docs.title: Roots & Rivers
docs.text:
An interactive guide to South Asian cultures for high school students. Learn where the traditions in your family (or your best friend's family) come from, and what they mean.

Start Chapter 1 See all chapters

docs.title: What this book is
docs.text:
South Asia is eight countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Together they're home to about 1.99 billion people (2025), roughly one in four people on Earth. Millions of families in the United States, including here in Minnesota, carry its traditions.

A lot of us grew up with those traditions and never learned the "why". Why does Diwali move every year? Why does your grandmother have a different word for your mother's brother and your father's brother? Why do so many scripts look different but work the same way? This book answers those questions, one chapter at a time.

Every chapter has:

  • A story with Zara and Ben, two Minnesota sophomores figuring this out together
  • An interactive MicroSim you can play with: spin a festival calendar, clap a rhythm cycle, draw a kolam, build a thali
  • A "Whose Story?" box that shows how different communities tell the same history
  • Ask Your Elders, a short interview guide for talking with your own family or community
  • A quiz, practice questions and sources you can check

docs.title: Who it's for
docs.text:
• Students who want to understand their own heritage, or a friend's. No background needed.
  • Teachers looking for free, sourced material for world history, geography or the new ethnic studies courses. See For Teachers.
  • Clubs: South Asian student associations can run a full year of meetings from the Club Kit.
  • Families: the Ask Your Elders guides are a good excuse for a long conversation at dinner.

docs.title: Free and open
docs.text:
Roots & Rivers is free, has no ads and needs no login. It's licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so teachers and clubs can copy and adapt it. Every fact is sourced. If you find a mistake, please report it; corrections are logged in public.

Created by Aaryav Sharma, a member of the board of the South Asian Student Association at Eastview High School in Apple Valley, Minnesota.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
Many South Asian American teens grow up inside traditions they were never taught to explain. They know the food, some of the words and the festival days. They don't always know why Eid moves every year, why their grandparents tell the story of 1947 or 1971 the way they do, or how the script on a wedding card works. Their friends are curious and have nowhere good to start.

Good free material is scattered. Some covers only ancient history or art. Some is written for teachers, not students. Some covers a single country, or only the diaspora. No single resource is interactive, covers all eight countries of South Asia, and sends readers back to their own families with good questions. Roots & Rivers tries to be that book.

It also comes at a useful time. Starting in the 2026-27 school year, Minnesota high schools must offer an ethnic studies course (Sahan Journal; Minn. Stat. 120B.021), and teachers need free, sourced material they can trust.

docs.title: What makes it different
docs.text:
• All eight countries. Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, in every theme and in four country chapters.
  • Interactive. Every chapter has a MicroSim you can use on a phone: a festival calendar, a rhythm cycle, a script family tree, a kolam you draw yourself.
  • Ask Your Elders. Every chapter ends its teaching with an interview guide, and the final chapter turns those interviews into an oral history project with a community Story Archive.
  • Whose Story? Every chapter shows how different communities, countries and historians tell the same thing differently. Disputed questions are presented as disputed.
  • Checked and sourced. Every number and date links to a source. See Accuracy and Corrections.

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text: Each chapter went through several separate passes by different reviewers. A script checked the structure. Every claim was fact-checked against its source. Another review looked at nuance, balance and whether facts were current. A final edit put the language in plain words, and a script checked that no fact changed. The details, and every correction made, are on the Accuracy and Corrections page. If you spot something wrong, please tell us.

docs.title: Who made it
docs.text:
Roots & Rivers was created by Aaryav Sharma, a student at Eastview High School in Apple Valley, Minnesota, and a member of the board of the school's South Asian Student Association (SASA). It was made for SASA's meetings and for any school, club or family that wants to use it.

It is built with Dan McCreary's open intelligent textbook framework, which also powers books on dozens of other subjects.

docs.title: Not affiliated
docs.text: Roots & Rivers is an independent student project. It is not an official publication of Eastview High School, Independent School District 196, or any government, religious body or organization named in it.

docs.title: Accuracy and Corrections
docs.text: A book about real people, real faiths and real history has to get the facts right and has to be fair. This page explains how Roots & Rivers is checked and lists the mistakes that were caught and fixed. Publishing corrections is part of being trustworthy.

docs.title: How every chapter was checked
docs.text:
Each chapter went through five separate layers. Each layer was done by someone other than the chapter's writer.

  1. Sourced writing. Every number, date and name was checked against a source the writer opened, and logged. Claims that couldn't be confirmed were removed or softened.
  2. Structure checks by script. A checker confirms every chapter has its required sections, every concept from the learning graph, a 10-question quiz with balanced answers, 8 to 10 references and a working MicroSim.
  3. Independent fact-check. A fresh reviewer re-verified the claims, the quiz answers, the links and the MicroSim's text.
  4. Expert edit for nuance, balance and currency. A second pass, held to the standard of a scholar of South Asia, looked for oversimplifications that had become false, one-sided framing, and facts that had gone out of date, and updated them to October 2026.
  5. Plain-language edit with a fact guard. A final edit made the writing clearer, and a script compared every file before and after to prove that no fact, number, name or link changed.

Disputed questions (borders, death tolls, the origins of ancient peoples) are presented as disputed, with each side's view and with ranges where scholars give ranges.

docs.title: What the checks found
docs.text: Across the 22 chapters, the independent fact-check (layer 3) logged more than 100 problems and fixed them, and the expert edit (layer 4) logged more than 80 more fixes and updates. Every chapter had at least one real error after writing, which is exactly why the layers exist. Most were small: a rounded number, an "only" that should have been "mostly", a date one year off. A few were serious.

docs.title: Notable corrections
docs.text: Where What was wrong Correction Ch 1 The Thar Desert was described as two-thirds in India About 85% lies in India Ch 1 The Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna system was called the second-largest river system by water carried It is third, after the Amazon and the Congo Ch 2 Varna and jati were blurred together Rewritten to separate the textual varna idea from local jati groups Ch 3 The Whose Story? box on how countries remember Aurangzeb, Shivaji and Ahmad Shah Durrani made unsourced claims Rewritten in careful, sourced wording Ch 5 The Guru Granth Sahib's other contributors were called "saints of the Hindu bhakti tradition, such as Kabir" Kabir was born into a Muslim weaver family and is honored by Hindus and Muslims; the chapter now names bhakti poets and the Sufi saint Sheikh Farid Ch 5 The Golden Temple was said to welcome over 150,000 visitors a day About 100,000 a day, per sourced reports Ch 5 Census figures for Pakistan and Bangladesh came from secondary summaries Updated to the official 2023 Pakistan and final 2022 Bangladesh census figures Ch 4 "44 of Pakistan's 69 million people spoke Bangla" 44 million was the population of East Bengal; most of them spoke Bangla Ch 4 The 1971 death toll was given as a single range Now gives the range most estimates fall in, and notes that some estimates are far lower Ch 6 Thaana script was said to be "in use by the early 1700s" The oldest surviving Thaana inscription is dated 1599 Ch 8 Ceylon tea was credited to the East India Company Commercial tea in Sri Lanka was started by British planters in 1867 Ch 9 Ravi Shankar was said to have told George Harrison about the 1971 refugees in August It was earlier in 1971 Ch 12 The oldest cotton at Mehrgarh was dated "about 8,500 years ago", which didn't match the sixth millennium BCE Roughly 7,500 to 8,000 years ago, from the original 2002 study (also fixed in the quiz) Ch 14 Rabindranath Tagore was called the first person from outside Europe to win any Nobel Prize He was the first from outside Europe to win the Literature prize and the first Asian Nobel laureate (Theodore Roosevelt won the Peace Prize in 1906) Ch 14 The English edition of Heart Lamp was dated 2024 in the Story Web sim First published in English in 2025 Ch 15 India and Pakistan were said to have played no bilateral cricket series since 2007-08 A short series was played in India in 2012-13 Ch 17 Potti Sriramulu's fast was said to last 56 days He died on the 58th day Ch 19 Sri Lanka's 2024 result was called the "first single-party majority since 1977" It was the first single party to win a two-thirds majority under proportional voting Ch 19 An unsourced "80% of Bangladesh's river water comes from outside" Softened to "most", which is well established Ch 20 Nepali was called Nepal's "national language" It is the official language; Nepal's constitution treats every mother tongue as a national language Ch 20 The 2009 Gurkha decision was described as being about pensions It gave Gurkha veterans the right to settle in Britain Ch 22 The AP Stylebook's decision to drop the hyphen in terms like "Asian American" was explained with an unsourced story Rewritten to match AP's stated reasons

docs.title: Found a mistake?
docs.text: Please tell us. Use the error report form, or the sensitivity review form if something feels unfair to a community. Every report is read. Corrections made after publication will be added in the next section, with the date.

docs.title: Corrections since publication
docs.text: None yet. Version 1.0 was published on 22 October 2026.

docs.title: What still needs a human expert
docs.text:
Automated and AI-assisted checks can't replace a scholar who has spent a career on a subject. These are the places where the reviewers asked for a human expert's eye first:

  • The wording of the Partition and 1971 death and displacement ranges (Chapter 4).
  • Kinship terms that vary by region and community, especially Sinhala and Bangla terms (Chapter 13).
  • Official-language details for a few Indian union territories where sources disagree (Chapter 17).
  • The current names of some festival processions that have recently changed (Chapters 7 and 22).

If you teach or research South Asia and can review a chapter, please volunteer. Reviewers who agree to be named will be credited here.

docs.title: Club Kit
docs.text:
This kit is for South Asian student associations and any club that wants to learn about South Asian cultures together. It is built for a club that meets once a month for 45 minutes, which is how many school clubs work (for example, the South Asian Student Association at Eastview High School in Apple Valley, Minnesota, meets one Friday a month). Twenty meetings over two school years cover all 22 chapters.

Everything here is free. You need a screen, an internet connection, paper and pencils. You don't need to be an expert to lead. The leader's job is to keep things moving and ask good questions. The book has the answers.

Start with one meeting

Don't try to plan two years at once. Pick next month's session below, give each officer one job, and run it. You'll learn more from one real meeting than from any plan.

docs.title: Before your first meeting
docs.text:
• Find a faculty advisor. Most schools require one. A social studies, world language or ethnic studies teacher is a natural fit. The For Teachers page explains the book to them.
  • Book a room with a projector. MicroSims also run on phones and Chromebooks, so members can follow along on their own devices.
  • Check your school's rules on food, posters, social media and events with other clubs. Your advisor will know.
  • Make it clear the club is for everyone. See How non-South Asian members belong below.

docs.title: Officer roles
docs.text:
Small clubs can combine roles. Rotate the meeting jobs (leader, quizmaster) so more people get a turn.

Role What they do President or co-presidents Set the year's calendar with the advisor, run the opener, keep the meeting on time, and speak for the club with the school. Meeting leader (rotates) Reads the chapter's Summary and Key Takeaways before the meeting and runs the MicroSim on the big screen. Quizmaster Builds the game from the chapter's quiz and Common Misconceptions, keeps score, and checks answers. Treasurer Tracks any money (many meetings need none) and collects ingredient lists when food is involved. Food and allergy lead Plans any food, checks the food notes for each session, labels everything, and makes sure there is always an option everyone can eat. Can be the treasurer. Story keeper Runs the Ask Your Elders share-out, collects stories only with permission, and helps members submit to the Story Archive if they want to. Outreach and social media Makes posters and posts, and reaches out to other clubs for joint events. Follows school rules on photos (always ask before posting anyone's face).

docs.title: The 45-minute meeting template
docs.text:
Every session uses the same five parts. A steady routine means less planning and more time for fun.

Part Time What happens 1. Opener 5 min A quick question everyone can answer, posted on the board as people walk in. 2. MicroSim activity 12 min The leader runs the chapter's MicroSim on the big screen. Use predict, then reveal: everyone guesses first, then the sim shows what happens. 3. Game 13 min A Kahoot-style quiz built from the chapter quiz, Jeopardy categories, or Two Truths and a Myth from Common Misconceptions. Play in teams. 4. Ask Your Elders share-out 10 min Members who did last month's interview share one short story. Always voluntary. 5. Wrap-up 5 min Hand out next month's Ask Your Elders questions, announce the next date, and clean up.

docs.title: The three games
docs.text:
• Kahoot-style quiz. The quizmaster copies 8 to 10 questions from the chapter's quiz page into a free quiz tool or onto slides, without the answers. Teams answer on paper or devices. Read the explanation from the quiz page after each question; that's where the learning happens.
  • Jeopardy. Five categories, three questions each. Good categories come from the chapter's section headings, plus one category called "Myth or Reality?" and one called "Say It Right" (pronounce a term from the chapter using its respelling).
  • Two Truths and a Myth. Read three statements: two true facts from the chapter and one myth from its Common Misconceptions. Teams pick the myth, then one member explains the reality in their own words. This is the best game for new members because it rewards listening, not prior knowledge.

docs.title: Food at meetings: the basics
docs.text:
Food brings people in, but it needs care. These notes apply to every session.

  • Label everything with its name and main ingredients, and mark it vegetarian, vegan, contains nuts, contains egg, or contains meat (and which meat).
  • Halal: many Muslim members eat only halal meat. The simplest choice is to keep shared snacks vegetarian.
  • Vegetarian: many Hindu, Jain, Sikh and Buddhist families are vegetarian, and many are not. Never assume. Always have a vegetarian option.
  • Jain diets often avoid root vegetables (such as onion, garlic and potato) as well as meat and eggs. If you have Jain members, ask them what works.
  • Nut allergies can be life-threatening. Many South Asian sweets contain cashews, almonds or pistachios. Follow your school's allergy rules, read labels, and keep nut items clearly separate or skip them.
  • Ramadan: many Muslim members fast from dawn to sunset during Ramadan. If a meeting falls during Ramadan, skip food or send it home in to-go bags.
  • No food is fine. Many great meetings have no food at all. Check your school's rules before bringing anything homemade.

docs.title: Festival dates for planning
docs.text:
The plan below places sessions near festivals. Many festival dates move every year, and Islamic dates depend on moon sighting, so check a calendar each fall. The book's Festival Calendar 2026-27 and the Festival Wheel explain why.

Festival 2026-27 2027-28 Diwali Sunday 8 November 2026 (timeanddate) Friday 29 October 2027 in US Central time; some calendars for the West Coast give 28 October (Daanyam) Ramadan begins Around 8 February 2027 (timeanddate) Check in the fall Eid al-Fitr Around Wednesday 10 March 2027, tentative (timeanddate) Around Sunday 27 February 2028, tentative (same source) Holi Monday 22 March 2027 (timeanddate, India) Saturday 11 March 2028 (same source) Pohela Boishakh (Bangladesh) 14 April 14 April Vaisakhi 13 or 14 April 13 or 14 April

Islamic holidays begin at sundown the evening before, and the exact day can shift by one depending on when the new moon is seen. Ask your Muslim members which date their families will celebrate.

docs.title: The two-year plan
docs.text: Each school year has ten meetings, September through June. If your school year ends in early June, combine the May and June sessions. Every session links to its chapter, quiz and MicroSim.

docs.title: September: What is South Asia?
docs.text:
• Chapter: 1: What Is South Asia? (quiz)
  • Goal: Everyone can name the eight countries and say why "South Asia" is not the same as "India".
  • Opener: "Put a sticky dot on the board for a place in South Asia you, your family or a friend has a connection to. No connection? Pick one you want to visit."
  • MicroSim: Region Explorer. Predict which country has the most people and which has the fewest, then click to check. Turn on the monsoon and ask where the rain arrives first.
  • Game: Two Truths and a Myth, using "South Asia = India" and "monsoon means constant rain" as myths.
  • Ask Your Elders: First meeting, so no share-out. Hand out Chapter 1's questions (where the family comes from, what the monsoon meant to them).
  • Food note: Skip food or keep it simple: a labeled, nut-free, vegetarian snack.

docs.title: October: Ancient roots
docs.text:
• Chapter: 2: Ancient Roots (quiz)
  • Goal: Put the big ancient periods in order and know that the Indus script is still not deciphered.
  • Opener: "What's the oldest object in your home? Who did it belong to?"
  • MicroSim: Ancient Timeline. Teams predict which city lights up next before the leader moves the slider.
  • Game: Jeopardy with categories "Indus Cities", "Empires", "Faiths Begin", "Myth or Reality?" and "Say It Right".
  • Ask Your Elders: Share-out from Chapter 1. Then hand out Chapter 2's questions.
  • Food note: None needed.

docs.title: November: Festivals through the year (Diwali season)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 7: Festivals Through the Year (quiz)
  • Goal: Explain why Diwali, Eid and Vaisakhi move on the calendar in different ways.
  • Opener: "What's one sound, smell or food that means 'festival' to you?"
  • MicroSim: Festival Wheel. Predict where Eid will be in five years, then slide the year to check.
  • Game: Kahoot-style quiz from the Chapter 7 quiz.
  • Ask Your Elders: Share-out from Chapter 2, then hand out Chapter 7's questions (a favorite festival as a child, how it's different in Minnesota).
  • Food note: Diwali sweets often contain nuts, ghee or milk. Label carefully and include a nut-free option. Remember that Diwali is marked by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, each for their own reasons, and not every member celebrates it.

docs.title: December: Food and the table
docs.text:
• Chapter: 8: Food and the Table (quiz)
  • Goal: Compare regional food across at least four countries and connect it to climate and trade.
  • Opener: "Describe an ordinary weekday dinner at your house in five words."
  • MicroSim: Thali Builder. Teams each take a region and report back one thing that surprised them.
  • Game: Two Truths and a Myth ("curry is one dish", "all South Asian food is spicy").
  • Ask Your Elders: Festival stories from November. Hand out Chapter 8's questions (a dish only your family makes).
  • Food note: A good month for a small potluck if your school allows it. Require ingredient cards, keep meat dishes separate and labeled (and say whether meat is halal), and have a vegetarian, nut-free table.

docs.title: January: Empires and encounters
docs.text:
• Chapter: 3: Empires and Encounters (quiz)
  • Goal: See that many powers overlapped in time instead of replacing each other neatly.
  • Opener: "Name a building from South Asia you've seen in a photo. Who built it?"
  • MicroSim: Empire Swim Lanes. Drop the year cursor on 1600 and count who overlaps.
  • Game: Jeopardy: "Dynasties", "Buildings", "Trade", "Myth or Reality?", "Say It Right".
  • Ask Your Elders: Food stories. Hand out Chapter 3's questions (the oldest building near home).
  • Food note: None needed.

docs.title: February: Languages and scripts (Mother Language Day)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 6: Languages and Scripts (quiz)
  • Goal: Explain that many South Asian scripts share an ancestor, and why 21 February matters (Language Martyrs' Day in Bangladesh, 1952, and International Mother Language Day, declared by UNESCO in 1999).
  • Opener: "Write your name in any script you know. If you only know one, ask a neighbor to teach you a letter."
  • MicroSim: Script Family Tree. Predict which scripts write "ka" the most alike, then click to compare.
  • Game: Kahoot-style quiz, plus a bonus "Say It Right" round.
  • Ask Your Elders: Empire and building stories. Hand out Chapter 6's questions (a word with no English translation).
  • Food note: In 2027, Ramadan begins around 8 February, so a February meeting may fall during the fast. Skip food or send it home.

docs.title: March: Faiths of South Asia (Eid and Holi)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 5: Faiths of South Asia (quiz)
  • Goal: Compare faiths on the same questions without ranking them.
  • Opener: "What's one value your family taught you? (It doesn't have to be religious.)"
  • MicroSim: Faith Explorer. Use Compare mode: each team picks a lens (like "a major festival") and compares two faiths.
  • Game: Two Truths and a Myth ("Hinduism has one holy book", "religion and country map one-to-one").
  • Ask Your Elders: "A word with no English translation" share-out. Many members love this one. Hand out Chapter 5's questions, including the option to ask about values if the family isn't religious.
  • Food note: Time this meeting after Eid al-Fitr if you can (around 10 March 2027). If it falls during Ramadan, skip food. Never ask anyone to explain or perform a prayer.

docs.title: April: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka (spring new years)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka (quiz)
  • Goal: Explain how a river delta and an island shape daily life, and name new-year festivals that fall in mid-April.
  • Opener: "How does your family mark a new year? Any new year counts: January, Lunar New Year, Nowruz, Pohela Boishakh, Vaisakhi, Sinhala and Tamil New Year, or none."
  • MicroSim: Delta and Island. Predict how much land floods when the monsoon slider goes up.
  • Game: Jeopardy: "Rivers", "Tea and Rice", "New Year", "Myth or Reality?", "Say It Right".
  • Ask Your Elders: Faith and values stories (handle with extra care; nobody explains their faith on demand). Hand out Chapter 19's questions.
  • Food note: A spring snack table works well. Keep it vegetarian and nut-free, or ask members who celebrate these new years what they would like to share.

docs.title: May: Music and dance
docs.text:
• Chapters: 9: Music and 10: Dance and Theater (quiz 9, quiz 10)
  • Goal: Count a tala cycle and tell two classical dance forms apart.
  • Opener: "Name a song you'd play at a family wedding."
  • MicroSim: Tala Clapper. Everyone claps Teentaal together and waves on the khali beat. Then a quick look at the Classical Dance Map.
  • Game: Two Truths and a Myth ("all Indian dance is Bollywood dance", "a raga is just a scale").
  • Ask Your Elders: New-year stories. Hand out Chapter 13's questions for June.
  • Food note: None needed.

docs.title: June: Family, names, and life events (Ask Your Elders night)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 13: Family, Names, and Life Events (quiz)
  • Goal: Explain why many South Asian languages have separate words for mother's and father's relatives.
  • Opener: "What do you call your father's older brother? Write it on the board in any language."
  • MicroSim: Kinship Explorer. Compare terms across five languages.
  • Game: Kahoot-style quiz. Keep it short to leave time for stories.
  • Ask Your Elders: This is the year's Ask Your Elders night. Members may invite an elder.
  • Food note: If elders are invited, ask families in advance about dietary needs, and plan for halal, vegetarian, Jain and nut-free guests.

docs.title: September: India
docs.text:
• Chapter: 17: India (quiz)
  • Goal: Connect India's language-based states to its federal structure. Welcome new members with a quick recap of Chapter 1.
  • Opener: "Two truths and a lie about yourself" as an icebreaker for new members.
  • MicroSim: India Explorer. Color by language family and predict which family covers the south.
  • Game: Jeopardy: "States", "Languages", "Capitals", "Myth or Reality?", "Say It Right".
  • Ask Your Elders: Hand out Chapter 17's questions, with the "place you visited or want to visit" option for members without Indian heritage.
  • Food note: None needed.

docs.title: October: Art, craft, and clothing (Diwali season)
docs.text:
• Chapters: 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft and 12: Clothing and Textiles
  • Goal: Make a symmetric kolam pattern and match garments and textiles to regions in several countries.
  • Opener: "Wear or bring something from home if you'd like" (never required). Members can say one sentence about it.
  • MicroSim: Kolam Maker on the big screen, then on paper with chalk or markers. Finish with the Textile Map.
  • Game: Two Truths and a Myth ("the saree is only Indian", "turbans mean one religion").
  • Ask Your Elders: India stories. Hand out Chapter 11's questions (a handmade object passed down).
  • Food note: Diwali falls on 29 October 2027 in Minnesota (some calendars say 28 October). Same notes as Year 1's November session: label, nut-free option, and remember not every member celebrates.

docs.title: November: Colonialism, independence, and Partition
docs.text:
• Chapter: 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition (quiz)
  • Goal: Explain how one colonial territory became several countries through two separate events, 1947 and 1971.
  • Opener: "Why might a family remember the same year very differently from a textbook?" (Keep it general.)
  • MicroSim: Borders Then and Now. Predict what happens at 1971 before moving the slider.
  • Game: Kahoot-style quiz only. Skip jokes and fast-paced games for this topic.
  • Ask Your Elders: Art and craft stories. Hand out Chapter 4's questions, and read the gentle note aloud: ask only if your elder wants to share, and stop if a memory is painful. Ask your advisor to read the sensitive topics guidance first.
  • Food note: None needed.

docs.title: December: Cinema, cricket, and pop culture
docs.text:
• Chapter: 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture (quiz)
  • Goal: Know that "Bollywood" is one of many film industries, and understand an over in cricket.
  • Opener: "First movie you remember watching with your family?"
  • MicroSim: Film Industries Map, then the Cricket Basics tab. Ben-style questions encouraged.
  • Game: Jeopardy: "Film Industries", "Cricket", "Music", "Myth or Reality?", "Say It Right".
  • Ask Your Elders: Partition and 1971 share-out, only if members want to, and with no follow-up questions unless the speaker invites them. Hand out Chapter 15's questions.
  • Food note: A relaxed, end-of-semester snack is fine. Label it.

docs.title: January: Science, math, and ideas
docs.text:
• Chapter: 16: Science, Math, and Ideas (quiz)
  • Goal: Explain why a symbol for zero makes place value work, without overclaiming.
  • Opener: "Write 2027 in Roman numerals. How long did it take?"
  • MicroSim: Zero and Place Value. Try a number with zeros in the Roman and South Asian digit views.
  • Game: Two Truths and a Myth ("Indians invented all of math", "zero was invented by one person on one day").
  • Ask Your Elders: Film and cricket stories. Hand out Chapter 16's questions (math tricks they learned).
  • Food note: None needed.

docs.title: February: Pakistan and Afghanistan (Ramadan and Eid season)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan (quiz)
  • Goal: Compare the two countries and trace the old road from Kabul to Lahore.
  • Opener: "What does a good host do when guests arrive at your house?"
  • MicroSim: Country Compare. Run the Khyber route animation and predict the next city.
  • Game: Kahoot-style quiz.
  • Ask Your Elders: Math and memory stories. Hand out Chapter 18's questions (hospitality customs).
  • Food note: Eid al-Fitr 2028 is expected around 27 February, so this meeting will likely fall during Ramadan. Skip food, or hold an after-Eid celebration in March with members' input.

docs.title: March: Stories and literature (Holi season)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 14: Stories and Literature (quiz)
  • Goal: See how one story can be told many ways across languages, faiths and borders.
  • Opener: "A bedtime story you heard as a kid, in one sentence."
  • MicroSim: Story Web. Filter by language and trace one story across borders.
  • Game: Jeopardy: "Epics", "Poets", "Fables", "Myth or Reality?", "Say It Right".
  • Ask Your Elders: Hospitality stories. Hand out Chapter 14's questions.
  • Food note: Holi falls on 11 March 2028. If you celebrate with color, use only skin-safe colors, do it outdoors with permission, and make it opt-in. Not every member celebrates Holi.

docs.title: April: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives (spring new years)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives (quiz)
  • Goal: Compare how altitude and sea level shape life in three smaller countries.
  • Opener: "Mountains or ocean? Pick one and say why."
  • MicroSim: Mountains to Atolls. Predict what a one-meter sea rise does to the atolls, then raise the slider.
  • Game: Two Truths and a Myth ("Sherpa means porter", "the Maldives is just a resort").
  • Ask Your Elders: Story share-out. Hand out Chapter 21's questions now so members have two months for the bigger diaspora interview.
  • Food note: If you mark Vaisakhi or Pohela Boishakh, ask members who celebrate to lead. Label everything.

docs.title: May: The South Asian diaspora
docs.text:
• Chapter: 21: The South Asian Diaspora (quiz)
  • Goal: Identify the major migration waves and their causes, including to Minnesota.
  • Opener: "Without naming anyone, what's one thing a family might bring when they move to a new country?"
  • MicroSim: Migration Waves. Predict the order of the waves, then run the timeline.
  • Game: Kahoot-style quiz.
  • Ask Your Elders: First share-out of the diaspora interviews. Keep immigration details general; nobody has to say when or how their family arrived.
  • Food note: None needed, or save food for June.

docs.title: June: Bring it home (capstone)
docs.text:
• Chapter: 22: Bring It Home (quiz)
  • Goal: Plan an ethical oral history interview, and celebrate two years of stories.
  • Opener: "One thing you learned in this club that you told someone at home."
  • MicroSim: Interview Builder. Each member builds and prints a plan for a summer interview.
  • Game: A "best of" Jeopardy with one category from each part of the book.
  • Ask Your Elders: A second Ask Your Elders night. Members who want to can submit a story to the Story Archive with permission.
  • Food note: If it's a celebration, plan as in Year 1's June session.

docs.title: How to run an Ask Your Elders night
docs.text:
Once or twice a year, make the share-out the whole meeting.

  1. Invite early. Two weeks ahead, members may invite one elder (a grandparent, parent, aunt or uncle, or a community member). Inviting is optional, and members can come alone.
  2. Set up a circle with chairs, and a small table for objects or photos people bring.
  3. Open with the ground rules (2 minutes): sharing is voluntary, we listen without interrupting, no recording or photos without permission, and nothing leaves the room unless the speaker says so.
  4. Story rounds (30 minutes): each member who wants to shares one story from an interview, in two minutes or less, using first names only. Elders can add a sentence if they want.
  5. Close (5 minutes): each person names one thing they want to keep. The story keeper reminds members how to submit to the Story Archive, with permission from the person who told the story and from a parent or guardian if the member is under 18.

Not everyone has an elder to interview, and some family stories are private. Members can share an interview with a community member, a story from a published oral history, or just listen. Listening is a full way to take part. See the Oral History Project for the method and consent script.

docs.title: How to run a culture day with other clubs
docs.text:
A culture day with an Asian Student Association, a Black Student Union, a Latino club, a world language club or another cultural group shows that the clubs are partners, not rivals.

  • Plan together from the start. Meet with the other club's officers and both advisors. Split the work evenly and put both clubs' names on every poster.
  • Pick a shared theme. Good ones from this book: new years around the world (Chapter 7 and Chapter 19), scripts and writing systems (Chapter 6), patterns and symmetry (Chapter 11), or migration stories (Chapter 21).
  • Stations work well. Each club runs two or three tables: a MicroSim on a laptop, a hands-on activity like writing your name in a script or drawing a kolam on paper, and a Two Truths and a Myth card game.
  • Let members represent themselves. Nobody has to perform, dress up or explain their culture. Volunteers lead what they're comfortable with.
  • Food rules double with more people. Use one shared allergy and ingredient label format for both clubs.
  • Get school approval for the date, room and any food, and follow your school's photo rules.

docs.title: How non-South Asian members belong
docs.text:
South Asian student clubs are better with friends in them. The book's own running character, Ben, is the club's first non-South Asian member, and he asks the questions other people are afraid to ask. Make that easy:

  • Say it out loud at the first meeting and on every poster: the club is open to everyone.
  • Use games that reward curiosity, like Two Truths and a Myth, where nobody needs prior knowledge.
  • Give everyone the Ask Your Elders alternatives: interview a community member, a family friend, or your own grandparents about their traditions and compare.
  • Give real roles. Any member can run a MicroSim, be quizmaster or be an officer.
  • Avoid "explain your culture" moments for anyone. South Asian members aren't spokespeople, and non-South Asian members aren't tourists.
  • Talk about appreciation and appropriation using Chapter 22: learning, asking and giving credit are different from taking.

docs.title: Budget-free ideas
docs.text:
Most of what makes a meeting good costs nothing.

  • Script name tags: members write their name in a South Asian script with the help of the Pronunciation and Script Guide.
  • Paper kolam: dot grids on scrap paper, after using the Kolam Maker.
  • Tala circle: clap a tala together with the Tala Clapper. No instruments needed.
  • Myth-buster wall: a poster where members add one myth and its reality each month.
  • Festival board: a hallway calendar of festivals for the year, with each date checked against a reliable calendar.
  • Story jar: members drop in one-line memories from interviews (first names only) to read aloud at the next meeting.
  • Teach a younger class: with teachers' permission, members run Two Truths and a Myth for a middle school class.
  • Library display: ask your school librarian to display books by South Asian authors during a festival month.

docs.title: Tell us how it went
docs.text: If your club uses this kit, please report it with the classroom and club use form. The form is public, so don't include members' names. Your notes help other clubs and improve the book.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text:
The best way to reach the project is through GitHub. You don't need to be a programmer; the forms are short.

  • Found a mistake? Report an error. Corrections are listed on the Accuracy page.
  • Something feels unfair or one-sided? Request a sensitivity review. We take these seriously.
  • Used the book in a class or club? Tell us. It helps us know who the book is reaching.
  • Have an idea? Suggest it.
  • Teach or study South Asia professionally? Volunteer as an expert reviewer for a chapter.

For the EVHS South Asian Student Association, see evhs-sasa.vercel.app or Instagram @evhs.sasa.

docs.title: Course Description: Roots & Rivers
docs.text: Title: Roots & Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students Audience: High school students in grades 9-12. Second-generation South Asian American students reconnecting with their heritage, and classmates of any background who are curious. Also usable in social studies, world history, world geography and ethnic studies courses, and in South Asian student clubs. Prerequisites: None. Basic reading and map skills. Duration: Self-paced. About 22 sessions of 45-60 minutes (one per chapter), or one semester at 1-2 chapters per week. A club can run it as one chapter per monthly meeting over two years.

docs.title: Course overview
docs.text:
South Asia, the eight countries of Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, is home to about one in four people on Earth. Its traditions shape the lives of millions of families in the United States, including in Minnesota. Yet most students meet it only through a few holidays, a few foods and a lot of stereotypes.

This course starts with the land and the long history that shaped the region: the Himalaya and the monsoon, the Indus cities, the great empires, colonial rule, Partition and the independence of eight nations. It then explores living culture: faiths, languages and scripts, festivals, food, music, dance, art, dress, family life, stories, cinema and cricket, and the region's contributions to science and mathematics. It tours each of the eight countries and follows South Asians around the world, to the Caribbean, East Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Every chapter has an interactive simulation, a Whose Story? box that shows how different communities tell the same history, and an Ask Your Elders interview guide. By the end, students have interviewed family or community members across 21 topics and can turn those interviews into an ethical oral history project for their school or club.

docs.title: Main topics covered
docs.text:
# Chapter 1 What Is South Asia? 2 Ancient Roots 3 Empires and Encounters 4 Colonialism, Independence, and Partition 5 Faiths of South Asia 6 Languages and Scripts 7 Festivals Through the Year 8 Food and the Table 9 Music 10 Dance and Theater 11 Art, Architecture, and Craft 12 Clothing and Textiles 13 Family, Names, and Life Events 14 Stories and Literature 15 Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture 16 Science, Math, and Ideas 17 India 18 Pakistan and Afghanistan 19 Bangladesh and Sri Lanka 20 Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives 21 The South Asian Diaspora 22 Bring It Home

Appendices: A. Pronunciation and Script Guide; B. Country Fact Sheets; C. Festival Calendar 2026-27.

docs.title: Topics not covered
docs.text:
• Current party politics, elections beyond basic facts, and opinions on present-day governments.
  • Religious instruction or theology beyond what is needed to understand practice and culture.
  • Fluency in any language (the book teaches about languages and scripts, not full grammar).
  • Medical, legal or immigration advice.
  • Detailed military history.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
Remember - List the eight countries of South Asia and locate them on a schematic map. - Name the major faiths, language families and festivals of the region. - Recall key dates: 1947, 1948, 1971 and the founding of SAARC in 1985. - Define core terms such as monsoon, raga, tala, abugida, diaspora and oral history.

Understand - Explain how mountains, rivers and the monsoon shape where people live and what they eat. - Summarize how British rule ended in Partition and how Bangladesh later became independent. - Explain why lunar, lunisolar and solar festivals fall on different dates each year. - Describe how many South Asian scripts descend from Brahmi.

Apply - Use the respelling guide to pronounce key terms from several languages. - Count a tala cycle and find its first beat. - Use a festival calendar to predict roughly when a moving festival will fall. - Apply the Ask Your Elders method in a real interview.

Analyze - Compare how two faiths, two countries or two regions approach the same practice. - Distinguish a region, a nation, a language and a script. - Analyze how one historical event is remembered differently across countries and communities. - Trace how a story, dish or word traveled across borders.

Evaluate - Judge whether a media portrayal of South Asians relies on stereotypes, using evidence. - Assess the difference between cultural appreciation and appropriation in a real case. - Critique a source about South Asia for bias, date and evidence.

Create - Design and conduct an ethical oral history interview with an elder. - Plan a club meeting or school event that teaches one tradition accurately. - Create a kolam pattern, a festival calendar or a family kinship chart. - Produce a short presentation that connects a family story to the history in this book.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• A 10-question multiple-choice quiz per chapter with explained answers (220 questions total).
  • Check Yourself questions and 12 Bloom-level exercises per chapter.
  • 21 Ask Your Elders interviews that build into a final oral history project (Chapter 22).
  • Optional pre/post test for clubs and classes (see the pilot study kit).

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: These are the questions readers ask most, from "Is this book for me?" to "Why does Eid move every year?" Each answer is short and links to the section of the book that explains it in full.

docs.title: What is South Asia?
docs.text: South Asia is a region in the south of the Asian continent made up of eight countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. These are the members of SAARC, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, which was founded in Dhaka in 1985; Afghanistan joined in 2007. A region is a group of places people talk about together, but it has no government of its own. See Region, Subcontinent, Country and Eight Countries and SAARC.

docs.title: Is "South Asia" the same as "the Indian subcontinent"?
docs.text: Not quite. "Indian subcontinent" is an older, physical term for the wedge of land south of the Himalaya, today divided mainly among India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, with Nepal and Bhutan along its edge and Sri Lanka often included. "South Asia" names a group of eight countries, including Afghanistan. Many people prefer "South Asia" because it doesn't put one country's name on everyone. See Region, Subcontinent, Country.

docs.title: How many people live in South Asia?
docs.text: About 1.99 billion people lived in the eight countries in 2025 (2025, World Bank), roughly one in four people on Earth. India alone had about 1.46 billion, more than the other seven countries put together. The World Bank's own "South Asia" total is smaller because, since 2025, it groups Afghanistan and Pakistan with the Middle East and North Africa. See How Many People Live in South Asia?

docs.title: Is this book only for South Asian students?
docs.text: No. The book is written both for teens who want to understand their own heritage and for friends who are curious and start with zero background. One of the two main characters, Ben, has Swedish and Norwegian roots and is the first non-South Asian member of his school's club. As he puts it in Chapter 22, the club is for anyone who wants to learn. See Being a Good Ally.

docs.title: Do I have to read the chapters in order?
docs.text: No. Chapter 1 is the best first stop because it introduces the eight countries, the land and the monsoon, but every chapter lists its prerequisites at the top, so you can jump straight to festivals or food. The How to Use This Book page explains the layout. Start with What Is South Asia? if you're not sure.

docs.title: Who are Zara, Ben and Mora? Are they real?
docs.text: They are all made up. Zara Hossain and Ben Lindqvist are fictional sophomores at a Minnesota high school; Zara's family is from Chattogram, Bangladesh, and Ben's is Swedish and Norwegian. Mora is a young peacock who pops up with tips and warnings. Each chapter opens with a question one of them can't answer yet, like Zara's in Wait, Isn't Bangladesh Part of India?

docs.title: What are the "Whose Story?" boxes?
docs.text: They show how different communities, countries or historians tell the same event differently. For example, the box on Partition explains why 14 August is mainly a day of celebration in Pakistan, why 15 August is Independence Day in India, and why many Punjabi and Bengali families remember 1947 first as the year they lost their homes. See the box in What Partition Was.

docs.title: How do I pronounce all the new words?
docs.text: The first time a key word appears, the book gives it in its original script, a simple respelling with the stressed syllable in capitals, and its meaning, like Diwali, dee-VAH-lee, "row of lamps." The respellings are approximate, so the best way to learn is to ask someone who speaks the language. See how it works for Diwali and the Pronunciation Guide.

docs.title: Why do the Himalaya and the monsoon matter so much?
docs.text: The Himalaya stretches about 2,400 km across Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan and China, and great rivers such as the Ganges rise in its mountains. The monsoon is a seasonal shift in wind direction that brings a rainy season most farming depends on. Rich river soil, warm weather and dependable rain make it possible to grow a lot of food, which is a big reason so many people live here. See The Mountain Walls and The Monsoon.

docs.title: What was the Indus Valley Civilization?
docs.text: It was a civilization of planned cities that flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, in an area bigger than ancient Egypt or Mesopotamia. Its best-known cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, are in present-day Pakistan. The cities declined gradually, likely because of floods, shifting rivers and a drier climate, and their script is still undeciphered. See The Indus Script and The Indus Valley Civilization.

docs.title: Did "Aryans" invade India?
docs.text: The explanation most scholars accept is the Indo-Aryan Migration: people speaking early Indo-Aryan languages moved into the northwest in gradual waves after about 2000 BCE and mixed with people already there. The evidence comes from language, ancient DNA and the texts themselves. The older "Aryan invasion" theory, in which conquerors destroyed the Indus cities, is rejected by scholars, and some writers and scholars in India dispute migration altogether. See The Indo-Aryan Migration.

docs.title: Who was Ashoka?
docs.text: Ashoka was an emperor of the Maurya Empire who fought a bloody war to conquer Kalinga around 260 BCE and then turned to Buddhism and dhamma. He had his ideas carved in edicts across his empire, including one in Greek and Aramaic near Kandahar in present-day Afghanistan. He still kept his army and his empire after his change of heart. See The Maurya Empire and Ashoka.

docs.title: How did Islam come to South Asia?
docs.text: By several routes. Muslim traders were living on the coasts of Kerala and Sri Lanka by the 7th and 8th centuries, the Maldives became Muslim after its king converted in the 12th century, and Sufi teachers drew many followers in Punjab, Sindh and Bengal. Conquest was one route among several. See Early Islam in South Asia and Sufism.

docs.title: What was the British Raj?
docs.text: The East India Company was a private trading company that built armies and ruled territory. After the Revolt of 1857, the Government of India Act of 1858 ended Company rule and handed its lands to the British Crown. The British Raj is the name for that direct Crown rule, from 1858 to 1947. See The East India Company and The British Raj.

docs.title: What was Partition?
docs.text: Partition was the division of British India into two independent countries, India and Pakistan, in August 1947, largely along religious lines. Punjab and Bengal were cut in two, about 14 million to 18 million people were displaced, and estimates of the dead range from about 200,000 to 2 million. People of every community were killed and forced from their homes, and there were also many acts of courage by neighbors. See What Partition Was and Partition Migration.

docs.title: Why is Kashmir disputed?
docs.text: When Britain left in 1947, the ruler of Jammu and Kashmir, a Hindu maharaja over a mostly Muslim population, joined India after fighters from Pakistan's northwest entered the state, and the first India-Pakistan war followed. India's position is that the accession was legal and final; Pakistan's position is that it was not valid and that Kashmiris should decide by a vote. Many Kashmiris hold their own views, and China also controls part of the wider region. As of 2026 the dispute is unresolved, and this book does not take a side. See The Kashmir Dispute.

docs.title: How did Bangladesh become a country?
docs.text: In 1947 the area became East Pakistan. On 21 February 1952, students in Dhaka were killed protesting for Bangla to be a state language, and in 1971, after a military crackdown, East Pakistan fought the Liberation War. Independence was declared on 26 March 1971 and the war ended on 16 December 1971. See The Language Movement of 1952 and The Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971.

docs.title: Which faiths are practiced in South Asia?
docs.text: Hinduism, Islam, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism and Christianity all have large communities, alongside smaller ones such as Zoroastrians (Parsis) and Jewish communities. No country lines up with only one faith: India's 14.2% Muslim share in 2011 was about 172 million people, and Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal all have sizable religious minorities. See A Faith Map of South Asia.

docs.title: Is Hinduism a religion or a way of life?
docs.text: The book describes Hinduism as a family of related traditions, beliefs and practices with no single founder, no single holy book and no single central authority. The word "Hindu" was first used by outsiders, from the name of the Indus River, and many Hindus prefer to call their tradition Sanatana Dharma, "the eternal way." In Hindi, dharm can simply mean "religion." How to label it is something followers themselves describe in different ways. See Hinduism: Origins and Variety.

docs.title: What do dharma and karma mean?
docs.text: Dharma is the idea of right order, duty and right conduct, which many Hindus see as depending on their stage of life and responsibilities. Karma is the belief that a person's actions and intentions have effects in this life and future lives. Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs also speak of karma and rebirth, each in their own way, and in a 2021 Pew survey of India, 77% of Hindus and 77% of Muslims said they believe in karma. See Three Key Ideas.

docs.title: What is langar?
docs.text: Langar is the free community kitchen of a Sikh gurdwara, where volunteers serve a vegetarian meal to anyone who comes, regardless of religion, caste, gender or wealth, and everyone sits together as equals. It is one of the practices that give Sikhism its distinct identity, along with its scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib. See Langar and Religious Pluralism.

docs.title: How can I ask about someone's faith without being rude?
docs.text: Describe, don't judge, and don't rank: say "many Hindus believe" or "in Sikh tradition" rather than stating beliefs as facts or myths. Remember that practice varies a lot inside every faith. A person's name, clothes or country don't tell you their faith, so ask politely and accept "I'd rather not say" as a full answer. See Five Lenses, No Ranking.

docs.title: Do people of different faiths in South Asia get along?
docs.text: South Asia has lived with religious pluralism for thousands of years, with shared ideas, shared pilgrimage sites and even shared scripture. But it has also seen real discrimination and communal violence, and a Pew survey of India found that many people value respect for all faiths while keeping close friendships and marriages mostly inside their own group. Pluralism is something communities build and protect. See Religious Pluralism.

docs.title: Are Hindi and Urdu the same language?
docs.text: Many linguists call them two standard forms of one spoken language, Hindi-Urdu (Hindustani), because everyday speakers understand each other well. They differ in script (Devanagari versus Perso-Arabic) and in formal vocabulary (more Sanskrit words versus more Persian and Arabic words). Many people in India and Pakistan see them as two separate languages, tied to history and identity. See One Language or Two? Hindi-Urdu.

docs.title: What's the difference between a language and a script?
docs.text: A language is spoken; a script is a way to write it. Punjabi is written in Gurmukhi in India and Shahmukhi in Pakistan, and one script, Devanagari, is used for Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and Sanskrit. See A Language Is Not a Script.

docs.title: I understand my family's language but answer in English. Have I lost it?
docs.text: No. Understanding a language you grew up hearing is real knowledge, and it makes you a heritage speaker. Heritage speakers usually understand far more than they speak and often learn to speak, read and write faster than beginners when they get the chance. Mixing languages, or code-switching, is normal across South Asia too. See Living Between Languages.

docs.title: Why do Diwali and Eid change dates every year?
docs.text: They follow different calendars. Islamic festivals like Eid follow a purely lunar calendar of 354 or 355 days, so they move about 11 days earlier every year and pass through every season. Diwali follows a lunisolar calendar that adds a leap month every two to three years, so it jumps back later and stays in autumn. See Three Ways to Count a Year.

docs.title: Who celebrates Diwali?
docs.text: Diwali, the festival of lights, falls on a new moon, usually in October or November. Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists all celebrate on the same night, each for their own reasons: for Sikhs it is Bandi Chhor Divas, and for Jains it marks Mahavira's nirvana. See Diwali.

docs.title: What's the difference between Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha?
docs.text: Eid al-Fitr ends the fasting month of Ramadan. Eid al-Adha honors Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice and falls during the Hajj. Both move through the year on the Islamic lunar calendar. See The Islamic Year.

docs.title: What happens during Ramadan?
docs.text: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, a month of fasting, prayer and charity. Adult Muslims go without food and drink from dawn until sunset, with exceptions for people who are ill, traveling, elderly or pregnant, among others. Many families eat a predawn meal (sehri) and break the fast at sunset with iftar, often starting with dates and water. See Ramadan.

docs.title: Why does the same autumn festival look so different from place to place?
docs.text: The same autumn nights are Garba in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Kolkata and Dhaka, Ramlila in North India and Dashain in Nepal. Each region and community tells its own stories and keeps its own customs. See Nine Nights and the Tenth Day.

docs.title: What is a thali?
docs.text: A thali is a large round plate, usually metal, holding a complete meal: a staple in the middle and several small dishes around it in bowls called katori. It tries to balance flavors and textures, from sour and salty to mildly bitter and sweet, and the same idea shows up across the region under other names. See The Thali.

docs.title: Are most South Asians vegetarian?
docs.text: No. In India, the most vegetarian country in the region, 39% of adults called themselves vegetarian in a 2019-2020 Pew survey, though 81% limit meat in some way. In Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and the Maldives most people eat meat or fish, and many people in Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan do too. See Vegetarianism in South Asia.

docs.title: What does halal mean?
docs.text: Halal is an Arabic word meaning "permitted," and in Islamic law it describes food Muslims may eat. Pork, alcohol and blood are forbidden, and halal meat must come from a permitted animal slaughtered in a set way. Most vegetarian food is halal as long as it has no alcohol or other forbidden ingredients. See Halal.

docs.title: Were chili peppers always part of South Asian cooking?
docs.text: No. Chilies come from the Americas, and Portuguese traders brought them to India in the 1500s, through Goa, as part of the Columbian Exchange. Before that, heat came from black pepper and other local spices. See Chili Peppers and the Columbian Exchange.

docs.title: What are raga and tala?
docs.text: A raga is a framework for creating melody: it sets which notes may be used, how to go up and down, which notes to stress and its signature phrases. A tala is a repeating cycle of beats, more like a clock face than a row of bars, and its first beat is called the sam. Musicians improvise inside these frameworks while landing exactly on sam. See Raga and Sargam and Tala.

docs.title: What's the difference between Hindustani and Carnatic music?
docs.text: They share raga, tala and sargam, but by about the 1500s they were treated as separate systems. Hindustani music belongs to the north (northern and central India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal) and often gives a lot of time to improvisation. Carnatic music belongs to southern India and Tamil communities in Sri Lanka and centers on composed songs, many of them devotional. See Two Classical Systems.

docs.title: What makes a dance "classical," and how many classical dances are there?
docs.text: In this book, a classical dance has a long written theory behind it, usually traced to the Natya Shastra, a fixed technique that takes years to learn, and official recognition. India's Sangeet Natak Akademi recognizes eight, including Bharatanatyam, Kathak and Odissi; the Ministry of Culture also lists Chhau, and others draw the line differently. "Classical" describes a trained, codified form, not something better than folk dance. See What Makes a Dance "Classical"?

docs.title: What's the difference between rangoli and kolam?
docs.text: They are related doorstep arts. Kolam is traditionally drawn in white rice flour, often as lines looping around a grid of dots, and is made daily in many Tamil homes; rangoli usually uses colored powders or petals and is made most often for festivals like Diwali. Alpona in Bengal is painted with wet rice paste. See Art at the Threshold.

docs.title: Who wears the saree and the shalwar kameez?
docs.text: The saree is worn in India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka and in parts of Pakistan; it is the national attire for women in Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka has its own Kandyan style. The shalwar kameez is Pakistan's national dress but is also widely worn in India (especially Punjab), Bangladesh and Afghanistan, by people of many faiths. See Draped Garments and Stitched Garments.

docs.title: Why are there so many versions of the Ramayana?
docs.text: Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana is the oldest well-known telling, but the story has been retold for centuries in Tamil, Bangla, Awadhi, Nepali, Thai, Javanese, Malay and more, plus Buddhist and Jain tellings. Scholars such as A. K. Ramanujan call them "tellings," because each is a real performance of the story for its own audience. See The Two Great Epics and One Story, Many Tellings.

docs.title: Is Bollywood the only South Asian film industry?
docs.text: No. Bollywood is the Hindi-language industry in Mumbai. India also has large Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali, Marathi and other industries, and in 2023 it certified films in more than 25 languages. Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bhutan have their own cinemas too. See Not Just Bollywood.

docs.title: Why is India versus Pakistan such a big deal in cricket?
docs.text: It is often called the most intense rivalry in the sport. The teams first played Test matches in 1952, politics has shaped the rivalry ever since, and no cricket was played between them from 1962 to 1977. When they meet, huge audiences watch, including Indian and Pakistani families in the diaspora who are friends and neighbors. See The India-Pakistan Rivalry.

docs.title: Did India invent zero?
docs.text: Zero grew over centuries, with placeholder marks in Babylon, Greece, the Maya world and South Asia. Brahmagupta, in 628 CE, was the first known writer to give rules for zero as a number, building on earlier Indian place value. The digits then traveled through scholars writing in Arabic, which is why historians say "Hindu-Arabic numerals." See Place Value and the Zero and How the Numbers Traveled.

docs.title: Can Ayurveda or yoga cure diseases?
docs.text: The book describes them as traditions, not cures. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says few well-designed studies have tested Ayurveda, and some products have contained dangerous levels of lead, mercury or arsenic. It says research suggests yoga may help with stress, sleep, balance and some kinds of pain, but it does not claim yoga cures any disease. This is not medical advice. See Ayurveda and Yoga.

docs.title: How is India organized?
docs.text: India is a federal republic with 28 states and 8 union territories, governed under the Constitution of India, which came into effect on 26 January 1950. Its capital is New Delhi, while Mumbai is its biggest business and film city. Many state borders were drawn along language lines. See The Constitution of India and States and Union Territories.

docs.title: What changed in Jammu and Kashmir in 2019?
docs.text: Until 2019, Jammu and Kashmir was a state with special autonomy under Article 370 of India's constitution. In August 2019, India's government revoked that status and split the state into two union territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, and in December 2023 India's Supreme Court upheld the change. These territories are part of a larger region whose status is disputed. See Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

docs.title: What languages do people speak in Pakistan?
docs.text: Urdu is the national language, but in the 2023 census only about 9% of Pakistanis spoke it as their first language. Punjabi (about 37%), Pashto (about 18%), Sindhi (about 14%) and Saraiki (about 12%) are all more common mother tongues, and most Pakistanis learn Urdu as a second language. See Urdu and Pakistan's Many Mother Tongues.

docs.title: Is Afghanistan part of South Asia or the Middle East?
docs.text: It depends on the purpose. Afghanistan is a landlocked country where South Asia meets Central Asia and Iran; it is a SAARC member, so this book counts it as South Asian, while some scholars group it with Central Asia. Since 2025 the World Bank has put Afghanistan and Pakistan in a "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan" region for statistics. See Eight Countries and SAARC and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Who governs Afghanistan today?
docs.text: The Taliban, an Islamist movement, took control in August 2021 as US and NATO forces withdrew, and call their government the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. Afghans are about 44 million people (2025, World Bank) of many ethnic groups, languages and opinions, and many inside and outside the country disagree with the government's policies. See Afghanistan Today.

docs.title: Why is 21 February important in Bangladesh?
docs.text: On 21 February 1952, students in Dhaka were killed while protesting for Bangla to be recognized as a state language. Bangladeshis remember them on Ekushey February, and in 1999 UNESCO declared 21 February International Mother Language Day, so the whole world now marks a date that began in Dhaka. See Ekushey February.

docs.title: What caused the Sri Lankan civil war?
docs.text: The war, from 1983 to 2009, was mainly about ethnicity, language, political power and land, fought between the government and the LTTE, which sought a separate Tamil state. Many Tamils had felt shut out by laws like the Sinhala Only Act, and the Black July riots of 1983 are often treated as its start. The UN estimated 80,000 to 100,000 people were killed; religion overlapped with ethnic identity but was not the main cause. See The Sri Lankan Civil War.

docs.title: Was Nepal ever a British colony?
docs.text: No. Nepal was never formally colonized, though it lost land to the East India Company in the 1816 Treaty of Sugauli and kept close ties with Britain. Bhutan was also never colonized, though it let Britain guide its foreign relations after 1910. See The Neighbors Britain Never Fully Ruled and Nepal.

docs.title: What is Gross National Happiness?
docs.text: Gross National Happiness (GNH) is Bhutan's idea that a country should measure progress by the well-being of its people and environment, not only by its economy. Bhutan built it into its 2008 Constitution. It is a policy goal, not a claim that everyone is happy: Bhutan's own 2022 GNH Index classed 6.4% of people as unhappy. See Gross National Happiness.

docs.title: What is a diaspora?
docs.text: A diaspora is a population that lives outside its ancestral homeland but keeps some connection to it, through memory, language, faith, food or family ties. South Asians moved in waves: indentured workers to the Caribbean and Fiji, workers and traders to East Africa, postwar migrants to Britain, workers to the Gulf, and immigrants to the US after 1965. Many of those waves were tied to the British Empire. See What Is a Diaspora?

docs.title: When did South Asians first come to the United States?
docs.text: Punjabi Sikh workers came to the US West Coast in the early 1900s, founded a gurdwara in Stockton in 1912 and farmed in California for decades. Laws in 1917 and the 1923 Thind decision then shut most South Asians out until the 1940s and 1960s. See Punjabi Pioneers in California.

docs.title: What was the Bhagat Singh Thind case?
docs.text: In 1923 the US Supreme Court ruled that South Asians were not "white persons" and so could not become naturalized citizens. Thind was a Sikh man from Punjab who had served in the US Army in World War I. After the ruling, the government moved to strip citizenship from many South Asians who had already naturalized. See The Bhagat Singh Thind Case.

docs.title: What changed in 1965?
docs.text: The Immigration Act of 1965 ended the "national origins" quota system that had heavily favored immigrants from northern and western Europe. It gave preference to people with family in the US and people with needed skills. Doctors, engineers, scientists and students came first, followed by their families. See The Immigration Act of 1965.

docs.title: What is the model minority myth?
docs.text: It is the stereotype that Asian Americans, including South Asian Americans, are all successful, wealthy and free of problems. It hides real differences: in 2023 the median household income of Bangladeshi Americans was about half that of Indian Americans, and 14% of Bangladeshi Americans lived in poverty (Pew). See The Model Minority Myth.

docs.title: How many South Asians live in Minnesota?
docs.text: About 64,000 people, a little over 1% of the state, according to US Census Bureau estimates for 2020 to 2024. The community includes families from every South Asian country, with temples, mosques, gurdwaras and student clubs across the Twin Cities and beyond. These are estimates with margins of error, especially for small groups. See South Asians in Minnesota.

docs.title: What does "desi" mean, and does everyone use it?
docs.text: "Desi" comes from desh, "homeland" or "country," and many people of South Asian heritage use it to mean roughly "one of us, from back home." But not everyone does: some Afghans, Nepalis, Sri Lankans, Bhutanese and Maldivians don't use it for themselves, and many Indo-Caribbean people have their own words. Ask people what they call themselves. See Desi Identity and Labels and the Hyphen.

docs.title: Can I wear a saree or get mehndi if I'm not South Asian?
docs.text: Often, yes, when it's appreciation: you're invited, you understand what it means, and you give credit. Wearing a saree to a friend's wedding when their family helps you dress is very different from wearing a bindi as a party costume or selling mehndi designs as "tribal tattoos." People inside South Asian communities don't all agree on where the line is, so when in doubt, ask. See Appreciation or Appropriation?

docs.title: What is colorism?
docs.text: Colorism is prejudice based on skin tone, usually favoring lighter skin, including among people of the same background. In many South Asian families and media, lighter skin has long been praised. After years of criticism, the cream Fair & Lovely was renamed Glow & Lovely in 2020, though it is still sold. See Colorism.

docs.title: Is South Asia just another name for India?
docs.text: No. South Asia is eight countries, and Bangladesh, Pakistan and the others are separate, independent countries with their own governments, languages and histories. India is the largest by far. See Eight Countries and SAARC.

docs.title: Did Partition in 1947 create Bangladesh?
docs.text: No. Partition created India and Pakistan, and the area that is now Bangladesh became East Pakistan. Bangladesh was created in a separate event, the Liberation War of 1971. See From the Language Movement to Bangladesh.

docs.title: Did India win independence through nonviolence alone?
docs.text: Gandhi's nonviolent campaigns were central, but independence also came from elections and political bargaining, armed revolutionaries, the Indian National Army, strikes and protests, and Britain's weakness after the Second World War. Historians still debate how much each mattered. See Organizing for Freedom.

docs.title: Is Sikhism a mix of Hinduism and Islam?
docs.text: Sikhs understand their faith as a distinct revelation through Guru Nanak and the Gurus who followed him, with its own scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, and its own practices such as langar. The scripture includes some hymns by Hindu and Muslim saints, but that doesn't make Sikhism a blend. See Sikhism.

docs.title: Is Hindi India's national language?
docs.text: India's Constitution does not name a national language. Hindi in Devanagari is the official language of the central government, English is also used officially, and 22 languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule. States choose their own official languages. See Official Languages and the Eighth Schedule.

docs.title: Is Sanskrit the mother of all South Asian languages?
docs.text: No. Sanskrit is an ancestor of many Indo-Aryan languages, like Hindi and Bangla, but Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to the separate Dravidian family, and Tibeto-Burman, Austroasiatic and Iranian languages have their own ancestors. Languages borrow words, but borrowing is not descent. See The Five Big Language Families.

docs.title: Is "curry" one dish everyone in South Asia eats?
docs.text: No. "Curry" is an English umbrella word, probably borrowed from the Tamil kari, that British traders applied to hundreds of different dishes. In South Asia people use the dishes' own names, such as dal, korma, sambar, karahi or jhol. See Regional Cuisines.

docs.title: Does a turban mean someone belongs to one religion?
docs.text: No. Turbans are worn by Sikhs, many Pashtun men, elders in Rajasthan, some Hindu monks and some Muslim scholars, among others. For Sikhs the dastar has a specific religious meaning, but the turban itself belongs to many traditions. See The Turban and the Dastar.

docs.title: Are all South Asian marriages forced?
docs.text: No. In an arranged marriage, families help find a partner, but both people freely agree and either can say no. Forced marriage, without real consent, is a human rights abuse that South Asian faiths and laws reject, and many South Asians choose their own partners. See Arranged Marriage.

docs.title: Does caste exist only in India, and only in the past?
docs.text: No. Caste is a historical and continuing social system that still shapes marriage and social life in India and Nepal and appears among people of many faiths. India's Constitution abolished "untouchability" in Article 17, and laws in India and Nepal make caste discrimination a crime, though rights groups say enforcement is uneven. In 2023, Seattle and Fresno added caste to their anti-discrimination laws, and South Asian Americans were divided over those laws. See Caste: Varna, Jati, and the Law.

docs.title: Is the Sri Lankan civil war a religious war between Buddhists and Hindus?
docs.text: No. It was mainly about ethnicity, language, political power and land, between the government and the LTTE. Religion overlapped with ethnic identity, but it was not the main cause, and there were Christians and others on both sides. See Not a Religious War.

docs.title: What is Ask Your Elders?
docs.text: It is a short interview guide near the end of every chapter. You talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the chapter's topic, using six suggested questions, and ten minutes is enough. The book calls it its most important part. See any chapter's guide, such as Ask Your Elders in Chapter 1.

docs.title: How do I get an elder talking?
docs.text: Start with something they can see or touch. The chapter guides suggest bringing a map and asking them to point to where they grew up, looking at old wedding or festival photos together, doing the interview in the kitchen over chai, or asking them to write their name in their own script. Always ask first whether it's okay to take notes. See the guides in Chapter 1 and Chapter 8.

docs.title: What if I don't have South Asian elders to ask?
docs.text: Every guide offers other options: interview a club advisor, a volunteer at a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center, or a classmate's family, with permission. Non-South Asian readers can also interview their own grandparents about their traditions and compare. See Ask Your Elders in Chapter 7.

docs.title: What if a topic is painful for my family?
docs.text: Some memories, such as 1947 and 1971, are painful. Ask first whether your elder wants to talk about those years at all, let them choose what to share and never push for details. If they ask you to keep a story private, it stays in the family: in Chapter 22, Zara's grandmother asks her to keep the 1971 story "just for the family," and Zara does. See Ask Your Elders in Chapter 4 and Informed Consent.

docs.title: Can I record the interview?
docs.text: Only with permission. Informed consent means the person understands what you're doing, how their words will be used and who might see them, and freely agrees, with the right to skip questions or stop at any time. If you're under 18 and want to share anything outside the family, get a parent or guardian's OK, and use first names or initials only. See Informed Consent.

docs.title: What if my family's version of history is different from the book's?
docs.text: That's normal, and it's what the Whose Story? boxes are for. One person's story is one person's experience: a Partition story from a family in Lahore and another from a family in Amritsar can both be true and still be very different. That's why oral historians collect many voices. See What Partition Was and Culture Lives in People.

docs.title: Why do my relatives have a different word for every uncle and aunt?
docs.text: Many South Asian languages give separate words to relatives English lumps together, so you can tell from one word which side of the family someone is on, and sometimes whether they are older or younger. English has one word, "uncle," for at least four different people. See Kinship Terms.

docs.title: What if my family celebrates differently from what the book describes?
docs.text: Practice varies inside every faith, region and family, and the book uses "many families" and "in some regions" for exactly that reason. Traditions also change from generation to generation, and adapting one to a new home is a normal part of keeping it alive. Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here. See Five Lenses, No Ranking and Who Am I?

docs.title: Can I use this book in my classroom?
docs.text: Yes. The book is free under a Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0 license: you can use it in class, print it, share it and adapt it if you give credit, share your version under the same license and don't sell it. It also fits Minnesota's 2023 law requiring every high school to offer an ethnic studies course starting in 2026-27. See For Teachers and Clubs, Organizing and Impact.

docs.title: How should I teach Partition and 1971?
docs.text: The book describes suffering on all sides, gives death and displacement figures as ranges, and avoids graphic detail. Tell students a day ahead what the chapter covers, offer a quiet alternative task without asking why, and never ask a student to explain "their side." See Partition Migration and the guidance in For Teachers.

docs.title: How should caste come up in class?
docs.text: Keep the discussion on the system, the laws and how people have resisted it, not on individuals. Never ask a classmate their caste or guess it from a surname, and never describe communities as "high" or "low." Use "Dalit" and "Adivasi" respectfully, as the book does. See Caste: Varna, Jati, and the Law.

docs.title: Do students have to share their family history?
docs.text: No. Ask Your Elders must never require students to disclose family history. Offer everyone the same choices without asking which applies: interview a family member, interview a community member, or do a "research interview" from a published oral history.
