docs.title: Kerala School
docs.text:
A line of astronomers and mathematicians in Kerala, beginning in the 1300s with Madhava of Sangamagrama, who found ways to write important quantities as infinite series.

Example: Jyesthadeva's Yuktibhasha, written in Malayalam around 1550, recorded the Kerala School's methods.

See also: Aryabhata, Srinivasa Ramanujan

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Khadi
docs.text:
Cloth that is both hand-spun and hand-woven, made from cotton, silk or wool, important for the role it played in India's freedom movement.

Script and sound: खादी, KHAH-dee

Example: In the freedom movement, many Indians wore khadi and refused foreign cloth.

See also: Mahatma Gandhi, Cotton in South Asia

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
docs.text:
Pakistan's northwestern province, bordering Afghanistan, with Peshawar as its capital. Until 2010 it was called the North-West Frontier Province.

Script and sound: KY-ber pukh-TOON-khwah

Example: The name joins "Khyber," after the pass, and "Pakhtunkhwa," roughly "land of the Pashtuns."

See also: Khyber Pass, Provinces of Pakistan

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Khyber Pass
docs.text:
The mountain pass, about 53 km (33 miles) long, that connects Peshawar in Pakistan with Kabul in Afghanistan, crossing the hills at the end of the Spin Ghar range.

Script and sound: KY-ber

Example: The pass runs from near Jamrud, Pakistan, to the border post of Torkham.

See also: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Kabul, Hindu Kush

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Kinship Terms
docs.text:
The words a language uses for relatives. Many South Asian languages use separate words for relatives on the father's and mother's sides and for older and younger relatives.

Example: Zara calls her maternal grandmother Nanu, a word that names her mother's mother specifically.

See also: Joint Family, Respect for Elders

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Kolam
docs.text:
A line drawing made with white rice flour on the swept, dampened ground outside a home, traditionally drawn each morning before dawn by women in Tamil Nadu. The Tamil word means "form" or "beauty."

Script and sound: கோலம், KOH-lum

Example: In Telangana and Andhra Pradesh the same practice is called muggu.

See also: Rangoli

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Kuchipudi
docs.text:
A classical dance named after a village in Andhra Pradesh that began as a dance-drama performed by troupes of men who played every role.

Script and sound: కూచిపూడి, KOO-chee-POO-dee

Example: Arjun Reddy, from a Telugu-speaking family, performs Kuchipudi.

See also: Classical Dance

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Kurta
docs.text:
A loose tunic, traditionally collarless, with straight sleeves and side seams left open at the bottom, worn by both men and women.

Script and sound: कुरता, KOOR-tah

Example: Lucknow is famous for kurtas decorated with chikankari, delicate white embroidery.

See also: Shalwar Kameez

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Kushan Empire
docs.text:
An empire founded by newcomers from Central Asia that ruled much of today's Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India from about the 1st to the 3rd century CE. Its most famous ruler, Kanishka, came to the throne around 127 CE.

Example: Kanishka's main capital was Purushapura, today's Peshawar in Pakistan.

See also: Maurya Empire, Gupta Empire

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Lahore
docs.text:
Pakistan's second-largest city and the capital of Punjab province, on the Ravi River, which has been a royal city under the Ghaznavids, the Mughals and the Sikh ruler Ranjit Singh.

Script and sound: لاہور, lah-HOR

Example: Ayesha Qureshi's family comes from Lahore.

See also: Punjab Region, Pakistani Cinema

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Langar
docs.text:
The free community kitchen of a gurdwara, where volunteers cook and serve a vegetarian meal to anyone who comes, regardless of religion, caste, gender or wealth. Everyone sits together on the floor as equals.

Script and sound: ਲੰਗਰ, LUN-gur

Example: Sikh tradition says the emperor Akbar sat and ate langar with ordinary people before meeting the third Guru.

See also: Sikhism, Guru Nanak, Hospitality Customs

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: Language Family
docs.text:
A group of languages that all descend from one older ancestor language. Linguists identify family members by comparing basic words and grammar.

Example: English and Swedish are both in the Indo-European family, which is why Swedish tre and English three sound alike.

See also: Indo-Aryan Languages, Dravidian Languages

Taught in Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts.

docs.title: Language Movement of 1952
docs.text:
A protest movement in East Bengal demanding that Bangla be recognized as a national language of Pakistan, which peaked on 21 February 1952 when police in Dhaka opened fire on student protesters.

Example: The Shaheed Minar in Dhaka honors the Language Martyrs killed on 21 February 1952.

See also: Ekushey February, Bengali Language

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Life-Cycle Rituals
docs.text:
Ceremonies that mark turning points in a life, such as a birth, coming of age, a wedding or a death. In South Asia they are shaped by faith, region and family.

Example: In Hindu tradition, the samskaras are the life-cycle rituals.

See also: Coming-of-Age Rites, Weddings, Funeral Customs

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Linguistic States
docs.text:
States whose borders were drawn so that most people inside share one main language, which usually becomes the state's official language.

Example: Most of India's states, such as Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, are linguistic states.

See also: States and Union Territories, Eighth Schedule

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Losar
docs.text:
The new year of the Tibetan lunisolar calendar, usually in February or March, celebrated for up to 15 days. It is observed in Bhutan and by Sherpa, Tibetan and other Himalayan communities.

Script and sound: ལོ་གསར, LOH-sar, "new year" (Tibetan)

Example: Families clean their homes, visit monasteries and hang new prayer flags for Losar.

See also: Lunisolar Calendar, Sherpa People, Bhutan

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Lumbini
docs.text:
A pilgrimage site in the Terai of southern Nepal that Buddhist tradition honors as the birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha.

Example: Lumbini's Sacred Garden includes the Maya Devi Temple and a sacred pond.

See also: Buddhism, Pilgrimage

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: Lungi
docs.text:
A length of cloth worn by men around the waist like a skirt, without passing between the legs, usually cotton in checks or stripes.

Script and sound: লুঙ্গি, LOONG-gee

Example: In Bangladesh the lungi is the most commonly seen everyday clothing for men.

See also: Dhoti

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Lunisolar Calendar
docs.text:
A calendar whose months follow the moon but whose years are kept in step with the sun and seasons by adding a leap month from time to time.

Example: In many Hindu calendars the extra month, adhik maas, is added about once every 32.5 months.

See also: Islamic Lunar Calendar, Calendar Conversion

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Madhubani Painting
docs.text:
A style of bold, colorful painting, also called Mithila painting, from the Mithila region of northern Bihar and southern Nepal, traditionally made by women on the mud walls and floors of their homes.

Example: Madhubani artists fill every space with pattern and outline figures in double lines.

See also: Rangoli

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Mahabharata
docs.text:
A Sanskrit epic, "the great story of the Bharatas," about a struggle for a throne between two sets of royal cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, that ends in a great war at Kurukshetra. It is traditionally credited to the sage Vyasa.

Script and sound: महाभारत, muh-haa-BHAA-ruh-tuh

Example: With more than 100,000 verses in its longest version, it is one of the longest poems ever composed.

See also: Bhagavad Gita, Ramayana

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Mahajanapadas
docs.text:
The sixteen large kingdoms and republics that ruled northern South Asia from about the 6th to the 4th century BCE. The word combines maha, "great," and janapada, a territory where a people had settled.

Script and sound: महाजनपद, muh-HAA-jun-uh-puh-duh, "great realms"

Example: The Mahajanapadas stretched from Gandhara in the northwest to Anga in today's Bihar.

See also: Rise of Buddhism and Jainism, Maurya Empire

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Mahatma Gandhi
docs.text:
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869 to 1948), a lawyer from Porbandar in present-day Gujarat who became the most famous leader of the Indian independence movement by leading mass campaigns of nonviolent resistance. Mahatma is an honorific meaning "great soul."

Example: Gandhi first developed his methods in South Africa before returning to India in 1915.

See also: Satyagraha, Indian National Congress

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Maldives
docs.text:
An island country of about 530,000 people (2025, World Bank) in the Indian Ocean southwest of India and Sri Lanka, made up of roughly 1,190 small coral islands. It is the smallest South Asian country by population and land area.

Example: All the Maldives' land adds up to only about 298 square km, spread over about 90,000 square km of ocean.

See also: Atolls, Malé, Sea-Level Rise

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: Malé
docs.text:
The capital and largest city of the Maldives, built on a tiny island in North Malé Atoll and one of the most densely packed places on Earth.

Script and sound: MAA-lay

Example: In the 2022 census about 212,000 people, roughly two in five Maldivians, lived in the city of Malé.

See also: Maldives, Atolls

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: Manipuri Dance
docs.text:
A classical dance from Manipur in northeastern India, part of the culture of the Meitei people, whose best-known form is the Raas Leela.

Example: The Meitei king Bhagyachandra is credited with designing Manipuri Dance's famous costume.

See also: Classical Dance, Northeast India

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Maratha Empire
docs.text:
A state founded by Marathi-speaking warriors in western India that grew in the 1700s into one of the largest powers in South Asia. It is also called the Maratha Confederacy.

Example: Its founder, Shivaji, was crowned Chhatrapati at the fort of Raigad in 1674.

See also: Mughal Empire

Taught in Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters.

docs.title: Masala
docs.text:
A mixture of spices, whole or ground; the word means "spices" or "seasoning." It can also mean a wet paste of onion, ginger, garlic, tomato and spices that forms the base of a dish.

Script and sound: मसाला, ma-SAH-lah

Example: Garam masala is a warm blend that often includes cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, cumin and black pepper.

See also: Tadka, Chai

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Maurya Empire
docs.text:
The first empire to rule most of the Indian subcontinent, lasting from about 321 to 185 BCE with its capital at Pataliputra.

Example: Ashoka, the third Maurya emperor, ruled an empire stretching from present-day Afghanistan to present-day Bangladesh.

See also: Ashoka, Edicts of Ashoka

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Mehndi
docs.text:
The art of decorating the skin, usually hands and feet, with a paste of powdered henna leaves that leaves a reddish-brown stain for about one to three weeks. It is also called henna.

Script and sound: مہندی, MEH-hn-dee (Urdu)

Example: Zara's cousins line up on Chand Raat to have mehndi patterns drawn before Eid.

See also: Mehndi Night and Sangeet, Eid al-Fitr

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Mehndi Night and Sangeet
docs.text:
Two pre-wedding celebrations popular in many North Indian, Pakistani and diaspora families: a mehndi night, when the bride's hands and feet are decorated with henna, and a sangeet, a night of singing and dancing.

Script and sound: संगीत, sun-GEET, "music" (sangeet)

Example: At many sangeets today, both sides of the family stage dance performances to film songs.

See also: Mehndi, Weddings

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Mehrgarh
docs.text:
An archaeological site on the Kachhi Plain in Balochistan, Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass, that is one of the earliest known places in South Asia where people farmed and herded animals. French archaeologists Jean-François and Catherine Jarrige discovered it in 1974.

Example: Finds at Mehrgarh show farming villages in the region long before the Indus cities were built.

See also: Indus Valley Civilization, Balochistan

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Microfinance
docs.text:
The practice of giving very small loans and other banking services to poor people, especially women, who have no property to offer as security and cannot borrow from ordinary banks.

Example: A small loan might let someone buy a cow, a sewing machine or stock for a shop.

See also: People's Republic of Bangladesh

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Mirza Ghalib
docs.text:
The most famous ghazal poet in the Urdu language (1797 to 1869), born in Agra, who lived most of his life in Delhi and wrote in both Urdu and Persian.

Example: Ghalib lived through the violence of 1857 in Delhi.

See also: Ghazal, Indo-Persian Culture

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Mithai
docs.text:
South Asian sweets, the kind sold in sweet shops and boxed for guests, many made from milk, fresh cheese curds or thickened milk.

Script and sound: मिठाई, mi-THAI; মিষ্টি, MISH-tee (Bangla)

Example: Boxes of mithai are shared with neighbors at Diwali and Eid.

See also: Diwali, Hospitality Customs

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Model Minority Myth
docs.text:
The stereotype that Asian Americans, including South Asian Americans, are all successful, wealthy, highly educated and free of problems, often used to compare them favorably with other minority groups. It hides real differences and struggles.

Example: Assuming every South Asian student finds math easy reflects the model minority myth.

See also: Stereotypes, Representation in Media

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: Mohiniyattam
docs.text:
Kerala's second classical dance, traditionally a solo dance by women, named after Mohini, the enchanting female form of the Hindu god Vishnu.

Script and sound: mo-hi-nee-YAHT-tum

Example: Mohiniyattam dancers wear an ivory-white sari with a gold border.

See also: Kathakali, Classical Dance

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Monsoon
docs.text:
A wind that reverses direction with the seasons, blowing from the southwest for about half the year and from the northeast for the other half along the Indian Ocean coasts. In everyday speech, the rainy season that the southwest winds bring in summer.

Script and sound: বর্ষা, BOR-sha, "rain" or "the rainy season" (Bangla)

Example: Farmers across South Asia time their planting to the arrival of the summer monsoon rains.

See also: Indian Ocean Trade, Rivers and Floods

Taught in Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?.

docs.title: Mount Everest
docs.text:
The highest mountain on Earth, 8,848.86 m (29,031.7 ft) above sea level by the 2020 China-Nepal measurement, with its summit on the border between Nepal and China.

Script and sound: सगरमाथा, Sagarmatha, suh-gur-MAA-thaa

Example: In Tibetan, Mount Everest is called Chomolungma.

See also: Himalaya, Sherpa People

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: Mudra
docs.text:
A hand gesture with a set shape and set meanings, used in dance. In Hindi the word can also mean a seal or a stamp.

Script and sound: मुद्रा, MOO-druh

Example: The Abhinaya Darpana describes 28 single-hand gestures.

See also: Bharatanatyam, Rasa

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Mughal Architecture
docs.text:
The building style that developed under the Mughal emperors, blending Persian and Central Asian ideas such as domes, arched gateways and walled gardens with Indian building skills and decoration.

Example: The charbagh, a garden divided into four parts by water channels, is a signature of Mughal Architecture.

See also: Taj Mahal, Jali, Calligraphy

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Mughal Empire
docs.text:
A Muslim-ruled empire, founded by a dynasty from Central Asia, that ruled much of South Asia from 1526 until it formally ended in 1857. Its founder, Babur, descended from the conqueror Timur.

Example: Akbar and Shah Jahan, the builder of the Taj Mahal, were Mughal emperors.

See also: Akbar, Taj Mahal, Mughal Architecture

Taught in Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters.

docs.title: Mughal Miniature Painting
docs.text:
The style of small, detailed paintings made in Mughal imperial workshops to illustrate books or fill albums. It grew out of Persian miniature painting and mixed with the styles of Indian painters.

Example: Under Akbar, senior artists drew outlines and junior artists filled in the colors.

See also: Indo-Persian Culture, Mughal Empire

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
docs.text:
A lawyer from Karachi (1876 to 1948) who led the All-India Muslim League and became the founder and first Governor-General of Pakistan.

Example: Jinnah's "two-nation theory" argued that Muslims and Hindus in South Asia were two nations.

See also: All-India Muslim League, Partition of 1947

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Nalanda
docs.text:
A great Buddhist monastery and center of learning in today's Bihar, India, founded around 427 CE under the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I, which operated for roughly 800 years.

Example: Students traveled from across Asia to study at Nalanda.

See also: Gupta Empire, Buddhism

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Naming Traditions
docs.text:
The customs a family follows to choose a child's name: who chooses, when, and what the name should mean or sound like.

Example: Many Sikh families choose a child's name from the Guru Granth Sahib, and many Bengali children have both a "good name" and a "call name."

See also: Surnames, Kinship Terms

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: National Symbols of India
docs.text:
The official emblems, chosen by the government, that stand for India as a whole, including a flag, an emblem, an anthem, a song, an animal, a bird and a flower.

Script and sound: तिरंगा, ti-RUNG-ah (tiranga, the national flag)

Example: The tiger is India's national animal, and the peacock has been its national bird since 1963.

See also: Republic of India, Rabindranath Tagore

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Natya Shastra
docs.text:
A Sanskrit handbook on the performing arts, "treatise on drama," credited by tradition to the sage Bharata. Most scholars place its first complete version between about 200 BCE and 200 CE.

Script and sound: नाट्य शास्त्र, NAHT-yuh SHAHS-truh

Example: The idea of rasa in dance and theater comes from the Natya Shastra.

See also: Rasa, Classical Dance

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Navaratri and Durga Puja
docs.text:
Two names for the great autumn festival of the goddess. Navaratri means "nine nights" and begins the day after the new moon of Ashvin; the tenth day is Vijayadashami, often called Dussehra.

Script and sound: नवरात्रि, nuh-vuh-RAHT-ree (Navaratri)

Example: Durga Puja in Kolkata was added to UNESCO's cultural heritage lists in 2021.

See also: Garba, Dashain and Tihar, Puja

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Nepal
docs.text:
A landlocked country of about 30 million people (2025, World Bank) on the southern slope of the Himalaya, between India and China's Tibet region, with Kathmandu as its capital.

Script and sound: नेपाल, nay-PAAL

Example: Nepal is one of the world's two Hindu-majority countries.

See also: Kathmandu Valley, Nepal's Republic (2008)

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: Nepal's Republic (2008)
docs.text:
The end of Nepal's monarchy, when the Constituent Assembly voted on 28 May 2008 to declare Nepal a federal democratic republic. Nepal's new constitution came into effect on 20 September 2015.

Example: The royal palace in Kathmandu became a museum after the last king left in June 2008.

See also: Nepal

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: New Delhi
docs.text:
The capital of India and seat of its national government, home to Parliament, Rashtrapati Bhavan and the Supreme Court, inside the larger city and union territory of Delhi on the Yamuna River.

Example: The British Raj moved its capital from Calcutta to New Delhi.

See also: Parliament of India, Republic of India

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Nikah
docs.text:
The Islamic marriage contract and ceremony, in which the bride and groom each give consent before witnesses and the groom agrees to give the bride the mahr, a gift that belongs to her alone.

Script and sound: نکاح, ni-KAAH

Example: In Pakistan and Bangladesh the couple and witnesses sign a marriage contract called a nikah nama.

See also: Weddings, Anand Karaj

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Northeast India
docs.text:
The easternmost region of India, made up of eight states, the "Seven Sisters" plus Sikkim, connected to the rest of India by the narrow Siliguri Corridor and bordering five countries.

Example: Assam, Manipur and Nagaland are states of Northeast India.

See also: Tibeto-Burman Languages, Manipuri Dance

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Nowruz
docs.text:
The Persian New Year, "new day," which begins at the March equinox on 20 or 21 March. In Afghanistan it is called Nawruz.

Script and sound: نوروز, noh-ROOZ

Example: Afghan families prepare haft mewa, a dish of seven dried fruits and nuts soaked in water.

See also: Afghanistan, Zoroastrians (Parsis)

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Odissi
docs.text:
A classical dance from Odisha on India's east coast, whose poses can be seen in the dancing figures carved on the state's old temples.

Script and sound: oh-DIS-ee

Example: The Sun Temple at Konark shows carved poses that Odissi dancers still use.

See also: Classical Dance

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Onam
docs.text:
The harvest festival of Kerala, celebrated by Malayali families of many faiths in the Malayalam month of Chingam (August to September). In Kerala tradition it marks the yearly return of the generous king Mahabali.

Script and sound: ഓണം, OH-num

Example: Families make a pookalam, a round carpet of flower petals, and share a sadya feast.

See also: Pongal and Makar Sankranti

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Oral History
docs.text:
The practice of recording people's memories of their own lives, in their own words, and keeping those recordings or notes so others can learn from them later.

Example: Recording Nanu's memories of growing up in Chattogram creates an oral history.

See also: Informed Consent, Oral Tradition, Active Listening

Taught in Chapter 22: Bring It Home.

docs.title: Oral Tradition
docs.text:
The passing of stories, poems, songs and knowledge from person to person by speaking, singing and memorizing, often across many generations, instead of by writing them down.

Script and sound: कथा, KUH-thaa, "story" (Hindi); গল্প, GOL-po, "story" (Bangla)

Example: Zara's Nanu telling her a golpo she heard as a child is part of an oral tradition.

See also: Oral History, Ramayana, Panchatantra

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Pakistani Cinema
docs.text:
The film industry of Pakistan, making films mainly in Urdu and Punjabi, with Pashto films made in Peshawar. Its old center in Lahore was nicknamed "Lollywood," and Karachi has since become a major center.

Example: Many filmmakers moved from Lahore's studios to Karachi after about 2000.

See also: Pakistani Dramas, Regional Cinemas

Taught in Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture.

docs.title: Pakistani Dramas
docs.text:
Pakistani television serials, usually in Urdu, known for family stories, romance and social issues, and for running a set number of episodes instead of going on for years.

Example: Fans in India and abroad watch Pakistani dramas online with subtitles.

See also: Pakistani Cinema, Streaming Era

Taught in Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture.

docs.title: Panchatantra
docs.text:
A Sanskrit collection of animal fables, "five treatises," set inside a frame story in which a wise teacher uses clever tales to teach three princes how to live and rule wisely. Its author is unknown.

Script and sound: पञ्चतन्त्र, PUNCH-uh-TUN-truh

Example: In each Panchatantra tale, animals argue, scheme and make friends, and the story ends with a lesson about trust or good judgment.

See also: Jataka Tales, Oral Tradition

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Panini's Grammar
docs.text:
The Ashtadhyayi, "eight chapters," a complete description of the Sanskrit language in just under 4,000 short rules called sutras, by Panini of Shalatula near Attock in present-day Pakistan.

Example: Scholars date Panini anywhere from about the 7th to the 4th century BCE.

See also: Sanskrit

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Parliament of India
docs.text:
India's national legislature, made up of two houses and the president, which makes the country's laws. The lower house, the Lok Sabha, has 543 elected seats.

Script and sound: लोकसभा, LOKE-sub-ha (Lok Sabha)

Example: Members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected by voters at least every five years.

See also: Elections in India, New Delhi

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Partition Literature
docs.text:
Poetry, fiction and memoir written about the 1947 Partition and its aftermath, in Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi, Bangla, Sindhi, English and other languages, often focused on ordinary people and loss.

Example: Short stories by Saadat Hasan Manto are classics of Partition Literature.

See also: Partition of 1947, Partition Migration

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Partition Migration
docs.text:
The movement of millions of people across the new India-Pakistan borders in 1947 and the years after, with Hindus and Sikhs moving into India and Muslims moving into Pakistan.

Example: In Punjab, people traveled in columns many kilometers long, on bullock carts and on overcrowded trains.

See also: Partition of 1947, Radcliffe Line

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Partition of 1947
docs.text:
The division of British India into two independent countries, India and Pakistan, in August 1947, largely along religious lines, with Muslim-majority areas becoming Pakistan.

Example: Pakistan celebrates its independence on 14 August and India on 15 August.

See also: Radcliffe Line, Partition Migration, Partition Literature

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Pashmina
docs.text:
The very fine wool from the soft undercoat of goats that live high in the Himalaya, and the shawls made from it. The word comes from pashm, Persian for wool.

Script and sound: पश्मीना, push-MEE-nah

Example: A shawl woven from pashmina wool is one of the region's most prized textiles.

See also: Himalaya

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Pashtunwali
docs.text:
The traditional, unwritten code of honor, hospitality and justice that guides Pashtun social life. It is a matter of custom, not religious law, and is older than Islam in the region.

Script and sound: push-toon-WAH-lee

Example: Melmastia, welcoming every guest generously, is one of Pashtunwali's main ideas.

See also: Hospitality Customs, Dari and Pashto

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: People's Republic of Bangladesh
docs.text:
The official name of Bangladesh: a parliamentary republic in the eastern part of the old region of Bengal, independent since 1971, with Bangla as its state language. The name means "country of the Bengalis."

Script and sound: বাংলা, BANG-lah (Bangla)

Example: Bangladesh had about 176 million people in 2025 (World Bank).

See also: Dhaka, Bangladesh Liberation War

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Perso-Arabic Script
docs.text:
The Arabic script as adapted for Persian and then for many South Asian languages, written right to left and working mostly as an abjad, which writes consonants and long vowels but usually leaves short vowels out.

Example: Urdu, Pashto, Dari, Sindhi and Shahmukhi Punjabi are written in Perso-Arabic Script.

See also: Hindi-Urdu (Hindustani), Calligraphy

Taught in Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts.

docs.title: Phonetic Respelling
docs.text:
Writing how a word sounds using ordinary English spelling patterns, with no special marks and the stressed syllable in capitals. It does not show how the word is spelled in its own script.

Example: Diwali is respelled dee-VAH-lee.

See also: Transliteration

Taught in Appendix A: Pronunciation and Script Guide.

docs.title: Pilgrimage
docs.text:
A journey to a sacred place for prayer, blessing, remembrance or renewal. Every faith in South Asia has its own pilgrimage places.

Example: Buddhists travel to Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace, and Bodh Gaya, where he reached enlightenment.

See also: Lumbini, Sri Pada (Adam's Peak)

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: Place Value System
docs.text:
A way of writing numbers in which a digit's value depends on its position, with each position worth a fixed multiple of the one beside it. The system in use today is base ten.

Example: In 352, the 3 means three hundreds because of its place.

See also: Zero, Hindu-Arabic Numerals

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Playback Singing
docs.text:
The practice of recording film songs with professional singers whose voices are played back while actors lip-sync on camera.

Example: In South Asia, many playback singers are as famous as the actors who appear on screen.

See also: Film Music (Filmi), Bollywood

Taught in Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture.

docs.title: Pohela Boishakh
docs.text:
The Bengali New Year, "the first of Boishakh," a national holiday in Bangladesh fixed on 14 April and falling on 14 or 15 April in West Bengal.

Script and sound: পহেলা বৈশাখ, po-HEH-la boy-SHAKH

Example: Bangladesh fixed the date by revising its Bengali calendar, officially adopted in 1987.

See also: Vaisakhi, Bengali Language

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Pongal and Makar Sankranti
docs.text:
Winter harvest festivals that mark the sun's move into Makara (Capricorn in the Indian zodiac), usually on 14 or 15 January. Because they follow the sun, their dates are very predictable.

Example: India's 2026 holiday list put both Pongal and Makar Sankranti on 14 January.

See also: Onam, Lunisolar Calendar

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Population of South Asia
docs.text:
The total number of people living in the eight countries of South Asia, about 1.99 billion in 2025 (World Bank). That is roughly one in four people on Earth.

Example: India alone had about 1.46 billion people in 2025 (World Bank), the largest share of the region's population.

See also: South Asia

Taught in Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?.

docs.title: Post-9/11 Backlash
docs.text:
The hate crimes, harassment, profiling and discrimination aimed at people perceived as Muslim or Middle Eastern after the 11 September 2001 attacks, including many South Asians.

Example: Sikh men wearing turbans were among those targeted in the post-9/11 backlash.

See also: Turban (Dastar), Stereotypes

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: Princely States
docs.text:
The kingdoms inside British-controlled South Asia that kept their own Indian rulers but accepted British control over their defense and foreign relations through treaties. There were officially about 565 of them when Britain left.

Example: Hyderabad, ruled by a Nizam, and Jammu and Kashmir, ruled by a Maharaja, were among the largest Princely States.

See also: British Raj, Kashmir Dispute

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Provinces of Pakistan
docs.text:
The four large regions into which Pakistan is divided, each with its own elected assembly: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.

Example: The capital has its own federal area, the Islamabad Capital Territory, separate from the provinces.

See also: Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan, Punjab Region

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Puja
docs.text:
The Hindu ritual of offering worship to a deity, often with light, flowers, water, incense or food. It can be a large temple ceremony with priests or a few quiet minutes at a home shrine.

Script and sound: पूजा, POO-jah, "worship" or "honor"

Example: Arjun's grandmother does a short puja every day at the small shrine in their kitchen.

See also: Hinduism, Navaratri and Durga Puja

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: Punjab Region
docs.text:
The cultural and geographic region of the five rivers that feed the Indus, today divided between Pakistan's Punjab province and India's Punjab state. The name comes from Persian words for "five" and "water."

Example: The Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej are the five rivers of the Punjab.

See also: Indus River, Lahore, Bhangra

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Punjabi Pioneers in California
docs.text:
South Asian men, mostly Sikhs from Punjab, who came to the US West Coast in the early 1900s to work in mills, on railways and on farms, and later farmed in California's agricultural valleys.

Example: Many Punjabi pioneers first worked on railways and farms, then farmed land of their own in California.

See also: Bhagat Singh Thind Case, Diaspora

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: Qawwali
docs.text:
A form of Sufi Muslim devotional music sung at Sufi shrines to help listeners feel closer to God. Its development is credited to Amir Khusrau in the 1200s and 1300s.

Script and sound: قوالی, kuh-WAH-lee (Urdu)

Example: Qawwali singers perform at dargahs, the shrines of Sufi saints.

See also: Sufism, Ghazal, Coke Studio

Taught in Chapter 9: Music.

docs.title: Rabindranath Tagore
docs.text:
A Bengali poet, songwriter, novelist, playwright, painter and educator from Calcutta (1861 to 1941) who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, the first Asian to win any Nobel Prize.

Example: Tagore wrote "Jana Gana Mana," India's national anthem.

See also: Kazi Nazrul Islam, National Symbols of India

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Radcliffe Line
docs.text:
The boundary drawn in 1947 to divide the provinces of Punjab and Bengal between India and Pakistan, based mainly on which districts had Muslim or non-Muslim majorities.

Example: The Radcliffe Line left Sikh holy sites and farmland on both sides of the new border in Punjab.

See also: Partition of 1947, Partition Migration

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Raga
docs.text:
A framework for creating melody that sets which notes to use, which to emphasize and which phrases give it its character. It is not just a scale: two ragas can share the same notes and still sound different.

Script and sound: राग, RAH-ga

Example: The Hindustani ragas Bhoopali and Deshkar use the same five notes but are treated as separate ragas.

See also: Tala, Sargam, Hindustani Music

Taught in Chapter 9: Music.

docs.title: Ramadan
docs.text:
The ninth month of the Islamic calendar, a month of fasting, prayer and charity lasting 29 or 30 days, during which adult Muslims go without food and drink from dawn until sunset.

Script and sound: رمضان, rah-mah-DAHN (Arabic); রমজান, rom-JAHN (Bangla)

Example: People who are ill, traveling, elderly, pregnant or breastfeeding are excused from the Ramadan fast.

See also: Eid al-Fitr, Islamic Lunar Calendar

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Ramayana
docs.text:
A Sanskrit epic, "the story of Rama," about Prince Rama of the kingdom of Ayodhya. Its best-known version is traditionally credited to the poet-sage Valmiki.

Script and sound: रामायण, raa-MAA-yuh-nuh

Example: Many families tell the story of Rama's return to Ayodhya at Diwali.

See also: Mahabharata, Oral Tradition, Diwali

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Rangoli
docs.text:
A design made on the floor or ground using dry materials such as colored powders, rice flour, colored sand or flower petals, most often for festivals.

Script and sound: रंगोली, rung-GOH-lee

Example: Many families draw a rangoli at the doorway for Diwali, or for Tihar in Nepal.

See also: Kolam, Diwali

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Rasa
docs.text:
In the arts, the emotional flavor that a performance creates in the audience. The word literally means "juice," "taste" or "essence."

Script and sound: रस, RUH-suh

Example: A dancer shows a feeling, or bhava, and a sensitive audience member "tastes" it as rasa.

See also: Natya Shastra, Mudra

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Regional Cinemas
docs.text:
The film industries that make movies in South Asia's many languages other than Hindi, each with its own stars, studios, history and fans.

Example: Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu and Bengali films come from regional cinemas.

See also: Bollywood, Pakistani Cinema

Taught in Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture.

docs.title: Regional Cuisines
docs.text:
Styles of cooking that grow up in one area, shaped by its grain, climate, coast or mountains, trade history and communities. Borders drawn in 1947 or 1971 often run right through them.

Example: Punjabi food is eaten on both sides of the India-Pakistan border.

See also: Staple Grains, Thali

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Regional Diversity
docs.text:
The idea that South Asia is many different places shaped by different land, water and history, rather than one place with one climate, language, faith or way of life.

Example: Snowy Himalayan valleys in Bhutan and the low coral islands of the Maldives are both part of South Asia.

See also: South Asia, Unity in Diversity

Taught in Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?.

docs.title: Religious Pluralism
docs.text:
Many faiths living side by side in the same society and, as an ideal, people of different faiths respecting each other's right to believe and practice. South Asia's long history of it includes shared traditions as well as real conflict.

Example: A city where a temple, a mosque, a gurdwara and a church stand on the same street shows religious pluralism.

See also: Unity in Diversity, Sufism

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: Remittances
docs.text:
Money that migrants send home to their families, which pays for food, school fees, weddings, medical care and new houses.

Example: A worker in Dubai sending part of each paycheck to family in Nepal is sending remittances.

See also: Gulf Migrant Workers, Transnational Families

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: Representation in Media
docs.text:
How a group of people is shown on screen and in the news: how often they appear, what roles they play, who writes their stories, and whether portrayals are accurate or rely on stereotypes.

Example: A show written by South Asian American writers about a South Asian American family is an example of representation in media.

See also: Stereotypes, Streaming Era

Taught in Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture.

docs.title: Republic of India
docs.text:
The official name of India: a sovereign, democratic republic and union of states with an elected parliament and a constitution in force since 1950. Its constitution also names the country Bharat.

Script and sound: भारत, BHAH-rut

Example: Article 1 of the Constitution begins, "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."

See also: Constitution of India, States and Union Territories

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Respect for Elders
docs.text:
The value that older relatives and community members deserve special honor, care and obedience, and that families should look after them as they age.

Example: In many Hindu and Sikh families, younger people bend to touch an elder's feet as a greeting, and the elder gives a blessing.

See also: Joint Family, Intergenerational Dialogue

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Revolt of 1857
docs.text:
A large uprising against East India Company rule that began on 10 May 1857 when sepoys at Meerut mutinied, marched to Delhi and declared the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader. It spread across much of northern and central India.

Example: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi fought on horseback in the Revolt of 1857.

See also: British Raj, East India Company

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Rickshaw Art
docs.text:
The painting and decoration of cycle rickshaws, best known in Dhaka, Bangladesh, with flowers, birds, heroes, movie stars and text.

Example: Because rickshaws move slowly through Dhaka's streets, they work like a moving art gallery.

See also: Truck Art, Dhaka

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Rise of Buddhism and Jainism
docs.text:
The growth of two traditions that began in the Ganga plain in the 6th or 5th century BCE, during the age of the Mahajanapadas, into religions followed by millions.

Example: The Buddha and Mahavira, the great teacher of Jainism, both taught in the kingdoms of the Ganga plain.

See also: Buddhism, Jainism, Mahajanapadas

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Rivers and Floods
docs.text:
In Bangladesh, the yearly rhythm in which monsoon rain and Himalayan meltwater raise the rivers, which spread across the low delta, bringing both fertile soil and danger.

Example: Farmers plant in the rich silt left behind when the floodwaters go down.

See also: Bengal Delta, Monsoon

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Roti and Naan
docs.text:
Two South Asian flatbreads. Roti is unleavened whole-wheat bread cooked on a flat griddle; naan is usually leavened white-flour bread baked on the inside wall of a tandoor.

Script and sound: रोटी, ROH-tee (roti); नान, Urdu نان, NAHN (naan)

Example: Many families in northern India and Pakistan eat roti at nearly every meal, while naan in India is mostly a restaurant bread.

See also: Staple Grains, Eating With Hands

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Sangam Age
docs.text:
The period in the Tamil-speaking south when the earliest Tamil poetry was composed, which most scholars place between about 300 BCE and 300 CE. Its dates are debated because the poems rarely mention datable events.

Example: Love poems and war poems collected in the Sangam anthologies come from the Sangam Age.

See also: Sangam Literature, Tamil Language

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Sangam Literature
docs.text:
The earliest known body of Tamil poetry, composed roughly between 300 BCE and 300 CE. Sangam means "gathering" or "academy."

Script and sound: சங்கம், SUNG-gum

Example: Tamil tradition says the poems were approved by great assemblies of poets in Madurai.

See also: Sangam Age, Tamil Language

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: Sanskrit
docs.text:
The classical language of ancient South Asia, part of the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family, whose oldest form is the Vedic Sanskrit of the Vedas.

Script and sound: संस्कृत, SUNS-krit, "refined" or "perfected"

Example: The grammarian Panini described Sanskrit in his Ashtadhyayi, "Eight Chapters."

See also: The Vedas, Panini's Grammar, Indo-Aryan Languages

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Saree
docs.text:
A long, unstitched length of cloth, usually 4.5 to 9 yards long, that a woman wraps around her waist and drapes over one shoulder, worn over a petticoat and a fitted blouse. The decorated end over the shoulder is the pallu.

Script and sound: Hindi साड़ी, Bangla শাড়ি, SAH-ree

Example: A jamdani saree from Dhaka is woven from fine, sheer cotton.

See also: Jamdani, Dhoti

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Sargam
docs.text:
The practice of singing notes with the syllables sa, re, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni, named after the first four. It works like "do, re, mi" in Western solfege.

Example: A music student warms up by singing sa re ga ma pa dha ni sa up and down the scale.

See also: Raga

Taught in Chapter 9: Music.

docs.title: Sattriya
docs.text:
A classical dance from Assam that began in the sattras, Vaishnava monasteries founded after the teacher Srimanta Sankardev in the 1400s and 1500s.

Script and sound: SUT-tree-yuh

Example: For centuries, male monks called bhokots performed Sankardev's dance-dramas as worship.

See also: Classical Dance, Northeast India

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Satyagraha
docs.text:
Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance in which people openly refuse to obey unjust laws, accept the punishment, and try to win over their opponents rather than defeat them. The Gujarati word combines satya, truth, and agraha, insistence.

Script and sound: સત્યાગ્રહ, SUT-yaa-gruh, "holding firmly to truth"

Example: Breaking an unjust law in public and calmly accepting arrest is an act of satyagraha.

See also: Mahatma Gandhi, Ahimsa

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Satyajit Ray
docs.text:
A Bengali filmmaker from Kolkata (1921 to 1992), widely considered one of the greatest directors in the history of cinema, who was also a writer, illustrator, magazine editor and composer.

Example: Ray's films are studied in film schools around the world.

See also: Regional Cinemas

Taught in Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture.

docs.title: Sea-Level Rise
docs.text:
The gradual increase in the average height of the ocean, caused mainly by warming seawater expanding and by melting glaciers and ice sheets.

Example: Low coral islands like those of the Maldives are especially threatened by sea-level rise.

See also: Maldives, Atolls

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: Shadow Puppetry
docs.text:
A form of storytelling in which flat cut-out figures are held between a light and a thin cloth screen, so the audience sees moving shadows.

Example: Tholu bommalata, "dance of leather dolls," is the shadow puppetry of Andhra Pradesh.

See also: Oral Tradition, Ramayana

Taught in Chapter 10: Dance and Theater.

docs.title: Shalwar Kameez
docs.text:
A two-piece outfit of loose drawstring trousers (the shalwar) and a long tunic with side slits (the kameez), worn by both men and women.

Script and sound: شلوار قمیض, SHUL-war ka-MEEZ (Urdu)

Example: In Pakistan, the shalwar kameez is everyday wear for both men and women.

See also: Dupatta, Kurta

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Sherpa People
docs.text:
An ethnic group of the high Himalaya, most of whom live in eastern Nepal, especially Solukhumbu and the Everest region. Their name means something like "people from the east."

Example: Nima Sherpa's family comes from Solukhumbu, Nepal.

See also: Mount Everest, Losar

Taught in Chapter 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives.

docs.title: Sigiriya
docs.text:
A royal fortress and palace built on top of a granite rock about 180 m (590 ft) high in central Sri Lanka by King Kashyapa I, who ruled from 477 to 495 CE. Its name comes from Sinhagiri, "Lion Rock."

Script and sound: SEE-gi-ri-ya

Example: Only the huge brick paws remain of Sigiriya's lion-shaped gateway.

See also: Sri Lankan Kingdoms

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Sikhism
docs.text:
A faith founded in Punjab by Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539) that teaches devotion to one God, honest work, sharing with others and the equality of all people.

Example: The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, created the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, on Vaisakhi in 1699.

See also: Guru Nanak, Guru Granth Sahib, Langar

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: Silk Weaving
docs.text:
Raising silkworms, unwinding or spinning their cocoon thread and weaving it into cloth, usually for festive and wedding clothes.

Example: Mulberry, tasar and eri silk are among the main kinds of silk India recognizes.

See also: Saree, Cotton in South Asia

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Sindh
docs.text:
Pakistan's southeastern province, the land of the lower Indus River and its delta, with Karachi as its capital. It takes its name from the river, known as the Sindhu.

Example: Mohenjo-daro, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is in Sindh.

See also: Provinces of Pakistan, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Sinhala Language
docs.text:
The Indo-Aryan language of the Sinhalese people, the majority of Sri Lankans, written in its own rounded script and most closely related to Dhivehi. It is spoken by about 16 million people.

Script and sound: සිංහල, SING-ha-la

Example: Dilan Perera's family in Kandy speaks Sinhala.

See also: Dhivehi, Indo-Aryan Languages

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Sitar
docs.text:
A long-necked plucked string instrument with a round gourd body and 18 to 21 strings, many of them sympathetic strings that ring by themselves. Its name comes from the Persian sehtar, "three strings."

Script and sound: सितार, si-TAAR

Example: Sitar players pull the string sideways across the curved frets to bend a note.

See also: Hindustani Music, Tabla

Taught in Chapter 9: Music.

docs.title: South Asia
docs.text:
The region in the south of the Asian continent made up of eight countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. It is a geographic and political label that does not put any one country at the center.

Example: When a news story compares rainfall in Nepal, Bangladesh and Pakistan, it is describing weather across South Asia.

See also: Indian Subcontinent, South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC)

Taught in Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?.

docs.title: South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC)
docs.text:
The regional organization that the eight countries of South Asia set up to work together on trade, health, education and culture. It was founded in Dhaka on 8 December 1985 by seven countries, and Afghanistan joined as the eighth member in 2007.

Example: SAARC's secretariat, its main office, is in Kathmandu, Nepal.

See also: South Asia

Taught in Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?.

docs.title: South Asian English Writing
docs.text:
Literature written in English by writers from South Asia and its diaspora, along with translated works that reach readers worldwide.

Example: Novels by South Asian authors winning major international prizes are milestones of South Asian English Writing.

See also: Rabindranath Tagore, Diaspora

Taught in Chapter 14: Stories and Literature.

docs.title: South Asians in East Africa
docs.text:
Communities of Indian, and later Pakistani, origin that grew up in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and neighboring countries from the late 1800s on, often holding a middle position under British rule.

Example: Many South Asian families in East Africa ran shops or worked as clerks.

See also: Uganda Expulsion of 1972, Diaspora

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: South Asians in Minnesota
docs.text:
Residents of Minnesota with roots in South Asia, a community that includes families from every South Asian country, with temples, mosques, gurdwaras, cultural associations and student clubs across the Twin Cities and beyond.

Example: Zara's family, who moved from Chattogram, Bangladesh, are South Asians in Minnesota.

See also: Diaspora, Student Clubs

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: South India
docs.text:
The southern part of the Indian peninsula, usually meaning Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana plus Puducherry and Lakshadweep, where the main languages are Dravidian.

Example: Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam are the main languages of South India.

See also: Dravidian Languages, Northeast India

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Sri Lanka
docs.text:
An island country in the Indian Ocean across the narrow Palk Strait from India, independent since 4 February 1948 and called Ceylon until 1972, when it became a republic. Its official name is the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka.

Script and sound: ශ්‍රී ලංකා (Sinhala)

Example: The Portuguese and Dutch ruled Sri Lanka's coasts, and the British ruled the whole island.

See also: Sri Lankan Independence, Colombo, Sinhala Language

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Sri Lankan Civil War
docs.text:
An armed conflict from 1983 to 2009 between the government of Sri Lanka and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), an armed group fighting for an independent Tamil state in the north and east.

Example: The war ended in 2009, after 26 years of fighting that caused suffering on all sides.

See also: Sri Lankan Tamils, Sri Lanka

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Sri Lankan Independence
docs.text:
The peaceful transfer of power from Britain to the island then called Ceylon, which became an independent country on 4 February 1948 under the Ceylon Independence Act of 1947.

Example: Don Stephen Senanayake became the first prime minister of independent Ceylon.

See also: Sri Lanka

Taught in Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition.

docs.title: Sri Lankan Kingdoms
docs.text:
The series of kingdoms, some Sinhala and some Tamil and often existing at the same time, that ruled the island of Sri Lanka before European colonial rule.

Example: Anuradhapura was the capital of one of the earliest Sri Lankan Kingdoms.

See also: Anuradhapura, Sigiriya

Taught in Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters.

docs.title: Sri Lankan Tamils
docs.text:
Tamil-speaking people whose ancestors have lived in Sri Lanka for many centuries, mostly in the north and east, with a long history centered on the Jaffna Peninsula. They differ from Hill Country Tamils, whose ancestors were brought by the British to work on plantations.

Example: Jaffna, in the far north, is a historic center of Sri Lankan Tamil culture.

See also: Tamil Language, Sri Lankan Civil War

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Sri Pada (Adam's Peak)
docs.text:
A cone-shaped mountain 2,243 m (7,359 ft) high in central Sri Lanka, sacred to people of several faiths because of a footprint-shaped mark in the rock near its summit. Its name means "sacred footprint."

Script and sound: ශ්‍රී පාද

Example: In Buddhist tradition the mark at the summit is the Buddha's footprint, while other faiths explain it differently.

See also: Pilgrimage, Religious Pluralism

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Srinivasa Ramanujan
docs.text:
A mostly self-taught mathematician from Tamil Nadu (1887 to 1920) whose discoveries about numbers, infinite series and fractions still keep mathematicians busy.

Example: In 1913 Ramanujan wrote to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, who invited him to England.

See also: Kerala School, C. V. Raman

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Staple Grains
docs.text:
The grains a community eats nearly every day and builds most meals around. In South Asia the three main families are rice, wheat and millets.

Example: Rice is the staple in the Bengal delta, while bread made from wheat is the staple on the plains of Pakistan.

See also: Regional Cuisines, Roti and Naan

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: States and Union Territories
docs.text:
The divisions of India: 28 states with their own elected governments that share power with the center, and 8 union territories governed more directly by the national government (as of October 2026).

Example: Kerala is a state, while Delhi is a union territory.

See also: Linguistic States, Republic of India

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Stereotypes
docs.text:
Fixed, oversimplified beliefs about a whole group of people, applied to every member of it.

Example: "They all speak Indian" is a stereotype, since there is no language called "Indian."

See also: Model Minority Myth, Representation in Media

Taught in Chapter 22: Bring It Home.

docs.title: Streaming Era
docs.text:
The period, mainly since the late 2010s, when films and TV shows began reaching audiences through online services such as Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+ and YouTube instead of only through theaters and TV.

Example: A Malayalam thriller can now be watched with subtitles anywhere in the world on the day it comes out.

See also: Global South Asian Pop, Representation in Media

Taught in Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture.

docs.title: Street Food
docs.text:
Food made and sold by vendors at stalls, carts and tiny shops, usually eaten standing up or on the go.

Example: Many South Asians who move abroad say street food is what they miss most.

See also: Regional Cuisines

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Student Clubs
docs.text:
Student-run groups at a school, usually with a faculty advisor, that meet regularly around a shared interest or identity.

Example: A South Asian Student Association is one kind of student club.

See also: Community Organizing, Community Impact

Taught in Chapter 22: Bring It Home.

docs.title: Stupa
docs.text:
A Buddhist monument shaped like a dome or mound, built over relics or sacred objects. Buddhists honor it by walking around it clockwise.

Script and sound: स्तूप, STOO-puh

Example: A classic stupa has a solid round dome topped by a railing and a pole with umbrella-like discs.

See also: Buddhism, Hindu Temple Architecture

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Sufism
docs.text:
The inward, devotional tradition of Islam, focused on the love of God and drawing closer to God through prayer, remembrance and a teacher's guidance. A Sufi usually belongs to an order, a chain of teachers and students.

Script and sound: صوفی, SOO-fee (Persian)

Example: Qawwali is devotional music that grew out of Sufi gatherings.

See also: Qawwali, Islam in South Asia, Bhakti Movement

Taught in Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters.

docs.title: Sundarbans
docs.text:
The world's largest mangrove forest, on the coast of the Bengal Delta, shared by Bangladesh and India. Its name means "beautiful forest" in Bangla.

Script and sound: সুন্দরবন, SHOON-dor-bon

Example: The name may refer to the sundari trees that grow in the Sundarbans.

See also: Bengal Delta, Bay of Bengal

Taught in Chapter 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Sunni and Shia Islam
docs.text:
The two main branches of Islam, which separated over a disagreement about who should lead the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad died in 632. Sunni Muslims accept Abu Bakr as the first caliph; Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet named Ali as his successor.

Example: Ashura is a day of mourning for Shia Muslims and a day of fasting for many Sunni Muslims.

See also: Islam in South Asia, Ashura

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: Surnames
docs.text:
Family names passed down from one generation to the next. In much of South Asia they exist but do not always work as they do in the United States, and some people have none.

Example: The Sri Lankan surname Perera dates from Portuguese rule in the 1500s and 1600s.

See also: Naming Traditions

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Sushruta Samhita
docs.text:
An old Sanskrit medical text linked to the physician Sushruta, famous for its detailed descriptions of surgical instruments and operations.

Example: It describes rebuilding a damaged nose using a flap of skin from the cheek.

See also: Ayurveda

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Tabla
docs.text:
A pair of hand drums that is the main drum of Hindustani music: the smaller wooden dayan produces clear tuned tones, and the larger bayan produces deep bass sounds.

Script and sound: तबला, TUB-la

Example: The black circle of paste on each tabla head gives the drum its ringing tone.

See also: Tala, Hindustani Music

Taught in Chapter 9: Music.

docs.title: Tadka
docs.text:
The cooking step called tempering, in which whole spices, and sometimes garlic, dried chili or curry leaves, are fried briefly in hot oil or ghee and poured over a finished dish.

Script and sound: तड़का, TUD-kah

Example: In Bangla the same step is called phoron, and in Urdu baghaar.

See also: Masala, Dal

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Taj Mahal
docs.text:
A white marble mausoleum in Agra built between about 1631 and 1648 by order of the emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1983.

Example: Shah Jahan himself was later buried in the Taj Mahal beside Mumtaz Mahal.

See also: Mughal Architecture, Mughal Empire

Taught in Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters.

docs.title: Tala
docs.text:
A repeating cycle of beats that organizes time in a piece of music, counted with claps, waves and finger taps. The first beat of the cycle, the sam, is its most important moment.

Script and sound: ताल, TAAL

Example: Musicians may improvise across the beat but aim to land together on sam at the end of each tala cycle.

See also: Raga, Tabla

Taught in Chapter 9: Music.

docs.title: Tamil Language
docs.text:
A Dravidian language spoken by about 69 million people in India in 2011, mostly in Tamil Nadu, and one of the two official and national languages of Sri Lanka. Its literature goes back roughly two thousand years.

Script and sound: தமிழ், THUH-mizh

Example: Tamil is also one of the official languages of Singapore.

See also: Dravidian Languages, Sangam Literature, Sri Lankan Tamils

Taught in Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts.

docs.title: Terracotta
docs.text:
Clay that is shaped and then fired, usually to an orange-red color. The Italian word means "baked earth."

Example: In the Bengal delta, temple walls were covered with terracotta panels showing gods, epics and daily life.

See also: Hindu Temple Architecture

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Thali
docs.text:
A large round plate, usually metal, holding a complete meal: a staple in the middle and several small dishes in bowls called katori around it. The word means both the plate and the meal.

Script and sound: थाली, TAH-lee, "plate"

Example: A Gujarati thali might hold rice and roti with dal, vegetables, pickle and a sweet.

See also: Regional Cuisines, Dal

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Thangka
docs.text:
A Buddhist painting on cotton or silk that can be rolled up like a scroll, showing a deity, a scene from the Buddha's life or a mandala. It is used for teaching and meditation.

Script and sound: ཐང་ཀ, TAHNG-kah (Tibetan)

Example: Thangkas are made in Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet and the Himalayan parts of India.

See also: Theravada and Vajrayana

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Thar Desert
docs.text:
A dry region of sandy plains and low hills, also called the Great Indian Desert, that lies mostly in the Indian state of Rajasthan and partly in Pakistan's Sindh and Punjab provinces. It usually gets less than 500 mm (20 inches) of rain a year.

Example: About 85 percent of the Thar Desert lies in India.

See also: Monsoon, Sindh

Taught in Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?.

docs.title: The Vedas
docs.text:
Four collections of sacred hymns, chants, ritual instructions and teachings composed in an early form of Sanskrit, which are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.

Script and sound: वेद, VAY-duh, "knowledge"

Example: The Rig Veda is the oldest of the four Vedas.

See also: Vedic Period, Hinduism

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Theravada and Vajrayana
docs.text:
Two of the main schools of Buddhism. Theravada, "teaching of the elders," is the school of Sri Lanka and follows the Pali Canon; Vajrayana, the "diamond" or "thunderbolt" vehicle, became the Buddhism of Tibet, Bhutan and Himalayan Nepal.

Example: A monk in Kandy follows Theravada, while a monk in a Bhutanese dzong follows Vajrayana.

See also: Buddhism, Thangka

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: Third Culture Kids
docs.text:
People who spent a large part of their childhood living in a culture different from their parents', usually because a parent's job moved the family between countries. The sociologist Ruth Useem first used the term in the 1960s.

Example: A child of diplomats who grew up in three countries is a third culture kid.

See also: Hyphenated Identity, Cultural Identity

Taught in Chapter 22: Bring It Home.

docs.title: Tibeto-Burman Languages
docs.text:
The South Asian members of the Sino-Tibetan family, spoken mostly in the Himalaya and in India's northeast. India's 2011 census counted 66 of them, more than any other family.

Example: Dzongkha in Bhutan and Sherpa and Newar in Nepal are Tibeto-Burman languages.

See also: Dzongkha, Language Family

Taught in Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts.

docs.title: Transliteration
docs.text:
Writing a word from one script in another script, letter by letter, so that a reader could rebuild the original spelling, often using extra marks.

Example: In one widely used system, दीवाली becomes dīvālī.

See also: Phonetic Respelling, Devanagari

Taught in Appendix A: Pronunciation and Script Guide.

docs.title: Transnational Families
docs.text:
Families whose members live in two or more countries but stay closely connected, sharing money, decisions, care and daily life across borders.

Example: A grandmother in Dhaka who joins dinner every night by video call is part of a transnational family.

See also: Remittances, Diaspora

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: Truck Art
docs.text:
The tradition of decorating trucks and buses with paintings, calligraphy, carved wood, mirrors and reflective strips, best known in Pakistan.

Example: A decorated Pakistani truck may carry mountain landscapes, poetry and a tall carved wooden "crown" above the cab.

See also: Rickshaw Art

Taught in Chapter 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft.

docs.title: Turban (Dastar)
docs.text:
For Sikhs, the dastar is an article of faith, a turban that covers uncut hair (kesh). In Sikh tradition, the Gurus adopted it to declare the sovereignty and equality of all people.

Script and sound: ਦਸਤਾਰ, dus-TAAR

Example: Many Sikh men, and some Sikh women, tie a dastar each day to cover their uncut hair.

See also: Sikhism, Post-9/11 Backlash

Taught in Chapter 12: Clothing and Textiles.

docs.title: Uganda Expulsion of 1972
docs.text:
The forced removal of nearly all South Asians from Uganda by the military ruler Idi Amin, who announced on 4 August 1972 that they had 90 days to leave.

Example: About 80,000 people of South Asian descent, many born in Uganda, had to abandon homes and businesses.

See also: South Asians in East Africa, British South Asians

Taught in Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora.

docs.title: Unani Medicine
docs.text:
A healing tradition that began with the Greek physicians Hippocrates and Galen, was developed by doctors writing in Arabic and Persian, and came to South Asia by the 1100s. It is based on the old idea of balancing four "humors."

Script and sound: یونانی, yoo-NAA-nee, "Greek"

Example: Unani practitioners are often called hakims.

See also: Ayurveda, Indo-Persian Culture

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Unity in Diversity
docs.text:
The idea that a country can hold many languages, faiths, peoples and cultures and still be one nation, with differences seen as a strength. Indian leaders and schools have used the phrase since independence.

Example: An Indian school assembly with songs in several languages celebrates unity in diversity.

See also: Regional Diversity, Religious Pluralism

Taught in Chapter 17: India.

docs.title: Urdu as National Language
docs.text:
The status of Urdu as the language Pakistan's constitution names for the whole nation, even though only a small share of Pakistanis speak it as a first language.

Script and sound: اردو, OOR-doo

Example: Article 251 of the 1973 constitution names Urdu the national language and lets provinces promote their own languages.

See also: Hindi-Urdu (Hindustani), Language Movement of 1952

Taught in Chapter 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Vaisakhi
docs.text:
A harvest festival and new year in Punjab and much of North India on 13 or 14 April, and one of the most important days of the Sikh year. It is also spelled Baisakhi.

Script and sound: VAI-saa-khee

Example: Sikhs mark Vaisakhi with prayers at the gurdwara and nagar kirtan, processions with hymn singing.

See also: Sikhism, Pohela Boishakh

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Varna and Jati
docs.text:
The two ideas behind what English speakers call caste. Varna is a fourfold social classification described in old Brahmanical Sanskrit texts; jati is the local group a person is born into, of which there are thousands.

Script and sound: वर्ण, VAR-na (varna); जाति, JAA-tee, "birth" or "kind" (jati)

Example: The Manusmriti lists four varnas and assigns each one duties.

See also: Caste System

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Vedic Period
docs.text:
The era from about 1500 to 500 BCE when the Vedas were composed in northern South Asia, between the end of the Indus cities and the rise of new cities and kingdoms around 600 BCE.

Example: The Rig Veda, the oldest of the Vedas, comes from the early part of the Vedic Period.

See also: The Vedas, Sanskrit

Taught in Chapter 2: Ancient Roots.

docs.title: Veena
docs.text:
An ancient name for stringed instruments used in Indian texts for about 3,000 years. In Carnatic music it usually means the Saraswati veena, a large plucked lute with 24 fixed frets.

Script and sound: वीणा, Tamil வீணை, VEE-nah

Example: The Hindu goddess Saraswati is usually shown holding a veena.

See also: Carnatic Music

Taught in Chapter 9: Music.

docs.title: Vegetarianism in South Asia
docs.text:
The practice of eating diets without meat, and often without fish or eggs, which is more common in South Asia than almost anywhere else, though most South Asians are not vegetarian.

Example: A Pew Research Center survey of nearly 30,000 adults in India, published in 2021, measured how many Indians are vegetarian.

See also: Ahimsa, Dietary Rules and Faith

Taught in Chapter 8: Food and the Table.

docs.title: Vesak
docs.text:
The most important Buddhist festival in South Asia, on the full moon of the month of Vesak, usually in May, when Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing away. It is also called Buddha Purnima.

Script and sound: වෙසක්, VAY-suck (Sinhala)

Example: In 1999 the United Nations General Assembly formally recognized the Day of Vesak.

See also: Buddhism, Lumbini

Taught in Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year.

docs.title: Vijayanagara Empire
docs.text:
A large Hindu-ruled empire of southern India from 1336 to 1646, named after its capital city, Vijayanagara, "city of victory."

Example: The ruins of the capital city stand at Hampi, in Karnataka.

See also: Delhi Sultanate, Chola Dynasty

Taught in Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters.

docs.title: Weddings
docs.text:
In South Asia, often multi-day events that join two families, not just two people, with separate ceremonies before, during and after the main rite. Details differ widely by faith, region and family budget.

Example: A wedding with a mehndi night, a nikah or other main ceremony, and a reception afterward can stretch across several days.

See also: Mehndi Night and Sangeet, Nikah, Anand Karaj, Arranged Marriage

Taught in Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events.

docs.title: Western and Eastern Ghats
docs.text:
The two mountain ranges that frame the Deccan Plateau, one along each coast of peninsular India. Ghat means a flight of steps down to a river, or a mountain pass.

Script and sound: घाट, GHAAT

Example: The ranges act like giant steps from the plateau down to the sea on India's west and east coasts.

See also: Deccan Plateau

Taught in Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?.

docs.title: Wootz Steel
docs.text:
A high-carbon steel made in South India and Sri Lanka by melting iron with carbon-rich material in sealed clay crucibles, famous for its strength and wavy surface pattern. "Wootz" comes from ukku, the Kannada and Telugu word for steel.

Example: Finds in Tamil Nadu suggest crucible steel was made there before the Common Era.

See also: Indian Ocean Trade

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Yoga
docs.text:
A set of practices rooted in South Asian philosophy that combines body postures, breathing and meditation, which began as a spiritual discipline for training the mind.

Script and sound: योग, YOH-guh, "joining" or "union"

Example: The poses taught at a gym are only one part of the much bigger yoga tradition.

See also: Ayurveda, Hinduism

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Zero
docs.text:
Both a symbol that marks an empty place in a number and a number in its own right, the result of subtracting any number from itself. The two ideas arrived at different times.

Example: Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero as a number in 628 CE.

See also: Place Value System, Brahmagupta

Taught in Chapter 16: Science, Math, and Ideas.

docs.title: Zoroastrians (Parsis)
docs.text:
Followers of Zoroastrianism, an ancient faith founded by the prophet Zoroaster in Iran; in South Asia most belong to the Parsi community, whose ancestors came from Iran. Parsi means "Persian."

Example: In the community's own story, the Qissa-i Sanjan, Zoroastrians from Iran landed on the coast of Gujarat.

See also: Religious Pluralism, Nowruz

Taught in Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia.

docs.title: How to Cite
docs.text:
If you use Roots & Rivers in a class, a project or a paper, please cite it.

APA (7th edition)

Sharma, A. (2026). Roots & Rivers: An interactive guide to South Asian cultures for high school students (Version 1.0). https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/

MLA (9th edition)

Sharma, Aaryav. Roots & Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students. Version 1.0, 2026, aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/.

Chicago

Sharma, Aaryav. Roots & Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students. Version 1.0. 2026. https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/.

BibTeX

@book{sharma2026rootsrivers,
  author    = {Sharma, Aaryav},
  title     = {Roots \& Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students},
  year      = {2026},
  edition   = {Version 1.0},
  url       = {https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/},
  note      = {Open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0}
}

To cite one chapter, add the chapter title and its URL, for example: Sharma, A. (2026). Festivals through the year. In Roots & Rivers (Chapter 7).

The repository also includes a CITATION.cff file, so GitHub's "Cite this repository" button gives you a ready-made citation.

docs.title: If you're a student
docs.text:
1. Start anywhere. Chapter 1 is the best first stop, but each chapter lists its prerequisites at the top, so you can jump to the festival or food chapter if that's what you're curious about.
  2. Play with the MicroSim. Each chapter has one interactive simulation. Most take two minutes. Try the controls before you read the paragraph that explains them.
  3. Do the Ask Your Elders interview. It's the most important part of the book. Ten minutes with a parent, grandparent or community elder will teach you things no book can.
  4. Check yourself. Each chapter has five quick questions, twelve exercises and a separate 10-question quiz with explained answers.
  5. Use the glossary. Every concept in the book has a short definition in the Glossary.

docs.title: How words from other languages are shown
docs.text: The first time a key word appears, you'll see it in its original script, a simple respelling and its meaning, like this: Diwali (दीवाली, dee-VAH-lee), "row of lamps". The CAPITAL letters show which part to stress. The respellings are approximate; the best way to learn a pronunciation is to ask someone who speaks the language. See Appendix A.

docs.title: Meet your guides
docs.text:
Mora is a young peacock who pops up in each chapter with a tip, a warning about a common mix-up, or a question to think about. The peacock motif runs through art across South Asia, from temple carvings to textiles.

Zara Hossain and Ben Lindqvist are two fictional sophomores at a Minnesota high school. Zara's family is from Bangladesh; Ben's is Swedish and Norwegian. They start a South Asian Student Association together, and each chapter begins with a question one of them can't answer yet. Their friends Arjun, Simran, Ayesha, Nima and Dilan show up along the way. All of them are made up.

docs.title: The boxes you'll see
docs.text: Box What it's for Mora's boxes A welcome, a tip, a common mix-up, a question to think about Whose Story? How different communities or historians tell the same thing Your interview for this chapter The Ask Your Elders guide Collapsible questions Click to reveal the answer after you've tried
