docs.title: Oral History Project and Story Archive
Oral History Project and Story Archive
docs.text:
Every chapter of this book ends with Ask Your Elders, a short interview guide. Do the ones in Chapters 1 to 21 and you'll have 21 conversations with the people who carry your family's or community's memory. This page shows how to turn those conversations into something lasting: a family archive, a club project, or a story shared with other readers.

Start small

You don't need a microphone or a plan for all 21 interviews. Pick the chapter you care about most, ask one person for ten minutes, and write down one story in their words. That's an oral history.

docs.title: What oral history is
docs.text: Oral history is the practice of recording people's memories of their own lives, in their own words, so that others can learn from them later. Libraries and museums collect oral histories because official records leave a lot out: what a festival smelled like, what it felt like to cross a new border, why a grandmother still sets an extra plate. The South Asian American Digital Archive (SAADA) collects stories like these from the diaspora.

docs.title: 1. Ask permission (informed consent)
docs.text:
Before you start, tell the person what you're doing, how long it will take, whether you'll record or take notes, and who might see it. Ask if it's OK. They can skip any question, stop at any time, or ask you not to share something later. This is called informed consent, and it's the first rule of oral history (Oral History Association).

A simple script:

"I'm doing a project for my school's South Asian club about [topic]. Can I ask you a few questions for about ten minutes? I'd like to take notes. You can skip anything you don't want to answer. Later, I might share one short story from our talk, with only your first name or initial, if you say that's OK."

docs.title: 2. Listen more than you talk
docs.text: Use the questions in the chapter's Ask Your Elders section, but follow the conversation. The best answers often come from a follow-up: "What happened next?" "What did that look like?" "How did that feel?" Don't correct them; memory isn't a test. If what they say differs from the book, that's interesting, not wrong. Write down the difference.

docs.title: 3. Save it carefully
docs.text: Write the date, who you talked to (relationship and first name), the chapter, and the best story in their words. If you recorded audio, keep it somewhere private and ask before sharing it with anyone. Never post an elder's full name, address, phone number or photo without clear permission.

docs.title: 4. Give something back
docs.text: Show the person what you wrote. Many elders love seeing their story taken seriously. Some families make a printed booklet of a year of interviews as a gift.

docs.title: Turn it into a project
docs.text:
• Family archive: collect all 21 interviews into one document with photos the family chooses to share.
  • Club night: at a South Asian Student Association meeting, each member shares one short story (with permission). See the Club Kit.
  • Class project: many of the Teacher Guide activities use these interviews.
  • Interview Builder: the MicroSim in Chapter 22 builds a printable interview plan for any chapter.

docs.title: The Roots & Rivers Story Archive
docs.text:
The Story Archive collects short stories from readers' interviews, shared with permission, so that other readers can hear how traditions are lived in real families.

The archive has no stories yet. Version 1.0 of the book has just been published. Every story here will come from a real reader, shared with consent, and approved before it appears. We will never write or invent stories for the archive.

docs.title: How to share a story
docs.text:
1. Pick one story from an interview, 150 words or fewer.
  2. Get permission from the person who told it, and from your parent or guardian if you're under 18.
  3. Use first names or initials only.
  4. Submit it with the Share a Story form on GitHub. That form is public, so if you'd rather not post publicly, share your story through your school's South Asian club instead.

Stories are reviewed, may be shortened (never changed in meaning), and are added here with the chapter they connect to.

docs.title: For Teachers
docs.text: Thank you for looking at this book for your students. This page explains what the book is, gives four ways to use it, and offers routines and cautions that make it work well in a real classroom. You don't need to read all 22 chapters first. Pick a plan below, open one chapter, and spend five minutes with its MicroSim yourself.

docs.title: What the book is
docs.text:
Roots & Rivers is a free, open textbook about the cultures of South Asia: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, plus the South Asian diaspora. It is written for students in grades 9 to 12 and assumes no background. Many readers are second-generation South Asian Americans. Many others are their friends.

Every chapter has the same parts:

  • a short opening scene with two fictional Minnesota teens, Zara and Ben
  • core content that starts with a familiar comparison before the details
  • a MicroSim, a small interactive simulation that runs in the browser
  • a Whose Story? box that shows how different communities, countries or historians tell the same thing differently
  • Ask Your Elders, a ten-minute interview guide
  • Common Misconceptions (Myth and Reality pairs), five Check Yourself questions, 12 exercises (two per Bloom level) and Key Takeaways
  • a 10-question quiz on its own page, and a references page

The 22 chapters are in four parts: Foundations (1 to 6), Living Culture (7 to 16), The Eight Countries (17 to 20) and Here and Now (21 and 22). After Chapter 1, most chapters stand on their own, and each one lists its prerequisites at the top. See the List of Chapters and the List of MicroSims.

docs.title: License
docs.text: The book uses Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0. In plain words: you can use it free in class, print it and share it with students; you can change it (shorten a chapter, translate it) if you share your version under the same license; give credit; and don't sell it. A credit line like this works: Adapted from "Roots & Rivers" by Aaryav Sharma, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. See How to Cite for more formats.

docs.title: Four ways to use it
docs.text: Times below assume class periods of about 50 minutes. Adjust them to your schedule.

docs.title: Option 1: A full semester (ethnic studies or a world history elective)
docs.text:
A semester of about 18 weeks covers all 22 chapters at one to two chapters per week, with time for the oral history capstone. The book's Chapter 22 turns the Ask Your Elders interviews into a final project, so students build toward it all term.

Weeks Chapters Focus 1 1: What Is South Asia? The region, its land and the monsoon 2 2: Ancient Roots Indus cities to the Guptas 3 3: Empires and Encounters Many powers, overlapping 4 to 5 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition Two weeks: read the sensitive topics section below first 6 5: Faiths of South Asia Comparing faiths without ranking them 7 6: Languages and Scripts Language families, scripts and identity 8 7: Festivals Through the Year, 8: Food and the Table Calendars, festivals and regional food 9 9: Music, 10: Dance and Theater Raga, tala and classical and folk forms 10 11: Art, Architecture, and Craft, 12: Clothing and Textiles Making and wearing 11 13: Family, Names, and Life Events Kinship, naming, caste (see the guidance below) 12 14: Stories and Literature How stories travel 13 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture, 16: Science, Math, and Ideas Media, sport and ideas 14 17: India, 18: Pakistan and Afghanistan Country tours, part 1 15 19: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, 20: Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives Country tours, part 2 16 21: The South Asian Diaspora Migration waves and Minnesota 17 22: Bring It Home Oral history method and project work 18 Capstone presentations Students share one interview story with permission

A weekly rhythm that works for many classes:

  • Day 1: the opening scene and the "intuition first" section, read together
  • Day 2: core content, ending with the Whose Story? box as a discussion
  • Day 3: the MicroSim, in pairs
  • Day 4: Common Misconceptions and exercises
  • Day 5: quiz questions as an exit ticket, and Ask Your Elders assigned for the weekend

docs.title: Option 2: A 6-week South Asia unit inside world history or world geography
docs.text:
This plan uses ten chapters and fits a unit of about 30 class days. The history-heavy chapters come first; the culture chapters show what that history means in people's lives.

Week Chapters MicroSims End-of-week check 1 1, 2 Region Explorer, Ancient Timeline Locate the eight countries; order the ancient periods 2 3, 5 Empire Swim Lanes, Faith Explorer Short written comparison of two empires or two faiths 3 4 Borders Then and Now Explain 1947 and 1971 as two separate events 4 6, 7 Script Family Tree, Festival Wheel Quizzes for Chapters 6 and 7 5 Two of 17, 18, 19, 20 The matching country sims Jigsaw: groups teach their country to the class 6 21 Migration Waves Short source analysis using the chapter's Whose Story? box

For a world geography course, swap Chapter 3 for Chapter 8: Food and the Table (crops, climate and trade) and give Chapter 1's monsoon section a full day.

docs.text:
Each chapter works as a one- or two-day lesson. Use the chapter's MicroSim and Whose Story? box as the core.

If you are teaching... docs.title: Option 4: A club or advisory period
docs.text: A South Asian student association, a multicultural club or an advisory group can use one chapter per meeting. The Club Kit has a two-year plan of 20 monthly 45-minute meetings, with games, festival timing and food notes. Advisory periods can use the Check Yourself questions and the Ask Your Elders share-outs on their own, without the full chapter.

docs.title: Standards connections
docs.text:
These are teacher-made connections

The connections below were made by the book's author to help with planning. The book is not aligned to, reviewed by or endorsed by the Minnesota Department of Education, the College Board or the National Council for the Social Studies. Check your own state or district standards.

docs.title: Minnesota K-12 Academic Standards in Social Studies (2021)
docs.text:
Minnesota's 2021 social studies standards were approved in 2024 and take effect in the 2026-27 school year (Sahan Journal). They are organized into five strands: (1) Citizenship and Government, (2) Economics, (3) Geography, (4) History and (5) Ethnic Studies. The codes and wording below come from the standards document as posted by Education Evolving. The Minnesota Department of Education's own site holds the official version; please confirm codes there before you put them in a lesson plan.

The Ethnic Studies strand has three anchor standards: Identity, Resistance and Ways of Knowing and Methodologies. In grades 9 to 12 they appear as standards 23, 24 and 25.

Benchmark What it asks (shortened) Chapters that connect 9.5.23.1 How definitions of racial and ethnic groups changed over time as a result of politics 21 (diaspora history in the U.S.) 9.5.23.3 The connection between language and power 6 (language movements, including 21 February 1952 in Dhaka), 19 9.5.23.6 How religions develop and change over time; the benchmark names Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Islam and others 5, 7 9.5.24.1 Compare liberation struggles in different regions of the world 4 (independence movements and 1971) Anchor standard 25 (Ways of Knowing and Methodologies) Use ethnic and Indigenous studies methods and sources 22 and the Oral History Project

Several geography and history benchmarks also connect:

Benchmark What it asks (shortened) Chapters that connect 9.3.15.3 Migration patterns, including forced migration and displacement 4, 21 9.3.15.6 The spread of culture through diffusion 8, 14 9.3.15.8 The impact of colonialism on new states, and tensions when borders don't match the people living within them 4, 18 9.3.17.1 Investigate one's multiple identities based on place and culture Every Ask Your Elders section; 22 9.4.18.6 Conflicting narratives about the past and how they can lead to conflict (World History Era 6) Every Whose Story? box, especially 4 9.4.19.5 Perspectives on revolutions, imperialism and nation-building, including in Asia (Era 5) 3, 4 9.4.20.6 Primary sources about global migration and refugees since 1900 (Era 6) 21 9.4.21.15 (U.S. History Era 8) Immigrant, migrant and refugee groups; the benchmark names Hmong, Somali, Indian, Ethiopian and Latinx people 21

Separately, the 2023 Legislature required Minnesota high schools to offer an ethnic studies course beginning in 2026-27 (Sahan Journal). This book can be one resource for such a course, but it covers one world region and is not a full ethnic studies curriculum on its own.

docs.title: AP World History: Modern
docs.text:
The College Board's AP World History: Modern Course and Exam Description (the version effective fall 2026) has nine units, listed on the course page. South Asia appears in many of them:

Unit Where South Asia appears in the framework Chapters that connect Unit 1: The Global Tapestry Topic 1.2 lists the Delhi sultanates among new Islamic states; Topic 1.3, Developments in South and Southeast Asia from c. 1200 to c. 1450, gives examples such as the Bhakti movement, the Vijayanagara Empire, the Rajput kingdoms and Sinhala dynasties 3, 5 Unit 2: Networks of Exchange Topic 2.3, Exchange in the Indian Ocean 3, 8 Unit 3: Land-Based Empires The Mughal Empire in topics on expansion, administration and belief systems; the framework notes that Sikhism developed in South Asia amid interactions between Hinduism and Islam 3, 5, 11 Unit 4: Transoceanic Interconnections Maritime empires and global trade; Indian cotton is an example of growing artisan labor 3, 12 Unit 6: Consequences of Industrialization The 1857 rebellion in India; Indian indentured servitude; Indian communities in East and Southern Africa, the Caribbean and Southeast Asia 4, 21 Unit 7: Global Conflict The Indian National Congress appears as an example of anti-imperial resistance 4 Unit 8: Cold War and Decolonization The Indian National Congress, the Muslim League, India's negotiated independence, the Partition of India, and South Asian migration to Britain 4, 19, 21 Unit 9: Globalization Caste reservation in India appears as an example 13, 17

Use the book as enrichment and as a source of perspectives. It is not an AP exam prep book.

docs.title: The C3 Framework
docs.text:
The National Council for the Social Studies' C3 Framework is built on an Inquiry Arc with four dimensions. Minnesota's 2021 standards say they used it. Each chapter of this book can carry one full inquiry:

C3 dimension How the book supports it 1. Developing Questions and Planning Inquiries Each chapter's opening scene ends on a real question (for example, "Is Bangladesh part of India?"). Students write their own supporting questions before reading. 2. Applying Disciplinary Concepts and Tools MicroSims practice geography (schematic maps, the monsoon), history (timelines, overlapping empires), economics (trade and food) and civics (federal states in India). 3. Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence Every number in the book is linked to a source on the chapter's references page. Whose Story? boxes ask students to weigh accounts that disagree. 4. Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action Ask Your Elders and the Oral History Project end with something real: a recorded story, a club presentation, or a contribution to the Story Archive.

docs.title: MicroSims: predict, observe, explain
docs.text:
Every MicroSim runs in a browser with no login or install, on phones, tablets and Chromebooks. You can link students straight to a sim's page from the List of MicroSims.

  1. Predict. Before touching the sim, students write what they expect. ("If I move the year slider forward ten years, will Eid be earlier or later in the year?")
  2. Observe. Pairs run the sim. One drives, one records, then they switch.
  3. Explain. Each pair writes two sentences explaining any surprise, using the chapter's terms.

Maps in this book are schematic on purpose: tiles, dots and rivers, never official borders. Tell students this before they start, and ask them why a textbook about eight countries might choose not to draw borders. It's a good opening for Chapter 4 or Chapter 18.

docs.title: Whose Story? boxes: one event, several tellings
docs.text:
Every chapter has a short box showing how different communities, countries or historians describe the same thing. A ten-minute routine:

  1. Read the box aloud.
  2. In pairs, students fill in a two-column chart: "Who tells it this way?" and "What might shape that view?"
  3. Ask: "What would you need to read or ask to know more?" Students list one source and one person.

Keep the goal clear: understanding why people see things differently, not deciding which community is right. The book never ranks faiths, countries or communities, and class discussion shouldn't either.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders, with a real choice
docs.text:
Ask Your Elders is the heart of the book, but it must never require students to disclose their family history. Some students have no South Asian elders. Some live with foster or adoptive families, have lost family members, or have family stories that are painful or private. Some simply don't want to share. Offer every student the same three choices, and never ask which one applies to them or why:

  • Option A: interview a family member or family friend, using the chapter's questions.
  • Option B: interview a community member instead: a club advisor, a volunteer at a temple, mosque, gurdwara, church or cultural center, a neighbor, or another teacher. The chapter template already offers this.
  • Option C: do a "research interview": read or listen to a published oral history (see the Oral History Project page for where to find them), then answer the chapter's questions as the narrator would have, with a citation.

Grade the process (questions prepared, notes taken, one story written in the person's words, a reflection), not the content of anyone's family life. Share-outs in class are always voluntary. A student can submit an interview to you and still decline to present it.

docs.title: Exit tickets
docs.text:
Each chapter's quiz is on its own page, with answers in "Show Answer" boxes. For an exit ticket, copy two or three questions into a form or onto paper so students can't see the answers. Other quick ideas:

  • Myth or Reality? Read one statement from the chapter's Common Misconceptions. Thumbs up or down, then one student explains.
  • 3-2-1: three new terms, two places named in the chapter, one question to ask an elder.
  • One-sentence Whose Story?: "One group tells it as , another as , because ___."
  • Sim screenshot: students paste a screenshot from the MicroSim and caption it with what it shows.

docs.title: Teaching sensitive topics with care
docs.text:
Some chapters touch history that is still personal for families in your room. A few principles help.

Partition (1947) and 1971. Chapter 4 describes suffering on all sides, gives death and displacement figures as scholarly ranges, and avoids graphic detail. Before teaching it:

  • Tell students a day ahead what the chapter covers. Offer a quiet alternative task without asking for a reason.
  • Don't ask students to speak for their family's country or community, or to explain "their side".
  • Some families carry memories of loss or violence. The chapter's Ask Your Elders section says to ask only if the elder wants to share; repeat that out loud.
  • If a student or family member contradicts the book, treat it as a perspective to explore, not an error to correct. The Whose Story? box is built for exactly this.

Caste. Chapter 13 describes caste as a historical and continuing social system. Discrimination by caste is illegal in India under Article 17 of the Constitution, and it still exists. In class:

  • Never ask students their caste, and never ask anyone to guess a classmate's caste from a surname. Stop that conversation if it starts.
  • Never use "high" or "low" to describe communities. Use "Dalit" and "Adivasi" respectfully, as the book does.
  • Keep the discussion on the system and how people have resisted it, not on individuals.

Religion. Chapter 5 describes beliefs in the words of believers ("many Hindus believe", "in Sikh tradition") and never as the book's own claims. Ask students to do the same. Practices vary widely within every faith, and students should not be asked to represent their faith or to perform a ritual or prayer. Visiting a place of worship can be wonderful, but make it optional and get permission from the community first.

Other topics that need a heads-up: the Sri Lankan civil war (Chapter 19), indenture and post-2001 hate crimes (Chapter 21), disputed territory such as Kashmir (described as disputed, with each side's position stated briefly), and health traditions such as Ayurveda, which the book describes as traditions, not medical advice.

When a student says the book is wrong

Thank them and ask where their version comes from. Sometimes families remember things the books leave out. If it's a factual error, please report it so we can fix it for everyone.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
• Devices and network. The book is a website and works on any modern browser. MicroSims load the p5.js library from a content delivery network; if a sim shows a blank area on school devices, ask your IT team whether that site is blocked.
  • Screen readers. MicroSims are visual and interactive, so pair students who use screen readers with a partner, and use the chapter text alongside the sim.
  • Language. Terms from South Asian languages are given in their original script, a simple respelling and a meaning. The Pronunciation and Script Guide helps everyone, including teachers, say names and words with respect.
  • Printing. See the Downloads page for printable versions as they become available.

docs.title: Tell us how it went
docs.text:
If you use the book with students, please report your classroom use. Tell us what worked, what confused students and what you changed. Please don't include student names or other personal information; the form is public. Reports help us improve the book and are summarized, as totals only, on the Impact page.

To report a factual error or something that feels unfair, use the links on the Contact page. Corrections are listed on the Accuracy page.

If you want to measure whether the book helps your students learn, the project's pilot study kit (in the Materials/pilot-study folder of the book's source files) has a 20-question pre and post test, a survey, consent and assent forms, and a simple analysis guide. It requires approval from your school before you collect any data.

docs.title: Appendix B: Country Fact Sheets
docs.text:
This appendix gives a one-table snapshot of each of the eight countries of South Asia, listed alphabetically. Use it for quick reference while you read, or as a starting point for a club presentation. The country chapters (17 to 20) tell the fuller stories.

How to read these tables

  • Official name is the formal name used by the United Nations (UNTERM country list, checked October 2026).
  • Population is the 2025 figure from the World Bank (SP.POP.TOTL, dataset updated October 2026).
  • Main faiths are Pew Research Center estimates for 2020, published in June 2025. We use one source for all eight countries so they can be compared fairly. National census figures, where the book uses them, appear in the country chapters, and they can differ a little from Pew's estimates. Percentages are rounded and may not add to 100.
  • Currency names and codes come from the international ISO 4217 list (September 2026 edition).
  • UNESCO World Heritage sites are counted from each country's page on the UNESCO World Heritage Centre website, checked in October 2026. A site shared between countries counts for each country that lists it.

Numbers have birthdays

Every number on this page has a year attached, because populations, faith shares and even site lists change. If you use one in a project, copy the year and the source along with it.

docs.title: Afghanistan
docs.text: Official name The Islamic Republic of Afghanistan (UN name). Since August 2021 the country has been governed by the Taliban, who call the state the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. As of October 2026, Russia (since July 2025) is the only country reported to have formally recognized the Taliban government. Capital Kabul Population (2025, World Bank) 43,844,111 (about 44 million) Official languages Pashto and Dari Main faiths (Pew, 2020) Muslim 99.9%; most are Sunni, with a Shia minority Currency Afghani (AFN) National day Independence Day, 19 August. Afghanistan was never formally colonized, but Britain controlled its foreign affairs until the 1919 Treaty of Rawalpindi. UNESCO World Heritage sites 2: Minaret and Archaeological Remains of Jam (2002); Cultural Landscape and Archaeological Remains of the Bamiyan Valley (2003) Learn more Chapter 18

docs.title: Appendix C: Festival Calendar 2026-27
docs.text: Planning a club celebration, or just want to know when your friends' big days fall? This appendix lists festivals and national days across South Asia's faiths and countries from November 2026 through December 2027. Before the table, a short guide explains why so many of these dates move around from year to year.

docs.title: C.1 Why Festival Dates Move: Calendar Conversion
docs.text:
The calendar on your phone is the Gregorian calendar, a solar calendar of 365 days (366 in leap years) that most of the world uses for school, work and government. But many festivals in South Asia are set by other calendars, and every year their Gregorian dates have to be worked out again. Calendar Conversion means finding the date in one calendar that matches a date in another, for example working out which Gregorian day will be the first day of the month of Shawwal, when Eid al-Fitr begins.

South Asia uses four main kinds of calendar:

Kind What it follows Year length Example festivals Solar The sun only about 365 days New Year's Day; Vaisakhi; Pongal; Sinhala and Tamil New Year Lunar The moon only 354 or 355 days Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Ashura (Hijri calendar) Lunisolar Moon for months, sun for the year months of about 29.5 days, with an extra month added some years Diwali, Holi, Dashain, Vesak, Guru Nanak Jayanti Gregorian (civil) The sun, with fixed month lengths 365 or 366 days National days such as 15 August or 16 December

Lunar calendars count only moons. The Hijri calendar, used by Muslims for religious dates, has twelve months of 29 or 30 days, so its year is about 11 days shorter than a Gregorian year. That's why Ramadan and the two Eids move about 11 days earlier every year and slowly travel through all the seasons. In many places a new month begins only when the new crescent moon is actually seen, so the exact day is often announced the night before.

Lunisolar calendars use moon-based months but add an extra month every few years, so that festivals stay in roughly the same season. Many Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh and Jain festivals follow these calendars. Diwali, for example, always falls in October or November, but its exact date jumps around within that window.

Solar festivals follow the sun's position, so they land on nearly the same Gregorian date each year. Vaisakhi and the Sinhala and Tamil New Year fall around 13 to 14 April, and Pongal and Makar Sankranti around 14 to 15 January.

Two national calendars are worth knowing:

  • Bikram Sambat is Nepal's official calendar. Its years are about 56 to 57 years "ahead" of the Gregorian count, and its new year begins in mid-April with the month of Baisakh.
  • The Bangla calendar (Bangabda) is used in Bangladesh and by Bengalis in India. Its new year, Pohela Boishakh, is fixed on 14 April in Bangladesh. In West Bengal and other parts of India, the traditional calculation can put it on 14 or 15 April.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Here is how three calendars line up on the same spring day in 2026, and what happens a year later.

  1. 14 April 2026 (Gregorian) was New Year's Day in two other calendars at once. In Nepal it was Baisakh 1, 2083 in Bikram Sambat. In Bangladesh it was Pohela Boishakh, the first day of the Bangla year 1433.
  2. Converting the year numbers. From mid-April to December, add 57 to the Gregorian year to get the Bikram Sambat year (2026 + 57 = 2083). From January to mid-April, add 56. For the Bangla year after 14 April, subtract 593 (2026 - 593 = 1433).
  3. Now follow a lunar festival. Eid al-Fitr was on 21 March 2026 in Pakistan and Bangladesh. In 2027 it is expected around 10 March. That is 11 days earlier, because the Hijri year is about 11 days shorter than the Gregorian year.
  4. And a lunisolar one. Diwali falls on 8 November 2026 and on 29 October 2027 in India. That's ten days earlier, but still in the same autumn season, because the lunisolar calendar adds an extra month every few years to catch up with the sun.

Check before you book the room

If your club is planning an Eid or Diwali party, confirm the date with a local mosque, temple or family a week or two before. Lunar dates can shift by a day, and communities sometimes celebrate on different days.

docs.title: Appendix A: Pronunciation and Script Guide
Appendix A: Pronunciation and Script Guide
docs.text: All through this book, a new word from a South Asian language shows up three ways at once: in its own script, in an English-style respelling, and with its meaning. Diwali, for example, appears as दीवाली, dee-VAH-lee, "row of lamps". This appendix explains how to read those respellings, why they are only a starting point, and where to find the words again.

docs.title: A.1 Transliteration and Respelling Are Not the Same
docs.text:
There are two common ways to write a word from another script in English letters.

Transliteration means writing a word from one script in another script, letter by letter, so that a reader could rebuild the original spelling. Scholars often use extra marks to do this. In one widely used system, दीवाली becomes dīvālī: the line over the ī and ā shows a long vowel. Transliteration is careful and exact, but you have to learn its rules before it helps you say anything.

Phonetic Respelling means writing how a word sounds using ordinary English spelling patterns, with no special marks. The same word becomes dee-VAH-lee. A respelling doesn't tell you how the word is spelled in its own script. It only tries to get your mouth close to the right sound on the first try.

This book uses respellings in the text because most readers can use them right away. The script form sits beside each one so you can see the real word, and you can always look up a scholarly transliteration in a dictionary.

Transliteration Phonetic respelling Goal Record the spelling exactly Help you say the word Looks like dīvālī, tamiḻ dee-VAH-lee, THUH-mizh Uses special marks? Often (ā, ī, ṭ, ṣ) Never Can you rebuild the original spelling? Yes No

docs.title: A.2 How to Read the Respellings
docs.text:
Hyphens split syllables. dee-VAH-lee has three syllables.

CAPITAL letters show stress, the syllable to lean on a little. In dee-VAH-lee, say "VAH" slightly louder and longer. Many South Asian languages put much less weight on stress than English does, so think of the capitals as a gentle hint, not a hammer.

Vowels follow this key. Some chapters write the long "a" as aa (as in BAANG-laa) and others as ah. Both mean the same sound.

Respelling Sounds like the vowel in Example from this book ah (or aa) father raga, RAHG uh up, sofa katha, KUH-thaa ee see Holi, HOH-lee i sit Hindi, HIN-dee oo moon Urdu, OOR-doo u put gurdwara, gur-DWAH-rah ay say namaste, NUH-mus-tay eh bed Telugu, TEL-oo-goo oh go gho, GOH ai my, sky chai, CHAI ow now (rare in this book) oi boy Boishakh, BOI-shakh

docs.title: Retroflex and dental t and d
docs.text:
Most South Asian languages have two kinds of t and two kinds of d, where English has only one.

  • Dental sounds are made with the tip of your tongue touching the back of your top front teeth. They sound soft and a little "flat". The t in Hindi tīn, "three", is dental.
  • Retroflex sounds are made by curling the tip of your tongue back and tapping the roof of your mouth, behind the ridge where English t and d live. They sound heavier, almost hollow. The ṭ in roṭī (roti) is retroflex.

English t and d sit in between, which is why South Asian speakers often hear English t and d as retroflex. Our respellings can't show this difference with plain letters, so when the book writes TH for a soft dental sound (as in Tamil, THUH-mizh), it does not mean the English "th" in "think". Listen to a speaker to catch it.

docs.title: Aspirated sounds: bh, kh, gh, ph, th, dh, chh
docs.text:
Hold your hand in front of your mouth and say "pin", then "spin". You'll feel a puff of air after the p in "pin" but not in "spin". In English that puff doesn't change meaning. In Hindi-Urdu, Bangla, Punjabi, Nepali and many other languages, it does. Writers mark the puff with an h after the consonant:

  • bh in bhangra or Bangla bhat (rice): a b with a puff of air, not a "b" and then an "h" sound.
  • kh in Dzongkha: a k with a puff, not the throaty sound in German "Bach".
  • ph is a p with a puff, not an f.

One exception: in Urdu, Pashto and Dari words, gh (as in ghazal) and kh can be throaty sounds made far back in the mouth, a little like gargling softly. The script tells you which one it is, which is a good reason to learn to recognize scripts.

docs.title: Nasal vowels
docs.text:
Some vowels are said partly through the nose, like the vowel in French "bon". Devanagari marks this with a small dot or moon-and-dot above the letter (ं or ँ). You can hear it at the end of Nepali दशैं (Dashain) and in Hindi मेहँदी (mehndi, henna). Our respellings show it with an n, but don't press your tongue down for a full "n" sound. Let the vowel hum through your nose instead.

Ask a real speaker

Every respelling in this book is approximate, and many words sound different from region to region and family to family. The best way to learn a word is to ask someone who grew up saying it. Most people are happy to be asked, and you'll learn far more than any table can teach.

docs.title: A.5 Where to Hear Words Said Aloud
docs.text:
Reading a respelling is a good start, but hearing a word is better. Try these, in this order:

  1. Someone you know. A parent, grandparent, classmate or club member who speaks the language.
  2. A community place. Volunteers at a temple, mosque, gurdwara, vihara or cultural center often teach greetings and festival words.
  3. Online dictionaries with audio. Many Wiktionary entries include recordings by native speakers. Check that the recording is labeled with the language you want, since the same spelling can belong to several languages.

If two speakers say a word differently, both may be right. Accents and dialects are part of what makes these languages alive.

docs.text:
1. What Is South Asia?: Meet the eight countries of South Asia and the mountains, rivers, plains, seas and monsoon that shape where about 2 billion people live. (Quiz · References)
  2. Ancient Roots: From the first farmers at Mehrgarh to the Indus cities, the Vedas, the Buddha, Ashoka and the Guptas: South Asia from about 7000 BCE to 550 CE. (Quiz · References)
  3. Empires and Encounters: Trace the kingdoms, empires, faiths and traders of South Asia from about 600 to 1800, and see how many powers lived side by side. (Quiz · References)
  4. Colonialism, Independence, and Partition: How British rule spread across South Asia, how people organized for freedom, and how one colony became India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. (Quiz · References)
  5. Faiths of South Asia: Meet the faiths of South Asia, from Hinduism, Islam and Buddhism to Sikhism, Jainism, Christianity, Parsis and Jewish communities, and compare them fairly. (Quiz · References)
  6. Languages and Scripts: Meet South Asia's language families and scripts, learn how an abugida works, and see why Hindi, Bangla and Tamil letters are cousins. (Quiz · References)

docs.title: Part 2: Living Culture
docs.text:
1. Festivals Through the Year: Why Diwali, Eid, Vaisakhi and other South Asian festivals land when they do: solar, lunar and lunisolar calendars, and how each festival is celebrated. (Quiz · References)
  2. Food and the Table: Explore how grain, climate, trade and faith shape what people eat across South Asia, from the thali and dal to biryani, chai, street food and hospitality. (Quiz · References)
  3. Music: Learn how raga and tala work, compare Hindustani and Carnatic music, and hear qawwali, ghazal, Baul, folk, bhangra and film songs across South Asia. (Quiz · References)
  4. Dance and Theater: Meet South Asia's classical dances, folk dances, theater and shadow puppets, and learn the hand gestures and emotions that let dancers tell stories. (Quiz · References)
  5. Art, Architecture, and Craft: Stupas, temples, Mughal tombs, miniature paintings, thangkas, kolam, mehndi, block prints, truck art and rickshaw art across South Asia. (Quiz · References)
  6. Clothing and Textiles: Cotton, silk and pashmina, the weaves and prints of eight countries, and the sarees, kurtas, ghos, turbans and bangles people wear today. (Quiz · References)
  7. Family, Names, and Life Events: Kinship words, joint families, names, caste and the law, and the rituals that mark birth, growing up, marriage and death across South Asia. (Quiz · References)
  8. Stories and Literature: Epics, fables, poets and novels from across South Asia, and how the same stories travel and change across languages, faiths and borders. (Quiz · References)
  9. Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture: Bollywood and the many other film industries of South Asia, playback singers, dramas, Coke Studio, global stars, and cricket, hockey, kabaddi and carrom. (Quiz · References)
  10. Science, Math, and Ideas: How zero and place value grew in South Asia and traveled the world, plus grammar, healing traditions, chess, steel and modern scientists. (Quiz · References)

docs.title: Part 3: The Eight Countries
docs.text:
1. India: Tour the Republic of India: its constitution, elections, 28 states and 8 union territories, languages, peoples, symbols, economy and space program. (Quiz · References)
  2. Pakistan and Afghanistan: Tour Pakistan's provinces and languages and Afghanistan's land, peoples and heritage, and follow the Khyber road that has linked them for centuries. (Quiz · References)
  3. Bangladesh and Sri Lanka: Tour Bangladesh's river delta, mangroves, language movement and garment economy, and Sri Lanka's island heritage, peoples, tea and recent history. (Quiz · References)
  4. Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives: Tour three small South Asian nations, from Everest and Himalayan dzongs to coral atolls barely above the sea, and see how altitude and water shape life. (Quiz · References)

docs.title: Part 4: Here and Now
docs.text:
1. The South Asian Diaspora: Follow South Asians to the Caribbean, East Africa, Britain, the Gulf and the US, including Minnesota, and learn why each wave of migration happened. (Quiz · References)
  2. Bring It Home: Identity, stereotypes, appreciation and allyship, then the oral history method and how a student club can turn stories into community action. (Quiz · References)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asia is a region of eight countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Together they were home to about 1.99 billion people in 2025, roughly one in four people on Earth. This chapter explains the difference between a region, a subcontinent and a country, then tours the land itself: the mountain walls in the north, the three great rivers, the plains, plateau, desert and coasts, and the monsoon that brings most of the year's rain. By the end you'll be able to find all eight countries on a map and explain why so many people live where they do.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
None, just curiosity. It helps to know north, south, east and west on a map, and that's all.

Welcome to Roots & Rivers!

Hi, I'm Mora! If your family is from South Asia, people have probably asked you "So where are you really from?" and expected a one-word answer. This chapter gives you the map you need to answer that question your own way, and it helps your friends ask better questions too. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 1.1 "Wait, Isn't Bangladesh Part of India?"
docs.text:
It's a Tuesday after school, and Zara Hossain and Ben Lindqvist are sitting in Ms. Okafor's classroom at Prairie Ridge High School. Zara is co-founding the school's South Asian Student Association, and the first meeting is in two weeks. Ben, her best friend since fourth grade, has already signed up as the club's first member who isn't South Asian. Ms. Okafor, their faculty advisor, has asked them for one thing: a single slide that answers "What counts as South Asia?"

Ben is typing notes. "Okay, so your parents are from Bangladesh. That's part of India, right? Like a state?"

Zara opens her mouth to say no, then stops. She knows Bangladesh is its own country. Her parents grew up in Chattogram, a port city in Bangladesh, and her Nanu (her mother's mother) still tells stories about it at dinner. But Zara has also heard her uncle say "the subcontinent," and her cousin in London say "South Asian," and a relative call everyone from that part of the world "desi." She realizes she can't explain the difference between a country, a subcontinent and a region. If the words themselves are confusing, how is one slide supposed to clear them up? This chapter is that slide, in long form.

docs.title: 1.2 Region, Subcontinent, Country: Three Different Words
docs.text:
Ben already knows this idea from his own family. His family's roots are in Sweden and Norway, two separate countries, each with its own government, flag and laws. People also talk about "Scandinavia," a region that groups those countries (and usually Denmark) because they share some history and culture. Nobody thinks Norway is "part of Sweden" just because both are in Scandinavia.

South Asia works the same way.

  • A country is a political unit with its own government and borders. India is a country. So is Bangladesh.
  • A region is a group of places that people choose to talk about together, because of geography, history, culture or politics. Regions don't have governments.
  • A continent is one of the very large landmasses, like Asia or Africa. A subcontinent is a large, distinct part of a continent.

South Asia is the region in the south of the Asian continent made up of eight countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, the members of SAARC (Section 1.3). It's a geographic and political label, and it doesn't put any one country at the center.

The Indian Subcontinent is an older, more physical term for the big wedge of land south of the Himalaya that pushes out into the Indian Ocean, between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. It sits on its own tectonic plate (Section 1.5). Today that wedge is divided mainly among India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, with Nepal and Bhutan along its northern edge and Sri Lanka just off its tip. Afghanistan is usually not counted as part of the subcontinent. In short, "subcontinent" describes the land, and "South Asia" describes a group of countries.

Term What kind of thing What it includes Who often uses it South Asia A region of countries Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka Governments, the World Bank, the United Nations, most universities in North America Indian Subcontinent A physical landmass The land south of the Himalaya: mainly India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, plus Nepal and Bhutan; Sri Lanka is often included Geologists, historians, many people in the UK and in South Asian families India A country One country, with 28 states and several union territories Everyone, for that one country

Why "Indian"? For centuries, outsiders used "India" to mean the whole land around and beyond the Indus River, and historians still sometimes write "India" for the whole subcontinent before 1947. Since 1947, though, India has been the name of one modern country. That's why many people prefer "South Asia" for the region: it doesn't make one country's name stand for everyone.

Try this

Notice how Zara's family uses its own word for home. In Bangla, দেশ (DAYSH), "desh," means "country" or "homeland," and the word is even inside the name Bangladesh. When your family says "back home," which do they mean: a village, a city, a country or a region?

docs.title: 1.3 Eight Countries and SAARC
docs.text:
So which countries count? The answer most governments and researchers use comes from a regional organization.

SAARC, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, is a group the countries of the region set up to work together on trade, health, education and culture. It was founded in Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, on 8 December 1985 by seven countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Afghanistan joined as the eighth member in 2007. SAARC's secretariat (its main office) is in Kathmandu, Nepal. SAARC's leaders last met for a full summit in Nepal in 2014. The next summit, planned for Pakistan in 2016, was postponed and, as of October 2026, has not been held. Even so, "the SAARC countries" is still the most common way to define South Asia.

Here are the eight countries, listed alphabetically. Population numbers are for 2025 from the World Bank.

Country Capital Population (2025, World Bank) Main language(s) Afghanistan Kabul 43,844,111 (about 44 million) Pashto and Dari Bangladesh Dhaka 175,686,899 (about 176 million) Bangla (Bengali) Bhutan Thimphu 796,682 (about 800,000) Dzongkha India New Delhi 1,463,865,525 (about 1.46 billion) Hindi and English are official; 22 languages are listed in the Constitution's Eighth Schedule Maldives Malé 529,676 (about 530,000) Dhivehi Nepal Kathmandu 29,618,118 (about 30 million) Nepali Pakistan Islamabad 255,219,554 (about 255 million) Urdu (national language) and English (official); Punjabi, Pashto, Sindhi, Saraiki, Balochi and others are widely spoken Sri Lanka Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte (legislative) and Colombo (executive) 21,756,000 (about 22 million) Sinhala and Tamil

The sizes are very uneven: India alone has more people than the other seven countries put together. The "main language" column also hides a lot. India's Constitution lists 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule, from Assamese to Urdu, and many more are spoken across the region. You'll meet them in Chapter 6. And two of the eight, Sri Lanka and the Maldives, are island countries.

Some lists differ a little. Afghanistan is sometimes grouped with Central Asia instead, and Myanmar or Tibet are occasionally included. This book follows the SAARC list of eight, which is the most widely used.

Whose Story?

Even the name of the region depends on who is talking. "The Indian subcontinent" became common in the British Empire in the early 1900s and is still widely used in Britain and in India, where many writers like it because it points to the culture the region shares. Many people in Pakistan and Bangladesh, which became separate countries in 1947 and 1971, find the phrase uncomfortable because it puts India's name on everyone, and they usually say "South Asia," as historians increasingly do. Afghans may describe their country as part of Central Asia, South Asia or both. Even international bodies differ: since mid-2025 the World Bank groups Afghanistan and Pakistan with the Middle East and North Africa in its regional statistics, though both remain SAARC members.

docs.title: 1.4 How Many People Live in South Asia?
docs.text:
The Population of South Asia is the total number of people living in its eight countries. Add up the 2025 World Bank numbers from the table and you get about 1.99 billion people (2025, World Bank). The whole world had about 8.2 billion people that year, so South Asia was home to roughly one in four people on Earth.

In 2025 India was the most populous country in the world, ahead of China, and Pakistan and Bangladesh were both among the ten most populous countries on Earth (World Bank).

Here's how the total breaks down.

Country Share of South Asia's 2025 population (approximate) India about 73.5% Pakistan about 12.8% Bangladesh about 8.8% Afghanistan about 2.2% Nepal about 1.5% Sri Lanka about 1.1% Bhutan about 0.04% Maldives about 0.03%

Watch out for this number trap

If you look up "South Asia population" on the World Bank website, you'll get a smaller number than 1.99 billion. That's because the World Bank's own "South Asia" group now leaves out Afghanistan and Pakistan, so always check which countries a total includes.

Why do so many people live here? Part of the answer is history: farming villages and cities have existed in the region for thousands of years (that's Chapter 2). But a big part of the answer is the land and water you're about to meet. Rich river soil, warm weather and a dependable rainy season make it possible to grow a lot of food, and food supports large populations.

docs.title: 1.5 The Mountain Walls: Himalaya and Hindu Kush
docs.text: Look at any physical map of Asia and you'll see South Asia's northern edge drawn in dark brown. That's a wall of the highest mountains on Earth.

docs.title: The Himalaya
docs.text:
The Himalaya (हिमालय, hi-MAA-lay, "abode of snow") is the mountain range that separates the plains of the subcontinent from the high Tibetan Plateau to the north. The name comes from Sanskrit: hima means frost or snow, and ālaya means dwelling or home. You'll also see it written "the Himalayas," with an s. Both are correct.

Some key facts:

  • The range curves in an arc about 2,400 km (1,500 miles) long, running from west-northwest to east-southeast.
  • It holds more than 100 peaks taller than 7,200 m (23,600 ft), including the highest mountain on Earth.
  • That mountain is Mount Everest, 8,848.86 m (29,031.7 ft) tall, according to a joint measurement by China and Nepal in 2020. Its summit sits on the border between Nepal and China. In Nepali it is called Sagarmatha.
  • The Himalaya spans five countries: Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. So it is not "in" any single country.

How did mountains this tall form? Through a very slow crash. About 80 million years ago, the land that is now the subcontinent was a separate piece of Earth's crust (a tectonic plate) sitting roughly 6,400 km south of Asia. It drifted north. Somewhere between 40 and 50 million years ago, it ran into the Eurasian plate. The crust crumpled and piled upward, and according to the US Geological Survey, the Himalaya is still rising by more than 1 cm a year. That's why it makes sense to think of the subcontinent as a distinct piece of Asia. It really did arrive as its own piece of land.

The mountains matter for people in two big ways. They block the cold air of Central Asia from blowing south, and their snow and glaciers feed the region's largest rivers. Many Himalayan peaks are also sacred in Hindu and Buddhist traditions.

A disputed area

The western end of the Himalaya runs through Kashmir, a region whose control is disputed among India, Pakistan and China, and each country has its own position on where its borders lie. That's one reason the maps in this book are schematic and never draw official borders.

docs.title: The Hindu Kush
docs.text:
West of the Himalaya, another range takes over. The Hindu Kush is a mountain range about 800 km (500 miles) long that stretches from central and eastern Afghanistan into northwestern Pakistan, with a small piece in far southeastern Tajikistan. Its highest peak is Tirich Mir, 7,708 m (25,289 ft), in the Chitral District of Pakistan. It is the highest mountain anywhere outside the Himalaya and Karakoram ranges.

The Hindu Kush has been both a wall and a doorway, with routes that carried traders, travelers and armies between Central Asia and South Asia. Buddhism was once widespread in its valleys, and the giant Buddha statues carved into the cliffs at Bamiyan, in Afghanistan, stood until they were destroyed in 2001. Today most people in the region are Muslim.

docs.title: 1.6 Three Great Rivers
docs.text: Mountains collect snow, the snow melts into rivers, and the rivers carry soil down to the plains. That chain is the reason so many people live in South Asia. Three rivers matter most.

docs.title: The Indus
docs.text:
The Indus River is about 3,180 km (1,980 miles) long. It begins on the Tibetan Plateau in China, flows northwest through the disputed Kashmir region (first through Indian-administered Ladakh, then Pakistani-administered Gilgit-Baltistan), then turns south and runs the full length of Pakistan before emptying into the Arabian Sea near Karachi. Along the way it collects five big tributaries in the Punjab: the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. The name Punjab means "land of five rivers."

Most of Pakistan's farming depends on the Indus. It's also the river that gave the whole subcontinent its outside name. Its old Sanskrit name is Sindhu, and through Old Persian and Greek that name became the English words "Indus" and "India," as well as "Hindustan," "land of the Indus." And it was along the Indus and its neighbors that one of the world's earliest city civilizations grew, a story for Chapter 2.

docs.title: The Ganges (Ganga)
docs.text:
The Ganges (Ganga) River is about 2,525 km (1,569 miles) long. In India it is called the Ganga (गंगा, GUNG-gaa), and in Bangladesh it is called the Padma. It rises in the western Himalaya in the Indian state of Uttarakhand, flows east across the northern plains of India, picks up major tributaries such as the Yamuna and several rivers coming down from Nepal, then crosses into Bangladesh.

Hundreds of millions of people depend on the Ganga, and many big cities stand on it or its connected rivers, including Varanasi, Patna, Kolkata and Dhaka. In Hinduism the Ganga is worshipped as a goddess, and many Hindus bathe in it as an act of devotion. You'll learn more in Chapter 5.

docs.title: The Brahmaputra
docs.text: The Brahmaputra River is about 3,000 km (1,900 miles) long. It begins in Tibet near Mount Kailash, where it's called the Yarlung Tsangpo, and flows east along the north side of the Himalaya. Then it turns and cuts south through the mountains in deep gorges, enters India in the state of Arunachal Pradesh, flows west through the Assam Valley, and turns south into Bangladesh, where it is called the Jamuna. It is a braided river, which means it splits into many shifting channels, and it floods often, especially when Himalayan snow melts.

docs.title: Where the rivers meet
docs.text:
In Bangladesh, the Padma (Ganga) and the Jamuna (Brahmaputra) join, then merge with the Meghna River and pour into the Bay of Bengal. Together they built the Ganges Delta, also called the Bengal Delta, which is the largest river delta in the world. It covers most of Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal. At its edge on the sea is the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world, shared by Bangladesh and India. The Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna system carries so much water that only two river systems on Earth, the Amazon and the Congo, pour more fresh water into the sea.

That's the land Zara's family comes from: wet, green, flat, crossed by rivers, and shaped by them.

River Approx. length Starts in Flows through Ends in Other names Indus 3,180 km Tibet (China) Kashmir region, Pakistan Arabian Sea Sengge Zangbo (in Tibet) Ganges (Ganga) 2,525 km Uttarakhand, India India, Bangladesh Bay of Bengal Padma (in Bangladesh) Brahmaputra 3,000 km Tibet (China) China, India, Bangladesh Bay of Bengal (through the delta) Yarlung Tsangpo, Jamuna

docs.title: 1.7 Plains, Plateau, Ghats and Desert
docs.text: Between the mountains and the sea, the land changes a lot. Four landforms explain most of the map.

docs.title: The Indo-Gangetic Plain
docs.text:
The Indo-Gangetic Plain is the huge, flat, fertile lowland that stretches across the north of the subcontinent, from Pakistan in the west, through northern India and southern Nepal, to almost all of Bangladesh in the east. It covers about 700,000 square km (270,000 square miles). It's named for the two river systems that drain it, the Indus and the Ganga.

The rivers built the plain themselves. Flood after flood, they spread fine mud called alluvium, so the plain is one of the largest unbroken stretches of river soil anywhere. It's among the most densely populated and most intensely farmed places on Earth, home to many of the region's biggest cities: Lahore, Delhi, Lucknow, Patna, Kolkata and Dhaka all sit on or near it.

docs.title: The Deccan Plateau
docs.text:
South of the plain, the land rises. The Deccan Plateau is a large raised tableland that covers much of central and southern India, about 422,000 square km. Its average height is about 600 m (2,000 ft). The name Deccan comes from the Sanskrit word दक्षिण (DUK-shin), "south."

The plateau tilts gently from west to east, so most of its big rivers, such as the Godavari, the Krishna and the Kaveri, flow east and empty into the Bay of Bengal. The northwest part of the plateau is made of thick layers of dark volcanic rock called the Deccan Traps, laid down by enormous lava flows about 66 million years ago. Much of the land there has dark black soil. Because mountains on its western edge block rain, much of the Deccan is drier than the coasts, with a semi-arid climate.

docs.title: The Western and Eastern Ghats
docs.text:
The Western and Eastern Ghats are the two mountain ranges that frame the Deccan Plateau, one along each coast of peninsular India. Ghat comes from the Hindi word घाट (GHAAT), which means a flight of steps leading down to a river, or a mountain pass. These ranges are like giant steps from the plateau down to the sea.

  • The Western Ghats run about 1,600 km along India's west coast, from the state of Gujarat south through Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Kerala to Tamil Nadu. They form an almost continuous wall, with peaks over 2,000 m. The highest is Anamudi, 2,695 m. They catch the rain-bearing monsoon winds coming off the Arabian Sea, so their western slopes and the coast below them get very heavy rain, while the land behind them stays drier. The Western Ghats are also famous for their forests and wildlife.
  • The Eastern Ghats run about 1,750 km along the east coast, from Odisha through Andhra Pradesh and Telangana to Tamil Nadu. Unlike the Western Ghats, they are broken into separate hills, with many gaps where rivers cut through to the Bay of Bengal. They are lower, about 600 m on average, so they affect the weather less.

The two ranges meet in the Nilgiri Hills in the far south.

docs.title: The Thar Desert
docs.text:
In the northwest, where India meets Pakistan, the land turns to sand. The Thar Desert, also called the Great Indian Desert, is a dry region of sandy plains and low hills. About 85 percent of it lies in India, mostly in the state of Rajasthan, and the rest lies in Pakistan's Sindh and Punjab provinces. It gets most of its little rain from the summer monsoon, usually less than 500 mm (20 inches) a year. Summers are extremely hot and winters are cooler.

The Thar is a good reminder that South Asia isn't one climate. People have lived in the Thar for a very long time, getting by with herding and careful water storage, and the desert has its own traditions of music and craft that you'll meet in later chapters.

A quick way to remember the layout: walk south from Tibet and you step down from the Himalaya to the Indo-Gangetic Plain, up onto the Deccan Plateau, then down the Ghats to the coast, with desert to the northwest and delta to the northeast.

docs.title: 1.8 The Monsoon
docs.text: Ask South Asian grandparents about the weather back home, and there's a good chance the first word they say is "monsoon." It's the most important weather pattern in the region.

docs.title: What the word means
docs.text:
The English word monsoon comes from the Arabic word موسم (MAW-sim), mawsim, which means "season." Sailors crossing the Arabian Sea between Africa, Arabia and India learned long ago that the winds blew from the northeast for half the year and from the southwest for the rest, and they used that pattern for their voyages. Ocean trade depended on it, as you'll see in Chapter 3.

So a monsoon is, first of all, a wind that reverses direction with the seasons. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) describes it as winds along the Indian Ocean coasts that blow from the southwest for about half the year and from the northeast for the other half. In everyday speech, though, "the monsoon" usually means the rainy season that the southwest winds bring in summer. In Bangla, Zara's Nanu calls that season বর্ষা (BOR-sha), borsha, which means both "rain" and "the rainy season."

docs.title: How the summer monsoon works
docs.text:
You can feel the basic idea at a beach. On a hot day the sand gets hot fast, but the water stays cooler, because land heats up faster than water.

  1. In spring and early summer, the huge landmass of South Asia and the rest of Asia heats up much faster than the Indian Ocean.
  2. Hot air over the land rises, which lowers the air pressure there.
  3. Cooler, moist air from over the ocean flows in toward the land to fill the gap. In South Asia that wind blows from the southwest.
  4. As the moist air is pushed up over hills and mountains, such as the Western Ghats and later the Himalaya, it cools, and its water falls as rain.
  5. In winter the pattern flips. The land cools faster than the sea, and cool, dry winds blow outward from the land, from the northeast.

The Himalaya matters here too. It acts like a wall that stops the monsoon clouds from simply drifting away north, so they drop their rain on the plains and foothills.

docs.title: When it arrives
docs.text:
The southwest monsoon arrives on a fairly regular schedule. According to the IMD, it normally reaches the state of Kerala, at India's southwest tip, around 1 June, then moves north in surges and covers the whole of India around 8 July. Rain moves up the west coast from the Arabian Sea, while low-pressure systems that form over the Bay of Bengal carry heavy rain westward across the land. The monsoon begins to pull back from northwest India in September and has usually withdrawn from the country by October. Those are average dates, though. In any real year the monsoon can come early or late, and people watch the forecasts closely.

The amount of rain changes a lot from place to place. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, two towns in the hills of the Indian state of Meghalaya, just north of Bangladesh, trade places as the wettest spots on Earth. Meanwhile, the Thar Desert gets only a little. And Afghanistan sits mostly outside the monsoon zone altogether; most of its rain and snow falls in winter and spring.

Not all monsoon rain comes in summer, either. In the southeast of India, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh get rain from the northeast monsoon during the winter months, after the summer monsoon has left, when winds crossing the Bay of Bengal pick up moisture on the way.

It doesn't rain all day

"Monsoon season" doesn't mean nonstop rain. The monsoon comes in active spells of heavy rain and "break" spells of days with little rain, and many monsoon days mix sun, sticky heat and a big afternoon downpour.

docs.title: Why it matters so much
docs.text:
The southwest monsoon brings most of the year's rain to most of India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Many farms in the region don't have large irrigation systems, so they depend on the monsoon to water their crops, especially rice, and to refill wells and underground water for the rest of the year. A late or weak monsoon can hurt harvests and the whole economy. A very strong one can cause floods and landslides. The monsoon also feeds the rivers that power hydroelectric dams.

The monsoon shows up in songs, poems, foods and festivals too, and in a lot of family memories of the first rain of the season.

docs.title: 1.9 Water All Around: The Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean
docs.text:
South Asia's southern half is a peninsula, which means water on three sides. Two big bodies of water shape the coasts.

The Bay of Bengal is the northeastern part of the Indian Ocean, lying east of India and south of Bangladesh, with Myanmar on its eastern side and Sri Lanka at its southwestern edge. It covers about 2.2 million square km (about 840,000 square miles). Many of the subcontinent's biggest rivers flow into it, including the Ganga, the Brahmaputra, the Godavari, the Krishna and the Kaveri.

The bay's coasts include the Sundarbans mangrove forest and some of the longest natural beaches in the world, such as Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh and Marina Beach in Chennai, India. Severe cyclones also form over the bay, which is one reason coastal Bangladesh and eastern India plan so carefully for storms. Chattogram, where Zara's parents grew up, is Bangladesh's busiest port, right on the bay.

The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceans, covering about 70.6 million square km, or about 20% of the water on Earth's surface. It has Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east. It's also the warmest ocean, and monsoons shape the climate all around it. The Arabian Sea, to the west of India and south of Pakistan, and the Bay of Bengal are both arms of it.

Two of South Asia's countries sit out in this ocean:

  • Sri Lanka is a large island just south of India's tip, mostly flat to rolling coastal plains with mountains rising in the south-central part.
  • The Maldives is a chain of 1,192 small coral islands grouped into 26 atolls (rings of coral reef around a lagoon), stretched across the equator southwest of India and Sri Lanka. More than 80% of its islands sit less than 1 m above sea level, which makes the Maldives the lowest-lying country in the world and very vulnerable to rising seas.

For thousands of years the Indian Ocean worked more like a highway than a barrier, carrying ships, goods, faiths and languages between South Asia, Arabia, East Africa and Southeast Asia. Arab and Persian traders helped bring Islam to the Maldives in the 12th century.

docs.title: 1.10 Putting It Together: Regional Diversity
docs.text:
Regional Diversity is the idea that South Asia is not one place with one climate, one language, one faith or one way of life, but many different places shaped by different land, water and history. The geography you've just read about is one of the biggest reasons for that diversity.

Here's how different everyday life can be, depending on where you stand:

Place Country Landscape What shapes daily life Kabul Afghanistan High valley ringed by mountains Most rain and snow from December to April; dry summers; little monsoon rain Lahore Pakistan Indo-Gangetic Plain, Punjab Hot summers, monsoon rain from June to September, farming on river-fed land Kathmandu Nepal Valley in the Himalayan foothills Summer monsoon rains, mountains all around Chattogram Bangladesh Coast of the Bay of Bengal, near the delta Heavy monsoon rain, rivers and floods, port life, cyclone risk Jaisalmer India Thar Desert Little rain, extremely hot summers, careful water use Kandy Sri Lanka Central highlands Cooler than the coast, green and rainy Malé Maldives Low coral island Ocean on every side; fishing and tourism; sea-level rise

Each of those places has its own foods, clothes, building styles and festivals, and the land is one big reason why. In the chapters ahead, every time you meet a tradition, try asking: what about the land and weather made this make sense?

Geography isn't the only reason. History, trade, migration, faith and language add their own layers, as the rest of this book shows.

Back in Ms. Okafor's classroom, Zara and Ben finally finish the slide. At the top, in big letters: "South Asia = a region of 8 countries, about 2 billion people." Below that, a simple tile map with the Himalaya across the top, three rivers running down, and the monsoon arrow coming up from the southwest. At the bottom, Zara adds one line: "Bangladesh is not part of India. Both are part of South Asia." Ben reads it and grins. "Okay," he says. "Now I get why your Nanu talks about the rain so much."
