MicroSim specification: Region Explorer

sim-id: ch01-region-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will locate the eight countries of South Asia on a schematic map and explain how the mountains and the southwest monsoon shape where rain falls and where people live.

Canvas: responsive width; 620 px drawing area plus 80 px control area.

Controls: Start monsoon / Pause button, Reset button, country menu, "Show mountains, rivers and seas" checkbox; click or tap any country tile.

Behavior: Eight country tiles sit roughly in their geographic positions (no borders). Selecting a tile shows its capital, 2025 population (World Bank) and main languages. The monsoon starts paused; Start animates a shaded rain zone spreading from the southwest sea (late May) to all of India (about 8 July, IMD normal date), with a Bay of Bengal branch. Most of Afghanistan and the far north stay dry. The caption "Schematic map, not to scale. Not an official depiction of borders." is drawn inside the drawing area.

Start by clicking each of the eight tiles and reading the panel. Which country has the most people? Which have the fewest? Then untick the checkbox to hide the labels and see if you can still name the Himalaya, the Hindu Kush, the two Ghats and the three rivers.

Next, press Start monsoon and watch carefully. Pause when the date banner says the monsoon reaches Kerala, and again when the rain covers Bangladesh. Notice where the rain shows up first (the sea near Sri Lanka and India's southwest coast), how the rain reaches Bangladesh from the Bay of Bengal side, and which country stays almost completely dry. Then compare the rainy areas with the places you know are crowded, like the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the delta. The map is simplified, so the exact edges aren't precise, but the pattern is real.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about where your family comes from: the village, town or city, the river or region nearby, what the land and weather were like, and what the monsoon meant to them. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Bring a printed or phone map of South Asia and ask them to point to the place they grew up. Ask if it's okay to take notes.

Questions to ask

  1. Where did you grow up? What was the nearest river, mountain, desert or sea?
  2. What did the place look like out your window or on your walk to school?
  3. What was the weather like through the year? Which season did you like most, and why?
  4. When the first monsoon rain came (or the first big rain of the year), what did people do? Was there a smell, a food, a song or a game you remember?
  5. How has that place changed since you were young, or since you moved away? Do you know what the weather is like there now?
  6. If I visit one day, what is the one thing about the land or the weather there that you'd want me to see or feel?

Listen for: names of rivers or mountains (is it near the Indus River, the Ganges (Ganga) River or the Brahmaputra River, or the Himalaya?), stories about the Monsoon, and details that show Regional Diversity, such as how different their home was from another relative's.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare your elder's description of the weather back home with what this chapter says about the monsoon in that part of South Asia. Did the monsoon arrive when the IMD's normal dates say it should? If a friend interviewed someone from a different country or region, list two ways the landscapes and seasons they describe were different.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: South Asia is just another name for India. Reality: South Asia is a region of eight countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. India is the largest by far, but Bangladesh, Pakistan and the others are separate, independent countries with their own governments, languages and histories.

Myth: The Himalaya is in Nepal (or in India). Reality: The Himalaya stretches about 2,400 km across five countries: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan and China. Mount Everest itself sits on the Nepal-China border.

Myth: Monsoon means it rains all day, every day for months. Reality: A monsoon is a seasonal shift in wind direction. The summer monsoon brings a rainy season, but rain comes in active spells and break spells, and many monsoon days include sun and heat between heavy showers.

Myth: All of South Asia is hot all the time. Reality: The region includes snowy Himalayan peaks, cold, dry high valleys on the northern side of the western Himalaya, and Sri Lanka's central highlands, where frost can occur on some winter nights, as well as hot plains, deserts and tropical coasts. Climate depends a lot on height and distance from the sea.

Myth: The "Indian subcontinent" and "India" mean the same thing. Reality: "Indian subcontinent" is a geographic term for the landmass south of the Himalaya, which today includes several countries. "India" is the name of one modern country since 1947. That's why many people prefer the term "South Asia" for the region.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. Name the eight countries of South Asia.

Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. They are the eight members of SAARC.

2. What is the difference between a region and a country?

A country has its own government, borders and laws. A region is a group of places people talk about together because of geography, history or culture; it has no government of its own.

3. About how many people lived in South Asia in 2025, and what share of the world is that?

About 1.99 billion people (2025, World Bank), roughly one in four people on Earth.

4. Which two rivers join in Bangladesh to form the world's largest delta, and what are they called there?

The Ganga (called the Padma in Bangladesh) and the Brahmaputra (called the Jamuna). They join and flow with the Meghna into the Bay of Bengal.

5. Why does the summer monsoon blow from the southwest?

In early summer the land heats up faster than the Indian Ocean. Hot air rises over the land, and cooler, moist air from the ocean to the southwest flows in to replace it, bringing rain.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the capitals of Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal and Pakistan.

    Answer

    Bangladesh: Dhaka. Bhutan: Thimphu. Nepal: Kathmandu. Pakistan: Islamabad.

  2. In what city and year was SAARC founded, and which country joined later?

    Answer

    SAARC was founded in Dhaka on 8 December 1985 by seven countries. Afghanistan joined as the eighth member in 2007.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain in your own words why the land south of the Himalaya can be called a "subcontinent."

    Answer

    The land that is now the subcontinent sits on its own tectonic plate. It drifted north for millions of years and collided with Asia between about 40 and 50 million years ago, pushing up the Himalaya. It is a distinct piece of the Asian continent.

  2. Explain why the Deccan Plateau is drier than the coast of Kerala, even though both are in southern India.

    Answer

    The Western Ghats stand between the Arabian Sea and the plateau. Monsoon winds rise over the Ghats and drop much of their rain on the western slopes and the coast, so the plateau behind them gets less.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Region Explorer. Pause the monsoon on 15 June. Which countries are getting rain on that date, and which are not? Write two sentences explaining the pattern. Hint: think about where the monsoon starts and which way it moves.

  2. A family member says they grew up "near the Jamuna, in the north of the country." Using this chapter, figure out which country and which big river they mean, and where that river starts. Hint: rivers can have different names in different countries.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Thar Desert. Using at least three facts from the chapter, explain why one supports so many more people than the other. Hint: think about water, soil and rain.

  2. The World Bank's "South Asia" total is smaller than the eight-country total in this chapter. Analyze why the two numbers differ and why it matters to check the definition behind any statistic. Hint: which countries are in each group?

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Some people prefer "South Asia" and others prefer "the Indian subcontinent." Which term would you use on your club's slide, and why? Consider who will be in the room. Hint: the Whose Story? box gives several points of view.

  2. Your friend says, "The monsoon is just bad weather." Evaluate this claim using evidence about farming, water supply, floods and culture from the chapter. Hint: a fair answer looks at both benefits and dangers.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design your own one-slide answer to "What counts as South Asia?" for a club meeting. Include a schematic map (no official borders), the eight countries, one population fact with its year and source, and one fact about land or weather. Hint: keep it to what fits on a single slide.

  2. Write a short postcard (100 to 150 words) from someone living in one of the places in the Regional Diversity table in 1.10, describing their weather and landscape during the monsoon season. Hint: use at least two concept words from this chapter.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• South Asia is a region of eight countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, the members of SAARC.
  • "Indian Subcontinent" describes the landmass south of the Himalaya; "South Asia" describes the group of countries. Many people prefer "South Asia" because it doesn't center one country.
  • About 1.99 billion people lived in South Asia in 2025 (World Bank), roughly one in four people on Earth.
  • The Himalaya and Hindu Kush form the region's northern mountain walls. The Himalaya spans five countries and was pushed up when the subcontinent's plate collided with Asia.
  • The Indus, the Ganges (Ganga) and the Brahmaputra carry snowmelt and soil to the plains; the Ganga and Brahmaputra build the world's largest delta in Bangladesh and India.
  • The southwest monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers India by about 8 July, bringing most of the year's rain to much of the region, but not to most of Afghanistan.
  • Mountains, plains, plateau, desert, delta and islands help explain South Asia's regional diversity in food, dress, buildings and ways of life.

You've got the map!

You can now find all eight countries and explain why rivers and rain matter so much here. Next, in Chapter 2, we travel back thousands of years to the cities that grew up along the Indus.

docs.title: Quiz: What Is South Asia?
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 1. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which list contains only countries that are part of South Asia as defined by SAARC?

  1. India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka
  2. Afghanistan, Bhutan, Maldives, Pakistan
  3. Bangladesh, Tibet, Bhutan, India
  4. Pakistan, Iran, Nepal, Sri Lanka
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Afghanistan, Bhutan, the Maldives and Pakistan are all among SAARC's eight members. Myanmar and Tibet are sometimes mentioned as border zones, but they are not SAARC members, and Iran is not part of South Asia.

Concept Tested: SAARC Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
About how many people lived in the eight countries of South Asia in 2025, according to the World Bank?

  1. About 500 million
  2. About 1.46 billion
  3. About 8.2 billion
  4. About 1.99 billion
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The eight countries together had about 1.99 billion people in 2025, roughly one in four people on Earth. About 1.46 billion is India's population alone (a common mix-up), and 8.2 billion is the whole world.

Concept Tested: Population of South Asia Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which body of water receives the combined flow of the Ganga and the Brahmaputra?

  1. The Bay of Bengal
  2. The Arabian Sea
  3. The Red Sea
  4. The Caspian Sea
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The Ganga (Padma) and the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) join in Bangladesh, flow with the Meghna, and empty into the Bay of Bengal through the world's largest delta. The Arabian Sea is where the Indus ends, on the other side of the subcontinent.

Concept Tested: Bay of Bengal Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
What is the best explanation of the difference between "South Asia" and the "Indian subcontinent"?

  1. They are two names for the country of India.
  2. South Asia is only the island countries, while the subcontinent is the mainland.
  3. South Asia is a group of eight countries; the subcontinent is a physical landmass south of the Himalaya.
  4. The subcontinent includes Afghanistan, but South Asia does not.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. "South Asia" names a region made up of eight countries, while "Indian subcontinent" is a geographic term for the landmass on its own tectonic plate. Option D has it backward: Afghanistan is usually counted in South Asia but not in the subcontinent.

Concept Tested: Indian Subcontinent Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why does the summer monsoon blow from the southwest toward South Asia?

  1. The Himalaya pushes air south in summer.
  2. The land heats up faster than the Indian Ocean, so moist ocean air flows in toward the warm land.
  3. The ocean is hotter than the land in summer, so air flows out to sea.
  4. Winds from Central Asia carry rain over the mountains.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In early summer the land warms faster than the ocean, air rises over the land, and cooler, moist air from the Indian Ocean flows in from the southwest, bringing rain. Option C reverses the pattern, which is closer to what happens in winter.

Concept Tested: Monsoon Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why is the Indo-Gangetic Plain one of the most densely populated places on Earth?

  1. Its rivers spread fertile alluvium, and water from Himalayan rivers supports large-scale farming.
  2. It is the highest and coolest part of the region.
  3. It is a desert with large oil reserves.
  4. It is an island chain with many ports.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra built the plain from river soil, and their water makes intense farming possible, which supports huge populations. Option B describes the Himalaya, not the plain.

Concept Tested: Indo-Gangetic Plain Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Ayesha's family is from Lahore, Pakistan, and Nima's family is from Solukhumbu, Nepal. Ben says, "So they both live near the Himalaya, which is in Nepal." Which response best corrects Ben?

  1. "The Himalaya is only in India."
  2. "Lahore is on the Deccan Plateau, far from any mountains."
  3. "Nepal has no mountains; they're all in Pakistan."
  4. "The Himalaya stretches across five countries, including Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan and China, so it isn't in just one country."
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Himalaya spans Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan and China, about 2,400 km in all. Option B is wrong because Lahore is on the Indo-Gangetic Plain in Punjab, and the Deccan Plateau is in central and southern India.

Concept Tested: Himalaya Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Zara's cousin in Dhaka is planning a June trip to visit family in India and asks Zara when the rains start there. Using the chapter, where does the southwest monsoon normally arrive on mainland India first, and around what date?

  1. Delhi, around 1 May
  2. Kerala, around 1 June
  3. Kabul, around 1 July
  4. The Thar Desert, around 15 June
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The India Meteorological Department's normal onset date over Kerala, at India's southwest tip, is around 1 June. The monsoon then covers all of India around 8 July. Kabul is wrong because Afghanistan lies mostly outside the monsoon zone.

Concept Tested: Monsoon Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
The Deccan Plateau is drier than the Kerala coast, even though both are in southern India. What is the best explanation?

  1. The Deccan is closer to the Thar Desert.
  2. The Eastern Ghats block all rain from the Bay of Bengal.
  3. The Western Ghats catch the monsoon winds from the Arabian Sea, so much of the rain falls on the coast side before the air reaches the plateau.
  4. The Deccan is at sea level, and rain only falls on mountains.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Monsoon winds rise over the Western Ghats and drop much of their rain on the western slopes and coast, leaving the plateau behind them drier. Option B can look right, but the Eastern Ghats are low and broken, so they affect the weather much less.

Concept Tested: Western and Eastern Ghats Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
A club member finds a website that lists South Asia's population as about 1.69 billion for 2025, not 1.99 billion. What is the most likely reason for the difference?

  1. The website is counting a different set of countries; the World Bank's own "South Asia" group now leaves out Afghanistan and Pakistan.
  2. The population of South Asia fell by 300 million people in one year.
  3. The website forgot to count India.
  4. The smaller number counts only people who speak Hindi.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Since mid-2025 the World Bank groups Afghanistan and Pakistan with the Middle East and North Africa, so its "South Asia" total covers only six countries. Leaving out India (option C) would make the number far smaller, about 0.5 billion.

Concept Tested: Population of South Asia Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: What Is South Asia?
docs.text:
1. Population, total (SP.POP.TOTL) - World Bank Open Data - The source for every 2025 population number in this chapter. You can look up any of the eight countries yourself and see how their populations have changed since 1960.

  2. World Bank Country and Lending Groups - World Bank Data Help Desk - Lists which countries the World Bank puts in each region. It shows why the World Bank's "South Asia" total is smaller than the eight-country total: Afghanistan and Pakistan are now in its "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan" group.

  3. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on Monsoon - India Meteorological Department - The official explanation of how monsoon rainfall is measured, what "normal" means, active and break spells, and the normal dates when the monsoon reaches Kerala (around 1 June) and covers India (around 8 July).

  4. Winds Connect Snow to Sea - NASA Earth Observatory (Rebecca Lindsey) - A clear, illustrated explanation of how uneven heating of land and ocean drives the Asian monsoon, and how snow cover can affect its strength.

  5. Monsoon - National Geographic Education - A short encyclopedia entry on what a monsoon is, how the South Asian summer and winter monsoons differ, and why farmers depend on the summer rains.

  6. The Himalayas - US Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth - Explains how the subcontinent's plate drifted north and collided with Asia about 40 to 50 million years ago, and why the Himalaya is still rising.

  7. Eighth Schedule: Languages - Constitution of India (constitutionofindia.net) - The full list of the 22 languages recognized in India's Constitution, with a note on how the list grew from 14 in 1949.

  8. Indian subcontinent - Wikipedia - A useful starting point on the history of the terms "Indian subcontinent" and "South Asia," with links to the scholarly sources behind the naming debate.

  9. Monsoon of South Asia - Wikipedia - An overview of how the southwest and northeast monsoons work, the role of the Western Ghats and Himalaya, and the monsoon's effects on farming. Use it to find primary sources such as IMD reports.

  10. South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation - Wikipedia - Background on SAARC's founding in Dhaka in 1985, Afghanistan's entry in 2007, its secretariat in Kathmandu, and its summits. Follow its citations to official SAARC documents.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter follows South Asia's long story from the farming village of Mehrgarh, about 7000 BCE, through the planned cities of the Indus Valley, the Vedic period and the birth of Buddhism and Jainism, to the empires of the Mauryas, Kushans and Guptas, ending around 550 CE. You will see what historians know for sure, what they still argue about, and why those arguments matter today. By the end you'll be able to put the major ancient periods in order and connect each one to real places across Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

docs.text:
1. Mehrgarh
  2. Indus Valley Civilization
  3. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
  4. Indus Script

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?, especially the Indus and Ganges (Ganga) rivers, the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Hindu Kush.

Welcome to the deep past!

The symbol on India's money, the wheel on its flag, the Sanskrit words in a wedding ceremony and the Buddha statue in your neighbor's garden all come from this chapter's time period. When people argue online about "who was here first," they are arguing about this history too. Knowing the real evidence helps you join those conversations calmly and fairly.

docs.title: 2.1 "Nobody Can Read It?"
docs.text:
It's the club's second planning meeting, and Ben Lindqvist is supposed to be making a sign-up sheet. Instead he's holding his phone out to Zara Hossain. "Look at this," he says. On the screen is a museum photo of a small square stone, about the size of a postage stamp. Carved into it is an animal that looks like a bull with one horn, and above it a short row of neat little symbols.

"It's a seal from Mohenjo-daro," Ben reads. "In Pakistan. About four thousand years old. People pressed it into clay, like a stamp." He scrolls. "It says the writing on it has never been deciphered." He looks up. "Wait. Nobody can read it? Like, nobody on Earth?"

Zara shakes her head slowly. Her Nanu talks about the old ruins in Bangladesh as if they were neighbors, so Zara knew South Asia was old. But she pictured "old" as a few kings and temples, not planned cities with writing that has stumped experts for a hundred years. "So how do we know anything about them?" she asks. "And what came after?" That is what this chapter is about: how we know what we know about ancient South Asia, from the first farmers to the end of the Gupta Empire.

docs.title: 2.2 How Do We Know? Clues from the Ground and from Memory
docs.text:
Think about how a detective works. There is no confession, so the detective reads small clues: a footprint, a receipt, a coffee cup. Historians of ancient South Asia work the same way. For the oldest periods, there are no books that anyone can read. The clues come from the ground.

Archaeology is the study of the human past through the things people left behind: buildings, tools, pots, beads, bones and seeds. Archaeologists dig carefully, layer by layer. The deeper layers are usually older. Scientists can measure the age of things like charcoal, seeds and bone using radiocarbon dating, which reads the slow, steady decay of a form of carbon. That gives a date range, not an exact year, which is why almost every date in this chapter has the word "about" in front of it.

For later periods there are words too: texts that were memorized and passed on by voice for centuries, then inscriptions carved in stone, coins with kings' names, and reports by travelers from Greece and China. Each kind of clue has limits. Pots can't tell you what people believed, and a king's inscription tells you what he wanted people to think. Good history uses all of them together.

A quick note on dates. BCE means "before the Common Era," and CE means "Common Era." They count the same years as BC and AD. When you count BCE dates, bigger numbers are further back in time, so 7000 BCE is older than 2600 BCE.

docs.title: 2.3 The First Farmers: Mehrgarh
docs.text:
Mehrgarh is an archaeological site on the Kachhi Plain in Balochistan, Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass, a gap in the hills that leads toward Afghanistan and Iran. It is one of the earliest known places in South Asia where people farmed and herded animals. French archaeologists Jean-François and Catherine Jarrige discovered it in 1974.

The first village at Mehrgarh is usually dated to about 7000 BCE. Its people grew wheat and barley and raised sheep, goats and cattle. They lived in houses made of mud brick and buried their dead with ornaments. Over thousands of years the village grew, and its people learned to make pottery and work copper.

Archaeology keeps changing, and Mehrgarh shows how. In 2025, a team led by the archaeologist Benjamin Mutin radiocarbon-dated tooth enamel from 23 of the oldest graves and got a much younger start, about 5200 to 4900 BCE (Scientific Reports, 2025). So the start of Mehrgarh is a live debate, but nobody disputes that it was a very early farming village.

There's one more surprising find. In 2006, scientists reported in the journal Nature that some teeth from Mehrgarh had tiny holes drilled in them while the people were still alive. It is some of the oldest known evidence of something like dentistry anywhere in the world (how old exactly depends on which Mehrgarh dates turn out to be right).

Mehrgarh matters because cities need food. Farming villages like it are the roots the region's first cities grew from.

docs.title: A civilization bigger than Egypt and Mesopotamia
docs.text:
The Indus Valley Civilization was a Bronze Age civilization that grew up along the Indus River and nearby rivers, mostly in what is now Pakistan and northwestern India, with outposts as far as northeastern Afghanistan. It is also called the Harappan Civilization, after Harappa, the first of its cities to be found. Its full city-building phase, which archaeologists call the Mature Harappan period, lasted from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Early Harappan towns go back to about 3300 BCE.

It was one of the world's three earliest civilizations, alongside Mesopotamia (in today's Iraq) and Egypt. Of the three, it covered by far the most land. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, its sites stretch from Sutkagen Dor near the Arabian Sea coast of Balochistan to Ropar at the foot of the Shimla Hills in India's Punjab, and as far east as the Yamuna River basin north of Delhi. A Harappan trading post, Shortugai, even sat on the Amu Darya (Oxus) River in northern Afghanistan. Of more than a thousand known sites, most were villages and small towns.

docs.title: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
docs.text:
Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are the two best-known cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, both in present-day Pakistan. Harappa, in Punjab, was identified as an ancient site in 1921. Mohenjo-daro, in Sindh, beside the Indus River, was identified in 1922. Other large cities include Dholavira and Rakhigarhi, both in India, and Ganeriwala in Pakistan's Cholistan Desert.

These cities stand out because they were planned so carefully. At Mohenjo-daro:

  • The streets meet at right angles, like a grid.
  • Most buildings were made of baked brick.
  • Many houses had a room for bathing, and waste water flowed into covered drains that ran along the main streets.
  • A large, watertight brick pool, now called the Great Bath, may have been used for ritual washing.
  • The city had a raised western area that archaeologists call the citadel, and a larger lower town.

UNESCO, which made the ruins of Mohenjo-daro a World Heritage Site in 1980, describes it as the best-preserved city in South Asia from the 3rd millennium BCE. The site covers about 240 hectares, and only about a third of it has been dug up since 1922. Britannica cites estimates of about 35,000 to 41,000 people at Mohenjo-daro and about 23,500 to 35,000 at Harappa, which would make them very large cities for their time.

Feature What archaeologists found What it suggests Grid streets Main streets crossing at right angles Planning by some kind of authority Standard weights Stone weights that follow the same system across a huge area Shared rules and well-organized trade Covered drains Brick drains along streets, fed by house bathrooms Care for cleanliness and public works Great Bath A watertight pool with steps at Mohenjo-daro Possibly ritual bathing; its exact use is unknown Seals Small stone stamps with animals and short inscriptions Trade, ownership marks, maybe religious symbols Few palaces or big temples No clear royal palace or royal tomb found Power may have been shared in ways we don't yet understand

Indus people grew wheat, barley, peas, sesame and some of the earliest known cotton, and Indus objects such as red carnelian beads have turned up as far away as Mesopotamia. A tiny bronze figure nicknamed the "Dancing Girl" and a stone bust nicknamed the "Priest-King" are two famous finds. Modern archaeologists invented both nicknames, and nobody knows who the figures really showed.

Spot the guess

Notice how many words in this section are labels that modern people made up: "Great Bath," "citadel," "Priest-King." When you read about the Indus cities, ask: is this something the evidence shows, or a guess dressed up as a name?

docs.title: Why did the cities fade?
docs.text: The big Indus cities did not end in one dramatic day. Britannica describes a decline in stages between about 2000 and 1750 BCE. Mohenjo-daro had been hit by serious floods more than once, and its houses got more crowded and more poorly built over time. Many scholars think shifting rivers and a drier climate made it harder to farm near the old cities. People did not vanish. They moved to smaller villages, many of them farther east and south, and kept farming and making crafts.

docs.title: 2.5 The Indus Script: A Puzzle Still Unsolved
docs.text:
The Indus Script is the set of signs that Indus people carved on seals, pottery, tools and small tablets. It has not been deciphered, which means nobody can read it with confidence.

Here's why it's so hard:

  • The inscriptions are tiny. The average one is about five signs long. Imagine learning a language from license plates.
  • There are many signs. Scholars count around 400 (the Indian scholar Iravatham Mahadevan listed 419 in the 1970s), too many for an alphabet.
  • There is no "Rosetta Stone." No inscription has been found with the same text in a language we can already read.
  • Nobody knows the language. Some scholars link it to the Dravidian family, which includes Tamil and Telugu, and others disagree. A few argue the signs were not full writing at all, more like merchants' marks.

The puzzle still makes news. In January 2025, M. K. Stalin, the chief minister of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, announced a prize of 1 million US dollars for anyone who deciphers the script to the satisfaction of archaeological experts. As of 2026, no decipherment has been accepted by scholars.

Be careful with 'solved!' headlines

Every few years, someone claims to have cracked the Indus Script. Until other experts can test a decipherment and read new inscriptions with it, treat those claims as ideas, not facts.

docs.title: 2.6 New Languages and the Vedic Period
The Indo-Aryan Migration
docs.text:
After the Indus cities faded, a new language family spread across northern South Asia. The languages most people in Pakistan, northern India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka speak today, including Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi, Bangla, Nepali and Sinhala, belong to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European language family. That family also includes Persian, Greek, Latin, English and Ben's family languages, Swedish and Norwegian.

How did related languages end up in places as far apart as Norway and Bangladesh? The explanation most scholars accept is the Indo-Aryan Migration: the idea that people speaking early Indo-Aryan languages moved into the northwest of the subcontinent from Central Asia in gradual waves, starting after about 2000 BCE, and that over centuries their languages spread and mixed with the languages and peoples already living there.

Three kinds of evidence support it:

  1. Language. Words in Sanskrit, Persian, Greek and Latin match in regular, predictable ways, which points to a common ancestor spoken far to the northwest.
  2. Genetics. A 2019 study of ancient DNA from 523 people, published in Science (Narasimhan and colleagues), found that ancestry linked to herders of the Central Asian steppe spread into South Asia starting around 4,000 years ago. A second 2019 study, in Cell, read the DNA of a person buried at the Indus city of Rakhigarhi in India and found little if any steppe ancestry. Together they suggest this ancestry arrived after the Indus cities were built.
  3. Texts. The oldest Vedic hymns were composed in the northwest of the subcontinent, the region where the languages first arrived, and only later texts describe lands farther east.

Just as important is what the evidence does not show. An older colonial-era theory imagined an "Aryan invasion" in which conquerors destroyed the Indus cities. Scholars reject it. The cities were already declining for other reasons, there's no sign of one great war, and the movement of people looks slow. The colonial version was also tied to racist ideas about skin color.

The word "Aryan" itself needs care. In the old texts, arya meant "noble," a name for people who shared a language and customs, not a "race." European racists, and later the Nazis, twisted it into a racist label.

Whose Story?

Most linguists, archaeologists and geneticists worldwide accept that Indo-Aryan languages arrived through gradual migration over centuries, mixing with the people already living in the region. Some writers and scholars in India dispute this. They argue that Vedic culture grew up locally, sometimes linking it directly to the Indus cities, and they point to cultural continuity across the region. In Pakistan, the Indus cities are taught as the deep roots of the nation's own land, from Mohenjo-daro in Sindh to Harappa in Punjab. Tamil scholars and politicians often stress a possible Dravidian link to the Indus Script. The same ancient DNA results have been quoted by people on different sides of these debates, so it is worth reading the actual studies, not just headlines about them.

docs.title: The Vedic Period
docs.text:
The Vedic Period is the era, from about 1500 to 500 BCE, when the Vedas were composed in northern South Asia. It sits between the end of the Indus cities and the rise of new cities and kingdoms around 600 BCE.

Early Vedic people lived mostly in the Punjab region, organized into tribes rather than kingdoms, and lived largely by herding. Priests performed rituals around a sacred fire while chanting hymns. Between about 1200 and 1000 BCE, Vedic culture spread east into the western Ganga plain, and the Kuru kingdom became its new center.

This is also when varna, a division of society into priests, warriors and rulers, farmers and traders, and laborers, appears in Vedic texts. Varna is an idea from the texts. In everyday life, people later belonged to thousands of local groups, called jati, that were usually inherited and married within the group. Over many centuries, the textual varna idea and these local jati groups together shaped what is now called caste, and how they fit together varied from region to region. You'll learn about that long and painful history, and about the movements against caste discrimination, in Chapter 13.

docs.title: The Vedas
docs.text:
The Vedas (वेद, VAY-duh, "knowledge") are four collections of sacred hymns, chants, ritual instructions and teachings composed in an early form of Sanskrit. They are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism. The four are:

  • the Rigveda, a collection of hymns of praise to gods such as Agni (fire) and Indra (storm and war);
  • the Samaveda, hymns arranged for singing;
  • the Yajurveda, prayers and formulas for priests to use during rituals;
  • the Atharvaveda, which includes prayers for health, protection and everyday life.

Most scholars date the bulk of the Rigveda, the oldest, to about 1500 to 1000 BCE. Later layers include the Upanishads, philosophical dialogues about the self and ultimate reality that shaped central ideas in Hinduism.

Maybe the most amazing thing about the Vedas is how they survived. For centuries nobody wrote them down at all. Teachers passed them to students by voice, using memory techniques so precise that the sound of each word stayed fixed for thousands of years. UNESCO recognized the Tradition of Vedic Chanting as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage (it was proclaimed in 2003 and inscribed on the list in 2008). In Hindu tradition, the Vedas are shruti, "what is heard," revealed to ancient sages rather than written by human authors.

docs.title: Sanskrit
docs.text:
Sanskrit (संस्कृत, SUNS-krit, "refined" or "perfected") is the classical language of ancient South Asia, part of the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family. The oldest form, used in the Vedas, is called Vedic Sanskrit. Later, a grammarian named Panini, who most scholars place around the 4th century BCE (some argue earlier), described the language in a famous grammar called the Ashtadhyayi, "Eight Chapters." His rules shaped Classical Sanskrit for the next two thousand years.

Sanskrit became the language of Hindu scripture, philosophy, drama, poetry and science, and many Buddhist and Jain texts used it too. For centuries it was a shared language of learning, a bit like Latin in medieval Europe. Its words live on in many modern languages and even in English: "yoga," "karma," "avatar" and "jungle" all trace back to Sanskrit.

docs.title: 2.7 Cities Return: The Mahajanapadas
docs.text:
Around 600 BCE, something happened in the Ganga plain that had not happened in South Asia since the Indus cities: big towns and cities appeared again. Historians call this the "second urbanization."

The Mahajanapadas (महाजनपद, muh-HAA-jun-uh-puh-duh, "great realms") were the sixteen large kingdoms and republics that ruled northern South Asia from about the 6th to the 4th century BCE. The word comes from maha, "great," and janapada, a territory where a people (jana) had settled. Old Buddhist texts list sixteen of them, stretching from Gandhara in the northwest (today's northern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan) to Anga in the east (today's Bihar, India).

Most were ruled by kings, but a couple were governed by councils of leading families, which historians sometimes call republics. Over time, the kingdom of Magadha, in today's Bihar, swallowed its neighbors. Its rulers built a fort at a village on the Ganga that grew into the city of Pataliputra, near modern Patna. Pataliputra would become the capital of two of the biggest empires in this chapter.

In the far northwest, the city of Taxila, near today's Islamabad in Pakistan, became an important stop on trade routes to Central Asia. UNESCO's description of the site notes that Alexander the Great entered Taxila in 326 BCE, during his campaign into the Punjab.

docs.title: 2.8 New Paths: The Rise of Buddhism and Jainism
docs.text:
The new cities brought new wealth and new kinds of work, and with them came new questions. Some people began to doubt that elaborate fire rituals were the only path to a good life. Wandering teachers, called shramanas, gave up home and possessions to search for answers through meditation and simple living. Two of these teachers started traditions that are still alive today.

The Rise of Buddhism and Jainism describes how these two traditions began in the Ganga plain in the 6th or 5th century BCE, during the age of the Mahajanapadas, and grew into religions followed by millions.

docs.title: The Buddha
docs.text:
Siddhartha Gautama, who became known as the Buddha, "the awakened one," lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE. Historians are not sure of his exact dates. According to Buddhist tradition:

  • He was born into a ruling family of the Shakya clan at Lumbini, in what is now southern Nepal.
  • He left his comfortable life to search for an end to suffering.
  • He reached awakening (enlightenment) while meditating under a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, in today's Bihar, India.
  • He gave his first teaching at the Deer Park at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
  • He died at Kushinagar, in today's Uttar Pradesh, India.

The Buddha taught a "Middle Way" between luxury and extreme self-denial. His core teachings are the Four Noble Truths (life involves suffering; suffering has a cause in craving; suffering can end; and there is a path to end it) and the Noble Eightfold Path, a practice of ethics, mindfulness and meditation. He founded a community of monks and, later, nuns, called the sangha.

docs.title: Mahavira and Jainism
docs.text:
Mahavira, "the great hero," was born Vardhamana in today's Bihar and lived around the same time as the Buddha. Jains consider him the 24th and last Tirthankara, or "ford-maker," of the present age: a teacher who made a crossing over the sea of rebirth for others. Jainism's most basic rule is ahimsa, non-violence toward every living being. Some Jain monks carry a soft brush to gently move insects out of their path.

Buddhism Jainism Key teacher Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha Mahavira (the 24th Tirthankara) When 6th or 5th century BCE 6th or 5th century BCE Where Ganga plain (Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath) Ganga plain (today's Bihar) Central idea The Middle Way; the Four Noble Truths Ahimsa, non-violence to all living things

Both traditions questioned the idea that rituals performed by priests were the only path to a good life. Hindu thought was changing at the same time, too, and the Upanishads were asking similar deep questions about the self, rebirth and freedom. You'll explore all three faiths, and more, in Chapter 5.

docs.title: The first great empire
docs.text:
The Maurya Empire was the first empire to rule most of the Indian subcontinent. It lasted from about 321 to 185 BCE, with its capital at Pataliputra.

It was founded by Chandragupta Maurya, who took the Punjab after Alexander the Great's death in 323 BCE and defeated Seleucus, one of Alexander's generals, around 305 BCE. A Greek ambassador, Megasthenes, lived at his court. His book is lost, but pieces survive in later Greek and Roman writers. Chandragupta's son Bindusara pushed the empire south into the Deccan. The Mauryas ran a large government with a standing army and officials, and built a great road linking eastern Afghanistan to Pataliputra.

docs.title: Ashoka: a ruler who changed course
docs.text:
Ashoka (also spelled Asoka) was the third Maurya emperor and Chandragupta's grandson. He ruled from about 268 to 232 BCE (Britannica gives two possible ranges, about 265 to 238 BCE or about 273 to 232 BCE). His empire stretched from present-day Afghanistan in the west to present-day Bangladesh in the east.

In the eighth year of his reign, about 260 BCE, Ashoka conquered Kalinga, a region on the Bay of Bengal coast in today's Odisha, India. The war was brutal. In one of his own inscriptions, Ashoka said that 150,000 people were carried away as captives, 100,000 were killed, and many times that number died. He wrote that he felt deep sorrow and regret.

After Kalinga, Ashoka gave up conquering new lands by war. He became a follower of Buddhism and promoted what he called dhamma (धम्म, DUM-muh, "righteousness" or "right conduct," the Prakrit form of the Sanskrit word dharma). For Ashoka, dhamma meant things like non-violence, tolerance of all religious groups and opinions, obedience to parents, respect for priests and religious teachers, and humane treatment of servants.

He ended the royal hunts, and Buddhist tradition says he built many stupas (dome-shaped shrines holding relics) and sent missions to other lands. The Sri Lankan chronicle Mahavamsa says he sent his son Mahinda and his daughter Sanghamitta to Sri Lanka as missionaries.

Ashoka is on your money

Look at an Indian rupee note or coin. The four lions are India's state emblem, adapted from a pillar top Ashoka put up at Sarnath, and the 24-spoked wheel in the middle of India's flag is the Ashoka Chakra.

docs.title: The Edicts of Ashoka
docs.text:
The Edicts of Ashoka are messages that Ashoka had carved on rocks and on tall polished stone pillars across his empire. They are some of the oldest readable written documents in South Asia. Most were written in Prakrit, an everyday form of the languages related to Sanskrit, using the Brahmi script. Brahmi is the ancestor of dozens of modern scripts, including Devanagari, Bangla, Tamil and Sinhala.

The edicts were written for local readers. In today's Pakistan, some used the Kharoshthi script, written right to left. Near Kandahar, in Afghanistan, one was carved in Greek and Aramaic. At Lumbini in Nepal, Ashoka put up a pillar marking the Buddha's birthplace, and UNESCO dates it to 249 BCE.

Over the following centuries Brahmi changed so much that nobody could read the edicts, and Ashoka was nearly forgotten. Between 1836 and 1838, James Prinsep, a British official and scholar in Calcutta (now Kolkata), worked out the Brahmi script, and Ashoka returned to history.

Not every Ashokan inscription fits the gentle image, though. Ashoka did not give back the lands he had conquered, and Kalinga stayed part of his empire. In the Kalinga region itself, his inscriptions leave out the edict that expresses regret for the war. One possible reason is that confessing to the people he had conquered did not seem politically wise. Ashoka really did rethink power after a terrible war, but he was still an emperor.

After Ashoka's death, the empire weakened. The last Maurya ruler was overthrown about 185 BCE.

docs.title: 2.10 Crossroads in the North: The Kushan Empire
docs.text:
After the Mauryas, many smaller kingdoms ruled the north, and new groups came through the northwest passes, including Greek kings from Bactria (today's northern Afghanistan and Central Asia). The most powerful newcomers built the Kushan Empire, which ruled from about the 1st to the 3rd century CE (some scholars extend it into the 4th). The Kushans came from Central Asia.

At its height, their empire covered much of today's Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India, along with parts of Central Asia. Its most famous ruler, Kanishka, came to the throne around 127 CE. His main capital was Purushapura (today's Peshawar, Pakistan), with a second major capital at Mathura in northern India.

The Kushan Empire sat on the Silk Road, the trade routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, India and the Roman world. Some Kushan kings honored the Hindu god Shiva, and Kanishka strongly supported Buddhism. Two things grew out of this crossroads:

  • Gandhara art. In the region of Gandhara, around Peshawar and Taxila, artists mixed Buddhist subjects with styles learned from Greek and Roman art. Some of the earliest surviving statues showing the Buddha in human form were made in Gandhara and in Mathura during Kushan rule.
  • Buddhism's journey east. Monks, merchants and pilgrims carried Buddhism from Gandhara across the Karakoram mountains into Central Asia and China.

docs.title: 2.11 The Tamil South: The Sangam Age
docs.text:
The south had its own kingdoms, language and literature. It wasn't simply a copy of the north.

The Sangam Age is the period in the Tamil-speaking south of the subcontinent when the earliest Tamil poetry was composed. Most scholars place it between about 300 BCE and 300 CE, though some argue for a narrower range (the Tamil literature scholar Kamil Zvelebil suggested about 100 BCE to 250 CE). The dates are debated because the poems rarely mention events that can be dated.

The word Sangam (சங்கம், SUNG-um) means "assembly" or "academy." Tamil tradition says poets gathered in academies under the Pandya kings at Madurai. Scholars treat the oldest parts of that story as legend, but the poems are real. They fall into two groups:

  • Akam ("inner") poems about love, each tied to a particular landscape, such as mountains, forests, farmland or seashore.
  • Puram ("outer") poems about war, kings, generosity, death and public life.

Three ruling families, called the "three crowned kings," dominated the Tamil country: the Cheras on the west coast (in today's Kerala), the Cholas in the Kaveri River delta, and the Pandyas around Madurai. They often fought each other.

The Tamil south grew rich from sea trade. Ports like Muziris, on the Malabar Coast in today's Kerala, traded pepper with the Roman world and the Middle East. Roman writers such as Pliny the Elder described it, and a Tamil poem describes foreign ships arriving with gold and leaving with pepper. You'll follow this ocean trade in Chapter 3.

docs.title: Meanwhile, in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh
docs.text:
Ancient history happened across the region, not only in today's India.

  • In Sri Lanka, Anuradhapura became the capital of a Sinhala kingdom in the 4th century BCE (377 BCE, according to the chronicles) and stayed a capital for well over a thousand years. Tradition says Sanghamitta brought a cutting of the Bodhi tree there in the 3rd century BCE, and a tree grown from it still stands. The city became a center of Theravada Buddhism. UNESCO listed the Sacred City of Anuradhapura as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
  • In Bangladesh, Mahasthangarh, in today's Bogra District, is the earliest city site found so far. A limestone slab carved with six lines of Prakrit in the Brahmi script, found there in 1931, shows the city existed by at least the 3rd century BCE, when it was an important town under the Mauryas. Zara's Nanu calls it "very, very old," and she's right.

docs.title: The Guptas
docs.text:
The Gupta Empire ruled much of northern and central South Asia from about 320 to 550 CE. Its kings came from Magadha, the same region as the Mauryas, and Pataliputra was again a major capital.

Chandragupta I (not the Maurya one) began the dynasty's rise around 319 or 320 CE. His son Samudragupta expanded it through war, and Chandragupta II extended it west to Ujjain, though his reign is remembered more for culture than conquest. Sanskrit literature and science did well under the Guptas. The poet and playwright Kalidasa wrote famous Sanskrit works such as the play Shakuntala. The mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata wrote his book, the Aryabhatiya, in 499 CE, when he was 23 years old, according to the book itself. You'll meet Aryabhata again in Chapter 16, along with the story of zero and the decimal place-value system.

Historians used to call the Gupta period India's "Golden Age." Many now question that label: some achievements once credited to the Guptas began earlier, and "golden" mostly describes life for the wealthy. The empire weakened under attacks by the Hunas from Central Asia and the breakaway of its own local rulers, and by the mid-500s it had shrunk to a small kingdom.

docs.title: Nalanda
docs.text:
Nalanda was a great Buddhist monastery and center of learning in today's Bihar, India. Most historians date its founding to the reign of the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I, around 427 CE. It grew into one of the most famous places of study in Asia and operated for roughly 800 years.

Monks and students there studied Buddhist philosophy along with grammar, logic, medicine, mathematics and astronomy. They lived in brick buildings called viharas, and the monastery had a famous library. Students and scholars came from as far away as China and Korea. The Chinese pilgrim and scholar Xuanzang studied there in the 7th century and carried many texts back to China. Nalanda was badly damaged in attacks around 1200 CE and was later abandoned.

UNESCO made the Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara a World Heritage Site in 2016, calling it the most ancient university of the Indian subcontinent. Some historians note that "university" is a modern word that fits imperfectly, since Nalanda was first of all a monastery.

Our story ends around 550 CE, as the Gupta Empire fades. New kingdoms, new faiths and new traders are about to arrive, and that is the story of Chapter 3.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the ancient past: stories they heard as children, old places they visited, and how history was taught in their school. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Pull up a photo of one ancient place from this chapter, such as Mohenjo-daro, Lumbini, Sarnath, Anuradhapura or Mahasthangarh, and show it to them first. Ask if it's okay to take notes.

Questions to ask

  1. When you were growing up, what stories did you hear about the very distant past? Who told them?
  2. Have you ever visited an ancient site, like Mohenjo-daro, Taxila, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Lumbini, Anuradhapura or Mahasthangarh? What do you remember about it?
  3. What did your school teach about the Indus cities, the Vedas, the Buddha or Ashoka? Was there a part of that history your teachers were especially proud of?
  4. Are there old words, prayers, chants or sayings in our family that you were told come from a very old language, like Sanskrit, Pali or old Tamil?
  5. Has the way people talk about ancient history changed since you were young, or since you moved here? Do people argue about it more now?
  6. What is one thing about the ancient past of our region that you hope I'll always remember?

Listen for: names of places tied to Harappa and Mohenjo-daro or the Rise of Buddhism and Jainism, any mention of Ashoka or the Vedas, and signs that your elder learned a different version of the story, like the debate over the Indo-Aryan Migration.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare what your elder learned in school with what this chapter says. Did they learn about periods or places this chapter mentions, such as Mehrgarh, the Indus Script or the Sangam Age? If a friend interviewed someone who went to school in a different country, such as Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Nepal or Sri Lanka, list two ways their versions of ancient history were different and one way they were the same.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: South Asian history begins with the Vedas. Reality: Farming villages like Mehrgarh go back to about 7000 BCE (some say later), and the planned cities of the Indus Valley Civilization flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, centuries before the Rigveda was composed.

Myth: Scholars have figured out how to read the Indus Script. Reality: The Indus Script is still undeciphered. Its inscriptions are very short, there is no bilingual text to help, and the language is unknown. In 2025 the government of Tamil Nadu offered a 1 million US dollar prize for a decipherment that experts accept.

Myth: "Aryans" invaded and destroyed the Indus cities. Reality: The Indus cities declined gradually between about 2000 and 1750 BCE, likely because of floods, shifting rivers and a drier climate. Most scholars think Indo-Aryan speakers arrived slowly over centuries and mixed with people already there. The violent "Aryan invasion" story is an outdated colonial-era theory that scholars reject.

Myth: Ashoka was always a peaceful Buddhist king. Reality: Ashoka fought a bloody war to conquer Kalinga, around 260 BCE, before turning to Buddhism and dhamma. Even afterward he kept his army and his empire, and the edict in which he expresses regret was left out of the inscriptions in Kalinga itself.

Myth: Ancient South Asian history happened only in what is now India. Reality: Mehrgarh, Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Taxila are in Pakistan; Lumbini is in Nepal; Ashoka's Greek and Aramaic edict is near Kandahar in Afghanistan; Mahasthangarh is in Bangladesh; and Anuradhapura is in Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is Mehrgarh important?

It is one of the earliest known farming villages in South Asia, usually dated to about 7000 BCE. Its people grew wheat and barley and herded animals, and villages like it were the base the later Indus cities grew from.

2. Name three features that show Mohenjo-daro was a planned city.

Any three of these: grid streets meeting at right angles, baked-brick buildings, covered drains along the streets, bathrooms in houses, and a raised citadel area with the Great Bath.

3. Give two reasons the Indus Script is so hard to decipher.

The inscriptions are very short (about five signs on average), there is no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone, and nobody knows what language it recorded. Any two are correct.

4. What changed after Ashoka's war in Kalinga?

Ashoka gave up conquering new lands by war, turned to Buddhism and promoted dhamma, or right conduct, through edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire.

5. Which empire founded Nalanda, and about when?

The Gupta Empire. Most historians date Nalanda's founding to the reign of Kumaragupta I, around 427 CE.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Put these in order from oldest to newest: Maurya Empire, Mehrgarh, Gupta Empire, Indus cities at their height, Vedic Period.

    Answer

    Mehrgarh (about 7000 BCE), Indus cities at their height (about 2600 to 1900 BCE), Vedic Period (about 1500 to 500 BCE), Maurya Empire (about 321 to 185 BCE), Gupta Empire (about 320 to 550 CE).

  2. Name the four Vedas.

    Answer

    The Rigveda, the Samaveda, the Yajurveda and the Atharvaveda.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why almost every date in this chapter starts with "about."

    Answer

    Ancient dates come from methods like radiocarbon dating, which give a range, and from texts that often don't name exact years. Scholars also disagree about some dates, such as Mehrgarh's start and the Sangam Age.

  2. Explain the difference between the Indo-Aryan Migration that most scholars accept and the old "Aryan invasion" theory.

    Answer

    The migration idea says Indo-Aryan speakers arrived gradually over centuries after about 2000 BCE and mixed with people already living there. The invasion theory claimed a violent conquest that destroyed the Indus cities. The evidence does not support a single invasion, and the cities were already declining for other reasons.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Ancient Timeline. Set the year to about 100 CE. List every place that is lit and the present-day country it is in. Which two period bands overlap? Hint: one band is in the north and one in the far south.

  2. A cousin says, "Buddhism is from Sri Lanka." Using this chapter, write two sentences that politely correct and add to that statement. Hint: think about Lumbini, Bodh Gaya and Ashoka's missions.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the kinds of evidence historians use for the Indus Valley Civilization and for Ashoka's reign. Why do we know so much more about what Ashoka believed? Hint: one of them left writing people can read.

  2. Ashoka's regret for the Kalinga war appears in edicts across his empire but not in the edicts placed in Kalinga itself. Analyze what this might tell us about Ashoka as a ruler. Hint: who was the audience for each inscription?

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Some historians call the Gupta period India's "Golden Age," and others reject the label. Which side do you find more convincing? Use at least two facts from the chapter. Hint: ask "golden for whom?"

  2. Your club wants to put "Ancient India" as the title of a slide about Harappa, Taxila and Lumbini. Evaluate whether that title is accurate and fair, and suggest a better one. Hint: check which present-day countries those sites are in.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Create a five-panel comic strip that follows one object through time, such as a Harappan seal, a Brahmi inscription or a Nalanda manuscript, from when it was made to when it was found or read again. Hint: James Prinsep or the 1922 Mohenjo-daro dig could be a panel.

  2. Write a short museum label (80 to 120 words) for an Indus seal that tells visitors what we know, what we don't know, and why the script matters today. Hint: use "about" for dates and avoid claims the evidence can't support.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Farming began early in South Asia: Mehrgarh, in Pakistan's Balochistan, is usually dated to about 7000 BCE.
  • The Indus Valley Civilization (about 2600 to 1900 BCE at its height) built planned cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, and its script is still undeciphered.
  • Most scholars think Indo-Aryan languages arrived through gradual migration after about 2000 BCE; the violent "Aryan invasion" story is rejected, and some people in India dispute migration altogether.
  • The Vedic Period produced the Vedas in Sanskrit, kept alive for centuries by careful memorization.
  • The Buddha and Mahavira lived in the world of the Mahajanapadas, the new cities and kingdoms of northern South Asia, and their teachings became Buddhism and Jainism.
  • The Mauryas, especially Ashoka, built the first empire across most of the subcontinent; the Kushans linked the north to the Silk Road; Tamil kingdoms of the Sangam Age traded across the sea; and the Guptas supported Sanskrit learning and founded Nalanda.
  • Ancient South Asian history belongs to the whole region: Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka all hold key sites.

Seven thousand years, done!

You just crossed about 7,000 years of history, and you can now explain why Ben's tiny seal is such a big deal. Next, in Chapter 3, new empires rise, Islam and Sikhism arrive and grow, and European ships appear on the horizon.

docs.title: Quiz: Ancient Roots
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 2. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Mehrgarh, one of the earliest farming villages in South Asia, is in which present-day country?

  1. India
  2. Afghanistan
  3. Pakistan
  4. Nepal
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Mehrgarh is on the Kachhi Plain in Balochistan, Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass. Afghanistan is a tempting guess because the pass leads toward it, but the site itself is in Pakistan.

Concept Tested: Mehrgarh Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
About when did the Mature Harappan cities of the Indus Valley Civilization flourish?

  1. About 2600 to 1900 BCE
  2. About 7000 to 5000 BCE
  3. About 1500 to 500 BCE
  4. About 321 to 185 BCE
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The planned Indus cities were at their height from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. About 1500 to 500 BCE is the Vedic Period, which came after the cities faded, and 321 to 185 BCE is the Maurya Empire.

Concept Tested: Indus Valley Civilization Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which statement about the Indus Script is accurate as of 2026?

  1. It was deciphered in the 1830s by James Prinsep.
  2. It has not been deciphered, partly because the inscriptions are very short and no bilingual text has been found.
  3. It is an early form of the Brahmi alphabet and can be read easily.
  4. It was deciphered after Tamil Nadu offered a prize in 2025.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Indus Script is still undeciphered: inscriptions average about five signs, there is no Rosetta Stone, and the language is unknown. Prinsep deciphered Brahmi, Ashoka's script, not the Indus Script, and the 2025 prize has not been claimed with a decipherment experts accept.

Concept Tested: Indus Script Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Which feature of Mohenjo-daro best supports the idea that the city was carefully planned?

  1. A huge royal palace at the center of the city
  2. Gold coins stamped with the names of kings
  3. Temples covered in readable inscriptions
  4. Streets crossing at right angles, with covered drains along them
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Grid streets and covered drains fed by house bathrooms show planning. Archaeologists have not found a clear royal palace, and Indus writing cannot be read, so the other options describe things that were not found.

Concept Tested: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Which description of the Indo-Aryan Migration matches what most scholars accept today?

  1. A sudden invasion around 1900 BCE that destroyed the Indus cities in battle
  2. A movement of Indo-Aryan speakers from the south of India to Central Asia
  3. A gradual movement of Indo-Aryan speakers into the northwest over centuries after about 2000 BCE, mixing with people already living there
  4. A myth with no supporting evidence from language or genetics
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Linguistic and ancient DNA evidence supports gradual migration after about 2000 BCE. The violent "invasion" story (A) is an outdated colonial-era theory that scholars reject, because the cities were already declining for other reasons.

Concept Tested: Indo-Aryan Migration Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
How did the Vedas survive for many centuries before they were written down?

  1. They were carved on stone pillars across the empire.
  2. Teachers passed them to students by voice, using precise memory techniques.
  3. They were painted on the walls of the Indus cities.
  4. They were copied onto paper by monks at Nalanda.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Vedas were passed on by voice, using very precise recitation methods, a tradition UNESCO recognizes as intangible cultural heritage. Carved pillars (A) were Ashoka's way of sharing his edicts, much later.

Concept Tested: The Vedas Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Dilan's grandmother in Kandy tells him that the Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura grew from a cutting brought from the place where the Buddha reached awakening. Using the chapter, where did that cutting come from, and which emperor's family is linked to it?

  1. Bodh Gaya, and Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta
  2. Lumbini, and Chandragupta Maurya's son
  3. Nalanda, and the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I
  4. Taxila, and the Kushan emperor Kanishka
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The Buddha reached awakening at Bodh Gaya, and Sri Lankan tradition says Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta brought the cutting in the 3rd century BCE. Lumbini (B) is the Buddha's birthplace, not the place of his awakening.

Concept Tested: Rise of Buddhism and Jainism Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Your club is making a map of ancient sites by present-day country. Which site belongs under Bangladesh?

  1. Taxila
  2. Anuradhapura
  3. Pataliputra
  4. Mahasthangarh
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Mahasthangarh, in Bogra District, is the earliest city site found in Bangladesh, dated by a Brahmi inscription to at least the 3rd century BCE. Pataliputra (C) was in Magadha, in today's Bihar, India, which is west of Bangladesh, not inside it.

Concept Tested: Maurya Empire Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Ashoka's edict expressing regret for the Kalinga war appears across his empire but was left out of the inscriptions placed in Kalinga itself. What is the best conclusion?

  1. Ashoka never actually fought in Kalinga.
  2. Ashoka's inscriptions were shaped for their audience, so they show both his new ideals and his political judgment as an emperor.
  3. The Kalinga inscriptions were carved before the war began.
  4. Ashoka stopped believing in dhamma after the war.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The omission suggests Ashoka chose his message for each audience, since confessing to the conquered people may not have seemed wise. His own inscriptions describe the war, so A is wrong, and he promoted dhamma for the rest of his reign, so D is wrong.

Concept Tested: Edicts of Ashoka Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
The Kushan Empire (about the 1st to 3rd century CE) and the Tamil kingdoms of the Sangam Age existed at the same time. What does that overlap show?

  1. That one empire ruled all of South Asia in the 2nd century CE
  2. That the Sangam poets were writing in Sanskrit for the Kushan court
  3. That different regions had their own rulers, languages and cultures at the same moment
  4. That the Kushans conquered Madurai
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. While the Kushans ruled the north from Peshawar and Mathura, Chera, Chola and Pandya kings ruled the Tamil south, where poets wrote in Tamil. Nothing in the chapter suggests a single empire (A) or a Kushan conquest of Madurai (D).

Concept Tested: Sangam Age Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Ancient Roots
docs.text:
1. Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - The official World Heritage listing (1980) for Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, Pakistan. It describes the grid streets, baked-brick buildings, drainage and citadel, and explains how flooding and salt threaten the ruins today.

  2. Indus civilization - Encyclopaedia Britannica - A detailed, regularly updated overview of the Indus cities: their dates (about 2600 to 1900 BCE), how far they spread, their crops, seals, weights and script, and the debate over how they declined.

  3. Officials Are Offering $1 Million to Anyone Who Can Decode This Ancient Script - Smithsonian Magazine (January 2025) - A short news story on Tamil Nadu's 2025 prize for deciphering the Indus Script and why the puzzle is so hard. It shows why this ancient question still makes headlines.

  4. The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia - Narasimhan and colleagues, Science (2019), PubMed record - The large ancient DNA study of 523 people behind the chapter's discussion of the Indo-Aryan Migration. The summary is technical, but the opening paragraph is readable with help from a teacher.

  5. Tradition of Vedic chanting - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - Explains the four Vedas and the memory techniques priests use to keep every sound exact, and why UNESCO recognized the tradition (proclaimed 2003, inscribed 2008).

  6. Lumbini, the Birthplace of the Lord Buddha - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - The listing for Lumbini in Nepal, with Ashoka's inscribed pillar and the remains of monasteries and stupas. Note that it gives Nepal's traditional date for the Buddha's birth, which differs from many historians' dates.

  7. Ashoka - Encyclopaedia Britannica - A clear biography of Ashoka covering the Kalinga war, his turn to Buddhism and dhamma, his rock and pillar edicts, and his support for Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka.

  8. Gupta dynasty - Encyclopaedia Britannica - A short overview of the Gupta kings from Chandragupta I to the Huna invasions, including why historians now question calling the period a "classical" or "golden" age.

  9. Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara at Nalanda, Bihar - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - The 2016 World Heritage listing for Nalanda, describing its monasteries, temples and art, and its 800 years as a center of Buddhist learning.

  10. Sangam literature - Wikipedia - An overview of the earliest Tamil poetry, the debate over its dates, the akam and puram poems, and the Madurai academy legends. Use it to find the scholarly books it cites, such as Kamil Zvelebil's work.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Between about 600 and 1800 CE, South Asia was shared by many powers at once: ocean traders and temple-building kings in the south, island kingdoms in Sri Lanka, sultans in Delhi and Bengal, the Vijayanagara emperors, the Mughals, the Marathas, the Durranis of Afghanistan, and, from 1498, European trading companies. This chapter follows those powers and the people who moved between them: merchants, poets, saints and teachers. It also follows ideas, such as the devotional poetry of the bhakti movement, the Sufi path in Islam, and the teachings of Guru Nanak. By the end you'll be able to explain why the history of this period looks less like a relay race and more like a crowded highway with many lanes.
