docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?, especially the monsoon and the Indian Ocean.
  • Chapter 2: Ancient Roots, especially the Maurya and Gupta empires.

Kings, saints and spice ships

Hi, it's Mora! Many of the buildings in your family's photos, the foods on your table and even some of the words you use at home were shaped in the centuries this chapter covers. When someone online argues about "who ruled whom," this chapter helps you see the bigger, more crowded picture. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 3.1 "How Many Empires Were There?"
docs.text:
It's the second meeting of Prairie Ridge High School's South Asian Student Association. Zara Hossain has asked everyone to bring a photo of one old building from their family's home city. Ayesha Qureshi goes first. Her photo shows a huge red sandstone mosque with white marble domes. "This is the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore," she says. "My Dada calls Lahore 'the city of the Mughals.'"

Arjun Reddy holds up his phone. It shows a square stone gateway with four tall minarets. "This is the Charminar in Hyderabad. My grandmother says Hyderabad was built by the Qutb Shahi sultans, not the Mughals." Zara shows a picture her Nanu sent from Bangladesh: a low brick mosque crowned with rows of small domes. "And this one is in Bagerhat. Nanu says it's from the Bengal Sultanate."

Ben Lindqvist has been writing names on the whiteboard: Mughals, Qutb Shahis, Bengal Sultanate. He stops, marker in the air. "Wait. If the Mughals ruled Lahore, who ruled Hyderabad and Bengal? Were these all the same empire with different names? How many empires were there?" That question is the whole chapter.

docs.title: 3.2 A Highway, Not a Relay Race
docs.text:
Ben's family history can help. In the year 1100, the place we now call Scandinavia did not have one ruler. There were kings in Norway, in Denmark and in Sweden, plus earls, chieftains and trading towns, all at the same time. Sometimes they fought, sometimes they married into each other's families, and sometimes they traded. If you drew their history as a timeline, you couldn't draw a single bar. You'd need several lanes, side by side.

South Asia between 600 and 1800 works the same way, but on a much bigger scale. Many people imagine history as a relay race, where one empire hands the baton to the next: first the Guptas, then the sultans, then the Mughals, then the British. That picture is wrong in two ways.

  • Powers overlapped. When the Mughals ruled Lahore and Agra, the Qutb Shahis ruled Hyderabad, the Kingdom of Kandy ruled the hills of Sri Lanka, and Portuguese ships controlled Goa.
  • No single power ever ruled everything. Even the largest empires left areas to local kings, chiefs and communities.

Historians often draw this period as a set of "swim lanes": one horizontal lane per power, with bars showing when each one existed. You'll build exactly that kind of picture with the MicroSim later in this chapter. As you read, keep a rough lane in your head for each power you meet.

docs.title: 3.3 The Ocean Highway: Indian Ocean Trade
docs.text:
Before we meet the kings, meet the sea. Indian Ocean Trade is the network of sea routes and ports that linked South Asia with East Africa, Arabia, Persia, Southeast Asia and China for many centuries. It worked because of the monsoon you met in Chapter 1. The winds blow from the southwest for part of the year and from the northeast for the rest, so sailors could ride the wind one way and come back on the reverse wind months later. Merchants were using this seasonal pattern at least as far back as Roman times.

South Asia sat right in the middle of this network. Its ports sold cotton cloth, pepper, cinnamon, gems and much more. Some of the busiest included:

Port or coast Today in Known for Kozhikode (Calicut), Malabar coast Kerala, India Pepper and spices, plus Arab, Persian, Chinese and later European visitors Gujarat ports such as Cambay Gujarat, India Cotton textiles, links to Arabia and East Africa Chattogram and the Bengal ports Bangladesh and West Bengal Rice, fine cotton and silk cloth Galle and other harbors Sri Lanka Cinnamon, gems, a stopping point between east and west Malé and the atolls Maldives A rest stop on the east-west route, and seafaring islanders

Kozhikode, ruled by kings called the Zamorins (Samoothiris), was one of the most important ports in the world in medieval times. It welcomed Persian, Arab and Chinese traders, and famous travelers such as Ibn Battuta. Zara's family city, Chattogram, was also a busy port in this era, at the head of the Bay of Bengal.

The ocean carried more than goods. It carried people, languages, food and faiths. Traders settled in port towns, married local families, and built places of worship. That's how one of South Asia's major faiths first arrived.

docs.title: Early Islam in South Asia
docs.text:
Early Islam in South Asia means the first centuries of Muslim presence in the region, which came along several different routes, peacefully and through conquest, over hundreds of years. Islam began in Arabia in the early 600s. Arab merchants were already sailing to South Asia before then, so Muslim traders appeared on its coasts very early.

  • The Malabar coast (Kerala). Muslim merchants settled in port towns. The Cheraman Juma Mosque in Kodungallur, Kerala, is traditionally dated to 629 CE, which would make it one of the oldest mosques in the world. Historians debate that date, and some suggest a much later building. Either way, Kerala's Muslim communities have deep roots in this trade.
  • Sri Lanka. Arab traders arrived by the 7th century. Many Sri Lankan Muslims, often called Sri Lankan Moors, trace their ancestry to these merchant families.
  • The Maldives. In 1153 (some records say 1193), the last Buddhist king of the Maldives became a Muslim, and the islands gradually became Muslim too.
  • Sindh (Pakistan). In about 711 to 712, an Arab army led by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim conquered Sindh in the lower Indus valley, and it became a province of the Umayyad Caliphate.
  • The northwest. From about 1000, Mahmud, the sultan of Ghazni (in present-day Afghanistan), led raids deep into northern India. Later rulers from the northwest founded kingdoms in North India itself.

So Islam reached South Asia through trade, through teachers and holy men, and through conquest, over many centuries. That variety is one reason Muslim communities in Kerala, Sindh, Bengal and the Maldives have such different languages, foods and customs today.

Map the routes

I like to imagine two arrows: one sailing across the sea to the coasts of Kerala, Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and one crossing the mountains into Sindh and Punjab. Can you guess which arrow reached your family's region first?

docs.title: The Cholas
docs.text:
The Chola Dynasty was a Tamil royal family from the Kaveri River delta in south India. A dynasty is a ruling family whose power passes from one generation to the next. Cholas are mentioned in very early Tamil poems, but the empire most people mean by "the Cholas" was founded around 848 CE by a king named Vijayalaya. For the next four centuries the Cholas were one of the strongest powers in South Asia, until they were absorbed by their Pandya rivals by 1279.

Two Chola kings stand out:

  • Rajaraja I built the enormous Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur between 1003 and 1010. Its main tower rises like a stone mountain over the town, and the temple is still in use today.
  • Rajendra I, his son, led an army north as far as the Ganga, then built a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, whose name celebrates that campaign. His great temple there was completed in 1035. He also sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya kingdom in Southeast Asia.

That last point surprises many people. The Cholas were a sea power. Tamil merchant guilds traded across the Bay of Bengal, and Chola fleets reached Sri Lanka, the Maldives and the Malay Peninsula. Three Chola temples (at Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram) are listed together by UNESCO as the "Great Living Chola Temples," a name that reminds us that people still worship in them.

docs.title: The Sri Lankan Kingdoms
docs.text:
Sri Lankan Kingdoms is the name for the series of kingdoms that ruled the island of Sri Lanka, some Sinhala and some Tamil, often at the same time. A quick tour:

Kingdom Approximate dates Capital One thing to know Anuradhapura from the 4th century BCE to about 1017 CE Anuradhapura A Sinhala Buddhist capital for over a thousand years. Chola armies captured its last king around 1017 Chola rule in the north 993 to 1070 Polonnaruwa Part of the island was ruled by the Cholas for decades Polonnaruwa 1070 to 1232 Polonnaruwa Parakramabahu I (ruled 1153 to 1186) built huge irrigation reservoirs Jaffna kingdom 1215 to 1619 Nallur, near Jaffna A Tamil kingdom in the north, taken over by the Portuguese Kingdom of Kandy 1469 to 1815 Kandy The last independent kingdom. It kept the Buddha's Tooth Relic from 1595 and fell to the British in 1815

Notice how the Sri Lankan lane splits in two. From the 1200s to the 1600s a Tamil kingdom ruled the north while Sinhala kingdoms ruled further south. Dilan Perera's family is from Kandy, and the Temple of the Tooth Relic there is still one of the most important Buddhist sites in the world.

docs.title: The Delhi Sultanate
docs.text:
The Delhi Sultanate was a series of Muslim-ruled kingdoms based in Delhi that controlled much of northern South Asia from 1206 to 1526. A sultan is a king, and a sultanate (سلطنت, sul-TUH-nut, in Urdu and Persian, "rule" or "kingdom") is the land he rules. Historians divide the Sultanate into five dynasties (ruling families):

  1. Mamluk, 1206 to 1290
  2. Khalji, 1290 to 1320
  3. Tughlaq, 1320 to 1414
  4. Sayyid, 1414 to 1451
  5. Lodi, 1451 to 1526

At various times the Sultanate covered parts of today's India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and southern Nepal. Its sultans fought off Mongol armies from Central Asia, built forts and mosques, and drew scholars, poets and soldiers from Persia and Central Asia. One of its rulers was a woman: Razia Sultan, who ruled from 1236 to 1240 and remains the only woman to have sat on the throne of Delhi. The 72.5 m (238 ft) Qutb Minar, a red sandstone tower in south Delhi begun in the early 1200s, is the Sultanate's best-known monument.

The Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta reached the Indus in 1333 and worked as a judge in Delhi under Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq. Later he sailed to the Maldives. His travel book is one of our best eyewitness sources for the 1300s, and it shows how connected the Muslim world, from North Africa to the Maldives, had become.

docs.title: The Bengal Sultanate
docs.text:
Far to the east, Bengal had its own lane. The Bengal Sultanate ruled the delta from 1352 to 1576, independent of Delhi for most of that time, until the Mughal emperor Akbar's armies conquered it. Persian was the language of government, but some sultans and their officials also supported poets writing in Bangla, and the sultans employed both Muslims and Hindus in their government.

In the 15th century, a general named Ulugh Khan Jahan founded a city at Bagerhat in what is now Bangladesh. Its Sixty Dome Mosque (which actually has 81 domes held up by 60 columns) is the photo Zara's Nanu sent, and the city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

docs.title: The Vijayanagara Empire
docs.text:
In 1336, two brothers named Harihara and Bukka founded a kingdom in the south. It grew into the Vijayanagara Empire, a large Hindu-ruled empire of southern India from 1336 to 1646, named after its capital city, Vijayanagara ("city of victory"). The ruins of that city are at Hampi, in Karnataka.

Vijayanagara was strongest under Krishnadevaraya, who ruled from 1509 to 1529. Its capital was one of the biggest cities in the world in its day, with markets described by foreign visitors such as the Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq and the Portuguese traveler Domingo Paes, and its kings supported poetry in Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit.

In 1565 an alliance of Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota. UNESCO notes that the capital was then plundered for six months and abandoned. The empire continued in a smaller form until 1646. Today Hampi's temples, bazaars and royal buildings are a World Heritage Site.

docs.title: The Deccan sultanates
docs.text:
Vijayanagara's northern neighbors were also important. The Bahmani Sultanate, founded in 1347, was the first independent sultanate of the Deccan Plateau. By 1518 it had split into five smaller sultanates. One of them, Golconda, was ruled by the Qutb Shahi family from 1518 until 1687.

This is where Arjun's grandmother comes in. In 1591, Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah moved his capital to a new city, Hyderabad, and built the Charminar at its center. The Qutb Shahis began with Persian as their court language, but in the 1600s Telugu came to be used alongside it, and many royal orders were written in both languages. Arjun's family speaks Telugu, so the language of his home was once a language of a sultan's court. The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb conquered Golconda in 1687.

Don't read today's politics backward

It's tempting to sort these wars into "Hindu side" and "Muslim side," but alliances crossed faith lines all the time. Sultans had Hindu generals and ministers, Hindu kings hired Muslim soldiers, and kingdoms of the same faith fought each other constantly.

docs.title: 3.7 Paths of Devotion: Bhakti, Sufism and Guru Nanak
docs.text: Not all of this period's big changes came from kings. Some of the most lasting came from poets and teachers who spoke to ordinary people in their own languages.

docs.title: The Bhakti Movement
docs.text:
The Bhakti Movement was a wave of devotional poetry and practice within Hinduism that taught that loving devotion to God is open to everyone, whatever their caste, gender or education. Bhakti (भक्ति, BHUK-tee) means "devotion." It began in the Tamil country around the 6th century CE with two groups of poet-saints, the Alvars, devoted to Vishnu, and the Nayanars, devoted to Shiva. Over the next thousand years it spread north, and from the 1400s it was strong across north and east India.

Bhakti poets usually wrote in everyday languages, not in Sanskrit, so people could sing their songs at home and in the street. A few you may hear about in your own family:

  • Basavanna (12th century, though sources give different dates), a Kannada poet in Karnataka linked with the Lingayat tradition, who criticized caste divisions.
  • Kabir (15th century, though his exact dates are uncertain), a weaver from the Varanasi area whose sharp, short verses questioned empty ritual in both Hinduism and Islam. Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs all honor him, and some of his verses are in the Sikh scripture.
  • Mirabai (16th century), a Rajput princess remembered for her songs of devotion to Krishna.

docs.title: Sufism
docs.text:
At the same time, a parallel path was growing within Islam. Sufism is the inward, devotional tradition of Islam, focused on the love of God and on drawing closer to God through prayer, remembrance and the guidance of a teacher. A Sufi (صوفی, SOO-fee, in Persian) usually belongs to an order, a chain of teachers and students.

In South Asia, the Chishti order became especially well known. Moinuddin Chishti (who died in 1236) settled in Ajmer, in Rajasthan, and his shrine there is still visited by huge numbers of people of many faiths. In Delhi, Nizamuddin Auliya (1238 to 1325) taught crowds of followers. The Chishtis are famous for sama, gatherings where devotional music and poetry, usually qawwali, help listeners focus on the love of God.

A Sufi saint's tomb is called a dargah (درگاہ, dur-GAAH, in Urdu, also meaning "threshold"). Dargahs across Pakistan, India and Bangladesh became places where Muslims and non-Muslims alike came to pray, ask for blessings and listen to music. Many historians see Sufi teachers as one important way that Islam spread among ordinary people, especially in Punjab, Sindh and Bengal, alongside trade, migration and the influence of rulers.

docs.title: Guru Nanak
docs.text:
Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539) was a spiritual teacher and poet from Punjab whom Sikhs honor as the founder of Sikhism and the first of the ten Sikh Gurus. A guru (ਗੁਰੂ, GOO-roo, in Punjabi) is a teacher or guide. Nanak was born in 1469 in the village of Talwandi, now called Nankana Sahib, in Punjab, Pakistan. Many historians give his birth date as 15 April, while Sikhs usually celebrate his birthday, Guru Nanak Gurpurab, on the full moon of the month of Kartik, in October or November. In Sikh tradition, he traveled widely, sharing his message in poetry and song, then settled in the town of Kartarpur (also in present-day Pakistan), where he lived as a farmer and householder until he died in 1539.

In Sikh tradition, Guru Nanak taught devotion to one God, honest work, sharing with others, and the equality of all people. His followers ate together regardless of caste, a practice that grew into the langar, the free community kitchen you'll meet in Chapter 5. Simran Kaur Gill's family keeps a picture of Guru Nanak in their home, and her grandparents have visited Kartarpur.

Bhakti, Sufism and Sikhism are three separate traditions with their own teachings. Each came out of its own faith world. But they shared some features: poetry in local languages, music, and a focus on personal devotion rather than status. That's one reason a single qawwali singer or bhajan singer today might draw a mixed audience.

docs.title: From Babur to Akbar
docs.text:
The Mughal Empire was a Muslim-ruled empire, founded by a dynasty from Central Asia, that ruled much of South Asia from 1526 until it formally ended in 1857. Its founder, Babur, was a prince descended from the Central Asian conqueror Timur. He took Kabul in 1504, and on 21 April 1526 he defeated the last Lodi sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, at the First Battle of Panipat, north of Delhi. Babur died in 1530. His son Humayun lost the throne to a rival, Sher Shah Suri, and only won back Delhi and Agra in 1555.

The emperor most people remember is Babur's grandson. Akbar was the third Mughal emperor, who ruled from 1556 to 1605 and built the Mughal state into a lasting empire. He became emperor as a teenager. Over almost fifty years he took control of most of northern and central South Asia, from Kabul to Bengal, including the rich trading region of Gujarat.

Akbar is famous for how he ruled such a mixed population:

  • He brought Hindu Rajput kings into his government and army as high-ranking officers, and married into Rajput families.
  • In 1575 he built a hall for religious debate, the Ibadat Khana ("house of worship"), at his new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, and later invited scholars of many faiths, including Hindus, the Jain teacher Hiravijaya and Jesuit priests from Goa, to discuss their beliefs.
  • He followed a policy called sulh-i kul, "universal peace," meaning the emperor should stand above any single faith.
  • He set up a translation house that turned Sanskrit works into Persian. The best known is the Razmnama, a Persian version of the Mahabharata, illustrated by his court painters, who included Persians, Indian Muslims and Hindus.

Historians admire Akbar's policies of tolerance and also point out that he was a conqueror whose wars caused great suffering. Both things are true.

docs.title: Indo-Persian Culture
docs.text:
The Mughals inherited and expanded a way of life that had been growing since the Delhi Sultanate. Indo-Persian Culture is the blend of Persian and South Asian languages, literature, art, architecture, music, food and manners that developed in Muslim-ruled courts and cities of South Asia. Persian was the official language of the Delhi Sultanate, the Bengal Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, so officials, poets and scholars of every faith learned it.

You can still see and hear Indo-Persian culture all around you:

  • Language. Mixing Persian and Arabic words with the everyday speech of the Delhi region produced Hindustani, the ancestor of today's Hindi and Urdu. The poet Amir Khusrau (who died in 1325), a follower of Nizamuddin Auliya, is honored as an early master of it.
  • Architecture. Domes, arches, minarets, inlaid marble and gardens divided into four parts appear in Mughal buildings from Kabul to Dhaka.
  • Painting. Mughal miniature painting mixed Persian styles with Indian subjects and artists.
  • Food. Many families' biryanis, kormas and kebabs come from this court cooking tradition.
  • Music. Instruments, styles like qawwali, and parts of North Indian classical music grew in this setting. You'll meet them in Chapter 9.

docs.title: The Taj Mahal
docs.text:
The most famous Mughal building is a tomb. The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum (a large tomb) in Agra, built between about 1631 and 1648 by order of the emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. The surrounding gardens, mosque and gateways were finished around 1653. Shah Jahan himself was later buried there beside her. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1983, calling it a jewel of Muslim art in India.

Shah Jahan also built the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid in Delhi and added marble palaces to the fort in Lahore. Lahore's fort, started under Akbar in 1566, and the Shalamar Gardens are a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Pakistan. Shah Jahan's son, Aurangzeb, built the Badshahi Mosque opposite the fort between 1671 and 1673. That's the mosque in Ayesha's photo, and it's why her Dada calls Lahore "the city of the Mughals."

docs.title: Height and decline
docs.text:
Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 to 1707. Under him the empire reached its largest size, stretching over almost all of the subcontinent, including Golconda in 1687. But his long wars in the Deccan were expensive, and after his death the empire broke apart quickly. Governors in Bengal, Hyderabad and Awadh became rulers in their own right, and new powers rose. By about 1760 the Mughal emperor controlled little more than the area around Delhi. The empire formally ended after the uprising of 1857, which belongs to Chapter 4.

Whose Story?

The same rulers are often remembered very differently depending on who tells the story. Aurangzeb is a clear example: historians note that some South Asian Muslims remember him as a model of a devout ruler, while many others, including many Hindus in India, remember him mainly for destroying temples. Arguments about him still flare up in Indian politics today. Shivaji (Section 3.9) is honored as a hero by many people in India, especially in Maharashtra, a view that grew stronger during the independence movement. Many Afghans call Ahmad Shah Durrani "Ahmad Shah Baba," the father of Afghanistan, while in Punjab, which he invaded again and again, and among the Marathas, who lost to him at Panipat, many people remember him mainly as an invader. Historians try to weigh all of these memories against the evidence: court chronicles, travelers' accounts, coins, inscriptions and buildings.

docs.title: The Maratha Empire
docs.text:
The Maratha Empire (also called the Maratha Confederacy) was a state founded by Marathi-speaking warriors in western India that grew, in the 1700s, into one of the largest powers in South Asia. Its founder, Shivaji, inherited land from his father, who had served the Bijapur sultanate. Shivaji built up his own kingdom in the hills of Maharashtra, fought both Bijapur and the Mughals, and was crowned Chhatrapati (sovereign) at the fort of Raigad in 1674.

After Shivaji, the Marathas kept fighting the Mughals and kept expanding. In the 1700s their real leaders were chief ministers called Peshwas, based in Pune, along with several powerful Maratha families who ruled their own regions. At their height, Maratha armies collected taxes across much of India. Their power ended in a series of wars with the East India Company, the last of which finished in 1818.

docs.title: The Durrani Empire
docs.text:
Meanwhile, a new power rose in the northwest. The Durrani Empire was an Afghan empire founded in 1747 by Ahmad Shah Durrani, a Pashtun military leader. From his capital at Kandahar (later moved to Kabul by his son), his empire stretched over Afghanistan, much of present-day Pakistan, and into Punjab and Kashmir. Many historians, and many Afghans, see it as the beginning of the modern country of Afghanistan.

The Durrani and Maratha lanes collided on 14 January 1761, at the Third Battle of Panipat, north of Delhi. The Durranis won, and the Marathas suffered enormous losses. Neither side gained lasting control of North India from the battle. Within a few decades, a different kind of power, a company, was in the strongest position of all.

docs.title: 3.10 Strangers from the Sea: European Traders
Who came, and why
docs.text:
European Traders were the merchants and companies from Portugal, the Netherlands, England, France and Denmark who came to South Asia by sea from 1498 onward to buy spices, cotton cloth, indigo and other goods. For most of this period they were guests and customers of South Asian rulers, not rulers themselves.

  • The Portuguese came first. Vasco da Gama crossed the Arabian Sea from Malindi, in present-day Kenya, and landed near Kozhikode on 20 May 1498. In 1510 the Portuguese captured Goa from the Bijapur sultanate and made it their capital in Asia. They held Goa until December 1961.
  • The Dutch founded the Dutch East India Company (VOC) on 20 March 1602. In Sri Lanka they pushed out the Portuguese and took over the island's coasts, while the Kingdom of Kandy kept the interior.
  • The English formed their own East India Company in 1600. The French and Danes followed with smaller companies.

Ask what the ships carried

For any trading company, ask three questions: what did it buy, who gave it permission to trade, and who protected its ships and warehouses? When the answer to the last one becomes "its own army," a trader is starting to turn into a ruler.

docs.title: The East India Company
docs.text:
The East India Company (EIC) was an English, later British, private company that received a royal charter (official permission) on 31 December 1600 to trade in Asia, and that later conquered and governed large parts of South Asia. Many readers are surprised to learn that it was not the British government. It was a business owned by investors, who hoped to profit from trade.

For its first century and a half, the Company depended on permission from Mughal emperors and regional rulers. It set up trading posts at Madras (now Chennai), Bombay (now Mumbai) and Calcutta (now Kolkata). When it picked a fight with the Mughal Empire in the war known as Child's War (1686 to 1690), it lost badly and had to beg Emperor Aurangzeb for pardon to keep trading.

Over time, though, the Company built its own armies. Most of its soldiers were South Asians called sepoys. The Company also got involved in the wars between regional powers. In the 1700s, as the Mughal Empire broke apart, the Company began to take over territory itself. Britain's Parliament began to limit and supervise it, renewing its charter only for twenty years at a time. How a trading company ended up ruling much of the subcontinent, starting with the Battle of Plassey in Bengal in 1757, is the story of Chapter 4. The Company was finally dissolved in 1874.

docs.title: 3.11 Back to the Whiteboard
docs.text:
Ben steps back from the whiteboard. It's covered in names now, with arrows everywhere. "Okay," he says, "so the answer to 'how many empires' is... a lot, and they were mostly at the same time?"

"Not just at the same time," Arjun says. "They were trading with each other, marrying into each other's families, fighting each other, and borrowing each other's languages."

Ayesha points at the Badshahi Mosque, the Charminar and the Sixty Dome Mosque. "Three photos, three different dynasties, all built by Muslim rulers, and none of them were the same empire."

Zara adds one line at the bottom: "South Asia had many lanes." Then she turns to the club. "Next meeting, everybody asks an elder about the oldest building near their family's home."

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the oldest building, ruin or monument they remember near their home, and the stories they heard about kings, sultans, nawabs, rajas or traders. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Look up a photo of a famous building from your elder's home region (a fort, temple, mosque, tomb or market) and show it to them to get the conversation going. Ask if it's okay to take notes.

Questions to ask

  1. What was the oldest building or ruin near the place you grew up? Did you ever visit it as a child?
  2. Who did people say built it, and when? Were there any legends about it?
  3. Did your family or town have stories about a king, sultan, nawab, raja or famous saint from long ago?
  4. Were there shrines, temples, gurdwaras or dargahs near home that people of different faiths visited?
  5. How has that building or place changed since you were young? Is it looked after, crowded with tourists, or forgotten?
  6. Which part of your region's history do you most want me to remember, and why?

Listen for: names that connect to the Mughal Empire, the Delhi Sultanate, the Vijayanagara Empire or the Sri Lankan Kingdoms; stories about saints that connect to Sufism, the Bhakti Movement or Guru Nanak; and memories of trading towns that link to Indian Ocean Trade.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Find the building your elder named in this chapter or in the Empire Swim Lanes sim. Does their story about who built it match the historical dates? If a friend interviewed someone from a different region, place both buildings on the swim lanes. Were they built under the same power, or under two powers that existed at the same time?

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Islam arrived in South Asia only by conquest. Reality: Muslim traders were living on the coasts of Kerala and Sri Lanka by the 7th and 8th centuries, the Maldives became Muslim after its king converted in the 12th century, and Sufi teachers drew many followers in Punjab, Sindh and Bengal. Conquest was one route among several.

Myth: The Mughals ruled all of South Asia. Reality: Even at its largest, under Aurangzeb, the Mughal Empire never included Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan or the Maldives, and many regional kings inside it kept real power. For most of the Mughal period other powers, such as the Deccan sultanates, the Kingdom of Kandy, the Portuguese and later the Marathas, existed alongside it.

Myth: The Taj Mahal is a palace. Reality: The Taj Mahal is a mausoleum, a tomb built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who is buried there. Shah Jahan was later buried beside her.

Myth: The East India Company was the British government. Reality: It was a private company owned by investors, with a royal charter to trade. It later built armies and ruled territory, and Parliament increasingly regulated it, but it only handed India over to direct rule by the British Crown in 1858.

Myth: Each empire neatly replaced the one before it. Reality: Powers overlapped for decades or centuries. The Delhi Sultanate, the Bengal Sultanate, Vijayanagara, the Bahmani Sultanate and the Kingdom of Kandy all existed in the 1400s at the same time.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What natural pattern made long-distance Indian Ocean Trade possible?

The monsoon winds, which blow from the southwest for part of the year and from the northeast for the rest, so sailors could travel one way and return months later.

2. Name two Chola achievements.

Rajaraja I built the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur (1003 to 1010), and Rajendra I built a new capital at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and sent a navy to Southeast Asia.

3. What do the Bhakti Movement and Sufism have in common, and how are they different?

Both stress personal, loving devotion to God, often through poetry and music in local languages. Bhakti grew within Hinduism, while Sufism is a tradition within Islam.

4. Why is Akbar remembered for his religious policies?

He included Hindu Rajput nobles in his government, held debates among scholars of many faiths at the Ibadat Khana, followed a policy of "universal peace" (sulh-i kul), and had Sanskrit works translated into Persian.

5. In what year was the English East India Company chartered, and what kind of organization was it?

It received its royal charter on 31 December 1600. It was a private trading company owned by investors, not the British government.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in order.

    Answer

    Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi (1206 to 1526).

  2. Who founded the Durrani Empire, and in what year?

    Answer

    Ahmad Shah Durrani founded it in 1747, with its capital at Kandahar.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain in your own words what Indo-Persian Culture means, with two examples you could find in a South Asian family today.

    Answer

    It is the blend of Persian and South Asian languages, art, food and manners that grew in Muslim-ruled courts. Examples include Hindustani words in Hindi and Urdu, biryani and kebabs, qawwali music, and buildings with domes and arches.

  2. Explain why Arjun's grandmother says Hyderabad was built by the Qutb Shahis, not the Mughals.

    Answer

    Hyderabad was founded by Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda, who built the Charminar in 1591. The Mughals only conquered Golconda in 1687, almost a century later.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Empire Swim Lanes sim to find a year when at least one power was active in every one of these regions: Sri Lanka, the Deccan, North India and the coast (European companies). Write the year and list the powers. Hint: try years between 1500 and 1650.

  2. A cousin visiting Lahore sends you photos of the Badshahi Mosque and the Lahore Fort. Write a three-sentence caption for each photo, using dates from this chapter. Hint: the fort and the mosque were built under different emperors.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire. Give two similarities and two differences. Hint: think about dates, founders, capitals, language and how they ended.

  2. The chapter says Islam reached South Asia "through trade, through teachers and holy men, and through conquest." Analyze which of these routes mattered most in Kerala, in Sindh and in the Maldives, using evidence from the chapter. Hint: different regions had different first contacts.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Some people call Akbar "the Great" because of his tolerance, while others point out that he was a conqueror. Write a short paragraph evaluating whether "Akbar the Great" is a fair title, using evidence from both sides. Hint: a strong answer can agree with part of each view.

  2. A website says, "The British conquered India in 1600." Evaluate this claim. What is right and wrong about it, and how would you rewrite it accurately? Hint: who received the charter in 1600, and what was it allowed to do?

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Draw your own swim-lane timeline for your family's home region (or another region you choose) from 1000 to 1800. Include at least four powers, with start and end dates, and one building for each. Hint: the Empire Swim Lanes sim and the Sri Lanka table are good models.

  2. Write a short dialogue (150 to 200 words) between a Persian-speaking official at the Mughal court and a Portuguese merchant in Goa in 1600, each explaining what they want from the other. Hint: use at least three concept labels from this chapter.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Between about 600 and 1800, South Asia was shared by many powers at once. History in this period looks like parallel lanes, not a relay race.
  • Indian Ocean Trade, powered by the monsoon winds, linked South Asia's ports with Africa, Arabia and Southeast Asia, and carried goods, people and faiths, including early Islam.
  • In the south, the Chola Dynasty and the Vijayanagara Empire built great temples and cities. In Sri Lanka, Sinhala and Tamil kingdoms ruled side by side until the Kingdom of Kandy fell in 1815.
  • The Delhi Sultanate (1206 to 1526) and the Mughal Empire (1526 to 1857) spread Indo-Persian Culture, from the Hindustani language to buildings like the Taj Mahal, a tomb built for Mumtaz Mahal.
  • The Bhakti Movement, Sufism and the teachings of Guru Nanak brought devotion to ordinary people in their own languages.
  • As the Mughal Empire weakened after 1707, the Maratha Empire and the Durrani Empire rose, and clashed at Panipat in 1761.
  • European Traders arrived by sea from 1498. The East India Company, a private company chartered in 1600, would later turn from trader to ruler.

You can read the lanes!

You can now explain how many powers shared South Asia, and why your family's favorite old building might belong to a dynasty you'd never heard of. Next, in Chapter 4, the trading company becomes a ruler, and South Asia's road to independence and Partition begins.

docs.title: Quiz: Empires and Encounters
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 3. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
In what year was the Delhi Sultanate established?

  1. 1206
  2. 1336
  3. 1526
  4. 1747
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206 and lasted until 1526. The year 1526 is when Babur founded the Mughal Empire, which is why it's a tempting distractor. The year 1336 is the founding of Vijayanagara, and 1747 is the founding of the Durrani Empire.

Concept Tested: Delhi Sultanate Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
What is the Taj Mahal?

  1. A royal palace where Shah Jahan lived with his family
  2. A Sufi shrine built for Moinuddin Chishti
  3. A white marble tomb built by order of Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal
  4. A fort built by Akbar to guard Agra
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The Taj Mahal is a mausoleum, built in Agra between about 1631 and 1648. Many people think it is a palace because of its size and beauty, but it was built as a tomb, and both Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan are buried there.

Concept Tested: Taj Mahal Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which teacher, born in 1469 in Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan), do Sikhs honor as the founder of their faith?

  1. Kabir
  2. Guru Nanak
  3. Nizamuddin Auliya
  4. Basavanna
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539) is the first of the ten Sikh Gurus. Kabir is a common distractor because some of his verses are in the Sikh scripture, but he was a separate poet-saint of the bhakti tradition.

Concept Tested: Guru Nanak Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why were the monsoon winds so important to Indian Ocean Trade?

  1. They blew from the same direction all year, so ships could sail quickly in one direction only.
  2. They kept pirates away from the coasts of South Asia.
  3. They brought rain that filled the harbors so large ships could enter.
  4. They reversed direction with the seasons, so sailors could travel out on one wind and return on the other.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The monsoon winds blow from the southwest for part of the year and from the northeast for the rest, which let ships make round trips across the ocean. Option A gets the key idea backwards: it's the reversal that made return voyages possible.

Concept Tested: Indian Ocean Trade Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Which statement best describes how Islam first reached South Asia?

  1. Through several routes over centuries, including traders on the coasts, Sufi teachers and conquest in the northwest
  2. Only through the Mughal conquest in 1526
  3. Only through Arab armies that conquered the whole subcontinent in 711
  4. Through European traders who arrived after 1498
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Muslim traders settled on the Kerala and Sri Lankan coasts very early, the Maldives' king converted in the 12th century, Arab forces conquered Sindh around 711 to 712, and Sufi teachers drew many followers. Option C is wrong because the 711 conquest covered Sindh, not the whole subcontinent.

Concept Tested: Early Islam in South Asia Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
What does the term Indo-Persian Culture refer to?

  1. The culture of Persian immigrants who lived only in Iran
  2. A blend of Persian and South Asian language, art, architecture, food and music that grew in Muslim-ruled courts and cities of South Asia
  3. A religion that combined Hinduism and Islam into one faith
  4. The European style of buildings brought by the East India Company
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Indo-Persian Culture includes things like the Hindustani language (ancestor of Hindi and Urdu), Mughal architecture and painting, and court cooking. It was a culture shared by people of many faiths, not a new religion, so C is wrong.

Concept Tested: Indo-Persian Culture Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Ayesha shows a photo of the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, and Arjun shows the Charminar in Hyderabad. Using the chapter, which statement about the two buildings is correct?

  1. Both were built by the Mughal emperor Akbar.
  2. Both were built by the Delhi Sultanate.
  3. The Charminar was built by the Qutb Shahi sultan of Golconda in 1591, and the Badshahi Mosque by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in 1671 to 1673.
  4. The Charminar was built by the Vijayanagara Empire, and the Badshahi Mosque by the Durrani Empire.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The two buildings come from two different powers that existed at the same time: the Qutb Shahis ruled Golconda until the Mughals conquered it in 1687. Assuming every Muslim-built monument is Mughal (option A) is exactly the mistake the chapter warns about.

Concept Tested: Mughal Empire Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
A classmate says, "In 1600, the British government took over India." Which correction is most accurate?

  1. In 1600 the Portuguese took over India, not the British.
  2. In 1600 the Mughal Empire invited the British government to rule Bengal.
  3. In 1600 the Dutch East India Company conquered Sri Lanka.
  4. In 1600 the East India Company, a private English trading company, received a royal charter to trade in Asia; it did not rule territory yet.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The East India Company was a private business chartered on 31 December 1600. For more than a century it traded with the permission of Mughal emperors and regional rulers. The Portuguese (option A) held Goa from 1510, but they never took over South Asia as a whole.

Concept Tested: East India Company Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Using the Empire Swim Lanes idea, which pair of powers existed at the same time?

  1. The Chola Dynasty and the Mughal Empire
  2. The Vijayanagara Empire and the Bengal Sultanate
  3. The Delhi Sultanate and the Maratha Empire
  4. The Anuradhapura Kingdom and the Durrani Empire
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Vijayanagara (1336 to 1646) and the Bengal Sultanate (1352 to 1576) overlapped for more than two centuries. The Cholas ended by 1279, long before the Mughals began in 1526, and the Delhi Sultanate ended in 1526, long before Shivaji's coronation in 1674.

Concept Tested: Vijayanagara Empire Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
What do the Bhakti Movement and Sufism have in common?

  1. Both are branches of Sikhism founded by Guru Nanak.
  2. Both rejected music and poetry as distractions from prayer.
  3. Both emphasized personal, loving devotion to God, often through poetry and music in local languages, within their own faith traditions.
  4. Both were started by the Mughal emperor Akbar to unite his empire.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Bhakti grew within Hinduism and Sufism within Islam, but both focused on devotion and used songs and poetry, such as bhajans and qawwali. They are separate traditions, so they are not branches of Sikhism (A), and both began centuries before Akbar (D).

Concept Tested: Sufism Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Empires and Encounters
docs.text:
1. Mughal dynasty - Encyclopaedia Britannica - A full overview of the Mughal Empire from 1526 to 1857, with sections on each major emperor, government, trade, architecture and the empire's decline. Good for checking dates and names.

  2. The Art of the Mughals before 1600 - The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History - A short museum essay on Babur, Humayun and Akbar, with images of paintings made by Akbar's mixed team of Persian, Muslim and Hindu artists. It shows Indo-Persian culture in action.

  3. Taj Mahal - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - The official World Heritage listing, with the building dates (1631 to 1648), the reason it was listed in 1983, and photos and maps.

  4. Group of Monuments at Hampi - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Describes the last capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, its temples and palaces, and what happened to the city after the Battle of Talikota in 1565.

  5. Great Living Chola Temples - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Covers the three Chola temples at Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram, including the temple Rajendra I completed in 1035.

  6. Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - The listing for the 15th-century city founded by Ulugh Khan Jahan in present-day Bangladesh, home of the Sixty Dome Mosque.

  7. Fort and Shalamar Gardens in Lahore - UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Explains why Lahore's Mughal fort and gardens, from the reign of Shah Jahan, are World Heritage sites in Pakistan.

  8. East India Company and Raj 1785-1858 - UK Parliament, Living Heritage - Shows how the British Parliament gradually took control of the East India Company by renewing its charter only for twenty years at a time. Useful for understanding that the Company and the government were not the same thing.

  9. Aurangzeb: Mughal Emperor - Origins: Current Events in Historical Perspective, The Ohio State University (2023) - A historian explains why Aurangzeb's memory divides people today, from those who see him as a model Muslim ruler to those who see him as a villain. Supports the Whose Story? box.

  10. Ahmad Shah Durrani - Encyclopaedia Britannica - Calls him the founder of the state of Afghanistan and describes his repeated invasions of north India, his wars with the Sikhs in Punjab, and his victory over the Marathas at Panipat in 1761.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Between 1757 and 1947, Britain went from running a trading company in Bengal to ruling most of South Asia. This chapter follows that story: the battle that gave the East India Company its first big territory, the revolt of 1857, the British Raj and the princely states, and the freedom movements that pushed Britain out. It then explains the Partition of 1947, which created India and Pakistan and forced millions of people from their homes, and the events that led to Sri Lanka's independence in 1948 and Bangladesh's in 1971. By the end you'll be able to explain how one colonial territory became several nations in separate steps, and why families on different sides of those borders remember the same years so differently.

docs.text:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia? for the eight countries, the rivers and the Bay of Bengal.
  • Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters, especially the Mughal Empire, the European traders and the East India Company.

A hard chapter, and an important one

Hi, I'm Mora! The years in this chapter, 1947 and 1971 most of all, still shape where many South Asian families live, which flag they salute and which stories they tell at dinner. Some of what you'll read is painful, so go slowly, and remember that real people lived every line of it. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 4.1 Three Countries, One House
docs.text:
It's a snowy Sunday, and Zara Hossain is helping her Nanu (her mother's mother) sort a box of old photographs for the South Asian Student Association's first "Family History Night." Ben Lindqvist, her best friend, is sitting on the floor of the Hossains' living room, carefully flattening a photo of a tin-roofed house surrounded by banana trees.

"That's my mother's house," Nanu says in Bangla, tapping the picture. "Near Chattogram. She was born there, she grew up there, and she died there." Then she switches to English, for Ben. "She was born in India. She grew up in Pakistan. And she died in Bangladesh."

Ben looks up. "So she moved a lot?"

"Never," says Nanu. "Not once. The countries moved around her."

Zara laughs, then stops. She knows Bangladesh became independent in 1971. She has heard her parents talk about "1947." But she can't explain how one woman could live in three countries without ever leaving her house. Who drew the lines, when, and why did they keep changing?

docs.title: 4.2 When the Map Changes Around You
docs.text:
Ben has a version of this in his own family history. For most of the 1800s, Norway was joined to Sweden under the Swedish king. In 1905 the union ended peacefully and Norway became fully independent. A Norwegian farmer who never left his farm went from one country to another without packing a bag.

South Asia's borders changed in a similar way, but on a much larger scale and, in 1947 and 1971, with terrible violence. Here is the short version of what happened to the land around Nanu's mother's house:

Year What the area near Chattogram was part of Before 1947 British India (the province of Bengal) 1947 to 1971 Pakistan (first called East Bengal, later East Pakistan) 1971 onward Bangladesh

To see how that happened, we have to start almost two hundred years earlier, with a trading company that became a government.

docs.title: 4.3 From Traders to Rulers
docs.text: In Chapter 3, you met the East India Company, a private English (later British) business that came to South Asia in the 1600s to buy cotton cloth, spices, indigo and tea. For more than a century it was one of many foreign trading companies, working with the permission of Mughal emperors and regional rulers. That changed in Bengal.

docs.title: The Battle of Plassey, 1757
docs.text:
The Battle of Plassey was the battle on 23 June 1757, near the village of Plassey (Palashi) in Bengal, in which the East India Company's forces, led by Robert Clive, defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab (ruler) of Bengal. The Company won mostly because the Nawab's own commander, Mir Jafar, made a secret deal with the British and kept his troops out of the fight. Afterward, the Company made Mir Jafar the new Nawab.

Plassey matters because of what came next. Bengal was one of the richest provinces in South Asia, and after Plassey the Company dominated its government and used its tax revenue for its own purposes. From this base the Company fought, signed treaties with, and took over one region after another for the next hundred years. Many historians treat 1757 as the start of British rule in South Asia, even though most of the region was not yet under British control.

docs.title: The Revolt of 1857
docs.text:
By the 1850s, the Company ruled large parts of the subcontinent and had a huge army made up mostly of Indian soldiers, called sepoys. Anger had been building for years: about land taxes, about the Company taking over kingdoms whose rulers died without a son, and about new rules in the army. The spark was a new rifle cartridge that soldiers believed was greased with cow and pig fat, which would offend both Hindu and Muslim soldiers.

The Revolt of 1857 was a large uprising against Company rule that began on 10 May 1857, when sepoys at Meerut, a town about 64 km (40 miles) northeast of Delhi, mutinied and marched to Delhi. There they declared the elderly Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, their leader. The revolt spread across much of northern and central India. Soldiers, peasants, landlords and some rulers joined, including Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, a queen who fought on horseback and is still remembered as a hero in India. Both sides committed massacres. By 1858, British forces had crushed the revolt, often with brutal reprisals against whole villages.

Even its name is debated. British writers long called it the "Sepoy Mutiny," a soldiers' revolt. Many Indians call it the "First War of Independence," the start of a national struggle, though some historians question that label because the rebels did not share one plan. This book uses the neutral name "Revolt of 1857."

docs.title: The British Raj
docs.text:
The revolt convinced the British Parliament that a private company should not govern millions of people. The Government of India Act, passed on 2 August 1858, ended Company rule and transferred its territory and army to the British Crown.

The British Raj (Raj means "rule" in Hindi-Urdu) is the name for direct rule of South Asia by the British Crown, from 1858 to 1947. A Viceroy, appointed in London, governed from Calcutta (now Kolkata) and later from New Delhi. In 1876, Queen Victoria was given the title "Empress of India." A small number of British officials ran it, relying on huge numbers of Indian clerks, police and soldiers.

Same company, two chapters

Notice the hand-off: from 1757 to 1858 a company ruled, and from 1858 to 1947 a government did. When your family says "the British," which of those two do you think they mean, and does it change the story?

docs.title: 4.4 A Patchwork, Not a Single Colony
docs.text: On a map of "British India" from 1900, it can look like one solid block of British pink. It wasn't. The Raj was really a patchwork.

docs.title: The princely states
docs.text:
Princely States were the hundreds of kingdoms inside British-controlled South Asia that kept their own Indian rulers (called maharajas, nawabs, nizams and other titles) but accepted British control over their defense and foreign relations through treaties. At the time Britain left, there were officially about 565 of them. Some were tiny, a few villages. Others were huge: Hyderabad, ruled by a Nizam, and Jammu and Kashmir, ruled by a Maharaja, were each larger than many European countries. In 1947, princely states covered about 40 percent of the land of pre-independence India and held about 23 percent of its people.

That detail becomes very important in 1947, when every one of those princes had to decide what to do.

docs.title: The neighbors Britain never fully ruled
docs.text:
Several of today's South Asian countries were never formally colonized, though Britain still shaped their history.

  • Afghanistan. Britain feared that the Russian Empire, expanding in Central Asia, would use Afghanistan as a route to India. This rivalry led to the Anglo-Afghan Wars, three wars Britain fought in Afghanistan: 1839 to 1842, 1878 to 1880, and 1919. In the first, a British army was destroyed during its retreat from Kabul. After the second, Britain controlled Afghanistan's foreign affairs, though not its internal government. After the third war in 1919, the Treaty of Rawalpindi recognized Afghanistan's full independence in foreign affairs. Afghans remember 1919 as the year they won back control of their own foreign relations.
  • Nepal. After a war with the Company, Nepal signed the Treaty of Sugauli in 1816 and gave up some territory, but it remained an independent kingdom.
  • Bhutan. Under the Treaty of Punakha in 1910, Bhutan agreed to be guided by Britain in its foreign relations, while keeping its own king and internal rule.
  • Ceylon (today's Sri Lanka) was a British colony, but it was run separately from British India, with its own governor.
  • The Maldives became a British protectorate in 1887. It kept its own sultan, and Britain handled its defense and foreign affairs.

docs.title: 4.5 Life Under the Raj and the Bengal Famine of 1943
docs.text:
What did British rule mean for ordinary people? Historians still argue about the balance. The Raj built railways, universities and courts, but decisions were made in London, most people had no vote, and many historians argue that colonial policies drained wealth from the region and weakened older industries such as handloom weaving.

One of the worst disasters of colonial rule was the famine in Bengal during the Second World War.

The Bengal Famine of 1943 was a famine in the province of Bengal (today's Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal) and parts of neighboring Orissa (now Odisha) during the Second World War, when a very large number of people died of starvation and of diseases such as malaria that spread among people weakened by hunger. Estimates of the death toll vary widely, from about 800,000 to as many as 3.8 million. The economic historian Cormac Ó Gráda describes the scholarly consensus as about 2.1 million deaths.

Several causes came together:

  • Japan had occupied Burma (now Myanmar) in 1942, cutting off rice imports that Bengal depended on.
  • War spending caused prices to rise sharply, and farm workers' wages did not keep up, so poor families could not afford rice even where it existed.
  • Fearing a Japanese invasion, the government removed or destroyed boats and rice stocks in coastal areas, a "denial policy" that hurt local fishermen and traders.
  • Officials were slow to declare a famine, and wartime priorities, including the use of ships for war supplies rather than food, slowed relief.

Historians weigh these causes differently, but most agree that government decisions, in London and in Bengal, made the disaster far worse. For many people in Bengal, it showed why they wanted to govern themselves.

docs.title: 4.6 Organizing for Freedom
docs.text: The movement to end British rule lasted about sixty years and took many forms, including petitions, marches, strikes and armed revolt. These were the main organizations and leaders.

docs.title: Two political parties
docs.text:
The Indian National Congress is a political party founded on 28 December 1885, at a meeting in Bombay (now Mumbai), that became the largest organization in the movement for independence from Britain. It grew from a small group of professionals into a mass movement. It wanted a single, independent India for people of all religions, and many of its leaders, such as Jawaharlal Nehru, became leaders of independent India. The Congress still exists today as a political party in India.

The All-India Muslim League was a political party founded in 1906 in Dhaka to represent the political interests of Muslims in British India. Muslims were about a quarter of British India's population, and many Muslim leaders worried that in a democracy with a large Hindu majority, their community's rights, jobs and culture would not be protected. For decades the League asked for safeguards inside a united India. In 1940, at a meeting in Lahore, it adopted the Lahore Resolution (later called the Pakistan Resolution), which called for independent states in the Muslim-majority areas of the northwest and the east. Pakistan marks 23 March each year as Pakistan Day in memory of that resolution.

docs.title: Mahatma Gandhi and satyagraha
docs.text:
Mahatma Gandhi (Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, 1869 to 1948) was a lawyer from Porbandar, in present-day Gujarat, who became the most famous leader of the Indian independence movement by leading mass campaigns of nonviolent resistance. Mahatma is an honorific from Sanskrit meaning "great soul." Gandhi first developed his methods in South Africa, where he lived from 1893 and fought discrimination against Indians there. He returned to India in 1915 and soon became the leading figure in the Congress.

Gandhi called his method Satyagraha (સત્યાગ્રહ, SUT-yaa-gruh), "holding firmly to truth" or "truth force": nonviolent resistance in which people openly refuse to obey unjust laws, accept the punishment, and try to win over their opponents rather than defeat them. The word comes from Gujarati, Gandhi's first language, combining satya (truth) and agraha (insistence).

The most famous example is the Salt March. The British government held a monopoly on salt and taxed it, which hit the poorest people hardest. On 12 March 1930, Gandhi and 78 followers set out from his ashram near Ahmedabad and walked about 387 km (240 miles) to the seaside village of Dandi. Crowds joined along the way. On 6 April 1930, Gandhi picked up natural salt from the shore, breaking the law. Across India, people began making and selling salt, and tens of thousands were arrested.

In August 1942, during the Second World War, Gandhi and the Congress launched the Quit India Movement, demanding that Britain leave immediately. Its main leaders were arrested almost at once.

Gandhi's ideas later inspired civil rights movements around the world, and Martin Luther King Jr. in the United States drew on them. Gandhi also opposed Partition. On 30 January 1948, a few months after independence, he was shot and killed at a prayer meeting in Delhi by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist.

Not only nonviolence

Gandhi's campaigns were huge, but freedom did not come only from nonviolence. Revolutionaries such as Bhagat Singh, the Indian National Army led by Subhas Chandra Bose, strikes, elections, and Britain's exhaustion after the Second World War all played a part, and historians still debate how much each mattered.

docs.title: B. R. Ambedkar: whose freedom?
docs.text:
B. R. Ambedkar (Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar, 1891 to 1956) was a lawyer, economist and political leader, born into a Dalit family (a community that faced "untouchability," the most severe form of caste discrimination), who fought for the rights of Dalits and chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution. As a boy he was segregated from other students at school. He went on to earn doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics.

Ambedkar asked a question many other leaders preferred to skip: if India became free of Britain, would Dalits become free inside India? He clashed with Gandhi in 1932 over whether Dalits should elect their own representatives separately. Gandhi went on a fast against the idea, and the two men reached a compromise, the Poona Pact, which reserved seats for Dalits instead.

After independence, Ambedkar became India's first law minister and chaired the Constitution's Drafting Committee. The Constitution, which came into effect on 26 January 1950, includes Article 17, which abolished "untouchability" and made its practice a crime. In 1956, shortly before his death, Ambedkar and a very large number of his followers converted to Buddhism, which he saw as a path free of caste. Today he is honored across India, and especially by Dalit communities, often as "Babasaheb." You'll read more about caste in Chapter 13.

docs.title: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
docs.text:
Muhammad Ali Jinnah (1876 to 1948) was a lawyer from Karachi who led the All-India Muslim League and became the founder and first Governor-General of Pakistan. Early in his career Jinnah was a member of the Congress and worked for Hindu-Muslim cooperation. Over time he concluded that Muslims needed their own homeland to protect their political future. His argument, often called the "two-nation theory," was that Muslims and Hindus in South Asia were two nations with their own religions, cultures and histories. In Pakistan he is honored as Quaid-e-Azam, "the Great Leader." He died on 11 September 1948, about a year after Pakistan's creation.

Leader Organization What he wanted for South Asia Mahatma Gandhi Indian National Congress A free, united India, won through nonviolent mass action Muhammad Ali Jinnah All-India Muslim League By 1940, a separate homeland for Muslims in the Muslim-majority regions B. R. Ambedkar Dalit political organizations; later chaired the Constitution's Drafting Committee Freedom from Britain together with equal rights and protections for Dalits

docs.title: 4.7 The Partition of 1947
docs.text: By the end of the Second World War, Britain was exhausted and in debt, and its government had decided to leave South Asia. The question was no longer whether Britain would go, but what it would leave behind: one country or more than one.

docs.title: The road to Partition
docs.text:
In 1946, a British Cabinet Mission tried to design a loose federation that would keep India united while protecting Muslim-majority provinces. The plan fell apart because the Congress and the Muslim League didn't trust each other. Jinnah called for 16 August 1946 to be "Direct Action Day," to press the demand for Pakistan. That day, riots broke out in Calcutta, and over the following days large numbers of people, Hindus and Muslims both, were killed. The violence spread: to Noakhali in eastern Bengal, where Muslims attacked Hindus; to Bihar, where Hindus attacked Muslims; and in March 1947 to Rawalpindi in the Punjab, where Hindus and Sikhs were attacked.

In March 1947, Lord Louis Mountbatten arrived as the last Viceroy. On 3 June 1947, he announced the plan: British India would be divided into two independent countries, and power would be handed over in August, much earlier than expected.

docs.title: What Partition was
docs.text:
The Partition of 1947 was the division of British India into two independent countries, India and Pakistan, in August 1947, largely along religious lines: Muslim-majority areas became Pakistan and the rest became India. The British Parliament passed the Indian Independence Act on 18 July 1947. Pakistan celebrates its independence on 14 August, and India celebrates on 15 August.

Pakistan was created in two parts, with India in between:

  • West Pakistan, made up of Sindh, Baluchistan, the North-West Frontier Province and the western half of Punjab.
  • East Pakistan (first called East Bengal), made up of the eastern half of Bengal and the Sylhet district of Assam. It had more people than the western wing: about 44 million of Pakistan's 69 million people lived there, and most of them spoke Bangla.

India was not created as a "Hindu country." Its leaders built a secular state, meaning it would not have an official religion, and many millions of Muslims stayed in India.

Two provinces, Punjab in the northwest and Bengal in the east, had populations that were roughly half Muslim and half non-Muslim. They could not simply be handed to one side. They had to be cut in two.

Whose Story?

The same August is remembered very differently. In Pakistan, 14 August is above all a day of celebration: the birth of a homeland, achieved under Jinnah's leadership. In India, 15 August is Independence Day, the end of colonial rule won by a long freedom struggle, and Partition is often remembered as the price of that freedom. For millions of Punjabi and Bengali families on both sides, especially Sikh and Hindu families who left West Punjab and Muslim families who left East Punjab, 1947 is remembered first as the year they lost their homes. Many British accounts once focused on the "transfer of power" and Mountbatten's speed, while more recent historians, on all sides, have centered the voices of ordinary survivors, including women, whose stories were missing from the official record.

docs.title: The Radcliffe Line
docs.text:
Someone had to decide where the new borders would run through Punjab and Bengal. The British appointed Sir Cyril Radcliffe, a London lawyer who, according to many accounts, had never visited India before. He arrived on 8 July 1947 and had about five weeks to divide two provinces home to tens of millions of people. He chaired two boundary commissions, each with members chosen by the Congress and the Muslim League, who usually disagreed, leaving the final decisions to him.

The Radcliffe Line is the boundary Radcliffe drew to divide the provinces of Punjab and Bengal between India and Pakistan in 1947. It was based mainly on which districts had Muslim or non-Muslim majorities, though Radcliffe could also weigh "other factors" such as canals, railways and roads. No line could separate the communities neatly. The Punjab was home to many Sikhs, whose holiest sites and farmland lay on both sides.

The Line was published on 17 August 1947, two days after independence. That meant many people celebrated freedom without knowing which country their village was in. Today the Punjab part of the Radcliffe Line is part of the India-Pakistan border, and the Bengal part is the India-Bangladesh border.

docs.title: Partition migration
docs.text:
As the new borders became known and violence spread, huge numbers of people began to move.

Partition Migration is the movement of millions of people across the new India-Pakistan borders in 1947 and the years after: Hindus and Sikhs moving into India, and Muslims moving into Pakistan. In Punjab, the migration was concentrated into a few terrible months. People traveled on foot in columns many kilometers long, on bullock carts and on overcrowded trains. In Bengal, the movement was slower and continued for years and even decades.

Historians don't know the exact numbers, and the estimates differ. Here's what the sources say:

  • People displaced: Stanford Libraries' Partition guide gives about 14 million refugees. A study based on census records (Bharadwaj, Khwaja and Mian, 2008) estimated about 14.5 million people arriving in the new countries and about 17.9 million leaving, which leaves about 3.4 million people unaccounted for. So a fair range is about 14 million to 18 million people displaced.
  • Deaths: Estimates range from about 200,000 to 2 million people killed. No one counted at the time, and many deaths were never recorded.

People were killed in every community. Hindus and Sikhs were attacked in areas that became Pakistan, and Muslims were attacked in areas that became India. Trains arrived carrying people who had been killed on the way. Tens of thousands of women were kidnapped and assaulted. After Partition, India and Pakistan each claimed that tens of thousands of women from their communities had been abducted and agreed to try to return them. There were also many acts of courage: neighbors who hid families of another faith, and villages that protected their minorities.

Survivors rebuilt their lives in new cities. Refugees from West Punjab helped reshape Delhi, and refugees from East Punjab helped reshape Lahore and Karachi, while Bengali Hindu refugees settled in and around Kolkata. Many never saw their childhood homes again. Today the 1947 Partition Archive and other projects record survivors' memories before they are lost.

If this feels heavy

It's okay if these numbers feel hard to hold. Historians use ranges here because every number stands for people who were never counted, and it's fine to take a break before reading on.

docs.title: The princely states choose
docs.text:
When Britain left, its treaties with the princes ended. In theory each prince could join India, join Pakistan, or stay independent. In practice, leaders on both sides, especially India's Vallabhbhai Patel, pressed them to join, and most did so by August 1947, largely based on geography.

A few did not. Hyderabad, the largest princely state, had a Muslim ruler, the Nizam, and a mostly Hindu population, and it was surrounded by Indian territory. The Nizam wanted to remain independent. In September 1948, Indian troops entered Hyderabad in a military operation and the state became part of India.

docs.title: 4.8 The Kashmir Dispute
docs.text:
The hardest case of all was Jammu and Kashmir, a large princely state in the far north, touching both India and Pakistan. Its population was mostly Muslim, but its ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh, was Hindu. He delayed choosing a side.

In October 1947, armed tribesmen from Pakistan's northwest, supported by Pakistan, entered Kashmir. The Maharaja asked India for military help and, in late October 1947, signed an Instrument of Accession joining India. Indian troops arrived, and the first war between India and Pakistan followed. A ceasefire arranged by the United Nations took effect on 1 January 1949. The ceasefire line became, after another war and the 1972 Simla Agreement, the Line of Control that still divides the region.

The Kashmir Dispute is the continuing disagreement, mainly between India and Pakistan, over who should control the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. Each side states its position this way:

  • India's position: the Maharaja's Instrument of Accession was legal and final, so the whole former state is part of India.
  • Pakistan's position: the accession was not valid, the region's Muslim majority should have joined Pakistan, and the people of Kashmir should decide their future through a vote, as early United Nations resolutions called for.
  • Many Kashmiris have their own views, which differ from region to region and person to person: some favor India, some Pakistan, and some want independence or more self-rule.

China also controls part of the wider Kashmir region, including Aksai Chin, which India claims. Today India controls roughly 55 percent of the region's land, Pakistan about 30 percent, and China about 15 percent. The dispute has led to several wars and much loss of life, and as of 2026 it remains unresolved. This book describes Kashmir as disputed and does not take a side, which is also why its maps never draw official borders.

docs.title: 4.9 Sri Lankan Independence
docs.text:
Sri Lankan Independence is the peaceful transfer of power from Britain to the island then called Ceylon, which became an independent country on 4 February 1948. Britain granted it under the Ceylon Independence Act of 1947, after years of negotiation, with no partition and none of the mass violence seen in Punjab and Bengal. Don Stephen Senanayake became the first prime minister. For its first years, the country stayed closely tied to Britain, which kept military bases there, and the British monarch remained head of state. In 1972, Ceylon became a republic and changed its name to Sri Lanka.

Sri Lanka's later history had its own deep conflicts, including a long civil war covered in Chapter 19, but independence itself was quiet. Sri Lankans celebrate 4 February as Independence Day.

The Maldives followed a different path again. It had been a British protectorate, not a colony, and became fully independent on 26 July 1965.

docs.title: 4.10 From the Language Movement to Bangladesh
docs.text: Now we come back to Nanu's mother's house near Chattogram. In 1947 it became part of East Pakistan. Why did East Pakistan become a separate country only 24 years later?

docs.title: The Language Movement of 1952
docs.text:
Pakistan's two wings shared a religion, Islam, but differed in language, food, dress and history. In 1948, Pakistan's government announced that Urdu, a language most people in East Bengal did not speak at home, would be the only national language. Bengalis protested, because most of Pakistan's people spoke Bangla.

The Language Movement of 1952 was a protest movement in East Bengal demanding that Bangla be recognized as a national language of Pakistan, which reached its peak on 21 February 1952, when police in Dhaka opened fire on student protesters and killed several of them. Those killed are honored in Bangladesh as Language Martyrs, and the Shaheed Minar (Martyrs' Monument) in Dhaka stands in their memory. In 1956, Pakistan's first constitution recognized Bangla as an official language alongside Urdu.

In Bangladesh, 21 February, often called Ekushey ("the twenty-first"), is a national day of mourning and pride. In 1999, UNESCO declared 21 February International Mother Language Day, an idea that came from Bangladesh, and it has been observed around the world since 2000.

docs.title: The Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971
docs.text:
That didn't solve the deeper problem. Many East Pakistanis felt that the western wing controlled the government, the army and much of the money, though the east had more people. The Awami League, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, demanded much more self-government for the east.

In the December 1970 national elections, the Awami League won 167 of East Pakistan's 169 seats, which gave it a majority in Pakistan's whole National Assembly. Pakistan's military government did not hand over power, and talks failed. On the night of 25 March 1971, the Pakistani army launched a military crackdown, called Operation Searchlight, in Dhaka and across the east.

The Bangladesh Liberation War was the 1971 war in which East Pakistan fought for and won independence from Pakistan, becoming Bangladesh. In Bangla it is called মুক্তিযুদ্ধ (MOOK-tee-jud-dho), Muktijuddho, "liberation war." Bangladesh's independence was declared on 26 March 1971, which Bangladesh celebrates as Independence Day. Bengali fighters, called the Mukti Bahini ("liberation force"), fought a guerrilla war. About 10 million refugees fled to India. On 3 December 1971, war broke out openly between India and Pakistan, and India's army joined the fight in the east. The Pakistani army in the east surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December 1971, which Bangladesh celebrates as Victory Day.

The human cost was enormous, and the numbers are disputed:

  • Deaths: most estimates range from about 300,000 to 3 million. Bangladesh's official figure is 3 million. Some researchers give lower figures, and there is no complete count.
  • Refugees: about 10 million people fled to India, where crowded camps had high death rates of their own.
  • Pakistani soldiers and allied militias killed large numbers of civilians, including students, teachers and the Hindu minority, and committed widespread sexual violence against women. Many Bangladeshis and many scholars describe these killings as a genocide.
  • There was also violence against Urdu-speaking Biharis (Muslims who had moved from India to East Pakistan around 1947), many of whom were seen as supporting Pakistan and were killed or driven from their homes by Bengali fighters and crowds.

So the answer to Zara's puzzle is that Bangladesh was not created by Partition. It was created in a second, separate event in 1971. Partition made the area part of Pakistan, and the Liberation War made it Bangladesh.

Two events, not one

Try saying the whole sequence out loud: British India in 1946, East Pakistan in 1947, Bangladesh in 1971. Which step was decided by a line drawn in an office, and which was decided by the people living there?

docs.title: Diagram: Borders Then and Now
docs.text:
Open the Borders Then and Now fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Borders Then and Now

sim-id: ch04-borders-then-and-now Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain how one colonial territory, British India, became several nations in separate steps (1947 and 1971), and how Ceylon and the princely states fit into that story.

Canvas: responsive width; 630 px drawing area plus 90 px control area.
