Controls: Back and Next buttons, Play/Pause (starts paused), a stage slider (1857, 1858, 1947, 1948, 1971, 1972), a "Show 1947 migration arrows" checkbox; tapping the diagram also advances one step.

Behavior: A schematic block diagram, not a map. In 1857 and 1858 one large block (East India Company territory, then British India) holds small purple tiles for princely states, with Ceylon below and Afghanistan, Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives as gray outside blocks. In 1947 the block splits into West Pakistan, India and East Pakistan; tiles change color as they join India or Pakistan, Hyderabad stays purple until 1948, and Jammu and Kashmir becomes a striped "disputed" tile. In 1948 Ceylon is labeled independent; in 1971 East Pakistan becomes Bangladesh; in 1972 Ceylon becomes Sri Lanka. A panel gives the dates and sourced ranges for each event. The caption says the diagram is schematic, not to scale and not an official depiction of borders.

Start at 1857 and press Next one step at a time. At each step, read the panel, then ask: what split, what joined, and what only changed its name? Watch the jump from 1858 to 1947, when the big block breaks into three and the princely-state tiles change color as they join a side.

Then go from 1947 to 1971 and watch East Pakistan. Its block doesn't move at all. Only its name changes. That's Nanu's point: the land and people stayed put while the country changed around them. Finally, compare Ceylon's single peaceful step with Bangladesh's two steps.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about what your family remembers or was told about independence, 1947, 1971 or 1948, and how those years are talked about at home. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Some memories of 1947 and 1971 are painful. Ask first whether they want to talk about those years at all, let them choose what to share, and never push for details. Ask if it's okay to take notes.

Questions to ask

  1. When you were young, how did your family celebrate Independence Day (14 August, 15 August, 4 February or 26 March), or Victory Day? What do you remember about it?
  2. Where was our family living in 1947, or in 1971? Did anyone have to move?
  3. Were there stories in the family about neighbors, friends or places left behind? You only need to share what you're comfortable with.
  4. What did people call these events at home? For example, "Partition," "independence," "the liberation war," or something else?
  5. How do you think people talk about these years now, compared with when you were young, or compared with how people talk about them here in the United States?
  6. What is one thing about our family's history in those years that you hope I remember and pass on?

Listen for: whether the story centers the Partition of 1947, Partition Migration or the Bangladesh Liberation War; places on either side of the Radcliffe Line; and how the memory compares with the "Whose Story?" box above.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare your elder's account with a friend's interview from a family with roots in a different country, such as India, Pakistan, Bangladesh or Sri Lanka. Did they use the same name for the events? Did one family remember celebration and the other loss? Write two sentences on why both memories can be true at once.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Partition in 1947 created Bangladesh. Reality: Partition created India and Pakistan. The area that is now Bangladesh became East Pakistan in 1947. Bangladesh was created in a separate event, the Liberation War of 1971.

Myth: India won independence through nonviolence alone. Reality: Gandhi's nonviolent campaigns were central, but independence also came from elections and political bargaining, armed revolutionaries, the Indian National Army, strikes and protests, and Britain's weakness after the Second World War. Historians still debate how much each mattered.

Myth: The violence of Partition happened on one side. Reality: People of every community were killed, attacked and forced from their homes: Hindus and Sikhs in areas that became Pakistan, and Muslims in areas that became India. Survivors on both sides carry the memory.

Myth: Britain ruled every part of South Asia directly. Reality: About 565 princely states kept their own rulers under British control. Afghanistan, Nepal and Bhutan were never British colonies, though Britain influenced their foreign affairs, and the Maldives was a protectorate. Ceylon was a colony governed separately from British India.

Myth: Pakistan was always one block of land. Reality: From 1947 to 1971 Pakistan had two wings, West and East, with India in between. Most of its people lived in the eastern wing and spoke Bangla.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What happened at the Battle of Plassey, and why does it matter?

On 23 June 1757, the East India Company under Robert Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal, helped by the betrayal of the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar. It gave the Company control of Bengal's wealth, the base from which it expanded across South Asia.

2. What changed in 1858?

After the Revolt of 1857, the Government of India Act of 1858 ended East India Company rule and placed its territories under the British Crown. That began the British Raj, which lasted until 1947.

3. What was the Radcliffe Line, and why did its timing cause problems?

It was the boundary drawn through Punjab and Bengal to divide them between India and Pakistan. It was published on 17 August 1947, two days after independence, so many people did not know which country they were in when independence came.

4. About how many people were displaced by Partition, and why do historians give a range?

About 14 million to 18 million people. No one kept a full count in the chaos, and different methods, such as refugee records and census comparisons, give different totals.

5. Why is 21 February important in Bangladesh and around the world?

On 21 February 1952, police killed student protesters in Dhaka who were demanding recognition for Bangla. Bangladesh honors them on that day, and since 1999 UNESCO has marked it as International Mother Language Day.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Give the independence dates of Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka (Ceylon) and Bangladesh.

    Answer

    Pakistan: 14 August 1947. India: 15 August 1947. Ceylon (Sri Lanka): 4 February 1948. Bangladesh declared independence on 26 March 1971, and the war ended on 16 December 1971.

  2. Name the leaders most closely linked to the Indian National Congress, the All-India Muslim League, and the drafting of India's Constitution.

    Answer

    Mahatma Gandhi (with Jawaharlal Nehru) led the Congress. Muhammad Ali Jinnah led the Muslim League. B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Constitution's Drafting Committee.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain in your own words what satyagraha means and give one example of it.

    Answer

    Satyagraha means "holding firmly to truth": openly and nonviolently refusing to obey an unjust law and accepting the punishment. The Salt March of 1930, when Gandhi walked to Dandi and made salt in defiance of the British salt law, is the best-known example.

  2. Explain why the Kashmir Dispute began in 1947.

    Answer

    Jammu and Kashmir was a princely state with a Muslim-majority population and a Hindu ruler. After armed tribesmen from Pakistan entered in October 1947, the Maharaja joined India in return for military help. Pakistan disputed the accession, war followed, and both countries have claimed the region ever since.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Borders Then and Now MicroSim. Step from 1858 to 1972 and, for each step, write one sentence saying which blocks split, joined or only changed their names. Hint: notice which step changes only a label.

  2. A classmate says her grandfather was "born in Pakistan" in 1950 in Sylhet. Using this chapter, explain which country Sylhet is in today and why her statement is still correct. Hint: Sylhet was part of East Pakistan.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the Partition of 1947 with Sri Lankan Independence in 1948. Identify two reasons one was so much more violent than the other. Hint: think about how the land and its people were divided, and how fast it happened.

  2. Analyze the causes of the Bengal Famine of 1943. Which causes came from the war, and which came from government decisions? Hint: sort the four causes in section 4.5 into two groups.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. The 1857 uprising has been called the "Sepoy Mutiny" and the "First War of Independence." Evaluate both names. Which would you use in a club presentation, and why? Hint: what does each name assume about who rebelled and why?

  2. Some people say Radcliffe should not be blamed for Partition violence because he was given an impossible task. Evaluate this claim using evidence from the chapter. Hint: consider the five-week timeline, the mixed populations and who decided the timing.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Create a timeline poster with six dates from this chapter, from 1757 to 1972. For each date, write one sentence and a symbol, and include at least one event from Sri Lanka and one from Bangladesh. Hint: the MicroSim stages can be your starting points.

  2. Write a short letter (150 to 200 words) from a fictional teenager in Lahore, Delhi or Dhaka in 1947 or 1971 to a friend on the other side of a new border. Show the friendship and the fear, without graphic detail. Hint: use at least two concept words from this chapter.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• British rule began with the East India Company's victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. After the Revolt of 1857, the British Crown ruled directly as the British Raj from 1858 to 1947.
  • British India was a patchwork: about 565 princely states kept their own rulers, and Afghanistan, Nepal and Bhutan were never British colonies.
  • Freedom came through many paths: the Indian National Congress, the All-India Muslim League, Gandhi's satyagraha, Ambedkar's fight for Dalit rights, Jinnah's call for Pakistan, revolutionaries and Britain's postwar weakness.
  • The Partition of 1947 split British India into India and a two-winged Pakistan along the Radcliffe Line; about 14 to 18 million people were displaced and between about 200,000 and 2 million were killed, in every community.
  • The Kashmir Dispute began in 1947 and remains unresolved, with India, Pakistan and many Kashmiris holding different positions.
  • Ceylon became independent peacefully on 4 February 1948 and was renamed Sri Lanka in 1972.
  • Bangladesh was not created by Partition: the Language Movement of 1952 and the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971 turned East Pakistan into an independent country.

You untangled the map!

You can now explain how a woman could live in three countries without leaving home. Next, in Chapter 5, we visit the mosques, mandirs, gurdwaras, temples and churches where so many South Asian families find meaning.

docs.title: Quiz: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 4. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What happened at the Battle of Plassey in 1757?

  1. The East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal, helped by the betrayal of the Nawab's commander
  2. Indian soldiers at Meerut rose up against the East India Company
  3. The British Crown took over the government of India from the East India Company
  4. Britain fought its first war in Afghanistan
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. At Plassey, Robert Clive's Company forces defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah after Mir Jafar kept his troops out of the fight, giving the Company control of Bengal. The Meerut uprising (B) was the start of the Revolt of 1857, a century later.

Concept Tested: Battle of Plassey Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which statement best describes the princely states?

  1. Provinces governed directly by British governors
  2. Independent countries outside the British Empire, like Nepal
  3. Kingdoms with their own Indian rulers who accepted British control of defense and foreign affairs
  4. Territories created by the Radcliffe Line in 1947
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. About 565 princely states kept their own rulers but were tied to Britain by treaties. They were not directly ruled provinces (A), and unlike Nepal they were inside the British system (B).

Concept Tested: Princely States Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Why is the Revolt of 1857 called by different names, such as the "Sepoy Mutiny" and the "First War of Independence"?

  1. Because historians disagree about the year it took place
  2. Because each name reflects a different view of who rebelled and why
  3. Because it happened in two separate countries
  4. Because the British Crown renamed it in 1858
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. "Sepoy Mutiny" treats it as a soldiers' revolt, while "First War of Independence" treats it as the start of a national struggle. The date (A) is not in dispute: it began on 10 May 1857.

Concept Tested: Revolt of 1857 Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Which pair of dates gives Pakistan's and India's independence days?

  1. 26 January 1950 and 15 August 1947
  2. 4 February 1948 and 14 August 1947
  3. 23 March 1940 and 26 March 1971
  4. 14 August 1947 and 15 August 1947
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Pakistan celebrates 14 August and India 15 August 1947. 26 January 1950 (A) is when India's Constitution took effect, and 4 February 1948 (B) is Sri Lanka's independence day.

Concept Tested: Partition of 1947 Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
What made satyagraha different from other ways of resisting British rule?

  1. It relied on secret armed attacks against officials
  2. People openly and nonviolently broke unjust laws and accepted the punishment
  3. It asked Britain to divide India into two countries
  4. It was a petition sent only by lawyers to Parliament
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Satyagraha, "holding firmly to truth," meant open, nonviolent refusal to obey unjust laws, as in the Salt March. Armed attacks (A) were the path of some revolutionaries, not Gandhi.

Concept Tested: Satyagraha Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why did the timing of the Radcliffe Line's publication add to the confusion of 1947?

  1. It was published two days after independence, so many people did not yet know which country they were in
  2. It was published a year before independence, giving people too long to argue
  3. It was never published, so the border was decided by the armies
  4. It was published only in English newspapers in London
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The Line was announced on 17 August 1947, after both countries had become independent, so many people celebrated without knowing where the border would fall. It was published (C), and it came after independence, not before (B).

Concept Tested: Radcliffe Line Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Zara's Nanu says, "I was born in Pakistan in 1960, near Chattogram." Which explanation is correct?

  1. She is mistaken, because Chattogram has always been in India
  2. She is mistaken, because Bangladesh was created by Partition in 1947
  3. She is right only if she later moved to Lahore
  4. She is right, because from 1947 to 1971 Chattogram was in East Pakistan
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Chattogram was in East Pakistan from 1947 until Bangladesh's independence in 1971. Option B repeats a common myth: Partition created India and Pakistan, and Bangladesh came later, in 1971.

Concept Tested: Bangladesh Liberation War Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
A student uses the MicroSim and notices that between 1948 and 1971 one block only changes its name. Which block is it, and what does that show?

  1. India; it shows India changed its borders in 1971
  2. Ceylon; it shows Sri Lanka was partitioned
  3. East Pakistan becoming Bangladesh; it shows a new country can form while the land and people stay in place
  4. West Pakistan becoming Afghanistan; it shows the Anglo-Afghan Wars changed borders
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The East Pakistan block keeps its size and place and becomes Bangladesh, showing that the country changed around people who never moved. Ceylon (B) was never partitioned. It changed its name to Sri Lanka in 1972.

Concept Tested: Bangladesh Liberation War Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Compare the Partition of 1947 with Sri Lankan Independence in 1948. Which is the best explanation of why Partition was far more violent?

  1. Partition divided mixed provinces like Punjab and Bengal in a few weeks, while Ceylon became independent as one unit after years of negotiation
  2. Ceylon had no British officials, so there was nothing to fight over
  3. Partition happened during the Second World War, while Sri Lanka's independence came after it
  4. Sri Lanka was a princely state, so its ruler kept order
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Splitting mixed provinces at high speed, with borders announced after independence, set off mass migration and violence, while Ceylon was handed over whole. Option C is wrong because Partition took place in 1947, after the war had ended.

Concept Tested: Sri Lankan Independence Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Why do historians give Partition migration as a range, about 14 million to 18 million people, instead of one exact number?

  1. Because the British government kept exact records but has not released them
  2. Because only people who crossed by train were counted
  3. Because Pakistan and India agreed to use different numbers
  4. Because no one kept a full count, and different methods, such as refugee records and census comparisons, give different totals
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Refugee counts and census-based estimates produce different totals, and a census study found about 3.4 million people unaccounted for. There is no hidden exact record (A). The gaps come from the chaos of 1947.

Concept Tested: Partition Migration Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition
docs.text:
1. Partition of British India - The National Archives (UK) - A classroom lesson built from original letters, maps, newspapers and oral history, made with SOAS for the 75th anniversary. It shows how the 3 June plan, the Boundary Commission and the 17 August announcement looked in real documents.

  2. Indian Independence, Part Two - The National Archives (UK) - Primary sources from 1947, including Mountbatten's June broadcast and official reports of refugee movements in Punjab and Delhi. Useful for an Analyze or Evaluate exercise on what officials knew at the time.

  3. The 1947 Partition of South Asia: Introduction - Stanford University Libraries - A research guide with a short, clear overview of Partition, including the figure of about 14 million refugees, and links to books, films and archives for deeper reading.

  4. The 1947 Partition Archive - The 1947 Partition Archive - A nonprofit that records the life stories of Partition survivors and trains volunteers to interview elders. A model for the Ask Your Elders interviews in this book.

  5. The Big March: Migratory Flows after the Partition of India - Bharadwaj, Khwaja and Mian, Economic and Political Weekly (2008), via Princeton University - A study that uses census records to estimate about 14.5 million people arriving and 17.9 million leaving, which is the source for the chapter's displacement range.

  6. The South Asia Crisis and the Founding of Bangladesh, 1971 - Office of the Historian, US Department of State - A short account of the 1970 election, the crackdown, the refugee crisis and the December war, from the point of view of US foreign policy at the time.

  7. Death toll among the Bangladeshi refugees of the 1971 war - Adhikari, Islam and Jalal, PLOS ONE (2025) - A recent peer-reviewed study of about 9.9 million refugees who fled to India in 1971. Its introduction shows how widely estimates of the war's total death toll vary, and why.

  8. International Mother Language Day - UNESCO - Explains the day that grew out of Bangladesh's Language Movement, approved at UNESCO's 1999 General Conference and observed worldwide since 2000.

  9. Article 17: Abolition of Untouchability - Constitution of India (constitutionofindia.net) - The text of Article 17 and a summary of how the Constituent Assembly debated and adopted it in 1948, part of B. R. Ambedkar's legacy.

  10. Kashmir conflict - Wikipedia - A detailed overview of the dispute from 1947 to today, with the positions of India, Pakistan, China and Kashmiri groups. Use it as a starting point and follow its citations to primary sources.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asia is home to many of the world's faiths. Four of them, Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, began in the region, and others, including Islam, Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Judaism, arrived long ago and put down deep roots. This chapter introduces each faith through the same five lenses: where it came from, its sacred texts, its place of worship, a major festival, and a core idea. It also looks at pilgrimage, at the places and practices that different faiths share, and at religious pluralism, the fact of many faiths living side by side, with all its friendships and tensions. The goal is understanding, not ranking: you'll learn how followers describe their own beliefs, in their own words where possible.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Hinduism
  2. Dharma
  3. Karma and Rebirth
  4. Puja
  5. Buddhism
  6. Theravada and Vajrayana
  7. Jainism
  8. Ahimsa
  9. Islam in South Asia
  10. Sunni and Shia Islam
  11. Sikhism
  12. Guru Granth Sahib
  13. Langar
  14. Christianity in South Asia
  15. Zoroastrians (Parsis)
  16. Jewish Communities
  17. Pilgrimage
  18. Religious Pluralism

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?, for the eight countries and the rivers.
  • Chapter 2: Ancient Roots, for the Vedic period and the early history of Buddhism and Jainism.
  • Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters, especially early Islam in South Asia, the Bhakti movement, Sufism and Guru Nanak.

Many ways of believing

Hi, it's Mora! You probably have classmates who fast in Ramadan, light diyas at Diwali, wear a turban or kara, go to Mass, or don't follow any religion at all. Knowing a little about each other's faiths helps you ask kind questions, avoid hurtful mix-ups, and maybe get invited to a great festival meal. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 5.1 Shoes Off, Three Times
docs.text:
On a Saturday in October, the Prairie Ridge South Asian Student Association goes on a field trip. Ms. Okafor has arranged three visits in the Twin Cities: a mosque in the morning, a gurdwara at lunchtime, and a mandir (a Hindu temple) in the afternoon. Zara Hossain's family prays at the mosque. Simran Kaur Gill's family goes to the gurdwara every Sunday. Arjun Reddy's grandmother volunteers at the mandir.

At the mosque, Zara shows Ben Lindqvist the shelves by the door, and everyone leaves their shoes there before entering the prayer hall. At the gurdwara, Simran hands Ben an orange scarf to cover his head, and again, shoes come off. Then they all sit in rows on the floor and eat dal, roti and kheer for free, side by side with strangers. At the mandir, Arjun points to a long rack of sneakers and sandals. Ben laughs. "Okay, three buildings, three religions, and I've taken my shoes off three times. So are these faiths basically the same, or totally different?"

Simran shakes her head. "Not the same. But you can't understand any of them from the outside in five minutes." On the bus home, Ben keeps asking questions. How do you learn about many faiths without mixing them up, and without deciding one is better than another?

docs.title: 5.2 Five Lenses, No Ranking
docs.text:
Ben already knows one faith from the inside. His family is Lutheran, a kind of Christian. If a friend asked him about it, he could answer a few basic questions: Where did it start? What book do you read? Where do you go to worship? What's your biggest holiday? What's one idea that matters most? Those answers wouldn't be the whole of his faith, but they'd be a fair start.

This chapter uses those same five questions, or lenses, for every faith:

  1. Origins: where and when it began, and who followers say founded or taught it.
  2. Sacred texts: the writings it treasures.
  3. Place of worship: the building where people gather.
  4. A major festival: one celebration among many.
  5. A core idea: one teaching that followers often describe as central.

Using the same lenses for every faith keeps the comparison fair. It also comes with three ground rules that this whole book follows:

  • Describe, don't judge. We say "many Hindus believe" or "in Sikh tradition," because these are the beliefs of followers, not claims the book is making.
  • No ranking. Older doesn't mean better, and bigger doesn't mean more important.
  • Practice varies. Inside every faith there are many communities, schools and family customs. When you read "Muslims do X," remember that real families are more varied than any summary.

Ask before assuming

A person's name, clothes or country don't tell you their faith, or how they practice it. If you're curious, ask politely, and accept "I'd rather not say" as a full answer.

docs.title: 5.3 A Faith Map of South Asia
docs.text:
Before meeting each faith, it helps to see where people of different faiths live. The table shows the largest groups in each of the eight countries, using each country's most recent census (or the best available estimate).

Country Largest faith Other important communities Source and year Afghanistan Islam (almost everyone; mostly Sunni) A Shia minority; very small Sikh and Hindu communities Estimates; no recent census Bangladesh Islam, 91.08% Hindus 7.96%; Buddhists 0.61%; Christians 0.30% 2022 census (final report, 2023) Bhutan Buddhism, about three-quarters Hindus, most of the rest Pew Research estimate India Hinduism, 79.8% Muslims 14.2%; Christians 2.3%; Sikhs just under 2%; Buddhists and Jains each under 1% 2011 census Maldives Islam The constitution requires citizens to be Muslim 2008 constitution Nepal Hinduism, 81.19% Buddhists 8.21%; Muslims 5.09%; Kirat (the faith of Kirati peoples such as the Rai and Limbu) 3.17%; Christians 1.76% 2021 census Pakistan Islam, 96.35% Hindus about 3.9 million, plus about 1.3 million in a separate Scheduled Castes category, many of them Hindu Dalit communities; Christians about 3.3 million 2023 census Sri Lanka Buddhism, 69.8% Hindus 12.6%; Muslims 10.7%; Christians about 6.9% 2024 census

A few things jump out. India's figures come from the 2011 census, so treat them as a snapshot from fifteen years ago. India's next census counts its population in February 2027. Even small percentages can mean huge numbers of people: India's 14.2% Muslim share in 2011 was about 172 million people, one of the largest Muslim populations in the world. And no country lines up with only one faith. Every country on the list is home to several.

docs.title: Origins and variety
docs.text:
Hinduism is a family of related traditions, beliefs and practices that grew in South Asia over thousands of years, with no single founder, no single holy book and no single central authority. Most Hindus live in India and Nepal, the two Hindu-majority countries of South Asia. There are also large Hindu communities in Bangladesh, in Sri Lanka (mostly among Tamils in the north and east), in Pakistan (mostly in Sindh), in Bhutan, and around the world.

The word "Hindu" was first used by outsiders, from the name of the Indus River (Sindhu). Many Hindus also call their tradition Sanatana Dharma, "the eternal way." Inside that family are many traditions. Some Hindus focus their devotion on Vishnu (often as Krishna or Rama), some on Shiva, and some on the Goddess (Devi) in forms such as Durga or Kali. Many worship several deities, and many describe them as forms of one divine reality. In Pew Research Center's 2021 survey of India, 84% of Hindus either picked more than one god as feeling close to them or said they have many personal gods, and 61% said there is one God with many manifestations.

docs.title: Sacred texts
docs.text: Hinduism has many sacred texts, not one. The oldest are the Vedas, hymns in Sanskrit passed down by memory for many centuries. The Upanishads explore questions about the self and ultimate reality. The great epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata (which includes the Bhagavad Gita), are known to almost everyone through stories, TV shows and festivals. The Puranas and devotional poems in Tamil, Bengali, Hindi and many other languages matter too. Different communities value different texts most.

docs.title: Three key ideas
docs.text:
Dharma (धर्म, DHUR-muh) is the idea of right order, duty and right conduct: the way things should be, and the way a person should act. In Hindi, dharm can also simply mean "religion." Many Hindus think of their own dharma as depending on their stage of life and responsibilities, such as being a student, a parent or a teacher.

Karma and Rebirth is the belief that a person's actions and intentions (karma, कर्म, KUR-muh, "action") have effects, in this life and in future lives, and that the soul is reborn again and again in a cycle called samsara. In many Hindu traditions, the highest goal is moksha, release from that cycle. Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs also speak of karma and rebirth, each in their own way. In the 2021 Pew survey of India, 77% of Hindus and 77% of Muslims said they believe in karma, a sign of how widely the idea has spread across faith lines.

Puja (पूजा, POO-jah, "worship" or "honor") is the Hindu ritual of offering worship to a deity, often with light, flowers, water, incense or food. Puja can be a big temple ceremony with priests, or a few quiet minutes at a home shrine in the morning. Arjun's grandmother does a short puja every day at the small shrine in their kitchen.

docs.title: Places and festivals
docs.text: Hindus worship at a mandir (मंदिर, MUN-dir, "temple"), and many families also keep a home shrine. Big festivals include Diwali, the festival of lights; Holi, the spring festival of colors; Navaratri and Durga Puja in autumn; and harvest festivals such as Pongal. In Bangladesh, Durga Puja is the largest Hindu festival, and Dhaka's Dhakeshwari National Temple is dedicated to the goddess many say gave the city its name. In Pakistan, the Hinglaj Mata temple in Balochistan draws the country's largest Hindu pilgrimage. You'll meet the festivals in Chapter 7.

docs.title: 5.5 Buddhism
docs.text:
Buddhism is the faith based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha ("awakened one"), who Buddhists believe found the path to freedom from suffering. He was born at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal, about 2,500 years ago (the exact dates are debated). Buddhists believe he reached enlightenment while meditating under a tree at Bodh Gaya, in present-day India. Both Lumbini and the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

In Buddhist teaching, the Buddha described Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering and dissatisfaction; suffering has a cause, especially craving; suffering can end; and the Eightfold Path of right understanding, ethical living and meditation leads to that end. Buddhists take refuge in the "Three Jewels": the Buddha, his teaching (the Dharma), and the community of monks, nuns and followers (the Sangha).

Buddhism spread from South Asia across Asia and developed different schools. In India itself, many Buddhists today are Dalits whose families followed the reformer B. R. Ambedkar into Buddhism after his conversion at Nagpur in 1956 (you met him in Chapter 4). Two schools matter most in South Asia today.

docs.title: Theravada and Vajrayana
docs.text:
Theravada and Vajrayana are two of the main schools of Buddhism. Theravada ("teaching of the elders") is the school of Sri Lanka, and its scriptures are the Pali Canon, preserved in the Pali language. Buddhism reached Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE, and the island has been a center of Theravada learning ever since. Vajrayana (the "diamond" or "thunderbolt" vehicle) developed later and became the Buddhism of Tibet, Bhutan and Himalayan Nepal. It uses Mahayana scriptures and Tibetan teachings, and is known for its rituals, chanted mantras and the close bond between students and their teachers.

Theravada Vajrayana Where in South Asia Sri Lanka; also most Buddhists in Bangladesh Bhutan, Himalayan Nepal, Ladakh and other Himalayan areas Scriptures Pali Canon Mahayana sutras and Tibetan Buddhist texts Typical place A vihara (monastery temple) with a stupa A monastery; in Bhutan, many sit inside dzongs (fortress-like centers) Example Dilan Perera's family in Kandy visits the Temple of the Tooth Relic Nima Sherpa's family follows the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism

The big Buddhist festival in Sri Lanka is Vesak (Sinhala වෙසක්, VEH-suk), held on the full moon of the month of Vesak, usually in May. In Theravada tradition it marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing. Streets and homes glow with lanterns called Vesak kudu, and volunteers set up stalls called dansalas that hand out free food and drinks to passersby. In Bangladesh, Buddhists are a small minority (0.61% in 2022), and almost all of them live in Chattogram Division, where Zara's parents grew up, especially in the Chittagong Hill Tracts to the east of the city.

docs.title: 5.6 Jainism and Ahimsa
docs.text:
Jainism is a faith from South Asia that teaches that every living being has a soul, and that souls can be freed from the cycle of rebirth through non-violence, self-discipline and right knowledge. Jains believe their path has been taught by 24 tirthankaras ("ford-makers," teachers who help people cross the river of rebirth). The 24th, Mahavira, lived in what is now Bihar, India, around the 6th or 5th century BCE, close to the time of the Buddha.

Jains belong to two main groups, Digambara and Svetambara, which differ in some practices and in which collections of scripture they accept. In India, Jains live in many states, with especially large communities in Maharashtra and Gujarat. Jain temples, often carved in white marble, are famous for their detail. Jain merchant families have long been prominent in trade, and Jain families have supported temples, libraries and charities for centuries.

docs.title: Ahimsa
docs.text:
Ahimsa (अहिंसा, uh-HIM-sah) means non-violence: not harming any living being, in action, word or thought. Hindus and Buddhists also value ahimsa, but Jains put it at the very center of their life. Many Jains follow a strict vegetarian diet that also leaves out root vegetables such as potatoes, onions and garlic, to avoid destroying the many tiny living things in and around them. In the 20th century, Mohandas K. Gandhi made ahimsa famous worldwide as a method of peaceful protest.

The most important Jain festival is Paryushan, a period of fasting, reflection and study, eight days long for Svetambara Jains. It ends with a day of asking forgiveness from everyone you may have hurt in the past year. Jains also celebrate Diwali, which in Jain tradition marks the anniversary of Mahavira's final liberation.

Same word, different weight

I notice that karma, dharma and ahimsa show up in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions, but each faith gives them its own meaning and its own weight. When you hear one of these words, try asking, "What does it mean in your tradition?"

docs.title: Origins and basic practice
docs.text:
Islam began in Arabia in the early 600s CE. Muslims believe that God (Allah, the Arabic word for God) revealed the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad, and they also follow the Hadith, reports of what the Prophet said and did. Muslims around the world share the Five Pillars of practice: declaring faith in one God and in Muhammad as God's messenger (shahada), praying five times a day (salah, called namaz in South Asia), giving to those in need (zakat), fasting from dawn to dusk in the month of Ramadan (sawm), and, for those who are able, making the pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj).

Islam in South Asia is the faith and culture of the region's Muslims, who today form one of the largest Muslim populations on Earth. As you read in Chapter 3, Islam arrived over many centuries, through Arab traders on the coasts, Sufi teachers and conquest in the northwest. Most South Asian Muslims are descended from people who lived in the region long before. Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and the Maldives are Muslim-majority countries. India had about 172 million Muslims in 2011, one of the largest Muslim populations in the world, and Sri Lanka and Nepal have significant Muslim communities too.

A Muslim place of worship is a masjid (Urdu مسجد, MUS-jid), or mosque. Many South Asian Muslims also visit Sufi shrines (dargahs), though some Muslims, especially in reformist movements, disapprove of some shrine practices. One of the largest in South Asia is Data Darbar in Lahore, the shrine of the 11th-century saint Ali al-Hujwiri. In the 2021 Pew survey, 37% of Muslims in North India said they identify with Sufism.

Zara's family celebrates two big festivals: Eid al-Fitr, which ends the month of Ramadan fasting, and Eid al-Adha, which comes at the time of the hajj. On Eid morning her family goes to prayer in new clothes, and her Nanu hands out money to the children.

docs.title: Sunni and Shia Islam
docs.text:
Sunni and Shia Islam are the two main branches of Islam, which separated over a disagreement about who should lead the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad died in 632. Sunni Muslims hold that the community rightly chose the Prophet's companion Abu Bakr as the first leader (caliph). Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet named his cousin and son-in-law, Ali, as his successor, and they honor a line of leaders called imams descended from Ali.

Both branches share the Quran, the Five Pillars and most beliefs, and in many South Asian towns they have lived side by side for centuries. Most South Asian Muslims are Sunni. Shia Muslims are an important minority: Pew Research Center has estimated them at about 10% to 15% of Muslims in both India and Pakistan (2009 estimate), and some scholars estimate more. During the month of Muharram, many Shia Muslims mourn the death of Imam Husain, the Prophet's grandson, at the Battle of Karbala in 680, with processions, poetry and gatherings.

docs.title: 5.8 Sikhism
docs.text:
Sikhism is a faith founded in Punjab by Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539), which teaches devotion to one God, honest work, sharing with others, and the equality of all people. You met Guru Nanak in Chapter 3. In Sikh tradition, nine more human Gurus followed him. The tenth, Guru Gobind Singh, created the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, on Vaisakhi in 1699. Initiated Sikhs keep five articles of faith, including uncut hair (often covered by a turban) and a steel bracelet called a kara.

Sikhs believe in one God, expressed in the phrase Ik Onkar, "one creator," the opening words of their scripture. Most Sikhs live in Punjab in India, where they are the majority. Some of Sikhism's holiest places, including Nankana Sahib, Guru Nanak's birthplace, and Kartarpur, where he died, are in Pakistan. In 2019 a visa-free corridor opened so pilgrims from India could cross to the gurdwara at Kartarpur. India suspended it in May 2025 amid tensions between the two countries, and as of October 2026 it remained closed to Indian pilgrims, although Pakistan says its side is open.

docs.title: The Guru Granth Sahib
docs.text:
The Guru Granth Sahib is the Sikh scripture, a collection of hymns that Sikhs honor as their living Guru. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, compiled its first version in 1604 and placed it in the Golden Temple at Amritsar. In October 1708, shortly before he died, Guru Gobind Singh declared that after him the scripture itself would be the Guru. It has 1,430 pages, and its hymns are meant to be sung. Most are by the Sikh Gurus, but it also includes hymns by fifteen other saints (bhagats), including bhakti poets such as Kabir and Namdev and the Muslim Sufi saint Sheikh Farid.

In a gurdwara (ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ, GUR-dwah-rah, "door to the Guru"), the Guru Granth Sahib sits on a raised platform under a canopy. Visitors remove their shoes and cover their heads, and they usually sit on the floor. The holiest gurdwara is the Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) in Amritsar, which receives about 100,000 visitors on a typical day.

docs.title: Langar
docs.text:
Langar (ਲੰਗਰ, LUN-gur) is the free community kitchen of a gurdwara, where volunteers cook and serve a vegetarian meal to anyone who comes, regardless of religion, caste, gender or wealth. Everyone sits together on the floor, in rows, as equals. Sikh tradition traces langar to Guru Nanak, and it shows his teaching that all people are equal. A Sikh tradition even says that the Mughal emperor Akbar sat and ate langar with ordinary people before meeting the third Guru, Guru Amar Das.

The cooking, serving and cleaning are done as seva (ਸੇਵਾ, SAY-vah), selfless service. Simran has helped make roti for langar since she was eight, and she's the reason Ben now knows how to hold out both hands to receive it.

Visiting a place of worship

Before visiting a mosque, gurdwara, mandir, church or temple, check its website or ask a member what to wear and do. Most welcome respectful visitors, and asking first shows you care.

docs.title: 5.9 Christianity in South Asia
docs.text:
Christianity in South Asia refers to the region's many Christian communities, some among the oldest in the world, others formed later through Portuguese, Dutch, British and other missions. Christians believe that Jesus is the Son of God, and they read the Bible. Their place of worship is a church, and their biggest festivals are Christmas and Easter.

  • Kerala's St. Thomas Christians trace their church to the apostle Thomas, who, according to their tradition, came to the Malabar coast in the 1st century CE. They speak Malayalam and have their own ancient forms of worship.
  • Goa, ruled by Portugal from 1510 until 1961, has many Catholic churches. Its old churches, including the Basilica of Bom Jesus, which holds the tomb of St. Francis Xavier, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
  • Northeast India: Christians are the majority in the states of Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya.
  • Pakistan: the 2023 census counted about 3.3 million Christians (1.37%), most of them in Punjab. Some church leaders say the real number is higher.
  • Sri Lanka: about 6.9% of people were Christian in the 2024 census, most of them Roman Catholic, among Sinhala, Tamil and Burgher communities.

In India as a whole, Christians were 2.3% of the population in 2011, about 28 million people. South Asian churches celebrate Christmas with local touches: star lanterns, carols in regional languages and festive sweets.

docs.title: 5.10 Smaller Communities, Long Histories
docs.text: Two communities in South Asia are small in number but have long, important histories.

docs.title: Zoroastrians (Parsis)
docs.text:
Zoroastrians (Parsis) are followers of Zoroastrianism, an ancient faith founded by the prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra) in Iran. In South Asia, most belong to the Parsi community, whose ancestors came from Iran. Parsi means "Persian." According to the community's own story, the Qissa-i Sanjan, Zoroastrians left Iran to keep practicing their faith and landed on the coast of Gujarat. Historians place the migration somewhere between the 8th and 10th centuries.

In the story, the local king worried that his kingdom was already full. A Parsi priest answered by stirring sugar into a vessel of milk: like the sugar, the newcomers would blend in and sweeten life without making it overflow. Parsis often tell this story to explain how they settled in.

Zoroastrians teach the ideals of good thoughts, good words and good deeds, and believe each person chooses between good and evil. They pray in fire temples, where a sacred fire is kept burning. The Iranshah fire at Udvada, Gujarat, is the most revered in India, and tradition dates it to the community's earliest years. Parsis celebrate Navroz, the New Year. Most Parsis in South Asia live in Mumbai (formerly Bombay), and there are smaller communities in Karachi and other cities.

docs.title: Jewish Communities
docs.text:
Jewish Communities in South Asia are the old Jewish groups that settled in India, especially on the west coast, long before modern times. Jews believe in one God and a covenant (a sacred agreement) between God and the Jewish people, and they study the Torah. Their place of worship is a synagogue.

There were three main communities:

  • Cochin Jews in Kerala. The Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi, built in 1568, is the oldest active synagogue in the Commonwealth.
  • Bene Israel, who lived for centuries in villages of the Konkan coast and later moved to Mumbai, where they opened their first synagogue in 1796.
  • Baghdadi Jews, traders from the Middle East who settled first in Surat (from 1730) and later in Mumbai and Kolkata.

India's Jewish population peaked in the 1940s and declined quickly after 1948, as most moved to the new state of Israel. Most Cochin Jews left in the mid-1950s. Small communities remain, and their synagogues are still cared for.

docs.title: 5.11 Pilgrimage: Journeys of Faith
docs.text:
Pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place for prayer, blessing, remembrance or renewal. Every faith in this chapter has pilgrimage places, and South Asia is full of them.

Faith Pilgrimage example Where Hinduism The Kumbh Mela, where millions bathe in a sacred river. It rotates among four cities Prayagraj (Allahabad), Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik, India Hinduism Hinglaj Yatra Balochistan, Pakistan Buddhism The Buddha's birthplace and place of enlightenment Lumbini, Nepal; Bodh Gaya, India Buddhism The Temple of the Tooth Relic Kandy, Sri Lanka Islam The hajj to Mecca, plus visits to Sufi shrines such as Ajmer and Data Darbar Saudi Arabia; Rajasthan, India; Lahore, Pakistan Sikhism The Golden Temple; Nankana Sahib and Kartarpur Amritsar, India; Punjab, Pakistan Christianity The Basilica of Bom Jesus Old Goa, India Zoroastrianism The Iranshah fire temple Udvada, Gujarat, India

UNESCO lists the Kumbh Mela as part of humanity's Intangible Cultural Heritage (2017) and calls it the largest peaceful gathering of pilgrims on Earth.

Some pilgrimage places are shared. Adam's Peak (Sri Pada) in Sri Lanka is a 2,243 m mountain with a footprint-shaped rock at the top. In Buddhist tradition it is the Buddha's footprint; many Hindus see it as Shiva's; and in some Muslim and Christian traditions it is the footprint of Adam or of St. Thomas. Pilgrims of all four faiths climb it, often through the night to watch the sunrise. The Ajmer dargah of Moinuddin Chishti, too, draws many Hindus as well as Muslims.

docs.title: 5.12 Religious Pluralism
docs.text:
Religious Pluralism means many faiths living side by side in the same society, and, as an ideal, people of different faiths respecting each other's right to believe and practice. South Asia has lived with pluralism for thousands of years. That history includes deep friendships and shared traditions, and also real conflict and discrimination.

Some signs of shared life:

  • Shared ideas. In Pew's 2021 survey of India, the same share of Hindus and Muslims (77%) said they believe in karma.
  • Shared places. Hindus visit Sufi dargahs; Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians climb Adam's Peak; anyone may eat at a gurdwara's langar.
  • Shared scripture. The Guru Granth Sahib includes hymns by Hindu and Muslim saints.
  • Shared values. In the same survey, most Indians of every major faith said respecting all religions is very important to being truly Indian.

But the same Pew report was titled "Tolerance and Segregation." It found that many people in India, while valuing respect for other faiths, said their close friends came mostly from their own group, and large majorities of both Hindus and Muslims said it was very important to stop members of their community from marrying outside the faith. Across the region, religious minorities have at times faced discrimination and violence, and communal violence has caused terrible suffering on all sides, as Chapter 4 shows for Partition. Pluralism is not automatic. It is something communities build and protect.

Whose Story?

Who gets to define a faith? Many Hindus prefer the name Sanatana Dharma to "Hinduism," a label that grew from an outsider's word. Many Sikhs object when textbooks call Sikhism a "mix" of Hinduism and Islam, because in Sikh understanding it is a distinct revelation through Guru Nanak. In Pakistan, some church leaders say the 2023 census undercounted Christians, whom it counted at 1.37% of the population. Ahmadis describe themselves as Muslims, but most other Muslims reject their belief that their founder, Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, was a prophet. Since 1974, Pakistan's constitution has classified them as non-Muslims, so the same people are counted differently depending on who is counting. That's why this book describes each faith the way its own followers usually describe it, and notes where counts are disputed.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about what faith practice meant in their childhood home, and how they practice now. If your family is not religious, ask about the values they grew up with and how those values were passed down. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Faith can be personal. Ask if they're comfortable talking about it, let them skip any question, and ask permission before taking notes.

Questions to ask

  1. When you were a child, what did a normal day or week of faith (or family values) look like in your home?
  2. Is there a prayer, song, story or ritual you remember from childhood? What did it mean to you then?
  3. Where did your family go to worship or celebrate, and what was it like inside?
  4. Did you have friends or neighbors of other faiths? What did you learn from them, or share with them?
  5. How has your practice changed over your life, or since moving to a new country?
  6. What do you most want younger people in our family to understand or keep?

Listen for: practices such as Puja, Langar or the Five Pillars of Islam in South Asia; moments of Pilgrimage; and stories of Religious Pluralism, such as neighbors of different faiths sharing festivals or food.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare your elder's description of their faith (or values) with how this chapter describes it. What did the chapter get right, and what did your elder add that a short summary can't capture? If a friend interviewed someone of a different faith, list one practice that is similar and one that is different, without ranking them.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Hinduism has one holy book, like a Hindu Bible. Reality: Hinduism has many sacred texts, including the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata (with the Bhagavad Gita) and the Puranas, and different communities value different ones most.

Myth: Sikhism is a mix of Hinduism and Islam. Reality: Sikhs understand their faith as a distinct revelation through Guru Nanak and the Gurus who followed him, with its own scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, and its own practices such as langar. The scripture includes some hymns by Hindu and Muslim saints, but that doesn't make Sikhism a blend.

Myth: All Buddhists are the same. Reality: Buddhism has several schools. Sri Lanka follows Theravada, with the Pali Canon, while Bhutan and Himalayan Nepal follow Vajrayana, with Tibetan teachings and rituals. Their temples, festivals and practices differ.

Myth: South Asian Muslims are recent converts or outsiders. Reality: Muslims have lived in South Asia for well over a thousand years, starting with traders on the coasts in the 600s and 700s. Most South Asian Muslims descend from families who have lived in the region for many centuries.

Myth: Religion and country map one-to-one: India is Hindu, Pakistan is Muslim, Sri Lanka is Buddhist. Reality: Every South Asian country is home to several faiths. India had about 172 million Muslims in 2011, Bangladesh has millions of Hindus, Sri Lanka has large Hindu, Muslim and Christian communities, and Sikhism's holiest sites include places in Pakistan.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. Name the four faiths in this chapter that began in South Asia.

Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism.

2. What is the difference between Theravada and Vajrayana Buddhism, and where is each found in South Asia?

Theravada uses the Pali Canon and is the Buddhism of Sri Lanka. Vajrayana developed later, uses Mahayana and Tibetan teachings and rituals, and is the Buddhism of Bhutan and Himalayan Nepal.

3. What is langar, and what idea does it express?

Langar is the free community kitchen of a gurdwara, where everyone sits together and eats the same meal regardless of religion, caste, gender or wealth. It expresses the Sikh teaching that all people are equal.

4. Why did Sunni and Shia Islam separate?

They disagreed about who should lead the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad died in 632: Sunnis accept the choice of Abu Bakr, while Shias believe the Prophet named Ali.

5. What does ahimsa mean, and which faith puts it at the very center of life?

Ahimsa means non-violence toward all living beings. Jainism puts it at the center, which is why many Jains are strict vegetarians.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Match each faith to its place of worship: Hinduism, Islam, Sikhism, Zoroastrianism, Judaism.

    Answer

    Hinduism: mandir (temple). Islam: masjid (mosque). Sikhism: gurdwara. Zoroastrianism: fire temple. Judaism: synagogue.

  2. Who compiled the first version of the Guru Granth Sahib, and in what year?

    Answer

    Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, in 1604.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain the idea of karma and rebirth in your own words, and name two faiths besides Hinduism that use the idea.

    Answer

    Karma is the belief that a person's actions and intentions have effects, in this life and in future lives, as the soul is reborn in a cycle. Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism also speak of karma and rebirth, each in its own way.

  2. Explain why India's 14.2% Muslim share in 2011 still meant one of the largest Muslim populations in the world.

    Answer

    India's total population is so large that 14.2% was about 172 million people, more than the total population of most countries.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Faith Explorer in Compare mode. Pick two faiths and one lens, and write three sentences comparing them without using the words "better," "worse," "real" or "true." Hint: start with "Both..." and "In contrast..."

  2. Your school is planning a multi-faith calendar for the club. Choose four faiths from this chapter and list one major festival for each, with one sentence explaining what it marks. Hint: the "A major festival" lens in the sim will help.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Look at the faith map table in 5.3. Identify two countries where a minority faith includes millions of people, and explain why "minority" doesn't mean "small" in South Asia. Hint: compare percentages with each country's total population from Chapter 1.

  2. Analyze Adam's Peak as an example of religious pluralism. What does it show, and what are the limits of using one shared site to describe relations between faiths? Hint: the Pew report title "Tolerance and Segregation" is a useful clue.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A classmate's slide says "Sikhism = Hinduism + Islam." Evaluate the slide and suggest a fairer one-sentence description. Hint: think about how Sikhs describe their own faith.

  2. Some people say it's impossible to compare faiths fairly. Using the five lenses and the ground rules in 5.2, evaluate whether this chapter's approach works, and suggest one improvement. Hint: what might the five lenses leave out?

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a respectful "visitor's guide" card for one place of worship in your area (or one from the chapter): what to wear, what to do with shoes, how to behave, and one question to ask a member. Hint: check the place's own website or ask a member before finishing.

  2. Write a short scene (150 to 200 words) in which two friends of different faiths explain one festival to each other. Show curiosity and respect. Hint: use at least three concept labels from this chapter.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• South Asia is home to Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, which began there, and to Islam, Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Judaism, which arrived long ago and took deep root.
  • Comparing faiths fairly means using the same lenses for each, describing beliefs as their followers do, and never ranking them.
  • Hinduism has no single founder or book. Its key ideas include dharma, karma and rebirth, and puja, the offering of worship.
  • Buddhism in South Asia includes Theravada (Sri Lanka) and Vajrayana (Bhutan, Himalayan Nepal). Jainism puts ahimsa, non-violence, at its center.
  • Most South Asian Muslims are Sunni, with an important Shia minority. Muslims are the majority in Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and the Maldives, and number about 172 million in India (2011).
  • Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as their living Guru, and the langar feeds everyone as equals.
  • Pilgrimage and shared sites show religious pluralism in action, but pluralism also involves real tensions that communities must work to overcome.

Shoes back on!

You can now explain eight faith traditions through the same five lenses, without ranking any of them. Next, in Chapter 6, we follow the languages and scripts in which so many of these prayers, songs and stories are written.

docs.title: Quiz: Faiths of South Asia
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 5. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which school of Buddhism is followed by most Buddhists in Sri Lanka?

  1. Vajrayana
  2. Zen
  3. Theravada
  4. Pure Land
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Sri Lanka follows Theravada Buddhism, whose scriptures are the Pali Canon. Vajrayana is the main distractor: it is the Buddhism of Bhutan and Himalayan Nepal, not Sri Lanka.

Concept Tested: Theravada and Vajrayana Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
What is the Guru Granth Sahib?

  1. The Sikh scripture, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru
  2. The founder of Sikhism
  3. The holiest gurdwara in Amritsar
  4. A collection of Hindu epics translated into Punjabi
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The Guru Granth Sahib is the Sikh scripture, first compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604. Guru Nanak founded Sikhism, and the Golden Temple is the holiest gurdwara, which is why B and C can sound plausible.

Concept Tested: Guru Granth Sahib Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
What does ahimsa mean?

  1. Devotional singing in a temple
  2. Non-violence toward all living beings
  3. A pilgrimage to a sacred river
  4. Fasting during a holy month
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Ahimsa means non-violence in action, word and thought. Jains put it at the center of their lives, and Hindus and Buddhists also value it. Fasting (D) is part of some Jain festivals, but it is not what the word means.

Concept Tested: Ahimsa Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Which statement best describes Hinduism?

  1. A religion founded by one teacher, with one holy book
  2. A branch of Buddhism that began in Nepal
  3. A religion that began in Arabia and spread to India
  4. A family of related traditions with no single founder and many sacred texts
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Hinduism grew over thousands of years from many traditions and has many sacred texts, including the Vedas, Upanishads, epics and Puranas. Option A describes the common misconception that Hinduism has "one holy book."

Concept Tested: Hinduism Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why did Sunni and Shia Islam become separate branches?

  1. They disagreed about who should lead the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad died.
  2. They use different holy books.
  3. Shia Muslims do not follow the Five Pillars.
  4. Sunni Islam began in South Asia, while Shia Islam began in Arabia.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Sunnis accept the community's choice of Abu Bakr as the first leader, while Shias believe the Prophet named Ali. Both branches share the Quran and the Five Pillars, so B and C are wrong.

Concept Tested: Sunni and Shia Islam Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
What idea does langar, the free community kitchen of a gurdwara, express?

  1. That only Sikhs may eat food blessed in a gurdwara
  2. That fasting is the most important form of worship
  3. That all people are equal, so everyone eats together regardless of religion, caste, gender or wealth
  4. That food should be offered to the scripture before anyone eats
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Langar is served free to anyone who comes, and everyone sits together as equals, reflecting Guru Nanak's teaching of equality. Option A is the opposite of the truth: visitors of every faith are welcome.

Concept Tested: Langar Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Ben visits a gurdwara for the first time with Simran. Based on the chapter, what should he expect to do?

  1. Keep his shoes on and stand during the service
  2. Remove his shoes, cover his head, and sit on the floor, possibly eating langar afterward
  3. Bring an offering of meat for the community meal
  4. Show proof that he is a Sikh before entering
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Visitors to a gurdwara remove their shoes and cover their heads, sit on the floor, and are welcome at langar. Option C is wrong because langar is vegetarian, and D is wrong because gurdwaras welcome respectful visitors of every faith.

Concept Tested: Sikhism Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
A classmate writes, "Pakistan is Muslim, India is Hindu, and Sri Lanka is Buddhist, so each faith has its own country." Which fact from the chapter best shows the problem with this claim?

  1. SAARC was founded in 1985.
  2. Bhutan follows Vajrayana Buddhism.
  3. The Kumbh Mela rotates among four cities.
  4. India had about 172 million Muslims in 2011, and Sri Lanka's 2024 census found large Hindu, Muslim and Christian communities.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Every South Asian country is home to several faiths, and even minority shares can mean millions of people. Option B is true but doesn't address the claim that religion and country line up one-to-one.

Concept Tested: Religious Pluralism Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Adam's Peak in Sri Lanka is visited by Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians, who each explain its footprint differently. What does this example best show?

  1. That the four faiths have merged into one religion in Sri Lanka
  2. That one faith's explanation of the footprint is the correct one
  3. That a single sacred place can hold different meanings for different faiths, an example of religious pluralism
  4. That pilgrimage is only important in Buddhism
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Shared sites like Adam's Peak show people of different faiths valuing the same place in their own ways. The faiths remain distinct (so A is wrong), and the book does not rank one explanation above another (so B is wrong).

Concept Tested: Pilgrimage Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Pew Research Center's 2021 report on religion in India was titled "Tolerance and Segregation." Which conclusion does the evidence in the chapter best support?

  1. Most Indians value respect for all religions, yet many keep their friendships and marriages within their own faith.
  2. Indians of different faiths share no beliefs at all.
  3. Religious tension in India has completely disappeared.
  4. Only Hindus in India believe in karma.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The survey found that respect for all religions is widely valued, but many people's friends come mostly from their own group, and many oppose interfaith marriage. Option D is contradicted by the finding that 77% of both Hindus and Muslims said they believe in karma.

Concept Tested: Religious Pluralism Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asia is one of the most multilingual places on Earth. India's 2011 census counted 121 languages with at least 10,000 speakers each, and Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Bhutan and the Maldives add many more. This chapter sorts those languages into five big families, explains the difference between a language and a script, and shows how most of the region's scripts grew from one ancestor, Brahmi. You'll learn how an abugida writes vowels, why Hindi and Urdu are so close in speech yet so different on paper, and what it means to grow up with a heritage language that you understand but don't always speak.
