docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asia's festivals follow three different kinds of calendar. Some follow the sun and land on almost the same date every year. Some follow the moon alone and slide about 11 days earlier each year. Many follow both, so they wobble by a few weeks but stay in the same season. This chapter explains those three calendars first. Then it goes through the year's major festivals across the eight countries: what each one marks, who celebrates it, and how celebrations differ from place to place. By the end you'll be able to predict, roughly, when a festival will fall next year and explain why.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Lunisolar Calendar
  2. Islamic Lunar Calendar
  3. Diwali
  4. Holi
  5. Navaratri and Durga Puja
  6. Dashain and Tihar
  7. Ramadan
  8. Eid al-Fitr
  9. Eid al-Adha
  10. Ashura
  11. Vaisakhi
  12. Pohela Boishakh
  13. Pongal and Makar Sankranti
  14. Onam
  15. Vesak
  16. Losar
  17. Nowruz
  18. Christmas in South Asia

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia? for the eight countries and the monsoon seasons.
  • Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia for the basic ideas of Hinduism, Islam, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism and Christianity.
  • Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts helps with the festival names, which come from many languages.

Festival season is every season

Hi, I'm Mora! If you've ever had to explain to a teacher why you'll miss a test for Eid, or why Diwali "moved" this year, this chapter is for you. Festivals are when families pass down food, stories and music, and knowing how their calendars work helps you plan for them and explain them to friends. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 7.1 Ben Builds a Calendar
docs.text:
It's a Thursday in late August, and Ben Lindqvist has volunteered for a job nobody else wanted: building the South Asian Student Association's calendar for the whole school year. Zara Hossain wants the club to mark every big festival its members celebrate, so nobody schedules a meeting on someone's Eid or Diwali. Ben figures it'll take ten minutes. He'll just copy last year's dates.

Twenty minutes later he's frowning at his laptop. "Zara, something's broken. Last year Diwali was on 20 October. This year it says 8 November. And Eid al-Fitr was 31 March in 2025, then 21 March in 2026, and next year it's around 10 March. Do people just pick new dates every year?" Zara laughs, then stops, because she realizes she doesn't know why. Her Nanu always says "Eid depends on the moon," but Diwali follows the moon too, and it moved later, not earlier. If both festivals follow the moon, why don't they move the same way?

docs.title: 7.2 Three Ways to Count a Year
docs.text:
Start with something Ben already knows. His birthday falls on the same date every year because the calendar on his wall follows the sun. The Gregorian calendar, the one used for school, sports schedules and taxes in the United States, is a solar calendar: its year is built to match one trip of the Earth around the sun, about 365.24 days. That's why the seasons stay put, and hockey season always starts when it's cold.

Now imagine a second calendar that ignores the sun and counts only the moon. The moon goes from new moon to full moon and back to new moon in about 29.53 days. That cycle is a lunar month. Twelve lunar months add up to about

\[ 12 \times 29.53 \approx 354.4 \text{ days}, \]

which is about 11 days shorter than a solar year. A calendar built only on the moon is a lunar calendar.

There's also a third option: count months by the moon, but every few years add an extra month so the calendar catches up with the sun. That's a Lunisolar Calendar, a calendar whose months follow the moon but whose years are kept in step with the sun and the seasons by adding a leap month from time to time. In many Hindu calendars of South Asia, this extra month is called adhik maas, "added month," and it is inserted about once every 32.5 months on average, roughly every two and a half to three years.

Calendar type Months follow Year length What happens to festival dates on the Gregorian calendar South Asian examples Solar The sun About 365 days Almost the same date every year Vaisakhi, Pohela Boishakh in Bangladesh, Pongal, Nowruz, Christmas Lunisolar The moon, with a leap month 354 days in most years, about 384 in a leap year Jumps back and forth by up to about a month, but stays in the same season Diwali, Holi, Navaratri, Dashain, Vesak, Losar Lunar The moon only 354 or 355 days About 11 days earlier every year, moving through all seasons Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Ashura

The Islamic Lunar Calendar (also called the Hijri calendar) is a purely lunar calendar of 12 months, with a year of 354 or 355 days and no leap month. It is the calendar Muslims use for religious dates, from the start of Ramadan to the two Eids. Because it never adds a month to catch up, its dates drift backward through the Gregorian year. A little arithmetic shows how fast:

\[ 365.24 - 354.37 \approx 10.9 \text{ days per year}. \]

To slide all the way around the Gregorian year, an Islamic date needs about

\[ \frac{365.24}{10.9} \approx 33.5 \text{ Gregorian years}. \]

So someone who fasts during Ramadan for most of their life will fast through every season, more than once.

That answers Ben's puzzle. Eid al-Fitr follows a lunar calendar, so it moved about 11 days earlier from 2026 to 2027. Diwali follows a lunisolar calendar. In most years it also lands about 11 days earlier than the year before, but whenever a leap month is added, it jumps about 19 days later instead. Between 2025 and 2026, a leap month was added, so Diwali jumped from 20 October to 8 November.

Try the math yourself

If Eid al-Fitr is on 21 March in 2026 and moves about 11 days earlier each year, roughly when will it fall in 2028? In what year might it land near New Year's Day? Check your guesses with the Festival Wheel at the end of the chapter.

docs.title: Why a festival can be "a day off"
docs.text:
Calendars that follow the moon raise one more question: who decides when a month starts? In Islamic practice, a new month traditionally begins when people see the thin crescent moon just after sunset, and committees in many countries confirm the sighting. The crescent can be visible in one place and not another, so Eid can fall on different days in, say, Saudi Arabia and Bangladesh, or even in two cities of one country.

In July 2025, for example, the Government of India published its holiday list for 2026 and set the Eid al-Adha holiday (often called Bakrid in India) for 27 May 2026, "subject to change" depending on the moon. On 22 May 2026, after the moon was sighted, the government moved the holiday in Delhi to 28 May. Lunisolar calendars have their own version of this: many Hindu festivals are tied to a tithi (a lunar day), and regional calendars sometimes disagree about which sunrise or evening it falls on, so a festival can be marked on two neighboring days in different places.

docs.title: 7.3 Festivals of Light and Color: Diwali and Holi
Diwali
docs.text:
Diwali (दिवाली, dee-VAH-lee), from the Sanskrit Deepavali, "row of lamps," is the festival of lights, held on the new moon at the end of the lunar month of Ashvin (Kartika in some regional calendars), usually in October or November. Families clean and decorate their homes, light small clay oil lamps called diyas, draw colored designs at the doorway (you'll learn about rangoli and kolam in Chapter 11), wear new clothes, share sweets and set off fireworks.

What Diwali celebrates depends on who you ask.

  • Many Hindus celebrate the victory of light over darkness and of good over evil. In much of North India, Diwali recalls the god Rama returning home after defeating Ravana. Many families worship Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and good fortune, on the main night. In Bengal and among Hindus in Bangladesh, the same new moon night is Kali Puja, honoring the goddess Kali.
  • Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, "day of liberation," on the same day. In Sikh tradition, it marks the release of the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment in Gwalior Fort by the Mughal emperor Jahangir, along with 52 imprisoned kings.
  • Jains mark Diwali as the anniversary of the nirvana (final liberation) of Mahavira, the last of the Jain Tirthankaras.
  • Newar Buddhists of Nepal's Kathmandu Valley also celebrate the festival, which they call Swanti.

Diwali is a public holiday in India (8 November in 2026, according to the Government of India's holiday list), and Hindu communities in Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka celebrate it too. In Nepal, the five-day festival of the same season is called Tihar (Section 7.4). In 2025, a resolution introduced in the US House of Representatives recognized Diwali as a festival celebrated by "Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, and others" across the United States.

docs.title: Holi
docs.text:
Holi (होली, HOH-lee) is the spring festival of colors, held on the full moon of the month of Phalguna and the day after it, usually in March. On the first evening, communities light a bonfire called Holika Dahan. On the main day, people of all ages chase each other through the streets throwing colored powder and water, and old arguments are supposed to be forgiven.

Holi carries several meanings at once. Many Hindus connect the bonfire to the story of the young devotee Prahlad, who survived when his aunt Holika tried to burn him. Holi also celebrates the love of Radha and Krishna, the end of winter and the coming spring harvest. In Bengal (West Bengal in India, and Bangladesh) it is often called Dol Jatra or Basanta Utsab, "spring festival." Nepal celebrates Holi as Fagu Purnima, and Hindu communities in Pakistan and Bangladesh celebrate it too. In 2026, India's holiday list put Holi on 4 March.

Because Holi follows a lunisolar calendar, it can fall anywhere from late February to late March, but the leap month keeps it from ever leaving spring.

docs.title: 7.4 Nine Nights and the Tenth Day
Navaratri and Durga Puja
docs.text:
Navaratri and Durga Puja are two names for the great autumn festival of the goddess. Navaratri (नवरात्रि, nuh-vuh-RAHT-ree) means "nine nights." It begins the day after the new moon of the month of Ashvin, usually in September or October, and the tenth day is Vijayadashami, often called Dussehra, "the tenth day of victory." In 2026, India's central government listed Dussehra on 20 October.

The same nine nights look very different across the region.

  • In Gujarat, people dance Garba, a circle dance around a lamp or an image of the goddess, night after night. UNESCO added the Garba of Gujarat to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2023.
  • In Bengal, Assam and Odisha, and among Hindus in Bangladesh, the festival is Durga Puja, the worship of the goddess Durga (दुर्गा, DOOR-gah), who in many Hindu traditions defeats the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Artisans spend months sculpting images of Durga and her children from clay. Communities build temporary decorated structures called pandals to house them, and on the last day the images are carried to a river and immersed. UNESCO inscribed "Durga Puja in Kolkata" on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2021.
  • In much of North India, the tenth day recalls Rama's victory over Ravana. Plays called Ramlila retell the story, and towering effigies of Ravana are burned with fireworks.

docs.title: Dashain and Tihar
docs.text:
Dashain and Tihar are Nepal's two biggest festivals, about three weeks apart in the autumn.

Dashain (दशैं, duh-SHAIN) is Nepal's version of the Navaratri season. It is the longest and most important festival in the country's calendar, lasting 15 days, usually in September or October. On the first day, families plant barley seeds indoors. By the tenth day the seeds have grown into pale yellow shoots called jamara. On that day, elders put a tika (a mark of red rice and yogurt) on the foreheads of younger relatives, tuck jamara behind their ears and give their blessing. Dashain is celebrated by Nepali families of many backgrounds, and also in Bhutan and in Nepali-speaking parts of India.

Tihar (तिहार, tee-HAAR) is Nepal's five-day festival of lights, in the same season as Diwali. Each day honors someone different: crows on the first day, dogs on the second (Kukur Tihar, when dogs get flower garlands and treats), cows and the goddess Lakshmi on the third, oxen on the fourth, and siblings on the last day, Bhai Tika, when sisters bless their brothers. Children go house to house singing songs called Deusi and Bhailo, a little like caroling. Among Newar communities of the Kathmandu Valley the festival is called Swanti.

Same night, different names

If a friend from Kolkata says "Durga Puja," a friend from Ahmedabad says "Navaratri," and a friend from Kathmandu says "Dashain," they're often talking about the very same days in the calendar. Ask how their family celebrates before you assume it's the same festival in every way.

docs.title: 7.5 The Islamic Year
docs.text: Muslims make up most of the population of Afghanistan, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Maldives, and large communities in India and Sri Lanka. For all of them, the year's most important religious dates follow the Islamic Lunar Calendar.

docs.title: Ramadan
docs.text:
Ramadan (Arabic رمضان, rah-mah-DAHN; in Bangla রমজান, rom-JAHN) is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, a month of fasting, prayer and charity that lasts 29 or 30 days, from one sighting of the crescent moon to the next. Fasting during Ramadan is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Adult Muslims go without food and drink from dawn until sunset. People who are ill, traveling, elderly, pregnant or breastfeeding are excused, and many can make up the days later.

Zara's family wakes up before dawn for sehri (the predawn meal; in Arabic it's called suhur) and gathers at sunset for iftar, the meal that breaks the fast, often starting with dates and water. In Minnesota, where summer days are long and winter days are short, the length of the fast changes a lot depending on which season Ramadan falls in. Over a lifetime, Zara will fast through Minnesota summers and winters alike.

docs.title: Eid al-Fitr
docs.text: Eid al-Fitr (Bangla ঈদুল ফিতর, EED-ul FIT-er), "the festival of breaking the fast," begins on the first day of the month of Shawwal, when the new crescent is sighted at the end of Ramadan. The night of the sighting is celebrated as Chand Raat, "night of the moon," with last-minute shopping and henna. On Eid morning, families put on new clothes and attend special prayers. Before the prayer, Muslims give a required charity called zakat al-fitr so that people in need can celebrate too. Children receive Eidi (gifts of money), and visits to relatives last all day, often with sweet vermicelli (shemai in Bangla, sheer khurma or seviyan in Urdu and Hindi). Eid al-Fitr is celebrated for one to three days depending on the country. In 2026, India's holiday list put it on 21 March.

docs.title: Eid al-Adha
docs.text: Eid al-Adha (Bangla ঈদুল আযহা, EED-ul AD-ha), "the festival of sacrifice," falls on the 10th day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last month of the Islamic year, during the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca. In Islamic tradition, it honors the prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) willingness to sacrifice his son at God's command. Families who can afford it sacrifice an animal (a goat, sheep, cow or camel) and share the meat with relatives, neighbors and people in need. In Pakistan and Bangladesh, busy animal markets appear in cities in the weeks before. In India it is often called Bakrid, and in 2026 it fell on 28 May in Delhi, one day after the date first printed on the holiday list.

docs.title: Ashura
docs.text:
Ashura (Persian عاشورا, aa-SHOO-rah, "the tenth") is the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic year. It means different things to different Muslims.

  • For Shia Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year, a day of mourning for Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed with his companions at the Battle of Karbala, in present-day Iraq, on 10 Muharram in 680 CE. During the first ten days of Muharram, Shia communities hold gatherings called majlis where Husayn's story is retold, and on Ashura they hold processions. In Dhaka, the Hussaini Dalan, a Shia hall first built in the 17th century under Mughal rule, is the center of Muharram gatherings. Large Muharram processions also take place in cities across Pakistan and India.
  • Sunni Muslims also regard Husayn's death as a tragedy and remember it in sermons. Many Sunnis also fast on Ashura, a practice linked in Islamic tradition to the day Moses and the Israelites were saved from Pharaoh.

Not every festival is a party

Wishing someone "Happy Ashura" can hurt, because for many Shia families it is a day of grief. If you're not sure how a friend's family observes a day, ask, and listen.

docs.title: 7.6 New Years and Harvests Set by the Sun
docs.text: A surprising number of South Asia's new years land in mid-April. That's because many regional calendars start the year when the sun enters Mesha (the sign of Aries in the Indian zodiac), around 13 to 15 April. Since these festivals follow the sun, their dates barely move.

docs.title: Vaisakhi
docs.text:
Vaisakhi (VAI-saa-khee), also spelled Baisakhi, falls on 13 or 14 April and is both a harvest festival and a new year in Punjab and in much of North India. For Sikhs, it is one of the most important days of the year. In Sikh tradition, on Vaisakhi in 1699 the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, at Anandpur. Sikhs mark the day with prayers at the gurdwara and nagar kirtan, processions with hymn singing through the streets. Because many of Sikhism's holiest sites are in present-day Pakistan, thousands of Sikh pilgrims from India cross the border each year for Vaisakhi, with the main gathering at Gurdwara Panja Sahib in Hasan Abdal, in Pakistan's Punjab province. Simran Kaur Gill, the club treasurer, tells Ben that her grandparents in Ludhiana start the day at the gurdwara and spend the afternoon at a fair.

The same mid-April date is also Vishu in Kerala, Puthandu (Tamil New Year) in Tamil Nadu, and Bohag Bihu in Assam. In Sri Lanka, Sinhala and Tamil families celebrate the Sinhala and Tamil New Year on 13 or 14 April. Dilan Perera's family in Kandy waits for the exact auspicious time, set by astrologers, to light the hearth and cook kiribath (milk rice), and many neighbors do the same at the same minute.

docs.title: Pohela Boishakh
docs.text:
Pohela Boishakh (পহেলা বৈশাখ, po-HEH-la boy-SHAKH), "the first of Boishakh," is the Bengali New Year. In Bangladesh it is a national holiday on 14 April every year. That date is fixed because Bangladesh revised its version of the Bengali calendar: a committee led by the scholar Muhammad Shahidullah proposed the reform in 1966, and Bangladesh officially adopted it in 1987. In West Bengal and other Indian states, which still use the traditional Bengali calendar, Pohela Boishakh falls on 14 or 15 April. India's 2026 holiday list put "Vaisakhadi (Bengal)" on 15 April.

In Dhaka, the day starts at dawn with songs by the cultural group Chhayanaut in Ramna Park. Students and teachers from the Faculty of Fine Art at the University of Dhaka lead a huge street procession with giant masks and floats. That tradition began in 1989, when students under military rule wanted to bring people hope, and UNESCO added it to its intangible heritage list in 2016 as Mangal Shobhajatra. Its official name was changed in 2025 and debated again in 2026, so you may hear it called by different names.

Shopkeepers close the old year's accounts and open new account books, a custom called haal khata. In recent decades many families in Dhaka have also made panta bhat (cooked rice soaked overnight in water) part of the day's breakfast.

Whose Story?

Who invented the Bengali year? Many Bangladeshi textbooks and writers credit the Mughal emperor Akbar, who in the 1500s wanted a calendar that matched the harvest so taxes could be collected after the crops came in. Other historians point to older Bengali rulers, and to temple inscriptions that suggest a Bengali year was counted before Akbar's time. Some writers stress the festival's roots in Hindu solar new year traditions, while in Bangladesh it is also celebrated as a shared, secular Bengali holiday by Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists and Christians alike. Even the date is a border story: Dhaka celebrates on the 14th every year, while Kolkata sometimes celebrates on the 15th, because the two cities now use different versions of the same calendar.

docs.title: Pongal and Makar Sankranti
docs.text:
Pongal and Makar Sankranti are winter harvest festivals that mark the sun's move into Makara (Capricorn in the Indian zodiac), usually on 14 or 15 January. India's 2026 holiday list put both on 14 January. Because they follow the sun, they're among the most predictable dates in the South Asian year.

Pongal (பொங்கல், PONG-gul), "boiling over," is the Tamil harvest festival, held over three or four days at the start of the Tamil month of Thai. On the main day, families cook rice with milk and jaggery (unrefined cane sugar) in a new pot outdoors until it boils over, and everyone shouts "Pongalo pongal!" On Mattu Pongal, cattle are bathed, their horns painted and garlanded, to thank them for their work. Tamil communities in Sri Lanka celebrate Thai Pongal too.

Makar Sankranti (मकर संक्रांति) is the name used in much of India for the same solar moment. In Gujarat it's a kite festival called Uttarayan; in Assam it's Magh Bihu; in Nepal it is Maghe Sankranti. In Punjab, the bonfire festival Lohri falls the night before, usually on 13 January, and Hindus, Sikhs and some Muslims also mark it in rural Pakistani Punjab and in cities such as Lahore and Faisalabad.

docs.title: Onam
docs.text: Onam (ഓണം, OH-num) is the harvest festival of Kerala, celebrated by Malayali families of many faiths. It falls in the Malayalam month of Chingam (August to September), on the day of the star Thiruvonam. In 2026, India's holiday list put Thiru Onam on 26 August. In Kerala tradition, Onam is when the generous king Mahabali, who once ruled Kerala, returns each year to visit his people. Families make a pookalam, a round carpet of flower petals at the doorway, and share a sadya, a feast of many dishes served on a banana leaf. In some towns, long snake boats race on the backwaters. Onam's date depends on both a solar month and the moon's position among the stars, so it moves around within late August and September.

docs.title: Nowruz
docs.text: Nowruz (نوروز, noh-ROOZ), "new day," is the Persian New Year, which begins at the March equinox, on 20 or 21 March. In Afghanistan, where it's called Nawruz, it was long the start of the official calendar year. Families prepare haft mewa, a dish of seven dried fruits and nuts soaked in water, and the biggest celebrations took place at Mazar-i-Sharif, where a banner-raising ceremony drew crowds from across the country. After the Taliban took power in 2021, their government stopped observing Nowruz as an official holiday in 2022, while saying people could celebrate privately. In India, Parsi and Irani families, who trace their roots to Iran, also celebrate Navroz. UNESCO lists Nowruz as shared heritage of many countries; its 2024 listing includes Afghanistan, India and Pakistan.

docs.title: 7.7 Full Moons and Mountain New Years
Vesak
docs.text:
Vesak (Sinhala වෙසක්, VAY-suck), also called Buddha Purnima in India and Nepal, is the most important Buddhist festival in South Asia. It falls on the full moon of the month of Vesak (Vaisakha), usually in May, and Buddhists in South Asia remember the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing away all on this one day. In 1999 the United Nations General Assembly formally recognized the Day of Vesak.

In Sri Lanka, Vesak is a two-day national celebration. Streets glow with colored paper lanterns called Vesak kudu, and huge electrically lit panels called pandols (or thoranas) tell Jataka tales, stories of the Buddha's earlier lives. Many people set up free food stalls for anyone passing by, and the sale of alcohol and meat is usually stopped for the celebrations. In Sri Lanka every full-moon day, called Poya, is a public holiday, and Vesak Poya is the biggest of them. Dilan's family visits the temple in Kandy dressed in white. Nepal, where Lumbini (traditionally the Buddha's birthplace) lies, celebrates Buddha Jayanti, and Buddhists in Bangladesh, Bhutan and India also mark the day. In 2026, India's holiday list put Buddha Purnima on 1 May.

docs.title: Losar
docs.text:
Losar (Tibetan ལོ་གསར, LOH-sar), "new year," is the new year of the Tibetan lunisolar calendar, usually in February or March, celebrated for up to 15 days with the main celebrations in the first three. In Bhutan it is called Dawa Dangpa Losar. It is also celebrated by Sherpa, Tibetan and other Himalayan communities in Nepal and by people in Ladakh and Sikkim in India. Families clean their homes thoroughly beforehand, make special foods, visit monasteries and hang new prayer flags.

Nepal is a good reminder that one festival name can cover several dates. Nima Sherpa's family in Solukhumbu celebrates Gyalpo Losar, the Tibetan-calendar new year, in February or March. The Tamang community's Sonam Lhosar usually comes about a month earlier (19 January in 2026), and the Gurung community's Tamu Lhosar falls in late December or early January. Tamu Lhosar is a public holiday in Nepal.

docs.title: 7.8 Christmas in South Asia
docs.text:
Christmas in South Asia is the celebration of the birth of Jesus on 25 December by the region's Christian communities. Christianity in South Asia goes back a long way. Christians in Kerala trace their church to the apostle Thomas, who in their tradition arrived on India's southwest coast in the first century. According to India's 2011 census, about 2.3% of Indians, roughly 28 million people, were Christian. Kerala has the largest Christian population of any Indian state, and Christians are the majority in the northeastern states of Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya. Goa has a long Catholic history from the centuries of Portuguese rule, and many families there go to midnight Mass on Christmas Eve.

Christmas is a public holiday in India. In Bangladesh it is called Borodin (বড়দিন, BOH-roh-din), "the big day." In Pakistan, 25 December is a public holiday for two reasons: Christmas, and Quaid-e-Azam Day, the birthday of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Pakistan's founder. Christians in Sri Lanka, both Sinhala- and Tamil-speaking, celebrate with church services and family gatherings. Because Christmas follows the Gregorian calendar, which is solar, it's the easiest date on Ben's calendar.

You can read any calendar now

Notice the pattern: the sun-based festivals (Vaisakhi, Pohela Boishakh, Pongal, Nowruz, Christmas) are the ones you could predict years ahead. You now know more about calendars than most people who use them every day.

docs.title: 7.9 The Whole Year at a Glance
docs.text:
Here is the full list, sorted by calendar type. The 2026 dates come from the Government of India's holiday list for central government offices in Delhi (where it lists the festival); dates in other countries can differ by a day or more.

Festival Calendar Usual time of year 2026 date in India's holiday list Celebrated in (examples) Pongal and Makar Sankranti Solar 14-15 January 14 January India, Sri Lanka (Tamil communities), Nepal (Maghe Sankranti) Losar Lunisolar February-March Not listed Bhutan, Nepal, India (Ladakh, Sikkim) Holi Lunisolar Late February-March 4 March India, Nepal, Hindu communities in Pakistan and Bangladesh Nowruz Solar 20-21 March Not listed in March (Parsi New Year listed 15 August) Afghanistan, Parsi communities in India Vaisakhi Solar 13-14 April 14 April India and Pakistan (Punjab), Sikh communities worldwide Pohela Boishakh Solar 14 April (Bangladesh); 14-15 April (India) 15 April Bangladesh, West Bengal, Tripura and Assam Vesak Lunisolar April-May full moon 1 May Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, India Onam Solar month, star day Late August-September 26 August Kerala and Malayali communities Navaratri and Durga Puja Lunisolar September-October Dussehra 20 October India, Bangladesh Dashain Lunisolar September-October Not listed (Nepal) Nepal, Bhutan, parts of India Diwali and Tihar Lunisolar October-November 8 November India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Bangladesh Christmas Solar 25 December 25 December Christian communities across South Asia Ramadan Lunar Moves through all seasons Not listed (computed: about 19 February to 20 March) Muslim communities across South Asia Eid al-Fitr Lunar Moves through all seasons 21 March Muslim communities across South Asia Eid al-Adha Lunar Moves through all seasons 28 May (moved from 27 May) Muslim communities across South Asia Ashura Lunar Moves through all seasons 26 June (listed as Muharram) Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Afghanistan

One curious entry: India's holiday list puts "Parsi New Year's Day" in August, not March, because many Parsi families in India also follow a traditional Zoroastrian calendar whose new year now falls in late summer.

docs.title: Diagram: Festival Wheel
docs.text:
Open the Festival Wheel fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Festival Wheel

sim-id: ch07-festival-wheel Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain why solar festivals keep the same Gregorian date, lunisolar festivals move within a season, and Islamic lunar festivals move about 11 days earlier each year.

Canvas: responsive width; 620 px drawing area plus 112 px control area.

Controls: Play years / Pause button, Year slider (1990 to 2060), "Color by" menu (calendar type or faith), festival menu, "Show Islamic dates from the past 4 years" checkbox; click or tap any festival dot or label.

Behavior: A 12-month wheel with 1 January at the top. Solar festivals sit at fixed dates. Diwali, Holi, Navaratri and Vesak are computed each year from new and full moons (Meeus's algorithm) and Hindu month rules; Onam and Losar show their usual windows. Ramadan, the two Eids and Ashura are computed from the Moon and a crescent-visibility rule, so they slide about 11 days earlier each year, with faint dots trailing behind for the past four years. The info panel shows the selected festival's computed date, where it is celebrated, and why it moves. Starts paused, set to 2026.

Start in 2026 and click a few dots to read about them. Then drag the Year slider forward one year at a time and watch the three colors. The gold dots (solar festivals) never move. The teal dots (lunisolar festivals) hop back and forth, but Holi always stays in spring and Diwali always stays in autumn. The orange dots (Islamic festivals) march steadily counterclockwise, and the faint trail behind them shows where they were in earlier years.

Now select Eid al-Fitr and press Play years. Pause when Eid reaches December. How many years did it take to get there from March? Try the year 2033, when Eid al-Fitr falls twice in one Gregorian year. And notice the small print in the panel: the sim's dates are calculated, so they can be a day off from the date your community actually uses. That isn't a bug. The Government of India had to move Eid al-Adha in 2026 for the same reason.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the festivals they grew up with and how they celebrate them now. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Pick a quiet time that isn't the busy day of a festival itself, and ask if it's okay to take notes. If your family has a calendar (a printed panjika, a mosque timetable or a wall calendar from a community center), bring it along.

Questions to ask

  1. What was your favorite festival when you were a child? What do you remember about the day?
  2. What foods, clothes, sounds or smells do you connect with that festival?
  3. How did your family find out the exact date each year? Did anyone check the moon, a printed almanac, a radio announcement or a phone?
  4. Which festivals did your neighbors celebrate that your family didn't? Did you join in?
  5. How is celebrating in Minnesota (or wherever you live now) different from celebrating back home?
  6. What is one festival tradition you hope I keep, and why?

Listen for: whether their festivals follow the Islamic Lunar Calendar or a Lunisolar Calendar, which of this chapter's festivals they mention (Eid al-Fitr, Diwali, Pohela Boishakh, Vaisakhi or others), and stories about how dates were decided.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare your elder's description of a festival with the description in this chapter. What did they mention that the chapter left out? If a friend interviewed someone who celebrates a different festival, compare the two: do both families describe new clothes, special food or visiting relatives?

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Diwali is only a Hindu festival. Reality: Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists all celebrate on the same night, each for their own reasons. For Sikhs it is Bandi Chhor Divas, and for Jains it marks Mahavira's nirvana.

Myth: Eid is "the Muslim Christmas." Reality: There are two Eids, with different meanings: Eid al-Fitr ends the fasting month of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha honors Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice and falls during the Hajj. Neither celebrates anyone's birth, and both move through the year on the lunar calendar.

Myth: Holi is just about throwing colors. Reality: Holi begins with the Holika Dahan bonfire and carries religious stories (Prahlad, and Radha and Krishna), the welcome of spring, and a tradition of forgiving old quarrels.

Myth: Festivals that follow the moon all move the same way. Reality: Islamic festivals follow a purely lunar calendar and move about 11 days earlier every year. Lunisolar festivals like Diwali add a leap month every two to three years, so they jump back later and stay in the same season.

Myth: Every festival is celebrated the same way everywhere. Reality: The same autumn nights are Garba in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Kolkata and Dhaka, Ramlila in North India, and Dashain in Nepal. Even the date of Pohela Boishakh differs between Bangladesh and West Bengal.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a lunar calendar and a lunisolar calendar?

Both count months by the moon. A lunar calendar, like the Islamic calendar, never adds extra months, so its year is about 354 days. A lunisolar calendar adds a leap month every two to three years to stay in step with the sun and the seasons.

2. Why does Eid al-Fitr come about 11 days earlier each year on the Gregorian calendar?

Twelve lunar months add up to about 354 days, roughly 11 days less than a solar year of about 365 days. The Islamic calendar never adds a month to catch up, so each new Eid comes about 11 days earlier.

3. Name the three groups who celebrate on Diwali night and one thing each group remembers.

Many Hindus celebrate light over darkness (Rama's return, Lakshmi puja); Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior Fort; Jains remember Mahavira's nirvana. Some Buddhists celebrate too.

4. Why is Pohela Boishakh always on 14 April in Bangladesh but sometimes on 15 April in West Bengal?

Bangladesh adopted a revised Bengali calendar in 1987 (based on a 1966 proposal), which fixes the new year on 14 April. West Bengal still uses the traditional calendar, whose new year falls on 14 or 15 April.

5. What is Ashura, and how do Shia and many Sunni Muslims observe it?

Ashura is the 10th of Muharram. For Shia Muslims it is a day of mourning for Husayn, killed at Karbala in 680 CE, with gatherings and processions. Many Sunni Muslims fast on Ashura.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List two festivals that follow a solar calendar, two that follow a lunisolar calendar, and two that follow the Islamic Lunar Calendar.

    Answer

    Solar: any two of Vaisakhi, Pohela Boishakh (Bangladesh), Pongal and Makar Sankranti, Nowruz, Christmas. Lunisolar: any two of Diwali, Holi, Navaratri and Durga Puja, Dashain, Vesak, Losar. Lunar: any two of Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Ashura.

  2. Which festival is celebrated with jamara and tika, and in which country is it the biggest festival of the year?

    Answer

    Dashain, the biggest and longest festival in Nepal.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why Holi always falls in spring even though it follows the moon.

    Answer

    Holi follows a lunisolar calendar. Every two to three years, a leap month is added so that the lunar months stay lined up with the solar year. That keeps Holi between late February and late March.

  2. Explain why many Indian holiday lists say Islamic holiday dates are "subject to change."

    Answer

    Islamic months traditionally begin when the new crescent moon is sighted. The government prints its list months in advance using an expected date, but the actual sighting can push the holiday a day later, as happened with Eid al-Adha in 2026.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Festival Wheel to find the first year after 2026 when Ramadan begins in January. Then calculate how many years that is after 2026 and check whether it fits the "about 11 days a year" rule. Hint: count how many days Ramadan's start has to move back from 19 February to reach January.

  2. Your club wants to hold a "festivals of spring" night in April. Using this chapter, list at least four festivals from at least three different countries that could be featured, with a one-line description of each. Hint: look for festivals that follow the sun into mid-April.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare how Navaratri is celebrated in Gujarat, Kolkata and Nepal. What stays the same across all three, and what changes? Hint: think about the dates, the goddess, and what people actually do.

  2. Ben's calendar shows Diwali moving from 20 October 2025 to 8 November 2026, but Eid al-Fitr moving from 31 March 2025 to 21 March 2026. Analyze why one moved later and the other moved earlier. Hint: what happened in the lunisolar calendar between those two Diwalis?

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A school is deciding whether to give students a day off for Diwali, for Eid, or for neither. Evaluate the challenge of fixing those dates a year in advance, and suggest a fair policy. Hint: consider moon sighting, different communities' dates, and how many students celebrate.

  2. Some people say a festival like Pohela Boishakh or Onam is "cultural, not religious." Others disagree. Using evidence from the chapter, evaluate this claim for one festival. Hint: the Whose Story? box is a good place to start.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design your club's festival calendar for the next school year. Include at least eight festivals from at least four countries, the expected date for each, its calendar type, and a note on any date that could shift. Hint: use the Festival Wheel for computed dates, then check an official holiday list.

  2. Write a short guide (150 to 200 words) for a new club member explaining how to greet friends respectfully during three different festivals, including one that is a day of mourning. Hint: include Ashura and explain why "happy" is the wrong word for it.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• South Asian festivals follow three kinds of calendar: solar (fixed dates), lunisolar (moves within a season) and lunar (moves through every season).
  • The Islamic Lunar Calendar has 12 months and about 354 days, so Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha and Ashura come about 11 days earlier each Gregorian year and circle the whole year in about 33 years.
  • Lunisolar calendars add a leap month about every 32.5 months, which keeps Diwali in autumn, Holi in spring and Vesak near May.
  • Many festivals are shared across faiths and borders: Diwali by Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists; Pohela Boishakh by Bengalis of every faith; Vesak across five South Asian countries.
  • The same season can carry different names and customs: Navaratri, Durga Puja, Dussehra and Dashain; Diwali and Tihar; Vaisakhi, Pohela Boishakh and the Sinhala and Tamil New Year.
  • Exact dates depend on local calendars and, for Islamic months, on sighting the moon, so official holiday lists sometimes change, as India's did for Eid al-Adha in 2026.

Your calendar is ready!

You can now explain why Eid moves earlier, why Diwali jumps around, and why Pohela Boishakh stays put. Every festival comes with a feast, so in Chapter 8 we head to the table to see what South Asia eats and why.

docs.title: Quiz: Festivals Through the Year
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 7. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
About how long is a year in the Islamic Lunar Calendar?

  1. 365 or 366 days
  2. 354 or 355 days
  3. 384 or 385 days
  4. 330 days
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Islamic calendar has 12 lunar months of about 29.5 days each, which adds up to 354 or 355 days. 365 or 366 days is the length of the solar Gregorian year, and about 384 days is the length of a lunisolar year that includes a leap month.

Concept Tested: Islamic Lunar Calendar Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
For Sikhs, the day of Diwali is also celebrated as Bandi Chhor Divas. What does it remember?

  1. The founding of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh
  2. The birth of Guru Nanak
  3. The nirvana of Mahavira
  4. The release of Guru Hargobind from Gwalior Fort
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In Sikh tradition, Bandi Chhor Divas marks Guru Hargobind's release from imprisonment in Gwalior Fort, along with 52 imprisoned kings. The founding of the Khalsa is remembered on Vaisakhi, and Mahavira's nirvana is what Jains remember on Diwali.

Concept Tested: Diwali Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which festival does UNESCO list as "Durga Puja in Kolkata," inscribed in 2021?

  1. The autumn worship of the goddess Durga, ending with immersion of clay images
  2. The spring festival of colors held on the full moon of Phalguna
  3. The new year procession held on 14 April in Dhaka
  4. The five-day festival of lights in Nepal that honors crows, dogs and cows
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Durga Puja is the autumn festival, part of the Navaratri season, in which communities worship Durga and then immerse the clay images. The spring festival of colors is Holi, the Dhaka procession is part of Pohela Boishakh, and the five-day festival in Nepal is Tihar.

Concept Tested: Navaratri and Durga Puja Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why does Diwali stay in October or November every year, even though it follows the moon?

  1. Because the Indian government fixes the date by law each year
  2. Because it is set by the sun entering Capricorn
  3. Because a lunisolar calendar adds a leap month every two to three years to keep in step with the sun
  4. Because the moon's cycle is exactly one-twelfth of a solar year
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Diwali follows a lunisolar calendar, which adds an extra month about every 32.5 months so the lunar months don't drift away from the seasons. The government publishes holiday lists but doesn't decide the festival's date, and the sun entering Capricorn is the moment for Makar Sankranti and Pongal, not Diwali.

Concept Tested: Lunisolar Calendar Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why do Shia Muslims and many Sunni Muslims observe Ashura differently?

  1. Shia Muslims celebrate it as a new year party, while Sunnis ignore it
  2. For Shia Muslims it is a day of mourning for Husayn, killed at Karbala, while many Sunnis observe it mainly by fasting
  3. Sunnis mourn Husayn, while Shia Muslims fast to remember Moses
  4. It falls on different months for the two groups
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Ashura, the 10th of Muharram, is the most solemn day of the year for Shia Muslims, who mourn Husayn and his companions killed at Karbala in 680 CE. Many Sunnis also regard his death as a tragedy but mark the day mainly by fasting. Ashura is not a celebration for either group, and both observe it on the same date, the 10th of Muharram.

Concept Tested: Ashura Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why is Pohela Boishakh fixed on 14 April in Bangladesh?

  1. Bangladesh officially adopted a revised Bengali calendar (adopted in 1987, based on a 1966 proposal) that fixes the new year on that date
  2. The date is set by the first sighting of the new moon in April
  3. It is the day the Mughal emperor Akbar was born
  4. It always falls on the full moon of Boishakh
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A committee led by Muhammad Shahidullah proposed a revised calendar in 1966, and Bangladesh officially adopted it in 1987, fixing the new year on 14 April. West Bengal still uses the traditional calendar, so there it falls on 14 or 15 April. The date isn't based on the moon at all, because the Bengali calendar follows the sun.

Concept Tested: Pohela Boishakh Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Eid al-Fitr fell on 21 March 2026 in India. About when would you expect it to fall in 2027?

  1. About 21 March 2027, the same date
  2. About 1 April 2027, 11 days later
  3. About 21 February 2027, one month earlier
  4. About 10 March 2027, 11 days earlier
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Islamic year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Islamic festivals arrive about 11 days earlier each Gregorian year. Staying on the same date is what a solar festival does, and the Islamic calendar never adds a leap month that could push Eid later.

Concept Tested: Eid al-Fitr Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Your club is planning an event for the week of 13 to 15 April. Which group of festivals could you feature, all from that week?

  1. Diwali, Tihar and Kali Puja
  2. Pongal, Lohri and Makar Sankranti
  3. Vaisakhi, Pohela Boishakh and the Sinhala and Tamil New Year
  4. Holi, Losar and Onam
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Vaisakhi, Pohela Boishakh and the Sinhala and Tamil New Year are all solar new years that mark the sun entering Mesha (Aries) in mid-April. Pongal, Lohri and Makar Sankranti are in mid-January, and Diwali, Tihar and Kali Puja fall in October or November.

Concept Tested: Vaisakhi Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Ben notices that Diwali moved from 20 October 2025 to 8 November 2026, while Eid al-Fitr moved from 31 March 2025 to 21 March 2026. What best explains the difference?

  1. Both follow the moon, but the Hindu calendar added a leap month in 2026, pushing Diwali later, while the Islamic calendar never adds one
  2. Diwali follows the sun and Eid follows the moon
  3. The Indian government moved Diwali to a weekend
  4. Eid is decided by moon sighting, but Diwali is chosen by a vote each year
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Both festivals follow lunar months. The Hindu lunisolar calendar inserted an extra month (Adhik Jyeshtha) in May and June 2026, so Diwali jumped about 19 days later. The purely lunar Islamic calendar never adds a month, so Eid kept sliding about 10 to 11 days earlier. Option B is wrong because Diwali does not follow the sun.

Concept Tested: Lunisolar Calendar Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
A friend from Kathmandu talks about Dashain, a friend from Kolkata about Durga Puja, and a friend from Ahmedabad about Navaratri and Garba. What is the best conclusion?

  1. These are three unrelated festivals held in different seasons
  2. Only one of them is a "real" Hindu festival
  3. They fall in the same autumn season and honor the goddess, but local customs differ a lot
  4. They are identical in every way, just with different names
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. All three belong to the autumn Navaratri season tied to the goddess and the tenth day, Vijayadashami. But the customs differ: jamara and tika from elders in Nepal, clay images and pandals in Bengal, and Garba dancing in Gujarat. No version is more "real" than the others, and they are not identical.

Concept Tested: Dashain and Tihar Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: There is no single "South Asian food." What people eat depends on which grain grows near them, how much rain falls, which traders and rulers passed through, and what their faith and family teach about food. This chapter starts with the staple grains and the regional cuisines built on them, then opens up a thali to look at its parts: dal, masala, tadka, breads and rice. It follows biryani, chili peppers and chai through history, visits street stalls and sweet shops, and ends at the table itself, with food rules, eating with hands and the customs of hospitality.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia? for the rivers, plains, deltas and monsoon that decide which crops grow where.
  • Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters for the Mughals and the traders who arrived by sea.
  • Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia for the faiths whose teachings shape many food rules.
  • Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year for the feasts and fasts that go with the calendar.

Pull up a chair

Food is often the first thing friends ask about, and the last tradition people let go of after they move far from home. If you've ever had to explain your lunch at school, or wondered why your family cooks the way it does, this chapter gives you the words and the history. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 8.1 "Your Plate Is Missing Something"
docs.text:
The South Asian Student Association's first potluck is set up on three folding tables in the Prairie Ridge cafeteria. Ben Lindqvist, who has been looking forward to this all week, takes a paper plate and puts a little of everything on it: a piece of naan, two samosas, a spoonful of chickpeas, a scoop of butter chicken, and one gulab jamun soaking through the plate.

He sits down proudly next to Zara Hossain and three other club members. Ayesha Qureshi, whose family is from Lahore, looks at his plate and says, "Where's the raita? And you need a proper biryani, not just bread." Arjun Reddy, whose family is from Hyderabad, shakes his head: "No rice? And no pickle? That's not a meal." Dilan Perera, whose family is from Kandy in Sri Lanka, laughs. "Where's the rice and curry? Where's the coconut sambol?"

Ben looks at Zara for help. She shrugs. "At my Nanu's table it would be rice, dal and fish. Every time." Ben stares at his plate. "Okay. So which one of you has the real South Asian meal?"

That's the question this chapter answers.

docs.title: 8.2 Start With the Grain
docs.text:
Think about food in the United States. A barbecue in Texas, a crab feast in Maryland, a hotdish at a church supper in Minnesota and a plate of tamales in New Mexico are all "American food," but nobody would call any one of them the only real version. Each grew from what was easy to farm or catch nearby, who settled there, and what they brought with them. South Asia works the same way, on a bigger scale, with about 1.99 billion people (2025, World Bank).

The best place to start is the grain. Staple Grains are the grains a community eats nearly every day and builds most meals around. In South Asia there are three big families of them.

  • Rice needs warm weather and lots of water. It grows best in the wet, low lands that the monsoon soaks every summer: the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta in Bangladesh and eastern India, the coasts of southern India, Sri Lanka's paddy fields, and the terraced valleys of Nepal and Bhutan. In Bangla, cooked rice is ভাত (BHAHT), and a meal without it can feel incomplete to many Bengali families.
  • Wheat prefers cooler, drier winters. It grows on the irrigated plains of the Indus and its tributaries in Pakistan and northwest India, and in Afghanistan. Here bread, not rice, sits at the center of most meals.
  • Millets are small, hardy grains such as pearl millet (bajra), sorghum (jowar) and finger millet (ragi). They grow in dry places with poor soil and little water, like parts of Gujarat, Rajasthan, the Deccan Plateau and the hills of Nepal. The United Nations named 2023 the International Year of Millets, at India's suggestion, to draw attention to grains that can handle a changing climate.

These lines are not neat. Many families in central India eat both rice and wheat. In the high hills of Nepal, where rice is hard to grow, many people have long eaten dhido, a thick porridge made from millet, maize or buckwheat flour. Still, if you know a family's staple grain, you can often guess a lot about the rest of their meal.

Look back at the map

Remember the monsoon from Chapter 1? Rice country lines up closely with the places that get the heaviest summer rain. Before you read on, guess which grain Zara's family in Chattogram eats most, and which one Ayesha's family in Lahore does.

docs.title: 8.3 Regional Cuisines: One Region, Many Kitchens
docs.text:
A Regional Cuisine is the style of cooking that grows up in one area, shaped by its grain, its climate, its coast or mountains, its history of trade, and the communities who live there. South Asia has dozens of them, and borders drawn in 1947 or 1971 often run right through them. Punjabi food is eaten on both sides of the India-Pakistan border, and Bengali food in both Bangladesh and India's West Bengal.

Here are a few regional cuisines from across the eight countries. The table shows only a handful, and every family cooks a little differently.

Region Country Staple A few well-known foods What shapes it Punjab Pakistan and India Wheat Roti, chickpeas, mustard greens with maize bread, lassi Irrigated wheat plains, dairy cattle, cool winters Sindh Pakistan Rice and wheat Sindhi biryani, sai bhaji (greens with lentils) The lower Indus valley, a hot, dry climate Bengal Bangladesh and India Rice Fish such as ilish (hilsa), red lentils, sweets made from milk A wet river delta full of fish Gujarat India Wheat, rice, millet Sweet-and-sour dal, steamed snacks like dhokla Dry land, and strong vegetarian traditions Kerala India Rice Coconut, fish curries, avial, banana-leaf feasts Heavy rain, coconut palms, the old pepper trade Sri Lanka Sri Lanka Rice Rice and curry, hoppers, pol sambol, kottu Island climate, coconut, cinnamon, many trading partners Nepal hills Nepal Rice, maize, millet Dal bhat tarkari, gundruk (fermented greens), momos Mountain farming, terraces, trade with Tibet Bhutan Bhutan Red rice Ema datshi (chili and cheese stew) Himalayan valleys, dairy from cows and yaks Maldives Maldives Rice, flatbread Mas huni (tuna, coconut, chili, lime) Coral islands surrounded by tuna fishing grounds Afghanistan Afghanistan Wheat, rice Naan, qabili palaw (rice with carrots, raisins and meat) Dry mountains and valleys, Central Asian trade routes

Notice how often the sea or the river shows up. Bengal, Kerala, Sri Lanka and the Maldives all eat a lot of fish. Bangladesh lists the ilish as its national fish and catches most of the world's supply. In dry, inland places, dairy, lentils and grains carry more of the meal.

docs.title: 8.4 The Thali: A Whole Meal on One Plate
docs.text:
If you want to see a regional cuisine at a glance, look at a thali. A Thali (थाली, TAH-lee, "plate") is a large round plate, usually metal, holding a complete meal: a staple in the middle and several small dishes around it. The small bowls along the edge are called katori (कटोरी, ka-TOH-ree, "small bowl"). The word "thali" means both the plate and the meal served on it.

A typical thali tries to balance flavors and textures: something soft and something crisp, something sour, something salty, something mildly bitter and something sweet. A Gujarati family might call their everyday thali "dal, bhat, rotli, shaak": lentils, rice, thin wheat bread and a vegetable dish. A festive Gujarati thali can hold more than a dozen items.

The same idea shows up across the region under other names.

  • In Kerala, a festival feast called a sadya is served on a banana leaf instead of a plate. Rice sits in the middle, and a long row of vegetarian dishes is placed in set spots on the leaf. Sadyas are cooked for the harvest festival Onam (see Chapter 7), for Vishu and for weddings.
  • In Nepal, the everyday meal is dal bhat tarkari: lentil soup, rice and a vegetable curry, often with a sharp pickle on the side.
  • In Sri Lanka, "rice and curry" means a mound of rice with several small curries around it, made from vegetables, lentils, fish or meat, plus a sambol (a fresh relish).
  • In Bangladesh and West Bengal, a family meal is often rice with dal, a vegetable dish or mashed vegetables, and fish, with sweet yogurt or a sweet to finish when there are guests.

A thali is a useful tool for comparing cuisines because it has slots. Every region fills the "staple," "lentil," "vegetable," "main" and "sweet" slots, but with different foods. The Thali Builder MicroSim later in this chapter works the same way.

docs.title: 8.5 The Building Blocks: Dal, Masala and Tadka
docs.text: Open the katori on almost any thali and you'll find three building blocks that most South Asian kitchens share.

docs.title: Dal
docs.text:
Dal (दाल, DAHL) means split pulses, the dried seeds of plants like lentils, peas and beans, and also the soupy or thick dish made from them. Red lentils (masoor), yellow split pigeon peas (toor), split mung beans (moong), black gram (urad) and split chickpeas (chana) are all dals. Pulses are cheap, keep for a long time and are full of protein, which matters a lot in a region where many people eat little or no meat.

Every region makes dal its own way. A Gujarati dal is thin and often a little sweet and sour, with jaggery (unrefined cane sugar) or a squeeze of lemon. A Bengali masoor dal is light and fragrant. Punjabi cooks slow-cook whole black urad; the rich restaurant version, dal makhani, with butter and cream, was created in Delhi in the 1950s by Punjabi cooks who had moved from Peshawar after Partition. In Nepal, cooks flavor dal with jimbu, a dried Himalayan herb fried in ghee. In Sri Lanka, red-lentil parippu is often cooked with coconut milk.

docs.title: Masala
docs.text:
Masala (मसाला, ma-SAH-lah) means "spices" or "seasoning," and it usually refers to a mixture of spices, whole or ground. Garam masala, for example, is a warm blend that often includes cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, cumin and black pepper, though the mix changes by region and by family; in Bengal and Bangladesh it may be just cardamom, cinnamon and cloves. A masala can also be a wet paste of onion, ginger, garlic, tomato and spices that forms the base of a dish.

There's no single correct masala. Cooks change the mix to fit the dish, the season and their own taste. Some families still roast and grind their own; others buy ready-made blends. Notice, too, that a spice mixture is about flavor, not just heat. Cumin, coriander, turmeric, cardamom and fennel aren't hot at all.

Curry is not one dish

The English word "curry" probably comes from the Tamil word kari, a spiced dish eaten with rice. British traders used it for hundreds of different dishes, and "curry powder" was a blend sold mostly to Europeans. In South Asia, people usually call a dish by its own name: dal, korma, sambar, jhol, karahi.

docs.title: Tadka
docs.text:
Tadka (तड़का, TUD-kah) is a cooking step called "tempering" in English: whole spices, and sometimes garlic, dried chili or curry leaves, are fried for a few seconds in hot oil or ghee (clarified butter) and then poured, sizzling, over a finished dish. The hot fat pulls flavor out of the spices and carries it through the food. It goes by many names: chhaunk in parts of north India, baghaar in Urdu, vaghar in Gujarati, and phoron in Bangla.

Each region has favorite tadka spices:

  • Many South Indian and Sri Lankan cooks use black mustard seeds and curry leaves.
  • Bengali and Bangladeshi cooks often use panch phoron, a "five-spice" mix of whole seeds: fenugreek, cumin, nigella, black mustard and fennel.
  • Gujarati cooks often add a pinch of asafoetida (hing), a strong-smelling resin, along with mustard and cumin.
  • Punjabi and Pakistani cooks often use cumin, onion, garlic and dried red chili.

Tadka is a good example of how the same technique can taste completely different from one kitchen to the next. Ask anyone who cooks at home what goes into their tadka, and you'll learn a lot about their region.

docs.title: 8.6 Breads and Rice Dishes: Roti, Naan and Biryani
Roti and naan
docs.text:
In wheat country, bread is the staple. Roti and Naan are the two names most people outside South Asia know, and they are not the same thing.

Roti (रोटी, ROH-tee) is a flat, unleavened bread made from whole-wheat flour (atta) and water and cooked on a flat griddle called a tava. It's also called chapati or phulka, and in Pakistan and Bangladesh a similar thin bread is also simply "roti." For many families in northern India and Pakistan, roti is eaten at nearly every meal, torn by hand and used to scoop up dal and vegetables. "Roti" can even mean "food" or "a living," the way "bread" sometimes does in English.

Naan (नान, Urdu نان, NAHN) comes from the Persian word nan, which simply means "bread." It is usually made from white flour, leavened (allowed to rise), and slapped onto the inside wall of a tandoor, a very hot clay oven. The earliest mention of naan in South Asia is in the memoirs of the poet Amir Khusrau, in the 1300s. Because few homes have a tandoor, naan in India is mostly a restaurant or special-occasion bread. In Afghanistan and in Pakistani cities, though, naan from a neighborhood tandoor bakery is an everyday bread. So naan is common in some places and rare in others, which surprises many people who only know it from restaurants abroad.

Other breads fill out the picture: paratha (layered, pan-fried bread), puri (puffed, deep-fried bread), bajra rotla (millet bread) in Gujarat, the Maldivian roshi, and the godamba roti of Sri Lanka.

docs.title: Biryani
docs.text:
Biryani (Urdu بریانی, bir-YAH-nee) is a dish of rice layered and slow-cooked with meat (or vegetables), yogurt and spices, often with saffron. The word comes from the Persian biryan, "fried" or "roasted." A biryani record appears in the Ain-i-Akbari, an account of the Mughal emperor Akbar's court written in the 1590s, which lists it alongside pilau.

Historians don't agree on where biryani was born. Some argue it developed in the Mughal court kitchens, where Persian rice cooking met the spicier rice dishes of the subcontinent. Others think rice-and-meat dishes from Persia had already reached the Deccan in the south before the Mughals. Either way, biryani spread and changed everywhere it went:

  • Hyderabadi biryani (India) is one of the best-known styles; in 2009 Hyderabad's biryani makers even tried, and failed, to get an official place-of-origin tag for it.
  • Kolkata biryani includes potato, a habit linked to the court of Wajid Ali Shah, the last king of Awadh, who was exiled to Kolkata in 1856 with his cooks and musicians.
  • Sindhi biryani (Pakistan), one of the most popular dishes in the country, adds potatoes, tomatoes and yogurt to meat or fish and rice.
  • Kacchi biryani with mutton is the classic wedding dish of Old Dhaka in Bangladesh.

Biryani shows how a dish can belong to many places at once, which comes up again in the Whose Story? box below.

docs.title: 8.7 Chili Peppers and the Columbian Exchange
docs.text:
South Asian cooking had no chili peppers until about 500 years ago, which surprises a lot of people.

Chili peppers come from the Americas. So do potatoes, tomatoes, maize (corn), peanuts, cashews, pineapples and papaya. After Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, plants, animals, people and diseases began moving between the Americas and the rest of the world. Historian Alfred Crosby named this the Columbian Exchange in a 1972 book. It changed diets on every continent: wheat and cattle went to the Americas, and corn, potatoes and chilies went to Europe, Africa and Asia.

The Portuguese reached India by sea in 1498 and took the port of Goa in 1510. Their ships carried chili peppers from Brazil, and by the 1500s chilies were growing in Goa. Chilies were easy to grow and cheaper than black pepper, the region's older source of heat, so farmers and cooks across the subcontinent took them up. Within a few centuries chilies were everywhere.

Think about how deep that change went:

  • Bhutan's national dish, ema datshi, is basically chilies cooked in cheese. Before chilies arrived, Bhutanese cooks seasoned food with other local plants.
  • Punjab's winter favorite, sarson da saag (mustard greens) with makki di roti, is eaten with a bread made from maize, another American crop.
  • Potatoes appear in Kolkata and Sindhi biryani, in Gujarati vegetable dishes and in countless street snacks.
  • Tomatoes now form the base of many masala pastes.

None of this makes these foods "less South Asian." Cooks took new ingredients and made them their own, just as Mexican and Italian cooks did.

docs.title: 8.8 Chai: How Tea Became Everyone's Drink
docs.text:
Chai (चाय, Urdu چائے, CHAI) just means "tea." In much of South Asia it means black tea boiled with milk and sugar, and often spiced with cardamom, ginger, cinnamon, cloves or black pepper (that spiced version is masala chai). Today a cup of chai is offered to guests, sold at railway stations and roadside stalls from Karachi to Kolkata, and drunk at nearly every break in the day.

Many people assume chai is thousands of years old, but it isn't. Tea plants grew wild in the hills of Assam, but for most of history most people in the region did not drink tea as an everyday drink. The change came in steps:

  1. The 1830s: The British East India Company wanted to stop depending on China, which controlled the world tea trade. It began growing tea on plantations in Assam. British planters later spread tea to Darjeeling and the Nilgiri hills, and from 1867 to Ceylon (Sri Lanka), where tea replaced coffee after a plant disease wiped out the coffee estates. Plantation work was hard and poorly paid, and many workers were brought in under harsh labor contracts.
  2. By 1900: Tea from India and Ceylon had largely replaced Chinese tea in Britain. Almost all of it was grown for export.
  3. The early 1900s to the 1940s: The Indian Tea Association, run by British planters, set out to sell tea to Indians too. It paid salesmen to visit grocers, set up tea stalls at factories, mines and railway stations, and later sent sellers door to door. The campaign took off in the 1930s.
  4. The result: People did start drinking tea, but they made it their own way, with lots of milk, sugar and spices, and fewer tea leaves than the planters hoped.

So chai is both a product of colonial business and a very South Asian creation. Sri Lanka still exports "Ceylon tea," Bangladesh grows tea in the Sylhet hills where commercial planting began in 1857, and in Pakistan and Bangladesh the tea stall is a meeting place for friends, workers and arguments about cricket and politics.

docs.title: Street food
docs.text:
Street Food is food made and sold by vendors at stalls, carts and tiny shops, eaten standing up or on the go. It's often cheap, fast, and the thing people miss most after they move abroad.

One snack shows how street food changes from city to city: a hollow, crisp ball of fried dough filled with potato or chickpeas and dipped in spiced, tangy water. In Mumbai and much of India, and in Nepal, it's called panipuri. In Delhi and Pakistan it's golgappa. In Kolkata and Bangladesh it's phuchka, often sour and very spicy, and in Bangladesh it's filled with chotpoti and topped with egg. Phuchka even crossed oceans: by 2018 a Bangladeshi immigrant was selling it from a cart in Jackson Heights, New York City.

Many other street foods belong to a family called chaat (चाट, CHAHT), from the Hindi word for "lick," because they're tangy, sweet and spicy all at once. And street food goes far beyond chaat:

  • Sri Lanka: kottu roti, chopped flatbread stir-fried on a hot griddle with vegetables, egg or meat. It began as an inexpensive street meal in eastern Sri Lanka in the 1960s or 1970s.
  • Nepal: momos, steamed dumplings filled with meat or vegetables and served with a tomato-based achar.
  • Pakistan: nihari, a slow-cooked meat stew whose name comes from the Arabic word for "morning" because it was first a breakfast dish, became a Karachi favorite after 1947, when migrants from north India opened restaurants there.
  • India and Bangladesh: samosas, pakoras, and endless fried and grilled snacks.

docs.title: Mithai
docs.text:
Mithai (मिठाई, mi-THAI) is the word for South Asian sweets, the kind sold in sweet shops and boxed for guests. In Bangla, sweets are মিষ্টি (MISH-tee). Many mithai are made from milk: fresh cheese curds (chhena), milk boiled down until thick (khoa), or sweet yogurt. Others use chickpea flour, nuts, semolina or jaggery.

Some well-known examples:

  • Gulab jamun: fried milk-dough balls in rose-scented syrup.
  • Rasgulla (roshogolla in Bangla): spongy balls of chhena cooked in light syrup.
  • Mishti doi: sweet set yogurt, a specialty of Bogura (Bogra) in Bangladesh and of West Bengal.
  • Barfi and ladoo: dense squares and balls of milk, nuts or chickpea flour.
  • Sel roti: a ring-shaped sweet bread of rice flour fried for the Nepali festivals Dashain and Tihar.
  • Watalappam: a Sri Lankan coconut and jaggery custard linked to the island's Malay community.

Mithai are tied to big moments. Families hand out sweets for good exam results, new babies, weddings, Eid and Diwali, and a box of sweets is one of the most common gifts when visiting someone's home.

Whose Story?

Who does a dish belong to? In 2017 India's registry of Geographical Indications (labels that tie a product to a place) gave West Bengal a tag for "Banglar Rasogolla," and in 2019 it gave Odisha one for "Odisha Rasagola." Many people in Odisha trace the sweet to offerings at the Jagannath temple in Puri, while many in Bengal credit a Kolkata confectioner, Nobin Chandra Das, in the 1860s, and food historians still disagree about how much evidence supports each story. Biryani's origin is debated in a similar way: some historians credit the Mughal court, others earlier Persian travelers to the Deccan, and Hyderabad, Lucknow, Kolkata, Karachi and Dhaka each defend their own version. The two tags were given to two different versions, not to one "true" origin, and that may be the fairest answer.

docs.title: 8.10 Food and Faith
docs.text:
Food in South Asia is closely tied to religion, and many families follow rules about what, when and with whom to eat. Dietary Rules and Faith is the name for those rules: the foods a tradition asks its followers to avoid, the ways food must be prepared, and the days for fasting and feasting. Practices vary a great deal, even inside one faith and one family, so the examples below say "many" on purpose.

Ask, don't assume

You can't tell what someone eats from their name, faith or country. If you're hosting, the polite move is simple: ask your guests if there's anything they don't eat, and label dishes at a potluck.

docs.title: Vegetarianism in South Asia
docs.text:
Vegetarianism in South Asia refers to diets without meat (and often without fish or eggs), which are more common here than almost anywhere else in the world. But "most South Asians are vegetarian" is a myth. A large Pew Research Center survey of nearly 30,000 adults in India, carried out in 2019-2020 and published in 2021, found:

Group (India) Say they are vegetarian All adults 39% Jains 92% Hindus 44% Christians 10% Muslims 8%

The same survey found that 81% of Indian adults limit meat in some way, for example by avoiding certain meats or not eating meat on certain days. People defined "vegetarian" for themselves, and the answers varied by region: among Hindus, vegetarianism was much rarer in the east (18%), northeast (19%) and south (30%) than in the north and west. So most people in India eat some meat, but many have rules about it.

India is only one country, though: in Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and the Maldives, where most people are Muslim, meat and fish are everyday foods for those who can afford them, and in Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan, many people eat fish or meat too.

docs.title: Rules in different faiths
docs.text:
Here is how a few traditions shape the plate. Remember that observance differs from person to person.

  • Hinduism: Many Hindu texts praise vegetarianism, and many Hindus avoid beef because the cow is traditionally seen as sacred. Some also avoid onion and garlic; in the Pew survey, about one in five Hindus said they don't eat root vegetables such as onion and garlic.
  • Jainism: Jains follow ahimsa, non-harm to living beings, very strictly. Their diet excludes meat, fish, eggs and honey, and many Jains avoid root vegetables such as potatoes, onions and garlic, because pulling them up destroys the whole plant and the tiny lives in the soil. Many avoid eating after sunset. Jain families in Gujarat and Rajasthan developed whole styles of cooking without onion and garlic.
  • Islam: Muslims eat food that is halal (see below) and avoid pork and alcohol. During the month of Ramadan, many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset and break the fast together at iftar, often with dates.
  • Sikhism: In the same Pew survey, 59% of Sikhs in India said they were vegetarian; others eat meat. Every gurdwara runs a langar (ਲੰਗਰ, LUNG-gur), a free community kitchen that serves a vegetarian meal to anyone who comes, of any faith, caste or background, seated together on the floor. Sikh tradition credits Guru Nanak with starting it around 1500, and the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, made eating together a rule. The langar at the Golden Temple in Amritsar serves about 100,000 people a day, cooked by volunteers (2023 report).
  • Buddhism: Buddhist teaching discourages killing, and some Buddhists are vegetarian, while many in Sri Lanka, Bhutan and Nepal eat fish or meat. Practices differ by community.

Sharing food has also been shaped by caste. For centuries, rules about who could cook for or eat with whom kept people apart. The langar's rule of eating side by side was one challenge to this, and India's Constitution outlawed "untouchability" in 1950. You'll read more in Chapter 13.

docs.title: Halal
docs.text: Halal (حلال, ha-LAHL) is an Arabic word meaning "permitted." In Islamic law it describes food Muslims may eat. Pork is forbidden (haram), and so are alcohol and blood. For meat to be halal, the animal must be a permitted kind and must be slaughtered in a set way, with the name of God (Allah) said at the moment of slaughter. Most vegetarian food is halal, as long as it has no alcohol or other forbidden ingredients. In Muslim-majority countries such as Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and the Maldives, halal is the everyday norm, and in the United States, many Muslim families look for a halal butcher or a halal symbol on packages. Halal is a matter of faith and care, much like kosher rules for Jewish families, though the two sets of rules differ in their details.

docs.title: 8.11 At the Table: Hands, Guests and Manners
Eating with hands
docs.text:
In many South Asian homes, people eat with their fingers. Eating With Hands is an old and widespread custom, not a sign of having no utensils. Rice is gathered with the fingertips and mixed with dal or curry, and the thumb pushes each bite into the mouth. Roti or naan is torn with one hand and used as a scoop. People usually eat with the right hand only, since the left is used for washing, and wash their hands before and after the meal.

Done well, it's a skill that children learn at the family table, and many people say food tastes better this way. Plenty of families use spoons and forks too, especially for rice in some regions, at restaurants, or outside the home. Neither way is "more correct."

docs.title: Hospitality Customs
docs.text:
Hospitality Customs are the expected ways of welcoming and feeding guests. Across South Asia, being a generous host is a matter of family honor. A Sanskrit line from the Taittiriya Upanishad, atithi devo bhava, "the guest is like a god," is still quoted in India today. Families in Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and Nepal have their own sayings and strong traditions of welcoming guests, too.

Some customs that many families share:

  • A guest is offered something right away, usually chai or a cold drink, and a snack or sweet.
  • Hosts may offer second and third helpings and insist, even after the guest says no. In many families, a polite guest refuses once before accepting.
  • Guests often bring sweets or fruit, and many families never send a guest away with an empty dish: a borrowed container goes back with food in it.
  • Elders, guests and sometimes men are served first in more traditional homes, while the cooks (often women) may eat last. Many families have changed this.

When Ben finally sits down with a second plate at the potluck, Zara puts a spoonful of her mother's dal and a piece of fish on it. "Rice in the middle," she says. "Now you're eating like my Nanu." Ayesha adds raita, Arjun adds a little mango pickle, and Dilan brings coconut sambol. Ben looks at the crowded plate. "So there's no one real South Asian meal," he says. "There's a whole map of them." Zara grins. "Now you get it. Every plate is somebody's real meal."
