docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?, for the map and the eight countries.
  • Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia, because many dances tell stories from Hindu, Buddhist and other traditions.
  • Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year, since many folk dances belong to festivals such as Navaratri and Vaisakhi.
  • Chapter 9: Music, for raga, tala and the drums that dancers move to.

Let's dance!

Hi, I'm Mora! Maybe you've been dragged onto the floor at a wedding, or watched a cousin's dance recital, or seen a viral Bhangra video and wondered where it came from. This chapter helps you see what is happening when a South Asian dancer moves, so the next time you watch, you can read the story, not just the costume. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 10.1 "Great Bharatanatyam, Arjun!"
docs.text:
It's culture night at Prairie Ridge High School, the first big event of the new South Asian Student Association. The cafeteria has been turned into a stage with string lights and a borrowed speaker. Zara Hossain is running the slideshow. Ben Lindqvist is in charge of snacks, which means he has already eaten half of them.

Their friend Arjun Reddy steps out in a bright silk costume with a pleated fan at the front, bells around his ankles, and his eyes lined in black. For eight minutes he stamps out fast rhythms, freezes into poses like a temple statue, and acts out a whole story with his face and hands. Near the end, he jumps onto the rim of a brass plate and keeps dancing on it. The room goes wild.

Afterward, Ben finds him by the water fountain. "Dude. Great Bharatanatyam!"

Arjun laughs so hard he has to sit down. "It's Kuchipudi! My family is from Hyderabad. Kuchipudi comes from a village in Andhra Pradesh. Bharatanatyam is from Tamil Nadu."

Ben looks at Zara for help. Zara shrugs. She has seen both at weddings and festivals, and honestly, she isn't sure she could tell them apart either. Both have bells, both have hand gestures, both have that bent-knee stance. So what makes one dance different from another, and who decides which ones count as "classical"?

docs.title: 10.2 Dance as a Language
docs.text:
Before learning any names, think about how you already "read" people's bodies. A referee's arm signals tell you a foul happened. A friend's raised eyebrow says "really?" without a word. American Sign Language turns hand shapes into full sentences. And a good actor can make you cry without saying anything.

Many South Asian dance traditions combine all of these at once. A dancer might:

  • keep a beat with the feet, like a drummer,
  • make hand shapes that stand for a lotus, a bird, a king or the moon,
  • use the face and eyes to show feelings such as love, anger or wonder,
  • and act out a story, often from an epic like the Ramayana or Mahabharata, or a poem about Krishna.

Teachers often break a performance into three layers, using Sanskrit words:

Layer What it means Example Nritta (pure dance) Rhythm and shapes with no story, like a drum solo for the body A fast run of footwork that lands exactly on the last beat Nritya (expressive dance) Movement that carries meaning through gestures and the face Hands become a blooming lotus while the face shows delight Natya (drama) Acting a full story with characters One dancer plays both a worried mother and her mischievous child

Once you can spot these three layers, you can start to see what a dancer is doing even if you've never seen that style before.

docs.title: 10.3 The Natya Shastra: An Old Handbook for the Stage
docs.text:
Where did these ideas come from? Many dancers trace them to one famous text.

The Natya Shastra (नाट्य शास्त्र, NAHT-yuh SHAHS-truh), "treatise on drama," is a Sanskrit handbook on the performing arts. Tradition credits it to a sage named Bharata. Nobody knows exactly when it was written. Scholars think it grew over a long time, and most place its first complete version somewhere between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, though estimates range more widely, from about 500 BCE to 500 CE.

It is a big book: about 6,000 verses in 36 chapters. It covers playwriting, stage building, acting, makeup, costumes, body movement, hand gestures and music. Think of it as a drama-class textbook, a choreography manual and a music theory guide rolled into one. Later writers added their own books on top of it. One of the most used by dancers today is the Abhinaya Darpana ("Mirror of Gesture"), credited to a writer named Nandikeshvara, which describes hand gestures in detail.

In April 2025, UNESCO added manuscripts of the Natya Shastra, together with the Bhagavad Gita, to its Memory of the World Register, a list of documents considered important to all of humanity.

Old text, living art

The Natya Shastra is old, but no dance today is a frozen copy of it. Each classical style took its present shape much later, often in the last few hundred years, and teachers keep changing it. A good question to ask any dancer is: "Which parts come from the old books, and which parts did your own teachers create?"

docs.title: 10.4 Rasa: The Flavor of a Performance
docs.text:
Have you ever left a movie feeling a mood you couldn't shake, like the warm glow after a happy ending or the shivers after a scary scene? The Natya Shastra has a word for that.

Rasa (रस, RUH-suh) literally means "juice," "taste" or "essence." In the arts, a rasa is the emotional flavor that a performance creates in the audience. The idea is that the performer shows a feeling (called a bhava), and a sensitive audience member "tastes" it as a rasa. In Sanskrit, an ideal audience member is called a sahridaya, "one who has heart."

The Natya Shastra lists eight rasas. Later thinkers argued for centuries about adding a ninth, shanta (peace), and it was eventually widely accepted. That's why dancers often talk about the navarasa, the "nine rasas."

Rasa Feeling A dancer might show it by... Shringara Love, beauty Soft eyes, a shy smile, a gentle tilt of the head Hasya Laughter, comedy Playful eyebrows, a cheeky grin Karuna Sorrow, compassion Drooping shoulders, eyes filling with tears Raudra Fury Wide eyes, flaring nostrils, sharp stamps Vira Heroism, courage Tall posture, firm gaze, strong steps Bhayanaka Fear Darting eyes, shrinking back Bibhatsa Disgust Turning away, wrinkling the nose Adbhuta Wonder, amazement Wide-open eyes, raised brows, an open mouth Shanta (added later) Peace, calm Stillness, a soft and even face

Rasa isn't only for dance. The same idea shaped music, poetry, painting and sculpture in South Asia.

docs.title: 10.5 Mudra: Speaking with Your Hands
docs.text:
If rasa is the feeling, mudras are a big part of the vocabulary.

A mudra (मुद्रा, MOO-druh) is a hand gesture with a set shape and set meanings. In Hindi the word can also mean a seal or a stamp, which fits: each mudra "stamps" an idea into the air. Dancers also use the Sanskrit word hasta, "hand." The Abhinaya Darpana describes 28 single-hand gestures (asamyuta hasta) and about two dozen two-hand gestures (samyuta hasta; versions of the text count 23 or 24), and teachers add many more.

A single mudra can mean many different things, depending on where the hand is, how it moves, and what the face is doing. It works like a word with several meanings, where context tells you which one is meant. Here are six of the first single-hand mudras that students learn, with a few of the meanings listed in a 1917 English translation of the Abhinaya Darpana:

Mudra Name means Hand shape A few meanings Pataka Flag Fingers straight and pressed together, thumb bent in Clouds, forest, waves, a blessing, saying "Go!" Tripataka Three parts of the flag Like Pataka, but the ring finger is bent A crown, a tree, an arrow, a lamp's flame Ardhapataka Half flag Like Tripataka, with the little finger also bent Young leaves, a knife, a tower, a riverbank Kartarimukha Scissors face First two fingers spread like scissor blades, the others folded Separation, lightning, the corner of the eye Mayura Peacock Ring finger touches the thumb tip, the other fingers up A peacock's beak, wiping away tears, putting a mark on the forehead Alapadma Full-bloomed lotus All fingers spread and curved, like a flower opening A blooming lotus, the full moon, a mirror, praise

Teachers and styles describe some of these shapes a little differently, so don't worry if your cousin's dance teacher holds Kartarimukha a bit differently from the drawing in the MicroSim.

Mudras aren't only for dance. You'll also see hand gestures in Hindu and Buddhist statues and paintings, such as an open palm raised to mean "do not fear." Dancers, sculptors and painters shared much of this visual language. (Chapter 11 looks at the sculpture and painting side.)

docs.title: 10.6 What Makes a Dance "Classical"?
docs.text:
Now back to Ben's question: what does "classical" mean?

In this book, Classical Dance means a dance tradition with a long, written theory behind it (usually traced to the Natya Shastra), a fixed technique that takes years of training with a teacher, a set order of pieces in a performance, and official recognition as a classical art. It's similar to how people use "classical" for Western ballet or for Carnatic and Hindustani music: it describes a trained, codified art form, not something better than other dance.

So who decides which dances count? In India, the main official body is the Sangeet Natak Akademi, the national academy of music, dance and drama, set up in 1953. It recognizes eight classical dances:

  1. Bharatanatyam
  2. Kathak
  3. Kuchipudi
  4. Odissi
  5. Kathakali
  6. Sattriya
  7. Manipuri
  8. Mohiniyattam

Sattriya was the most recent addition. The Akademi recognized it on 15 November 2000.

Is it eight, nine or more?

Be careful with "India has eight classical dances." That's the Sangeet Natak Akademi's list, but India's Ministry of Culture also lists Chhau, a masked dance from eastern India, which makes nine, and some lists add more. Scholars disagree too, so the honest answer is "eight, according to the national academy."

Chhau comes from eastern India and has three main styles, named after the places they grew up: Seraikella, Purulia and Mayurbhanj. It mixes dance with martial-arts moves and is traditionally taught to men. The Seraikella and Purulia styles use masks. UNESCO added Chhau to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage in 2010.

Other countries draw the line differently. In Bangladesh, Banglapedia (the national encyclopedia) says classical dance there mainly means Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Kathakali, Odissi and Manipuri, learned from teachers of those schools. In Sri Lanka, the Kandyan dance tradition has its own long training and rules, even though it isn't on India's list.

docs.title: 10.7 A Tour of the Eight Classical Dances
docs.text:
Here's a quick guide to all eight. Use it like a field guide: notice where each comes from, what the dancers wear, and one or two things that make it easy to spot.

Dance Home region (today) Easy-to-spot features Bharatanatyam Tamil Nadu Half-sitting bent-knee stance, crisp geometric lines, fan-pleated costume Kathak North India, also Pakistan and Bangladesh Straight legs, fast spins, hundreds of ankle bells, footwork "conversations" with the tabla Odissi Odisha S-shaped tribhangi pose, square chauka stance, silver jewelry Kathakali Kerala Painted green faces, huge skirts and crowns, all-night dance-dramas Kuchipudi Andhra Pradesh Dance-drama roots, quick leaps, dancing on the rim of a brass plate Manipuri Dance Manipur, also Sylhet (Bangladesh) Soft rounded moves, no stamping, stiff barrel-shaped mirrored skirt Mohiniyattam Kerala Gentle swaying, white-and-gold sari, a hair bun to one side Sattriya Assam Born in monasteries, played with the khol drum, Krishna stories

docs.title: Bharatanatyam
docs.text:
Bharatanatyam (பரதநாட்டியம், BHUH-ruh-tuh-NAHT-yum) comes from Tamil Nadu in southern India. Its older name was Sadir. For centuries the dance was closely linked to Hindu temples and royal courts in the Tamil region. Later, four musicians and teachers known as the Thanjavur Quartet organized much of the order of pieces still used today.

In the late 1800s and early 1900s, colonial officials, missionaries and some Indian reformers attacked temple dance, and it nearly disappeared. In the 1930s, revivalists including Rukmini Devi Arundale and E. Krishna Iyer helped bring it to concert stages under a new name, Bharatanatyam, in 1932.

You can spot Bharatanatyam by its aramandi, a half-sitting position with bent knees turned out, a steady upper body, and sharp, geometric arm lines. The dancer usually performs solo for up to two hours, with a singer, drummer and a nattuvanar (conductor) keeping the rhythm with small cymbals.

docs.title: Kathak
docs.text:
Kathak (KUH-thuk) comes from northern India. Its name comes from katha, the Sanskrit word for "story," and it grew from traveling storytellers who acted out tales, especially about Krishna. Later it was also danced in royal courts, including Mughal courts and the court of Awadh in Lucknow, where Persian poetry and music shaped it. That double history, in temples and storytelling on one side and Muslim-ruled courts on the other, is part of why Kathak is danced today in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.

Kathak dancers keep their legs straight and wear ankle bells called ghungroo, sometimes with more than a hundred bells on each ankle. Footwork patterns called tatkar trade rhythms with the tabla player, and dancers finish phrases with dizzying spins. Different schools, called gharanas, are named after cities such as Jaipur, Lucknow and Banaras (Varanasi).

docs.title: Odissi
docs.text:
Odissi (oh-DIS-ee) comes from Odisha on India's east coast. Dancing figures carved on the walls of Odisha's old temples, such as the Sun Temple at Konark, show poses that dancers still use. Like Bharatanatyam, Odissi was attacked under colonial rule and rebuilt in the twentieth century.

Look for two poses. The chauka is a strong, square stance with bent knees. The tribhangi ("three bends") curves the body into an S-shape at the neck, waist and knee, like a statue come to life. Many pieces are devotional poems about Jagannath (a form of Vishnu) and Krishna, especially from the twelfth-century Sanskrit poem Gita Govinda.

docs.title: Kathakali
docs.text:
Kathakali (കഥകളി, KUH-thuh-kuh-lee), "story play," comes from Kerala in southwest India. It developed from older temple and folk arts and took its full form a few centuries ago. Unlike most classical dances, it grew up mainly in the courts and theaters of local kings.

Kathakali is easy to recognize. Performers wear thick makeup, giant skirts and tall crowns, and the makeup color tells you who a character is. Pacha (green) faces with bright red lips are noble heroes and gods such as Krishna and Rama. Kathi ("knife") faces, green with red marks, are proud or villainous characters, and kari (black) is for demons and forest beings. Performances were traditionally all-night shows by male actors, with the story sung by vocalists while the actors "speak" only through mudras, eyes and face.

Kerala is also home to Kutiyattam, a form of Sanskrit theater that UNESCO describes as one of India's oldest living theater traditions. Male actors traditionally performed it in special theaters inside Hindu temples, and a full performance can last up to 40 days. UNESCO first recognized it in 2001.

docs.title: Kuchipudi
docs.text:
Kuchipudi (కూచిపూడి, KOO-chee-POO-dee) is named after a village in Andhra Pradesh. As Arjun said, it's from the Telugu-speaking region. It began as a dance-drama performed by troupes of men from the village, who played every role. Tradition credits a seventeenth-century devotee named Siddhendra Yogi with shaping it. In the twentieth century it also became a solo dance, often performed by women.

Kuchipudi shares a lot with Bharatanatyam, which is why Ben mixed them up. Both use a bent-knee stance, mudras and Carnatic music. But Kuchipudi tends to be faster and bouncier, with more leaps and a strong acting side, and the songs are usually in Telugu. Its best-known feature is the tarangam, where the dancer performs on the rim of a brass plate, sometimes balancing a pot of water on the head.

docs.title: Manipuri Dance
docs.text:
Manipuri Dance comes from Manipur in northeastern India, where it is part of the culture of the Meitei people. The best-known form is the Raas Leela, dances about Krishna and Radha. A Meitei king, Bhagyachandra (who ruled 1759 to 1798), is credited with organizing the style and designing its famous costume.

Manipuri movement is soft and rounded, with no hard stamping, and the dancers' faces stay calm and gentle. Women playing the gopis (cowherd girls who love Krishna) wear the potloi, a stiff, barrel-shaped skirt decorated with mirrors and embroidery that makes them look as if they're floating. Manipuri is also danced in Bangladesh, especially in Sylhet. In 1919 the poet Rabindranath Tagore saw a Manipuri performance in Sylhet and later brought Manipuri teachers to his school at Shantiniketan, which helped make the dance known across Bengal.

docs.title: Mohiniyattam
docs.text:
Mohiniyattam (mo-hi-nee-YAHT-tum) is Kerala's second classical dance. It is named after Mohini, the enchanting female form of the Hindu god Vishnu. Mohiniyattam is traditionally a solo dance by women. Its movements sway gently from side to side, a little like palm trees in the breeze or waves on the backwaters, and it uses the soft, graceful style that the Natya Shastra calls lasya. Dancers wear an ivory-white sari with a gold border, and a round hair bun worn to one side.

In the 1930s, laws against temple dancing and colonial-era prejudice pushed Mohiniyattam almost out of sight. The Malayalam poet Vallathol Narayana Menon led its revival and founded the Kerala Kalamandalam, a school for Kerala's performing arts.

docs.title: Sattriya
docs.text:
Sattriya (SUT-tree-yuh) comes from Assam in northeastern India. It began in the sattras, Vaishnava (Krishna-worshipping) monasteries founded after the teacher, poet and playwright Srimanta Sankardev in the 1400s and 1500s. Sankardev wrote short dance-dramas, and for centuries male monks called bhokots performed them as part of worship.

In the second half of the twentieth century, Sattriya moved from the monasteries to public stages, and women began to perform it too. Its music features the khol, a two-headed clay drum played with the fingers, along with cymbals. When the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognized it in 2000, it became the eighth classical dance on the list.

docs.title: 10.8 Folk Dance: Dance for Everyone
docs.text:
Classical dance usually needs years of lessons, but most dancing in South Asia doesn't. A folk dance is a dance that grows out of a community's everyday life: harvests, weddings, festivals, worship and seasons. Anyone in the community can join. The steps are passed on by watching and doing rather than from textbooks, and they change from village to village.

"Folk" doesn't mean simple or less skilled. Bhangra dancers and Garba circles can be fiercely athletic and complex. The difference is about who dances, where and how the dance is learned, not about quality.

docs.title: Garba (India)
docs.text:
Garba (ગરબા, GUR-bah) comes from Gujarat in western India. It's danced during Navaratri, the "nine nights" festival honoring the Hindu goddess (see Chapter 7). Traditionally, dancers move counterclockwise in circles around a clay pot with holes in it and a lamp burning inside, or around an image of the goddess Amba. The circle starts slowly with clapping and singing, then speeds up into fast, whirling steps. A related dance, dandiya raas, uses pairs of decorated sticks that dancers clack together.

In 2023, UNESCO added Garba of Gujarat to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Today Garba nights draw huge crowds in Indian cities and in diaspora communities, and many community and campus Garba nights in North America welcome anyone who wants to join the circle.

docs.title: Bhangra and Luddi (India and Pakistan)
docs.text:
Bhangra comes from Punjab, a region split between India and Pakistan in 1947 (see Chapter 4). It began with farmers celebrating the harvest, especially around the spring festival of Vaisakhi. Dancers leap, kick and pump their shoulders with raised arms to the heavy beat of the dhol, a big two-headed drum, while singers shout short verses called boliyan. Bhangra today has grown into a whole music genre and a competitive college sport in the UK, US and Canada.

Luddi is another Punjabi folk dance, danced on both sides of the border. Men and women dance it in circles at weddings and celebrations, clapping, snapping their fingers and doing half-turns.

docs.title: Attan (Afghanistan and Pakistan)
docs.text:
Attan (اتڼ, uh-TUN) is a Pashtun circle dance and is widely called the national dance of Afghanistan. Pashtuns in Pakistan dance it too, and other Afghan communities have taken it up. Dancers move in a big circle around the drummer, clapping and spinning, with the dhol starting slow and building to a fast finish. A performance can last from about 5 to 30 minutes. Historically it was danced before battles to build courage. Today it's most often seen at weddings and celebrations, including in Afghan communities around the world.

Different regions have their own versions, such as Kabuli and Kandahari styles. In northwestern Pakistan, the Khattak dance, a fast sword-and-handkerchief version danced by men of the Khattak tribe, is a famous relative of Attan.

docs.title: Kandyan Dance (Sri Lanka)
docs.text:
Kandyan Dance comes from the hill country around Kandy in Sri Lanka's central highlands. In Sinhala it's called Uda Rata Natum, "up-country dance." Legend traces it to a healing ritual called the Kohomba Kankariya, and for generations its dancers served the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic in Kandy and performed in the city's great yearly procession, the Perahera.

Kandyan dancers are known for high leaps, fast spins and strong, athletic footwork. The most famous costume is the ves, with a shining metal headdress, a beaded net over the chest and rattling anklets. The music is mostly drumming, led by the geta bera, the main drum of Kandyan dance, though some pieces also have sung verses. There are 18 classic vannam, solo dances that each describe an animal or idea, such as the elephant, the monkey or the eagle. Traditionally only men trained in the dance, but today many schools teach women too. Kandyan dance is one of the strongest symbols of Sri Lankan culture, at home and in the diaspora.

docs.title: More dances across the region
docs.text:
• Bhutan: Buddhist monasteries hold festivals with cham, masked dances that teach moral lessons and honor Buddhist teachers. One of them, the Drametse Ngacham ("mask dance of the drums from Drametse"), features sixteen masked men and ten musicians. UNESCO first recognized it in 2005.
  • Nepal: In the Kathmandu Valley, Newar communities perform the Lakhey dance at festivals. A dancer in a fierce mask with fangs and a long mane of hair plays a forest demon who became a protector of the town.
  • The Maldives: Boduberu ("big drum") is the Maldives' best-known music and dance. About 20 performers, including drummers and a lead singer, start slow and build to a frenzied finish while one or two dancers move to the beat.
  • Bangladesh: Besides Manipuri in Sylhet, Bangladesh has many folk dances and a famous folk theater, jatra, described in the next section.

docs.title: 10.9 Theater and Shadow Puppetry
docs.text:
Many South Asian dance forms are really dance-drama. The same region also has theater traditions where acting, singing and puppetry come first.

Jatra (যাত্রা, JAH-trah), "journey," is a lively folk theater of Bengal, performed in Bangladesh and in India's West Bengal, Odisha and Assam. It goes back at least to the 1500s, when it grew out of devotional plays about Krishna. Jatra was traditionally played on open ground with the audience all around, and it mixed songs, dances, loud dialogue and comic characters. Over time it took up history, social issues and, in the twentieth century, patriotic themes. Jatra troupes still tour villages and towns today.

Yakshagana from coastal Karnataka is an all-night dance-drama with huge headdresses, painted faces and a lead singer who narrates the story. Like many strong traditions, it isn't on any official "classical" list.

Shadow Puppetry is a form of storytelling in which flat cut-out figures are held between a light and a thin cloth screen, so the audience sees moving shadows. South India has several shadow puppet traditions, and they share a word for leather:

Tradition Where What the name means Tholu bommalata Andhra Pradesh "Dance of leather dolls" (Telugu) Togalu gombeyaata Karnataka "Play of leather dolls" (Kannada) Tholpavakoothu Kerala and Tamil Nadu "Leather doll play" (Malayalam and Tamil)

The puppets are cut from animal hide, scraped so thin that light shines through, and painted in bright colors, so the shadows glow with color. Puppeteers sit behind the screen, move the jointed puppets with sticks, sing and speak all the voices, and often perform stories from the Ramayana all night. In Kerala, Tholpavakoothu is performed in temples of the goddess Bhadrakali, and a full Ramayana cycle can run for weeks of night-long shows. Many historians think South Asian shadow theater influenced shadow puppet traditions in Southeast Asia, though how and when are still debated.

Whose Story?

Who gets to say which dances are "classical"? India's Sangeet Natak Akademi lists eight, India's Ministry of Culture adds Chhau, and dancers in West Bengal and elsewhere have argued for other styles to join the list. In Bangladesh, the national encyclopedia uses "classical dance" mainly for styles such as Kathak and Manipuri that Bengali dancers learned from teachers of those schools, while Sri Lankans see Kandyan dance as their own classical tradition with its own rules. Historians also tell the revival story of the 1930s in different ways. Some celebrate the revivalists who saved Bharatanatyam and Odissi from colonial attacks. Others point out that the hereditary women performers who had kept these dances alive for generations were often pushed aside in the process.

docs.title: 10.10 Dance Today
docs.text:
A week after culture night, Arjun is teaching Ben the basic Kuchipudi stance in the school hallway. Ben's knees are shaking. "How long did you have to practice this?"

"Eight years," Arjun says. "And I still have a teacher." He shows Ben a Pataka hand, then turns it into a wave rolling across the sea.

Many classical dancers study for years before a first full-length solo recital, which in Bharatanatyam is called an arangetram.

At the same time, dance keeps changing. Film songs from Mumbai (formerly Bombay), Lahore, Dhaka and Chennai mix classical gestures, folk steps and hip-hop. College teams compete in Bhangra, Garba-Raas and "fusion" contests. Kandyan dancers perform at Sri Lankan community events abroad, and Afghan families dance Attan at weddings far from Afghanistan. "Bollywood dance" (popular film dance from India's Hindi film industry) is its own fun, mixed style. It borrows from many traditions, but it isn't the same as any one classical dance.

How to watch a dance like an expert

Next time you watch a performance, ask three questions: Is this pure rhythm (nritta), expression (nritya) or drama (natya)? Which rasa is the dancer showing right now? And what is that hand saying? You'll notice far more than before.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about dance in their life: dances at weddings and festivals, whether anyone in the family learned a classical dance, and folk dances from their village, town or region. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Ask if they have any old photos or videos of a wedding, festival or recital, and look at them together. Ask permission before taking notes or recording.

Questions to ask

  1. What is the first dance you remember seeing or doing, and where were you?
  2. What dances happened at weddings, festivals or religious events in your family or community?
  3. Did you or anyone in the family learn a classical dance? What was the teacher like, and how long did it take?
  4. Was there a folk dance special to your village, town or region? Can you show me a step?
  5. How has dancing at weddings or festivals changed since you were young, or since moving to a new country?
  6. Is there a dance, song or step you hope I'll learn and keep?

Listen for: names of classical styles such as Bharatanatyam, Kathak or Kandyan Dance; folk dances such as Garba, Bhangra or Attan; and any mention of hand gestures (Mudra) or the feelings a dance should bring out (Rasa).

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare your elder's memories with a friend's interview. Did one family talk mostly about classical dance and the other about folk dance at weddings? List two things that were the same and two that were different, and connect one of them to this chapter's idea that "folk" is about who dances and how it's learned, not about skill.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: All Indian dance is basically Bollywood dance. Reality: Bollywood dance is a modern, mixed film style. South Asia has many separate classical dances, such as Bharatanatyam, Kathak and Odissi, plus hundreds of folk dances, each with its own steps, music and history. Film choreographers borrow from them, but they are not the same thing.

Myth: Classical dance is only religious. Reality: Many classical pieces tell religious stories, but dancers also perform pure rhythm pieces, love poetry, court traditions (Kathak grew up partly in Mughal and Awadh courts) and modern themes. Dancers of many faiths learn and perform these styles.

Myth: There is one official list of classical dances. Reality: India's Sangeet Natak Akademi recognizes eight, the Ministry of Culture also lists Chhau, and scholars and other countries draw the line differently. It's more accurate to say "eight, according to the Sangeet Natak Akademi."

Myth: Folk dances are just simple party dances. Reality: "Folk" describes how a dance is passed on, through community life rather than formal schools. Folk dances such as Bhangra and Attan can be highly athletic and skilled, and UNESCO has listed some, such as Garba, as world heritage.

Myth: Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi are the same dance. Reality: They're related and share some technique, but Bharatanatyam comes from Tamil Nadu and is usually performed as a solo with Tamil and other songs, while Kuchipudi comes from Andhra Pradesh, grew out of Telugu dance-drama, and is known for leaps, acting and the brass-plate tarangam.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What is the Natya Shastra, and roughly when was it compiled?

It is a Sanskrit handbook on the performing arts, credited to the sage Bharata. Most scholars date its first complete version to between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, though estimates range wider.

2. What is rasa? Give two examples.

Rasa is the emotional "flavor" a performance creates in the audience. Examples include shringara (love), karuna (sorrow), vira (heroism) and adbhuta (wonder).

3. How many classical dances does the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognize, and which was added most recently?

Eight. Sattriya, from Assam, was the most recent, recognized in 2000.

4. Name one way to tell Kathakali apart from Mohiniyattam, even though both come from Kerala.

Kathakali uses heavy painted makeup, huge costumes and crowns, and was traditionally performed by men in all-night dance-dramas. Mohiniyattam is a gentle, swaying solo dance traditionally performed by women in a white-and-gold sari.

5. What makes shadow puppetry work, and where in South Asia is it found?

Flat, see-through leather puppets are held between a light and a cloth screen, so the audience sees colored shadows. Traditions include Tholu bommalata in Andhra Pradesh, Togalu gombeyaata in Karnataka and Tholpavakoothu in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the eight classical dances recognized by the Sangeet Natak Akademi and the home state of each.

    Answer

    Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (North India, such as Uttar Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Kathakali (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Manipuri (Manipur), Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Sattriya (Assam).

  2. Name the folk or regional dance from each place: Gujarat, Punjab, Kandy (Sri Lanka), and the Pashtun regions of Afghanistan and Pakistan.

    Answer

    Gujarat: Garba. Punjab: Bhangra (or Luddi). Kandy: Kandyan dance. Pashtun regions: Attan.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain the difference between nritta, nritya and natya in your own words.

    Answer

    Nritta is pure rhythm and movement with no story. Nritya adds meaning through gestures and facial expression. Natya is full drama, with characters and a story acted out.

  2. Explain why a single mudra, such as Pataka, can mean many different things.

    Answer

    A mudra works like a word with several meanings. Where the hand is held, how it moves, and what the face shows tell the audience which meaning is intended. Pataka can be clouds, a wave or "Go!" depending on context.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Classical Dance Map. Choose two dances from different regions and write a short "how to tell them apart" guide for a friend, using region, movement and costume. Hint: the info panel has all three.

  2. Watch a short performance clip chosen by your teacher or club leader. Identify one moment of nritta, one of nritya, and the main rasa the dancer seems to show. Hint: look at the face during the expressive part.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare how Bharatanatyam and Kathak were each shaped by the places where they were performed (temples, courts, concert stages). How do those places show up in the dance today? Hint: think about Mughal and Awadh courts, temple sculpture and the 1930s revival.

  2. The Sangeet Natak Akademi lists eight classical dances, while the Ministry of Culture includes Chhau. Analyze what criteria might lead two official bodies to different lists. Hint: think about written theory, training, history and who is on the committee.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Some people say folk dances should be put on official "classical" lists so they get more funding and respect. Others say this would change them. Which side do you find more convincing, and why? Hint: use Garba, Yakshagana or shadow puppetry as an example.

  2. Ben says, "Bollywood dance is fake Indian dance." Evaluate his claim using what you learned about how dance traditions mix and change. Hint: a fair answer looks at what film dance borrows and what makes it different.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Choreograph a 30-second "mudra story" using at least four of the six mudras in this chapter. Write out the story, the mudra for each moment and the rasa you want the audience to feel. Hint: Pataka can be waves, Alapadma the moon.

  2. Design a one-page program for your club's culture night that introduces three dances from at least three different South Asian countries, with two sentences on each that would help a newcomer like Ben enjoy them. Hint: include one classical and one folk dance.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The Natya Shastra, a Sanskrit handbook credited to Bharata and usually dated between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, gave South Asian performing arts many of their core ideas.
  • Rasa is the emotional flavor a performance creates; the Natya Shastra lists eight, and a ninth, shanta (peace), was added later.
  • Mudras are hand gestures with set shapes and many meanings; context tells the audience which meaning is intended.
  • India's Sangeet Natak Akademi recognizes eight classical dances: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Kathakali, Sattriya, Manipuri and Mohiniyattam. Other bodies and countries draw the list differently.
  • Folk dances, such as Garba, Bhangra, Luddi, Attan and Kandyan dance, grow from community life and can be just as skilled as classical forms.
  • Theater and shadow puppetry, from Bengal's jatra to South India's leather puppets, tell epic and everyday stories across the region.
  • Dance in South Asia and its diaspora keeps changing, mixing classical, folk, film and global styles.

You can read a dance now!

You can now tell a Kuchipudi dancer from a Bharatanatyam dancer, and you know what their hands and faces are saying. Next, in Chapter 11, we look at the art that stays still: temples, mosques, paintings and the kolam patterns drawn fresh on doorsteps every morning.

docs.title: Quiz: Dance and Theater
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 10. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What is the Natya Shastra?

  1. A Mughal court history that describes Kathak performances
  2. A Sanskrit handbook on the performing arts, credited to the sage Bharata
  3. A list of classical dances published by the Sangeet Natak Akademi
  4. A Tamil epic poem about a dancer
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Natya Shastra is a Sanskrit treatise on drama, dance and music, traditionally credited to Bharata and usually dated between about 200 BCE and 200 CE. It is much older than the Sangeet Natak Akademi's list, which dates from modern India.

Concept Tested: Natya Shastra Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
How many classical dances does India's Sangeet Natak Akademi recognize?

  1. Six
  2. Nine
  3. Twelve
  4. Eight
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Akademi recognizes eight: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Kathakali, Sattriya, Manipuri and Mohiniyattam. Nine is a common mix-up because India's Ministry of Culture also lists Chhau.

Concept Tested: Classical Dance Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which dance is widely called the national dance of Afghanistan?

  1. Attan
  2. Bhangra
  3. Kandyan dance
  4. Garba
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Attan is a Pashtun circle dance danced around a dhol drummer, and Pashtuns in Pakistan dance it too. Bhangra is a Punjabi harvest dance, Kandyan dance is from Sri Lanka, and Garba is from Gujarat.

Concept Tested: Attan Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
In the Natya Shastra's theory of rasa, what is a rasa?

  1. A hand gesture with a fixed meaning
  2. The rhythm cycle a drummer keeps
  3. The emotional flavor that a performance creates in the audience
  4. A costume worn only for religious stories
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Rasa, literally "juice" or "taste," is the feeling the audience experiences, such as love, wonder or sorrow. A fixed hand gesture is a mudra, not a rasa.

Concept Tested: Rasa Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why can a single mudra, such as Pataka, stand for clouds in one moment and the word "Go!" in another?

  1. Because its meaning depends on context: where the hand moves and what the face shows
  2. Because each dance style gives every mudra exactly one meaning
  3. Because the audience is expected to guess randomly
  4. Because Pataka is only decorative and has no real meaning
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Like a word with several meanings, a mudra's meaning comes from context, including its position, movement and the dancer's expression. The idea that each mudra has only one meaning is a common misunderstanding.

Concept Tested: Mudra Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Which statement best explains the difference between folk dance and classical dance, as this chapter describes it?

  1. Folk dances are always simpler and less skilled than classical dances.
  2. Classical dances are never performed at festivals.
  3. Folk dances come only from India, while classical dances come from all eight countries.
  4. Folk dances grow out of community life and are learned by joining in, while classical dances follow a codified technique learned over years with a teacher.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The difference is about how a dance is learned and who dances it, not about skill. Option A is the misconception the chapter corrects: Bhangra and Attan can be highly athletic and complex.

Concept Tested: Folk Dance Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
At a culture night, a dancer from Andhra Pradesh performs fast footwork, acts out a story in Telugu songs, and ends by dancing on the rim of a brass plate. Which dance is this most likely to be?

  1. Bharatanatyam
  2. Kuchipudi
  3. Odissi
  4. Manipuri Dance
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Kuchipudi comes from Andhra Pradesh, uses Telugu songs, and is famous for the brass-plate tarangam. Bharatanatyam is the most likely mix-up because the two share a bent-knee stance and mudras, but it comes from Tamil Nadu.

Concept Tested: Kuchipudi Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Your club wants to show one dance that uses green painted faces for heroes, huge skirts and crowns, and all-night storytelling. Which dance should you look for?

  1. Mohiniyattam
  2. Sattriya
  3. Kathakali
  4. Kathak
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Kathakali, from Kerala, uses color-coded makeup such as green pacha faces for noble heroes. Mohiniyattam also comes from Kerala, but it is a gentle solo dance with natural makeup and a white-and-gold sari.

Concept Tested: Kathakali Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Kathak is danced today in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Which part of its history best explains this?

  1. It grew from storytellers and was also danced in royal courts across northern India, including Mughal and Awadh courts.
  2. It was invented in the twentieth century for film.
  3. It began in Buddhist monasteries in Bhutan.
  4. It was created by the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 1953.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Kathak's roots in traveling storytellers and in courts across northern India, including Muslim-ruled courts, made it part of the shared culture of a region now divided among several countries. The Akademi recognized Kathak; it did not create it.

Concept Tested: Kathak Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
The Sangeet Natak Akademi lists eight classical dances, India's Ministry of Culture also lists Chhau, and Bangladesh's national encyclopedia names its own set. What is the best conclusion?

  1. Only one of these lists can be correct, so the others are mistakes.
  2. Chhau must be older than the eight Akademi dances.
  3. Lists made in Bangladesh do not count because the dances are from India.
  4. "Classical" is a label that institutions apply using their own criteria, so the list depends on who is counting.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Different bodies use different criteria and serve different communities, which is why the chapter says "eight, according to the Sangeet Natak Akademi." Option A assumes there is one true list, which is the misconception the chapter warns against.

Concept Tested: Classical Dance Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Dance and Theater
docs.text:
1. About Us - Sangeet Natak Akademi - The official page of India's national academy of music, dance and drama, set up in 1953. It explains the Akademi's role, its awards, and its dance institutions such as the Kathak Kendra and the Manipur dance academy in Imphal.

  2. Garba of Gujarat - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - UNESCO's 2023 listing for Garba, with a description of the circle dance around a lit clay pot during Navaratri and how the tradition is passed on. Includes photos and a short video.

  3. Chhau dance - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - Describes the three styles of Chhau (Seraikella, Purulia and Mayurbhanj), the use of masks, and its link to the spring festival Chaitra Parva. Inscribed in 2010.

  4. Kutiyattam, Sanskrit theatre - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - An overview of Kerala's temple theater, its long training and performances that can last up to 40 days. A good companion to the Kathakali section.

  5. Mask dance of the drums from Drametse - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - Bhutan's masked monastery dance honoring Padmasambhava, with sixteen masked dancers and ten musicians. Shows how dance carries Buddhist teaching in the Himalaya.

  6. Classical Dance - Banglapedia, National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh - Explains what "classical dance" means in Bangladesh and how Bengali dancers learned Kathak, Manipuri and other styles. Useful for the "Whose Story?" question of who defines the term.

  7. Kuchipudi - Akademi: South Asian Dance in the UK - A short, clear introduction to Kuchipudi's village origins, its change from all-male dance-drama to solo dance, and the famous brass-plate tarangam. The same site has pages on other South Asian dance styles.

  8. The Mirror of Gesture: Being the Abhinaya Darpana of Nandikesvara - Ananda Coomaraswamy and Gopala Kristnayya Duggirala, 1917 (Internet Archive) - A public-domain English translation of the classic handbook of dance gestures. It lists the hand shapes and meanings of Pataka, Tripataka, Mayura, Alapadma and many more, with photographs.

  9. Manuscripts of Bhagavad Gita, Natyashastra inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of World Register - The Week (PTI), 18 April 2025 - News report on UNESCO's April 2025 decision to add Natya Shastra manuscripts to its Memory of the World Register.

  10. Indian classical dance - Wikipedia - An overview of the classical forms, the eight recognized by the Sangeet Natak Akademi and the longer lists used by others. Follow its citations to scholarly books on each dance.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asian art is everywhere: carved into hillside monasteries, built into temple towers and marble tombs, painted on palace walls and paper, and drawn in rice flour on a doorstep every morning. This chapter starts with the art people make at home, kolam and rangoli, and the dots and symmetry behind them. It then tours the region's great buildings, from Buddhist stupas and Hindu temples to Mughal tombs and gardens, and its traditions of painting, from Mughal miniatures and Sri Lanka's Sigiriya to Himalayan thangkas and Mithila painting. It ends on the street, with mehndi, terracotta, block printing, and the painted trucks and rickshaws of Pakistan and Bangladesh.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters for the Mauryas, the Cholas and the Mughals, who built many of the monuments here.
  • Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia for the basic ideas behind Buddhist, Hindu, Jain and Islamic sacred buildings.
  • Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year for the festivals when rangoli, alpona and mehndi appear.

Art is something you do

Hi, I'm Mora, and yes, I have opinions about color! Some of the most skilled art in South Asia isn't in a museum. It's on a doorstep, a pair of hands, or the back of a truck, and you might already have some of it at home. This chapter helps you see it, name it and maybe make some yourself. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 11.1 Rice Flour on the Doorstep
docs.text:
It's the morning of Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year, and Zara Hossain comes downstairs to find her Nanu kneeling at the front door with a bowl of white rice paste. Nanu dips her fingertips in the paste and draws a flower, then vines curling out from it, then a border of tiny leaves, all without lifting her eyes from the floor. "This is alpona," she tells Zara in Bangla. "We did it at home in Chattogram every new year."

That afternoon at the South Asian Student Association meeting, Zara shows the club a photo. Arjun Reddy leans over. "My grandmother does something like that in Hyderabad, but every single morning, before sunrise. She calls it muggu. In Tamil it's called kolam. First she puts down a grid of dots, then she draws lines around them." Ben Lindqvist zooms in on the photo, then on Arjun's. "Wait. How do they get them so perfect? It's not like they use a ruler." Arjun shrugs. "She just knows." But how do you "just know" a design that perfect, and what else across South Asia is made with that same kind of knowledge?

docs.title: 11.2 Art at the Threshold: Rangoli, Kolam and Their Cousins
docs.text:
Start with something you've probably done: drawing on graph paper. The little squares tell you where to put each line, so even a complicated pattern comes out even. Or think of cutting a paper snowflake: fold once, cut once, and the shape repeats around the center by itself. South Asian floor art uses both tricks: a hidden grid and symmetry.

All across the region, families decorate the floor at the doorway, especially for festivals, weddings and new years. The threshold matters because it's where the outside world meets the home. Each region has its own name and style.

Rangoli (रंगोली, rung-GOH-lee) is a design made on the floor or ground using dry materials such as colored powders, rice flour, colored sand, crushed limestone or flower petals. Rangoli is made most often for Diwali (and for Tihar in Nepal), and also for Onam, Pongal and other festivals. Rangolis can be geometric, floral, or pictures of deities, peacocks and lamps, and modern ones often use bright synthetic colors.

Kolam (கோலம், KOH-lum), a Tamil word meaning "form" or "beauty," is a line drawing made with white rice flour on the swept and dampened ground outside a home, traditionally drawn each morning before dawn by women in Tamil Nadu. In Telangana and Andhra Pradesh the same practice is called muggu (ముగ్గు, MOOG-goo), and Tamil families in Sri Lanka and around the world draw kolams too. The artist holds a pinch of flour between thumb and first finger and lets it fall in a steady line as her hand moves.

The most traditional style is the pulli kolam, "dot kolam." The artist first sets down a grid of dots (pulli). Then she draws lines that loop around the dots, usually without touching them. In the hardest designs, a single line winds around every dot and joins back to where it started, with no loose ends. That answers Ben's question. The dots work like graph paper, and the rules (go around, don't touch, keep the line moving) work like a recipe. Learning those rules takes years of watching relatives draw, and many women keep a notebook of designs and swap the hardest ones.

Kolams are meant to disappear. During the day, feet, wind and rain wear them away, and ants and birds eat the rice flour. Many families see that as part of the point: a kolam is thought to welcome prosperity into the home, the flour feeds small creatures, and the next morning it's drawn again.

Kolam meets computer science

In 1974, the Indian mathematicians and computer scientists Gift Siromoney, Rani Siromoney and Kamala Krithivasan published a paper describing kolam patterns with "array grammars," a way of writing drawing rules a computer can follow. Why do you think a pattern drawn by hand on a doorstep turned out to be a good puzzle for computer scientists?

The region has many more cousins. In Bangladesh and West Bengal, alpona (আলপনা, AL-po-na) is painted, not sprinkled: a wet paste of rice flour and water is applied with the fingertips or a twig or cloth, for Pohela Boishakh, Durga Puja and weddings. In Bangladesh, alpona is also painted for national days such as International Mother Language Day on 21 February. In Kerala, the Onam flower carpet is called pookalam. Gujarat has sathiya, Rajasthan mandana and Odisha chita.

Tradition Where Material How it's made Typical occasions Rangoli Across India and Nepal Dry colored powder, rice flour, sand, petals Sprinkled by hand, often freehand or from outlines Diwali, Tihar, festivals, weddings Kolam / muggu Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh; Tamil communities in Sri Lanka Dry white rice flour Lines drawn around a grid of dots, often in one continuous line Every morning; bigger designs in the month of Margazhi and at Pongal Alpona Bangladesh and West Bengal Wet rice-flour paste Painted with fingertips, twig or cloth Pohela Boishakh, Durga Puja, weddings, national days Pookalam Kerala Flower petals Petals arranged in circular designs Onam

docs.title: The stupa
docs.text:
A Stupa (स्तूप, STOO-puh) is a Buddhist monument shaped like a dome or mound, built over relics, such as the remains of the Buddha or of revered teachers, or sacred objects. Buddhists honor a stupa by walking around it clockwise, a practice called pradakshina, and by meditating near it. A classic stupa has a round, solid dome, a small square railing on top, and a pole with umbrella-like discs, a sign of honor.

The Great Stupa at Sanchi, in central India, was first commissioned by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE as a simple brick dome over relics of the Buddha. In the 1st century BCE, four richly carved stone gateways (toranas) were added, covered with scenes from the Buddha's life and earlier lives. UNESCO, which made Sanchi a World Heritage Site in 1989, calls it the oldest Buddhist sanctuary still in existence.

As Buddhism spread, the stupa took new shapes and names.

  • In Sri Lanka, a stupa is called a dagoba. The huge white Ruwanwelisaya in Anuradhapura, a city UNESCO lists as the Sacred City of Anuradhapura (1982), was built by King Dutugemunu more than 2,000 years ago.
  • In Nepal, the Kathmandu Valley (a World Heritage Site since 1979) includes the great stupas of Swayambhu and Boudhanath. Boudhanath is one of the largest spherical stupas in the world.
  • In Bhutan, stupas are called chortens. Chorten Kora in eastern Bhutan, built in 1740, was modeled on Boudhanath.
  • In Pakistan, the hilltop Buddhist monastery of Takht-i-Bahi, founded in the 1st century CE in the old region of Gandhara, is so well preserved that UNESCO listed it in 1980.
  • In Afghanistan, the Bamiyan Valley held two giant Buddha figures carved into a cliff, possibly in the 6th century, surrounded by painted caves. They were destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001, an act UNESCO describes as a tragedy that "shook the world." The valley became a World Heritage Site in 2003.
  • In Bangladesh, the great Buddhist monastery at Paharpur (Somapura Mahavihara), built under the Pala kings from the late 8th century, was a center of learning until the 12th century and is a World Heritage Site (1985).

docs.title: The Hindu temple
docs.text:
Hindu Temple Architecture is the set of shared design traditions used to build Hindu temples as homes for a deity. At the heart of a temple is the garbhagriha ("womb chamber"), a small, dark sanctum holding the image of the deity. Above it rises a tower: a shikhara (शिखर, SHIK-huh-ruh, "mountain peak") in the north, or a vimana in the south. In front there is usually a mandapa, a hall where worshippers gather, and a path for walking around the sanctum. The tower is often shaped like a mountain, and the walls are covered with sculpture.

Historians describe two main regional styles.

Nagara (northern) style Dravida (southern) style Tower over the sanctum Curved shikhara, often with smaller towers clustered around it Stepped, pyramid-like vimana Gateways Usually modest Huge, sculpture-covered gate towers called gopuram (கோபுரம், GO-pu-rum), often taller than the main tower in later temples Famous examples Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh, India (built mostly 950 to 1050 under the Chandella kings; about 20 Hindu and Jain temples survive) Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, India (built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I, 1003 to 1010)

The Brihadisvara Temple is part of the Great Living Chola Temples, a World Heritage Site since 1987, and its granite vimana is one of the tallest in South India. Nepal developed its own style of tiered, pagoda-roofed temples, like Pashupati in the Kathmandu Valley, and Bangladesh and West Bengal developed temples made of brick and terracotta (Section 11.6).

docs.title: 11.4 Mughal Architecture: Domes, Gardens and Stone Lace
docs.text:
Mughal Architecture is the building style that developed under the Mughal emperors, who ruled much of the subcontinent from the 1500s to the 1700s (you met them in Chapter 3). It blended Persian and Central Asian ideas, such as tall domes, arched gateways and walled gardens, with Indian building skills, materials and decoration. Its signatures are red sandstone and white marble, perfect symmetry, and the charbagh, a garden divided into four parts by water channels, which in Islamic tradition recalls the four rivers of Paradise.

Three sites show how the style grew.

  1. Humayun's Tomb, Delhi. Commissioned in 1558 by Bega Begum, Emperor Humayun's widow, and designed by Persian architects Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son, it was finished around 1570. It was the first garden-tomb in the subcontinent and the first building to use red sandstone on such a scale. UNESCO calls it the model that inspired the Taj Mahal.
  2. The Taj Mahal, Agra. Shah Jahan ordered it in 1631 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died that year. The white marble mausoleum was built between 1631 and 1648, and the whole complex, with its gardens and red sandstone buildings, was finished around 1653. More than 20,000 workers and artisans worked on it under a board of architects led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori. It is a World Heritage Site (1983).
  3. The Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens, Pakistan. The fort holds marble palaces, a hall of mirrors (Sheesh Mahal) and the enormous Picture Wall, covered in glazed tile mosaics of court life, begun under Jahangir and finished under Shah Jahan around 1632. Shah Jahan's Shalimar Gardens (1641 to 1642) step down three terraces with pools, cascades and fountains. Both became a World Heritage Site in 1981. Across from the fort stands the Badshahi Mosque, built by Emperor Aurangzeb from 1671 to 1673, which was the largest Mughal mosque.

Islamic architecture in the region didn't start with the Mughals. In southern Bangladesh, the Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat (a World Heritage Site since 1985) was founded in the 15th century by Khan Jahan Ali. Despite its name, its great brick Sixty Dome Mosque has 81 domes held up by 60 columns. And in the Maldives, builders cut mosques from coral stone: the Malé Friday Mosque (Hukuru Miskiy), completed in 1658, is built from blocks of coral that fit together without mortar. It is on UNESCO's tentative list, and on 21 January 2026 the Maldives submitted a full World Heritage nomination for it and four other coral stone mosques, which was still being evaluated in 2026.

docs.title: Jali
docs.text: A Jali (जाली, JAA-lee, "net") is a stone screen carved with holes in a geometric, floral or calligraphic pattern. Jalis let in air and soft, filtered light while blocking harsh sun and rain and giving privacy, which is a clever answer to South Asia's hot climate. Geometric jalis appear by 1311 in the Alai Darwaza gateway in Delhi. The Mughals carved finer, plant-like designs, as in the marble screens of the Taj Mahal. Some of the most famous jalis are in the Sidi Saiyyed Mosque in Ahmedabad, built in 1572 to 1573, whose stone windows are carved with intertwining trees and leaves.

docs.title: Calligraphy
docs.text:
Calligraphy is the art of beautiful writing. In Islamic art it holds a special place, because many Muslims believe the words of the Qur'an deserve the most beautiful form possible, and because Islamic religious art usually avoids pictures of people in mosques and tombs. So instead of statues, Mughal buildings carry words. The Taj Mahal's gateways and walls are framed with Qur'anic verses in a flowing script called thuluth, made of jasper or black marble set into white marble. The calligrapher was Abdul Haq, whom Shah Jahan honored with the title Amanat Khan.

Calligraphy runs through the region in many scripts. Urdu is usually written in the elegant, slanting Nastaliq style (see Chapter 6). Sikh scripture is written in the Gurmukhi script, and Buddhist monasteries in Bhutan and Nepal treasure texts written in Tibetan script. You'll even find calligraphy on the back of a Pakistani truck (Section 11.6).

Whose Story?

Who gets the credit for a masterpiece? Tour guides say Shah Jahan "built" the Taj Mahal, but historians point to a board of architects led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori, a calligrapher, inlay workers, stone carvers and more than 20,000 laborers whose names were mostly never recorded. Some historians call Mughal buildings "Islamic architecture," others "Indian architecture," and many prefer "Indo-Islamic," because the style mixed Persian designs with local craftsmanship. The same question comes up for art made at home: kolam, alpona and Mithila wall paintings were made for centuries by women who were rarely called "artists" at all. Museums and scholars now debate whether labels like "folk art" honor these traditions or rank them below "fine art."

docs.title: 11.5 Painting on Paper, Rock and Cloth
Mughal Miniature Painting
docs.text:
Mughal Miniature Painting is the style of small, detailed paintings made in the workshops of the Mughal emperors, either to illustrate books or to be collected in albums. It grew out of Persian miniature painting, made a tentative start under Emperor Humayun, and soon mixed with the styles of Indian painters. Under Akbar, a large workshop of artists often worked in teams: senior artists might draw the outlines, and junior artists fill in the colors, especially the backgrounds. Akbar's most ambitious project was the Hamzanama, a giant illustrated adventure story begun around 1562. According to his court historian, it had illustrations for 1,400 passages of the story.

Mughal painters were known for realistic portraits, court scenes and nature studies. Under Emperor Jahangir, the artist Ustad Mansur became famous for his studies of birds, animals and flowers. He was the first to illustrate the Siberian crane. Pages were made with fine brushes and rich colors, sometimes on paper flecked with gold. Hindu Rajput and Pahari kings in the hills also kept painters at court, so related miniature styles flourished in Rajasthan and the Himalayan foothills.

docs.title: Sigiriya
docs.text:
Sigiriya (SEE-gi-ri-ya, from Sinhagiri, "Lion Rock") is a royal fortress and palace built on top of a granite rock about 180 m (590 ft) high in central Sri Lanka by King Kashyapa I, who ruled from 477 to 495 CE. Visitors once entered through a gateway shaped like a giant lion. Today only its huge brick paws remain on either side of the stairs.

Partway up, the king had the rock face painted with colorful frescoes, and some still survive. Next to them runs the polished Mirror Wall, where visitors scratched well over a thousand poems and comments, most of them between the 8th and 10th centuries. Below the rock lie water gardens with pools and channels. After Kashyapa's reign, the site became a Buddhist monastery until the 13th or 14th century. UNESCO listed the Ancient City of Sigiriya in 1982.

docs.title: Thangka
docs.text:
Thangka (Tibetan ཐང་ཀ, TAHNG-kah) is a Buddhist painting on cotton or silk that can be rolled up like a scroll, showing a deity, a scene from the Buddha's life, or a mandala (a circular diagram of the universe used in meditation). Thangkas are made in Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet and the Himalayan parts of India, and they are used as teaching tools and as aids for personal meditation. Painters follow precise, traditional rules about the proportions, postures and measurements of each figure, a little like the kolam artist's rules for her dot grid. Thangka painting grew in part from the Newar painting tradition of Nepal's Kathmandu Valley, called paubha.

Bhutan makes the biggest thangkas of all. A thongdrel is a giant appliqué religious image, sewn from colored cloth, that covers the side of a building. It is unveiled only once a year, usually on the last day of a district's tsechu, Bhutan's main religious festivals. Nima Sherpa tells the club that her family's monastery in Solukhumbu keeps its thangkas rolled up and brings them out for special days.

docs.title: Madhubani Painting
docs.text:
Madhubani Painting, also called Mithila painting, is a style of bold, colorful painting from the Mithila region, which spans northern Bihar in India and the Terai lowlands of southern Nepal around Janakpur. For centuries, women of the region painted gods, goddesses, lotus ponds, fish, birds and wedding scenes on the freshly plastered mud walls and floors of their homes, especially for marriages. Every space is filled with pattern, and figures are outlined in double lines. Artists use fingers, twigs, brushes, nib pens and even matchsticks, with natural pigments such as ochre and lampblack.

In the late 1960s, during a severe drought, a few women began painting these designs on paper to sell for family income. Over the following decades, hundreds of women from many different castes and communities took it up, and Madhubani painting became known worldwide. It's named after Madhubani district in Bihar, still its busiest center.

docs.title: 11.6 Craft at Home and on the Road
Mehndi
docs.text:
Mehndi (Urdu مہندی, MEH-hn-dee), also called henna, is the art of decorating the skin, usually hands and feet, with a paste made from the dried, powdered leaves of the henna plant (Lawsonia inermis). The paste leaves a reddish-brown stain that lasts about one to three weeks. Across South Asia, mehndi is part of weddings (many families hold a separate "mehndi night" before the wedding), Eid, Karva Chauth, Teej and other festivals. Zara's cousins line up on Chand Raat, the night before Eid, to have fine, detailed vines and paisleys piped onto their palms from a cone.

Real henna isn't black

Natural henna stains orange-brown to reddish-brown. "Black henna" often contains a hair-dye chemical called PPD, which the US Food and Drug Administration warns can cause dangerous skin reactions and scarring in some people. This is safety information, not medical advice: if you react to any skin product, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Terracotta
docs.text:
Terracotta (Italian for "baked earth") is clay that is shaped and then fired, usually to an orange-red color. In the delta of Bengal, where there is plenty of river clay but little building stone, builders turned brick and terracotta into an art form. Temple walls were covered with fired-clay panels showing gods, epics, hunting scenes and daily life.

  • The Kantajew Temple in Dinajpur, Bangladesh, built between 1704 and 1752, is a celebrated example of terracotta architecture, with walls covered in clay panels.
  • The Malla kings of Bishnupur, in West Bengal, India, built a group of terracotta temples in the 17th and 18th centuries.
  • Earlier still, the walls of the great Buddhist monastery at Paharpur in Bangladesh were covered with carved decoration.

Terracotta is also a living village craft. The long-necked Bankura horse, made in Panchmura village in West Bengal, was first made for village rituals and is now a symbol of Indian folk art around the world.

docs.title: Block Printing
docs.text:
Block Printing is a way of printing patterns on cloth by carving a design into a wooden block, dipping it in dye, and stamping it by hand, over and over, to build up the pattern. A single cloth may need several blocks, one for each color, lined up by eye.

In Sindh, Pakistan, the block-printed cloth called ajrak is a symbol of Sindhi identity. It uses deep indigo blue and crimson red, with white and black outlining geometric patterns, and it is made with carved wooden blocks and resist-dyeing, where parts of the cloth are covered so dye can't reach them. Ajrak is also made by Sindhi communities in Kutch, Gujarat, in India, in the village of Ajrakhpur. In Rajasthan, the town of Bagru is known for hand block printing with natural dyes by the Chhipa community of printers. You'll see more of South Asia's textiles in Chapter 12.

docs.title: Truck Art
docs.text:
Truck Art is the tradition of decorating trucks (and buses) with paintings, calligraphy, carved wood, mirrors and reflective strips, best known in Pakistan and also common in India and Afghanistan. A decorated Pakistani truck can carry mountain landscapes, birds, film stars, the winged horse Buraq, poetry and religious verses in calligraphy, and painted eyes meant to ward off bad luck. A tall carved wooden "crown" rises above the cab. The art grew up in the colonial era, when trucks first came into the region and drivers began decorating them with local folk designs.

Karachi is one of the biggest centers of the trade. In 2002, the Karachi truck painter Haider Ali and bodywork expert Jamil Uddin decorated a 1976 Bedford truck on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, and the finished truck joined the Smithsonian's permanent collection. Ayesha Qureshi tells the club her uncle in Lahore insists the most beautiful trucks are the ones that carry poetry. In India, painted trucks often carry the phrase "Horn OK Please."

docs.title: Rickshaw Art
docs.text:
Rickshaw Art is the painting and decoration of cycle rickshaws, best known in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Almost every part of a rickshaw, from the back panel to the hood and seat, is painted with flowers, birds, animals, scenes from history and fables, national heroes, movie stars and text, then decorated with tassels, plastic flowers and tinsel. Because rickshaws move slowly through the streets, they work like a moving art gallery. Traditionally, the craft is passed down in workshops by hands-on training, and both men and women paint. In 2023, UNESCO added "Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka" to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, partly because the craft is under pressure as motorized rickshaws spread.

You're surrounded by art

Look around your own home: a block-printed tablecloth, a brass lamp, a framed calligraphy panel, a henna cone in the kitchen drawer. Every one of them came from a craft with a long history. Pick one and find out who made it and where.
