docs.title: Diagram: Kolam Maker
docs.text:
Open the Kolam Maker fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Kolam Maker

sim-id: ch11-kolam-maker Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Create Bloom Verb: design Learning Objective: The learner will create a symmetric dot-grid design and explain how the dots (pulli) and rotational symmetry guide the drawing of a kolam.

Canvas: responsive width; 565 px drawing area plus 115 px control area.

Controls: grid size menu (3 x 3 to 7 x 7 dots), ink color menu, "4-fold symmetry" checkbox, Trace demo / Pause button, Clear button, Save button; draw with mouse or finger.

Behavior: A dark "ground" square with a grid of white dots. The sim starts with a demo pulli kolam already drawn: on odd grids it is one continuous line around every dot; on even grids, several closed loops. Trace demo animates the drawing. Learner strokes are copied four times around the center when symmetry is on. Save downloads the design as a PNG. The demo is computed as a mirror curve (diagonal lines through the gaps between dots, bouncing off the edge and off a few symmetric inner walls).

Start by tracing the demo with your eyes, or press Trace demo and watch. On the 5 x 5 grid, the line is a single unbroken loop that passes around all 25 dots and never touches one. Notice the two rules that make it work: the line always travels diagonally through the gaps between dots, and when it reaches the edge, it swings around the outside of the edge dot and heads back in.

Then press Clear and make your own. With 4-fold symmetry on, draw one small curve near a corner and watch it appear in all four corners at once. Try to make a design that loops around the dots the way the demo does. Then turn symmetry off and try to draw the same design by hand. You'll quickly see why kolam artists rely on the dot grid, and how much skill it takes to make a balanced design on a doorstep at dawn without any help from a computer. Finally, switch to the 4 x 4 grid and notice that the demo needs four separate loops instead of one.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the art and craft in their home and life: floor designs, mehndi, embroidery, pottery, painted objects, or buildings they love. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Ask them to show you one handmade object in the house (a cloth, a dish, a painting, a piece of jewelry) and hold it while you talk. Ask if you can take a photo of it for your notes.

Questions to ask

  1. When you were young, who in your family made art or did crafts at home? What did they make?
  2. Did anyone draw alpona, kolam, rangoli or other designs at the door? When, and how did they learn?
  3. Who put mehndi on your hands for weddings or Eid or festivals? What designs do you remember?
  4. What is the most beautiful building you have ever seen, in South Asia or anywhere? What made it beautiful to you?
  5. Have the crafts you grew up with changed, or are fewer people making them now? Why do you think that is?
  6. Is there a handmade object or a skill in our family that you hope I keep?

Listen for: mentions of Kolam, Rangoli or alpona at the doorway, Mehndi at celebrations, and buildings that show Mughal Architecture, Hindu Temple Architecture or a Stupa.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare the object or craft your elder described with one from this chapter. Was it made for a ritual, for beauty, for sale, or all three? If a friend interviewed someone from a different country, compare: did both elders learn their craft by watching relatives, or in another way?

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Rangoli and kolam are the same thing. Reality: They are related doorstep arts, but kolam is traditionally drawn in white rice flour, often as lines looping around a grid of dots, and is made daily in many Tamil homes. Rangoli usually uses colored powders or petals and is made most often for festivals like Diwali. Alpona in Bengal is different again: it's painted with wet rice paste.

Myth: The Taj Mahal is the only Mughal building worth knowing. Reality: Humayun's Tomb in Delhi was the model the Taj Mahal grew from, and the Lahore Fort, Shalimar Gardens and Badshahi Mosque in Pakistan are among the greatest Mughal works. Earlier Islamic buildings like Bagerhat's Sixty Dome Mosque in Bangladesh are worth knowing too.

Myth: Folk art is less skilled than fine art. Reality: A pulli kolam that circles every dot in one unbroken line takes years to master and follows rules complex enough to interest mathematicians and computer scientists. Madhubani and rickshaw painting are recognized worldwide, and rickshaw painting is on UNESCO's heritage list.

Myth: Truck art is just graffiti. Reality: Pakistani truck art is a skilled, commissioned trade with specialist painters, woodcarvers and metalworkers who follow established styles. One Karachi-decorated truck is in the Smithsonian's permanent collection.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What is a pulli kolam, and what are the dots for?

A pulli kolam is a kolam drawn on a grid of dots (pulli). The dots guide the drawing: lines loop around them without touching, which keeps the design even and symmetric.

2. Name the two main styles of Hindu temple architecture and one difference between them.

The northern Nagara style has a curved shikhara tower over the sanctum. The southern Dravida style has a stepped, pyramid-like vimana and often huge gateway towers called gopurams.

3. Why are Mughal tombs and mosques decorated with calligraphy rather than statues?

Islamic religious art usually avoids images of people in sacred buildings, and many Muslims believe the words of the Qur'an deserve the most beautiful form. So builders decorated with calligraphy, geometric patterns and plant designs.

4. What is a thongdrel, and when is it shown?

A thongdrel is a giant appliqué thangka made in Bhutan. It is displayed only once a year, usually at dawn on the last day of a district's tsechu festival.

5. What did UNESCO add to its heritage list in 2023 from Bangladesh?

"Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka," the colorful painting and decoration of cycle rickshaws.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Match each place to its country: Sigiriya, Takht-i-Bahi, Bagerhat, Boudhanath, Sanchi.

    Answer

    Sigiriya: Sri Lanka. Takht-i-Bahi: Pakistan. Bagerhat: Bangladesh. Boudhanath: Nepal. Sanchi: India.

  2. What material is a kolam traditionally made from, and at what time of day is it usually drawn?

    Answer

    White rice flour, drawn in the early morning before or around dawn.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why a jali is both beautiful and practical in South Asia's climate.

    Answer

    Its carved holes create patterns of light and shadow, while letting in air and soft light and blocking harsh sun, rain and outside views, which keeps rooms cooler and private.

  2. Explain how Madhubani painting changed from a wall art to a famous art on paper.

    Answer

    Women of the Mithila region painted it on the mud walls of their homes for centuries. During a drought in the late 1960s, some began painting on paper to sell for income, and over the following decades hundreds of women took it up and it became known around the world.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Kolam Maker to design a kolam on a 5 x 5 grid with 4-fold symmetry. Describe in two sentences where the center of rotation is and how many times each of your strokes appears. Hint: look for the small gold circle.

  2. Your club wants to decorate the entrance for a Pohela Boishakh event and a Diwali event. For each, choose a floor art tradition from this chapter and list the materials you'd need. Hint: compare alpona and rangoli in the table in Section 11.2.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the stupa at Sanchi with a Hindu temple like the Brihadisvara at Thanjavur. How does each building guide what visitors do with their bodies? Hint: think about walking around, entering, and where the most sacred spot is.

  2. Truck art and rickshaw art are both "moving art." Analyze two ways they are similar and two ways they differ. Hint: think about vehicle, country, materials and recognition.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Should everyday crafts like kolam or mehndi be displayed in museums next to Mughal paintings? Evaluate the pros and cons. Hint: the Whose Story? box raises the question of labels like "folk art."

  2. UNESCO says rickshaw painting is under pressure as motorized rickshaws spread. Evaluate one way a community could keep a craft like this alive. Hint: think about who learns it, who pays for it, and where people see it.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a club poster or slide that teaches one South Asian craft in five steps, with a simple drawing for each step. Hint: kolam, alpona, block printing or mehndi all work well.

  2. Create a short "museum label" (80 to 120 words) for a handmade object from your own home or an elder's home, including what it is, where it comes from, who made it and why it matters. Hint: use your Ask Your Elders interview.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Doorstep arts differ by region: kolam (rice flour lines around dots, Tamil Nadu and Sri Lankan Tamil homes), muggu, rangoli (colored powder, festivals) and alpona (wet rice paste, Bengal).
  • Dots and symmetry are the hidden structure of a pulli kolam, and the best designs use one unbroken line around every dot.
  • Stupas (Sanchi, Anuradhapura, Boudhanath, Takht-i-Bahi) and Hindu temples (Nagara and Dravida styles) are designed for walking around and approaching a sacred center.
  • Mughal Architecture blended Persian and Indian traditions, from Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal to the Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens, with jalis and calligraphy as signature details.
  • South Asian painting ranges from Mughal miniatures and Sigiriya's frescoes to Himalayan thangkas and Mithila (Madhubani) painting.
  • Living crafts like mehndi, terracotta, block printing (ajrak), truck art and rickshaw art (UNESCO 2023) connect art to everyday life across all eight countries.

What a gallery!

From rice flour to marble, you've toured South Asia's art in every size. Next, in Chapter 12, we look at what people wear: cotton, silk, jamdani, ikat and the stories woven into saris, kurtas and shalwar kameez.

docs.title: Quiz: Art, Architecture, and Craft
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 11. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
In which country is the rock fortress of Sigiriya, built by King Kashyapa I in the 5th century CE?

  1. Nepal
  2. Bangladesh
  3. Sri Lanka
  4. Pakistan
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Sigiriya, the "Lion Rock," is in central Sri Lanka, and Kashyapa I ruled from 477 to 495 CE. The Buddhist monastery of Takht-i-Bahi is the major ancient site in Pakistan from this chapter, and Bagerhat is in Bangladesh.

Concept Tested: Sigiriya Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
What is a jali?

  1. A carved stone screen with holes that lets in air and filtered light
  2. A dome built over the relics of the Buddha
  3. A gateway tower on a South Indian temple
  4. A garden divided into four parts by water channels
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A jali is a perforated stone screen carved in geometric, floral or calligraphic patterns. A dome over relics is a stupa, a temple gateway tower is a gopuram, and a four-part garden is a charbagh.

Concept Tested: Jali Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
In 2023, UNESCO added which Bangladeshi tradition to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity?

  1. Truck art in Karachi
  2. Terracotta temples in Dinajpur
  3. Alpona painting for Pohela Boishakh
  4. Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. UNESCO inscribed "Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka" in 2023. Truck art is best known in Pakistan, not Bangladesh, and the terracotta temples and alpona are Bangladeshi traditions but were not the 2023 listing.

Concept Tested: Rickshaw Art Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why do pulli kolam artists start by placing a grid of dots?

  1. The dots are where the colored powder will be piled highest
  2. The dots guide the lines, which loop around them, keeping the design even and symmetric
  3. The dots mark where guests should step
  4. Each dot stands for one member of the family
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In a pulli kolam, lines loop around the dots, usually without touching them, so the dots work like graph paper for an even, symmetric design. Kolam is traditionally drawn in white rice flour lines, not piles of colored powder, which is closer to rangoli.

Concept Tested: Kolam Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why is Mughal Architecture described as a blend of traditions?

  1. It combined Persian and Central Asian ideas like domes and walled gardens with Indian materials, skills and decoration
  2. It copied Greek temples exactly
  3. It was designed entirely by European architects
  4. It used only wood and bamboo from the Himalaya
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Mughal buildings such as Humayun's Tomb, designed by Persian architects and built with Indian red sandstone and craftsmanship, mixed Persian and Central Asian forms with local building traditions. They were not copies of Greek or European buildings.

Concept Tested: Mughal Architecture Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why is calligraphy, rather than statues of people, the main decoration on the Taj Mahal?

  1. Statues were too heavy for marble walls
  2. Shah Jahan did not like sculpture of any kind
  3. Islamic religious art usually avoids images of people in sacred buildings, and the words of the Qur'an are honored in beautiful script
  4. Calligraphy was cheaper than carving
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Islamic religious buildings are usually decorated with calligraphy, geometric patterns and plant designs instead of human figures, and Qur'anic verses are given the most beautiful form possible. Cost and weight had nothing to do with it. The Taj's inlaid calligraphy was itself expensive, skilled work.

Concept Tested: Calligraphy Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A friend offers to give you a "black henna" design before a wedding, saying it's darker than regular mehndi. Based on the chapter, what's the best response?

  1. Accept, because all henna is made from the same plant
  2. Be cautious, because "black henna" often contains PPD, a hair-dye chemical the FDA warns can cause dangerous skin reactions
  3. Accept, as long as it's washed off within an hour
  4. Refuse, because mehndi is only for Eid
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Natural henna stains reddish-brown, but "black henna" often contains PPD, which can cause dangerous reactions and scarring. Mehndi is used for weddings, Eid, Diwali, Karva Chauth and many other occasions, so it isn't "only for Eid." This is safety information, not medical advice.

Concept Tested: Mehndi Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Your club is decorating for a Pohela Boishakh celebration and wants to use the floor art Zara's Nanu made. Which materials and method should you use?

  1. Dry colored powders sprinkled in a freehand design
  2. Flower petals arranged in circles
  3. White rice flour dropped in lines around a grid of dots
  4. A wet rice-flour paste painted on with fingertips
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Alpona, the Bengali floor art made for Pohela Boishakh, is painted with a wet paste of rice flour and water using the fingertips, a twig or cloth. Dry colored powder describes rangoli, petals describe pookalam, and rice flour lines around dots describe kolam.

Concept Tested: Rangoli Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Compare a stupa with a Hindu temple. Which statement is most accurate?

  1. Both are built only in India
  2. A stupa is a solid mound walked around by worshippers, while a temple has an inner sanctum (garbhagriha) that worshippers approach
  3. Both always have gopuram gateway towers
  4. A stupa holds an image of a Hindu deity, while a temple holds relics of the Buddha
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A stupa is a solid dome over relics, honored by walking around it clockwise, while a Hindu temple is built around a sanctum holding the deity's image, with a tower above it. Stupas are found in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Pakistan and Bangladesh as well as India, and gopurams belong to South Indian temples, not stupas.

Concept Tested: Stupa Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Madhubani painting moved from mud walls to paper in the late 1960s. What does this change best show about the tradition?

  1. It stopped being made by women
  2. It was invented in the 1960s
  3. Women adapted a long-standing wall art to a new material during hard times, which helped it reach audiences worldwide
  4. It became a form of truck art
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Women of Mithila had painted walls for centuries. During a severe drought in the late 1960s, some began painting on paper to earn income, and hundreds of women from many communities later took it up. The art was not invented in the 1960s, and women remained its main artists.

Concept Tested: Madhubani Painting Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Art, Architecture, and Craft
docs.text:
1. Significance of Kolam in Tamil Culture - Sahapedia - A clear introduction to kolam as a daily women's art in Tamil Nadu: rice flour, the grid of dots (pulli), how the lines are drawn, why the designs are meant to disappear, and the names of related floor arts in other regions.

  2. Array Grammars and Kolam - Gift Siromoney, Rani Siromoney and Kamala Krithivasan, Computer Graphics and Image Processing 3 (1974): 63-82 - The paper that described kolam patterns with formal drawing rules a computer can follow. Advanced reading, but a good example of art and computer science coming together.

  3. Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - Describes the painted rickshaws of Dhaka, how the craft is taught in workshops, and why it was added to UNESCO's Representative List in 2023.

  4. Masterpieces to Go: The Trucks of Pakistan - AramcoWorld (2005) - A magazine feature on Karachi's truck painters: what they paint, how the decorations are made, and how a Pakistani truck ended up in the Smithsonian.

  5. Painted Truck (The Silk Road, 2002) - Smithsonian Folklife Festival - Photos and notes from 2002, when Karachi artists Haider Ali and Jamil Uddin decorated a truck on the National Mall.

  6. Tibetan Thangka Painting (Sacred Pictures) - Asian Art Museum of San Francisco - A teacher-friendly guide to what thangkas are, how they are made and used, and what their images mean.

  7. The Politics of Mithila Painting - David L. Szanton, ORIAS, University of California, Berkeley - A short scholarly essay on how women's wall paintings in Mithila moved onto paper during the drought of the late 1960s and became an art known worldwide.

  8. Temporary Tattoos, Henna/Mehndi, and "Black Henna": Fact Sheet - US Food and Drug Administration - Explains the difference between natural henna and "black henna," and why PPD in black henna can cause serious skin reactions.

  9. Mughal painting - Wikipedia - An overview of Mughal miniature painting from Humayun to Shah Jahan, including the Hamzanama, court workshops and famous artists, with links to museum collections.

  10. Hindu temple architecture - Wikipedia - Explains the parts of a Hindu temple (sanctum, tower, hall, gateways) and the differences between the Nagara and Dravida styles, with many examples.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asia has been growing, spinning and weaving fiber for thousands of years, and its cloth has traveled the world. This chapter starts with three fibers (cotton, silk and pashmina wool), then looks at famous ways of weaving and dyeing them, such as Jamdani from Bangladesh, ikat from India and ajrak from Pakistan. Next it sorts everyday clothes into draped garments (the saree, dhoti and lungi) and stitched garments (the kurta, shalwar kameez and dupatta), and visits national dress in Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan. It ends with the turban, the bindi and bangles, and the many meanings people give them.

Clothes that carry stories

Hi, it's Mora! Maybe you have a kurta you only wear to weddings, or an aunt's saree folded in a closet that nobody explains. Clothes are one of the first ways people read your background, sometimes wrongly. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to tell the story behind what's in that closet, and answer the questions your friends ask about it.

docs.title: 12.1 Culture Day Guessing Game
docs.text:
The South Asian Student Association at Prairie Ridge High School is holding its first culture day, and everyone has been asked to wear something from home. Zara Hossain comes in a cream-and-gray cotton saree her Nanu brought from Bangladesh, covered in tiny woven flowers. Ayesha Qureshi, whose family is from Lahore, wears a green shalwar kameez with a long scarf. Simran Kaur Gill wears a shalwar kameez too, with a bright embroidered scarf from her grandmother in Ludhiana. Dilan Perera wears a white shirt and a checked cloth wrapped around his waist, and Nima Sherpa has brought a small brimmed cloth cap with a busy pattern.

Ms. Okafor turns it into a game. Ben Lindqvist has to guess which country each outfit comes from. "Saree, so India," he says, pointing at Zara. Wrong: Bangladesh. "Shalwar kameez is Pakistani," he says. Right for Ayesha, but Simran's family is from India. He guesses Dilan's wrap is "a Bangladeshi lungi," which is close but not quite: Dilan's family is from Sri Lanka, where a similar wrap is called a sarama. He gets Nima's cap right only because she gives him a hint. Ben scores two out of five and groans. "How is anyone supposed to know? Half of these are worn in, like, four countries." He has stumbled onto the big question of this chapter: if the same clothes cross so many borders, what can a garment tell you about where someone is from?

docs.title: 12.2 Clothes Speak a Language
docs.text:
Ben already knows the answer from his own family. His grandmother in Minnesota has a Norwegian bunad, a folk costume with embroidery and silver jewelry. Norway has hundreds of kinds of bunad (counts run from about 200 to more than 400, depending on what is counted), and each is tied to a region. People usually choose the one from the place their family comes from, then wear it for weddings, confirmations and especially Norway's National Day on 17 May. A bunad doesn't tell you "Norwegian" so much as "my grandmother's people came from this valley."

South Asian clothing works in a similar way, with one big difference: the region is far bigger and its borders are much newer than its clothes. The saree, the kurta and the turban are much older than the countries of India, Pakistan or Bangladesh, which became independent in 1947 and 1971. So a garment usually tells you less about a passport and more about these things:

  • Where the cloth was made. A Jamdani weave points to Dhaka. An ajrak print points to Sindh.
  • What the occasion is. Many families keep everyday cotton for home and heavy silk for weddings.
  • Sometimes, faith or community. A Sikh man's dastar, a married Bengali Hindu woman's white and red bangles, or a Bhutanese man's white ceremonial scarf each carry a specific meaning.
  • Personal taste. Plenty of teens wear a kurta with jeans simply because they like it.

To read clothes well, it helps to start one layer down, with the fibers themselves.

docs.title: 12.3 Three Fibers: Cotton, Silk and Pashmina
Cotton
docs.text:
Cotton in South Asia is the long history of growing, spinning and weaving the cotton plant's soft seed fibers in the region, a history that goes back more than 7,000 years. The oldest known cotton fibers in the world come from Mehrgarh, an early farming village in Balochistan, Pakistan. Archaeologists found a set of eight copper beads next to the wrist of a skeleton buried there in the first half of the sixth millennium BCE, roughly 7,500 to 8,000 years ago. (Some news stories round this up to 8,500 years.) When the copper corroded, its salts soaked into the thread that once strung the beads and preserved it. Under a microscope, French researchers identified the fibers as cotton.

Cotton suited South Asia well. It grows in warm places, and cotton cloth is light and breathable in the heat and humidity of the monsoon. Later, cotton cloth from the region became one of the most traded goods in the world. Merchants carried fine Indian cotton to the Roman Empire, to Baghdad and Basra, and east toward China.

The finest of all was muslin from Bengal, especially around Dhaka and Sonargaon in present-day Bangladesh. Weavers there used a local cotton called phuti karpas, which grew along the banks of the Meghna River, and spun it into thread so thin that travelers wrote that a whole length of muslin could be pulled through a ring. Mughal emperors prized it, and so did European nobles in the 1700s. Under British colonial rule the trade collapsed as cheap machine-made cloth from British factories flooded the market and weavers lost their livelihoods. The special cotton plant was eventually lost. In recent years, researchers and artisans in Bangladesh have been working to revive Dhaka muslin.

Count the cotton

Check the labels on three things in your closet right now. How many say "cotton," and how many say "Made in" Bangladesh, India, Pakistan or Sri Lanka? The cloth trade I'm describing never really stopped. It just moved into factories.

docs.title: Silk
docs.text:
Silk comes from the cocoons of silkworms, the caterpillars of certain moths. Silk Weaving in South Asia means raising silkworms, unwinding or spinning their cocoon thread, and weaving it into cloth, usually for festive and wedding clothes. India's government recognizes four main kinds of silk:

Kind of silk What the silkworms eat Where it is mostly made What it is known for Mulberry Mulberry leaves Karnataka, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir By far the most common; smooth and shiny Tasar Oak, asan and arjuna tree leaves Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Bihar and nearby states A rougher, textured silk Eri Castor leaves Assam and the northeast Spun rather than reeled; warm, with a copper tint Muga Som and soalu leaves Almost entirely in Assam A natural golden color

Some of the most famous silk sarees are named after the towns that weave them:

  • Banarasi sarees come from Varanasi (also called Banaras or Benares), on the Ganga. They are known for zari, thread wrapped in gold or silver color, woven into flowers, vines and net-like patterns. A complex Banarasi saree can take from about two weeks to several months to finish. In 2009, weavers' groups in Uttar Pradesh won Geographical Indication (GI) status for Banaras brocades and sarees. A GI is a legal label, like the one that protects the name "Champagne," which says a product's quality comes from a particular place.
  • Kanjivaram (or Kanchipuram) sarees come from the town of Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu. They are woven from mulberry silk with wide borders in a contrasting color, often with a classic "temple" border design. In a traditional Kanjivaram saree the border and the body are woven separately and then interlocked so firmly that the border stays attached even if the saree tears. The Government of India recognized Kanchipuram sarees as a GI in 2005-06.
  • Rajshahi silk comes from Rajshahi in northwestern Bangladesh, where people trace silk production back to the 13th century. Bangladesh gave it GI status in 2021.

docs.title: Pashmina
docs.text:
Pashmina is the very fine wool from the soft undercoat of goats that live high in the Himalaya, and also the name for the shawls made from it. The word comes from pashm, the Persian word for wool. In Hindi it is written पश्मीना (push-MEE-nah).

The classic source is the Changthangi goat, raised by nomadic Changpa herders on the high, cold Changthang plateau of Ladakh. Winter temperatures there can fall below −30 °C (−22 °F), so the goats grow a thick, fine undercoat. Each spring, when the goats shed, herders comb the undercoat out by hand rather than shearing it. Weavers in Kashmir turned this wool into the famous Kashmir shawl. Mughal emperors gave pashmina shawls as "robes of honor" to reward nobles, and in the 1800s the shawls became high fashion in Britain and France.

One pashmina design traveled farther than the wool itself. The teardrop-shaped buta motif on Kashmir shawls was copied by factories in the town of Paisley, Scotland, in the early 1800s. That's why English speakers today call the shape "paisley," even though it began on South Asian looms.

Nepal has its own pashmina tradition. There the high-mountain goat is called the chyangra, and Nepal's pashmina makers, working with the International Trade Centre, created a "Chyangra Pashmina" brand to mark genuine Nepali products.

A disputed region

Kashmir, where the famous shawls are woven, is a region whose control is disputed among India, Pakistan and China, and people from all sides claim its crafts with pride. When I say "Kashmir shawl," I mean the craft of the region, not a statement about whose territory it is.

docs.title: 12.4 Weaving and Dyeing: Making Pattern
docs.text:
Once you have thread, there are two main ways to put a pattern on cloth. You can weave the pattern in, by choosing which colored threads go over and under each other. Or you can dye or print the pattern on, by blocking color from some parts of the thread or cloth. South Asia has famous examples of both.

A quick piece of vocabulary helps here. On a loom, the warp threads run the long way and are stretched tight. The weft thread is passed back and forth across them.

docs.title: Jamdani
docs.text:
Jamdani (জামদানী, JAHM-dah-nee) is a fine, sheer cotton cloth from the Dhaka region of Bangladesh, with patterns woven directly into it on a hand loom. Its name comes from Persian. The weaver adds each little flower, leaf or diamond by hand, using extra weft threads that go back and forth only across that one small motif instead of the full width of the cloth. This is called a discontinuous weft technique. It is slow, careful work, so a single saree can take weeks or months, and the result is light and breathable.

In 2013, UNESCO added the traditional art of Jamdani weaving to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. UNESCO notes that the skills pass mostly from parents to children in home workshops around Dhaka, and that many Bengali women wear Jamdani sarees as a symbol of identity, both in Bangladesh and abroad. In 2016, Bangladesh also gave the Jamdani saree GI status. Zara's culture-day saree, with its woven flowers, is a Jamdani.

docs.title: Ikat
docs.text:
Ikat (EE-kaht) is a way of patterning cloth in which the threads are tied and dyed before they are ever woven. The word comes from Indonesia, where it means "to bind," and similar techniques grew up independently in many parts of the world. It works in four steps:

  1. The weaver wraps tight bindings around small sections of a bundle of threads, following a planned pattern.
  2. The threads are dyed. The tied sections resist the dye and stay their original color.
  3. The bindings are moved or added, and the threads are dyed again in a new color. This can repeat many times.
  4. Finally the bindings are removed, and the patterned threads are set up on the loom and woven.

Because the pattern is in the threads, the edges of each shape come out slightly feathery and blurred, which is ikat's signature look. In double ikat, both the warp and the weft are tie-dyed, and the weaver has to line them up exactly. It's so hard that it is woven in only a few places in the world.

India has several famous ikat centers:

  • Pochampally, in Telangana, known for bold geometric ikat sarees in cotton and silk.
  • Sambalpur and nearby districts in Odisha, where ikat is called bandha and often uses motifs such as the conch, the wheel and the flower.
  • Patan, in Gujarat, home of patola, a silk double ikat. Dutch traders once used patola as prized trade cloth in the spice trade with Indonesia.

docs.title: Ajrak
docs.text:
Ajrak is a cloth printed by hand with carved wooden blocks, made mostly in the Sindh region of Pakistan, and also by families in Kutch, in the Indian state of Gujarat, who trace their craft to Sindh. The printers use natural dyes, especially deep indigo blue and crimson red, and "resist" techniques that keep some areas from taking the dye, skills passed down through generations of the same families. Its dense patterns of stars, circles and lattices are easy to recognize.

For many people in Sindh, ajrak is a badge of identity. Families give an ajrak shawl to honor a guest, and it appears at weddings and cultural events. Some writers even point out that the famous stone bust of a "priest-king" from Mohenjo-daro, more than 4,000 years old, wears a robe with a trefoil (three-lobed) pattern that looks a little like ajrak. That link can't be proven, but it shows how strongly people feel the cloth belongs to the Indus region.

Whose Story?

Cloth often crosses borders that were drawn long after the craft began, so different groups tell its story differently. In Pakistan, ajrak is celebrated as a symbol of Sindhi culture, and in 2025 the Government of Sindh even put an ajrak-inspired design on new vehicle license plates. Across the border, block printers in Kutch in India make ajrak too, and they tell it as the story of their own families, who brought the craft from Sindh. In Bhutan, the government describes the gho and kira as national dress that protects a distinct Bhutanese identity, but when the dress code became mandatory in 1989, some Lhotshampa (Nepali-speaking Bhutanese in the south) resented being required to wear clothes from another community's tradition. Asking "whose cloth is this?" usually has more than one true answer.

docs.title: 12.5 Khadi: Cloth as Protest
docs.text:
Khadi (खादी, KHAH-dee) is cloth that is both hand-spun and hand-woven, made from cotton, silk or wool. Its importance comes from the role it played in India's freedom movement.

Under British rule, raw cotton was often shipped from India to mills in Britain, woven there by machine, and sold back to Indians as finished cloth. Mohandas K. Gandhi, the leader of the Indian independence movement, argued that buying that cloth kept India poor and dependent. He called on people to boycott foreign cloth and to spin their own thread on a charkha, a hand-turned spinning wheel. This was part of swadeshi, a movement whose name means "of one's own country."

The first piece of hand-woven cloth at Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram, in Gujarat, was made in 1917-18. He began spinning himself in 1919 and asked members of the Indian National Congress to spin and even pay their dues in yarn. In 1921, he began wearing only a simple dhoti, often without a shirt, to show his solidarity with India's rural poor. That same year he visited the Comilla region, now in Bangladesh, to encourage local weavers, and weaving centers grew up there.

After independence, India's government set up the Khadi and Village Industries Commission in April 1957, under a 1956 law, to support khadi and other village crafts. Khadi is still sold across India today. In Bangladesh, a khadi tradition continued in the Comilla area too, and in 2025 Bangladesh gave Comilla khadi Geographical Indication status.

Khadi is also a symbol of self-reliance, and many politicians in India still wear it for that reason.

docs.title: 12.6 Draped Garments: Saree, Dhoti and Lungi
docs.text: Many South Asian clothes are not cut and sewn at all. They are long, unstitched rectangles of cloth that are wrapped, pleated and tucked around the body. This makes them easy to weave on a hand loom and easy to adjust to any body size.

docs.title: The saree
docs.text:
The Saree (also spelled sari; Hindi साड़ी, Bangla শাড়ি, SAH-ree) is a long, unstitched length of cloth that a woman wraps around her waist and drapes over one shoulder. A saree is usually between 4.5 and 9 yards (about 4 to 8 meters) long. It is worn over a petticoat (a long underskirt) and a fitted blouse, which is called a choli in northern India and a cholo in Nepal. The loose end that hangs over the shoulder is the pallu, and it is often richly decorated.

The saree is worn in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and parts of Pakistan. It is the national attire for women in Bangladesh, which is why Zara's Jamdani makes perfect sense there. Sri Lanka has its own famous style, the osariya or Kandyan saree, which comes from the old Kandyan kingdom in the hill country. It has a frill at the waist and is worn with a full blouse that covers the midriff, and many women in Sri Lankan public life wear it.

There isn't one right way to drape a saree. The most common style today is the Nivi drape, with pleats tucked in at the front and the pallu over the shoulder. But there are many regional drapes. In the Deccan region of western and central India, for example, the Nauvari style passes the pleats between the legs and tucks them in at the back, which makes it easy to move in. Some Newar women in Nepal traditionally fold the saree to knee length and wrap a shawl across the chest instead of the pallu.

Ask for a draping lesson

If someone in your family wears sarees, ask them to show you their drape slowly, step by step. Many people learned their style from their own mother or grandmother, so the way they pleat and tuck is a little piece of family history.

docs.title: The dhoti
docs.text: The Dhoti (धोती, DHOH-tee) is a man's unstitched lower garment, a rectangle of cloth about 4 yards (3.7 meters) long that is wrapped around the waist and then passed between the legs and tucked in, so it looks a bit like loose trousers. It is often white or cream cotton, and silk dhotis are worn for weddings and religious occasions. It has local names too. In parts of South India, the formal style is called panchakacham. The dhoti is common in India and in Nepal, and it is the garment Gandhi made famous worldwide in the 1920s.

docs.title: The lungi
docs.text:
The Lungi (লুঙ্গি, LOONG-gee) is a length of cloth worn by men around the waist like a skirt, without passing between the legs. It is usually cotton, often in checks or stripes, and it is loved for staying cool in hot, humid weather. In Bangladesh, the lungi is the most commonly seen everyday clothing for men, usually sewn into a tube, though it is not worn for formal occasions. Elaborate silk lungis are often given to a Bangladeshi groom as a wedding gift.

Wrapped garments like this have different names in different places. In Kerala, a white or cream wrap with a decorative border is called a mundu. In Sri Lanka, it is a sarama, which is what Dilan wore to culture day. Across the Bay of Bengal in Myanmar, it is a longyi. They are cousins, not copies.

docs.title: 12.7 Stitched Garments: Kurta, Shalwar Kameez and Dupatta
docs.text: Other South Asian clothes are cut and sewn. Many of these styles came to South Asia from Central Asia and Persia over centuries, then took on local forms.

docs.title: The kurta
docs.text:
The Kurta (कुरता, KOOR-tah) is a loose tunic, traditionally collarless, with straight sleeves and side seams left open at the bottom. It can be short or long, plain or embroidered, cotton for every day or silk for festivals. Both men and women wear kurtas, over loose trousers, fitted trousers or, increasingly, jeans. Lucknow in India is famous for chikankari, a delicate embroidery traditionally done in white thread on light cotton or muslin, often seen on kurtas.

Two close relatives show how widely the idea spread. In Nepal, men's national dress is the daura-suruwal: the daura is a kurta-like shirt that closes with ties, and the suruwal is a pair of trousers that is loose at the hips and narrow at the ankles. It is often worn with a patterned cloth cap, the Dhaka topi, the cap Nima brought to culture day. Under King Mahendra, who ruled from 1955 to 1972, men were required to wear the Dhaka topi in official photos for passports and documents. In Afghanistan, many men wear the perahan tunban, a long, loose shirt over very full trousers. The style from Kandahar is known for fine geometric embroidery on the chest.

docs.title: The shalwar kameez
docs.text:
The Shalwar Kameez (Urdu شلوار قمیض, SHUL-war ka-MEEZ) is a two-piece outfit of loose trousers and a long tunic, worn by both men and women. The shalwar is wide at the waist, held up by a drawstring, and narrows to the ankle. The kameez is a long shirt with slits up both sides, which makes it easy to walk, sit and move in.

The shalwar kameez spread across northern South Asia over many centuries, especially in the Punjab region. Today it is Pakistan's national dress, and it is worn every day by millions of men and women there. It is also very common in India, especially in Punjab, where many people call the women's version a "Punjabi suit," and in Bangladesh and Afghanistan. So Ben was half right: Ayesha's outfit is Pakistani national dress, and Simran's matching outfit is just as much a part of her family's Punjabi Sikh tradition in India.

docs.title: The dupatta
docs.text:
The Dupatta (Hindi दुपट्टा, Urdu دوپٹہ, doo-PUT-tah) is a long scarf or shawl, usually worn by women with a shalwar kameez or with a long skirt and blouse. Its name roughly means "a doubled strip of cloth." A dupatta can be draped over one or both shoulders, wrapped across the chest, or worn over the head, for example in a place of worship or in front of elders. Families and communities have different customs about when and how to wear it.

Dupattas are often where the most beautiful handwork goes. In Punjab, on both sides of the India-Pakistan border, women have long made phulkari, which means "flower work," a bright darned embroidery in silk thread on coarse cotton. Simran's culture-day scarf is a phulkari dupatta.

Garment Draped or stitched Mainly worn by Countries where you'll often see it Saree Draped Women India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, parts of Pakistan Dhoti Draped Men India, Nepal Lungi (and mundu, sarama) Draped Men Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka Kurta Stitched Men and women India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, the diaspora Shalwar kameez Stitched Men and women Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Afghanistan Dupatta Draped over stitched clothes Mostly women Pakistan, India, Bangladesh

docs.title: 12.8 National Dress: Bhutan and Its Neighbors
docs.text: Some countries in South Asia have an official or widely accepted national dress. The clearest example is Bhutan.

docs.title: Gho and kira
docs.text:
Gho and Kira are the national dress of Bhutan: the gho (བགོ, GOH) for men and the kira (KEE-rah) for women.

  • The gho is a heavy, knee-length robe that is folded and tied at the waist with a woven belt called a kera. The fold creates a large pouch above the belt that people use like a pocket. Under it, men wear a white jacket called a tego, whose long white cuffs are folded back over the gho's sleeves.
  • The kira is an ankle-length dress made from one large rectangle of woven cloth. It is wrapped around the body, pinned at both shoulders with brooches called koma, and belted at the waist. Women wear a long-sleeved blouse called a wonju underneath and often a short jacket called a toego on top.

Everyday gho and kira are usually cotton or wool in simple checks and stripes. For festivals, many people wear richly patterned silk kira woven by hand. Weaving, called thagzo, is one of Bhutan's traditional arts, and the Royal Textile Academy of Bhutan, founded in 2005 in Thimphu, runs a weaving school and a textile museum to keep it alive.

Bhutan's national dress is connected to the driglam namzha, Bhutan's official code of etiquette and dress. Its roots go back to the 17th century, when Ngawang Namgyal, the first Zhabdrung, worked to unify Bhutan and give it a distinct identity.

In 1989, the government made the dress code mandatory in public during business hours. Today men who work in government offices or schools are required to wear the gho, and both gho and kira are worn for formal occasions. When visiting a dzong (a fortress-monastery) or meeting officials, men add a ceremonial scarf called a kabney. Ordinary citizens wear a white one, while other colors are reserved for officials and monks. Women wear a narrow embroidered cloth called a rachu over the shoulder.

docs.title: Other national dress in the region
docs.text:
Country Often-named national dress Notes Bhutan Gho (men), kira (women) Required in government offices and schools and for formal occasions Nepal Daura-suruwal with Dhaka topi (men); saree with cholo blouse (women) Many communities in Nepal also have their own dress Pakistan Shalwar kameez (men and women) Worn every day across the country Bangladesh Saree (women) Jamdani is the best-known weave Sri Lanka Osariya, the Kandyan saree (women) Widely treated as national dress for women Afghanistan Perahan tunban (men) Regional styles, such as Kandahari embroidery

"National dress" is always a simplification. Each of these countries has many communities with their own clothing, and a single official outfit can leave some of them out, as the Whose Story? box showed.

docs.title: 12.9 Head, Forehead and Wrist: Turbans, Bindis and Bangles
docs.text: Some of the most noticeable things people wear are small, and they often carry the deepest meanings.

docs.title: The turban and the dastar
docs.text:
A turban is a long cloth wound around the head. Turbans are worn in many parts of the world and by people of many faiths. In South Asia, you can see turbans on Sikh men and some Sikh women, on many Pashtun men in Afghanistan and Pakistan, on village elders in Rajasthan, where it's often called a pagri (पगड़ी), on some Hindu monks, and on some Muslim religious scholars. Its style, color and way of tying can show region, occasion or community.

The Turban (Dastar) is, for Sikhs, an article of faith. The dastar (ਦਸਤਾਰ, dus-TAAR) is the Sikh turban, and the word comes from Persian through Punjabi. In Sikh tradition, the Gurus adopted the turban, which in South Asia was once worn mainly by royalty, as a way of declaring the sovereignty and equality of all people. Sikhs who have formally committed to the faith keep their hair uncut (kesh), one of the five articles of faith, and the dastar covers it. According to the Sikh Coalition, a US Sikh civil rights group, both men and women may wear a turban, and wearing one is a public commitment to values such as service, compassion and honesty. Tying a dastar neatly every day, turn by turn, is a skill many Sikh children learn from a parent.

A good question to ask

If you're curious about a friend's turban, it's fine to ask a respectful question like "What does your dastar mean to you?" Just never touch someone's turban or ask them to take it off. For many Sikhs it's as personal and sacred as anything they own.

docs.title: The bindi
docs.text:
The Bindi (बिंदी, BIN-dee) is a dot, traditionally red or maroon, worn in the center of the forehead, often between the eyebrows. The word comes from the Sanskrit bindu, meaning "point" or "drop." Traditional bindis are made with powders such as kumkum. Today many people wear small stick-on bindis in every color and shape.

The bindi is worn mainly by Hindu women, and also by some Jains and Buddhists, in India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and in Hindu communities in Pakistan and Bhutan. In Hindu tradition, many people link the spot between the eyebrows with spiritual focus. For some women, a red bindi has also been a sign of being married, though customs vary a lot by region and family, and many unmarried girls wear decorative bindis too. In Nepal, a related forehead mark, the tika, is placed on people's foreheads by elders as a blessing during festivals such as Dashain.

docs.title: Bangles
docs.text:
Bangles are rigid bracelets, usually worn in sets, made from glass, metal, shell, lac, plastic or other materials. They have a very long history in the region. The famous "Dancing Girl," a small bronze figure from Mohenjo-daro in what is now Pakistan, made sometime between about 2300 and 1750 BCE, wears a stack of bangles on her left arm. Hindi speakers call a bangle a चूड़ी (CHOO-ree), and Urdu speakers call it a چوڑی, the same word in a different script.

Bangles can carry very specific meanings:

  • Weddings: many brides across South Asia wear sets of glass or gold bangles, and the sound of bangles is part of wedding celebrations. Many Punjabi Hindu and Sikh brides wear a chooda, a set of red and white bangles, on their wedding day.
  • Marriage in Bengal: many married Bengali Hindu women, in both Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal, wear a white conch-shell bangle called a shankha (শাঁখা, SHAN-kha) together with a red bangle called a pola. These are traditionally given to the bride at her wedding.
  • Faith: many Sikhs wear a kara, a single plain steel or iron bangle, which is one of the five articles of faith in Sikh tradition. It is worn by men and women.
  • Everyday style: gold bangles are often given to babies and little girls, and plenty of people wear bangles just because they like them.

The town of Firozabad in Uttar Pradesh, India, is famous as a center of glass bangle making.

docs.title: 12.10 The Textile Map
docs.text: Now that you know the fibers, techniques and garments, it's time to put them on the map. Look back at how many of these traditions are tied to a single town or region: Jamdani to Dhaka, ajrak to Sindh, Banarasi to Varanasi, Kanjivaram to Kanchipuram, kira weaving to Bhutan. That's the main idea of the sim below.

docs.title: Diagram: Textile Map
docs.text:
Open the Textile Map fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Textile Map

sim-id: ch12-textile-map Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Remember / Understand Bloom Verb: identify, explain Learning Objective: The learner will connect ten South Asian garments and textiles to the regions where they are made and to their fiber and technique.

Canvas: responsive width; 740 px drawing area plus 100 px control area.

Controls: textile menu, Previous and Next buttons, Quiz me / Show answer button, "Show place names" checkbox; click or tap any dot.

Behavior: A schematic tile map shows the eight countries (no borders) with ten labeled dots. Selecting a dot shows the textile's place, fiber, technique and the garment it is often used for, a simple drawing of that garment in the textile's colors, and a procedurally drawn pattern swatch (for example scattered woven flowers for Jamdani, feathery diamonds for ikat, buta shapes for pashmina, indigo and crimson stars for ajrak). In quiz mode the name is hidden and the learner clicks the dot they think matches the swatch. The caption "Schematic map, not to scale. Not an official depiction of borders." is drawn inside the drawing area.

Start by clicking every dot and reading the panel. For each one, notice three things: the fiber (cotton, silk or wool), whether the pattern is woven in, dyed into the thread first, or printed on, and which garment it usually becomes. Then press Quiz me. The sim will show you only a pattern swatch and a garment, and you have to find the right dot.

As you play, look for the pattern behind the details. The cotton traditions cluster in hot, humid places like the Bengal delta and Sindh. The pashmina dots sit high in the mountains, where goats need warm undercoats. The silk dots are in places with long weaving traditions and wealthy patrons, such as the old temple town of Kanchipuram and the holy city of Varanasi. The map is simplified, but the link between land, fiber and cloth is real.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the clothes they wore growing up, the clothes they wear for special days, and any garment in the family that has a story. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Ask if they have one special garment, like a wedding saree, a shawl, a turban or a set of bangles, that they would be willing to show you. Ask permission before you take a photo of it.

Questions to ask

  1. What did you wear on an ordinary school day when you were my age? What did you wear for festivals or weddings?
  2. Is there one piece of clothing in our family that has a story? Who made it, wore it or gave it?
  3. How is a saree, turban, dupatta, gho or other garment tied or worn in our family? Who taught you?
  4. Where did your family buy cloth or clothes? Did a tailor make them, or did anyone weave, embroider or block-print at home?
  5. How have the clothes you wear changed since you were young, or since you moved to a new country?
  6. Is there a garment, a weave or a way of dressing you hope I'll keep wearing or pass on?

Listen for: names of weaves or fibers (Jamdani, Ikat, Pashmina, silk, Khadi, Cotton in South Asia), which garments are draped and which are stitched (Saree, Dhoti, Lungi, Kurta, Shalwar Kameez, Dupatta), and the meaning of anything worn for faith or marriage, such as a Turban (Dastar), a Bindi or Bangles.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare your elder's description of everyday clothes with a friend's interview. Did one family wear mostly draped clothes and the other mostly stitched ones? Did either garment cross a border, like a saree in Bangladesh or a shalwar kameez in India? Write two sentences about what surprised you.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: The saree is only Indian. Reality: The saree is worn in India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka, and in parts of Pakistan. It is the national attire for women in Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka has its own Kandyan style, the osariya.

Myth: The shalwar kameez is only Pakistani. Reality: It is Pakistan's national dress, but it is also widely worn in India (especially Punjab), Bangladesh and Afghanistan, by people of many faiths.

Myth: A turban means a person belongs to one particular religion. Reality: Turbans are worn by Sikhs, by many Pashtun men, by elders in Rajasthan, by some Hindu monks and by some Muslim scholars, among others. For Sikhs, the dastar has a specific religious meaning, but the turban itself belongs to many traditions.

Myth: Khadi is just another word for cotton. Reality: Khadi means cloth that is both hand-spun and hand-woven. It can be cotton, silk or wool, and it became a symbol of self-reliance in India's freedom movement.

Myth: "Paisley" is a Scottish design. Reality: The shape began as the buta motif on Kashmir shawls. Factories in Paisley, Scotland, copied it in the 1800s, and the town's name stuck to the pattern.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. Where were the oldest known cotton fibers found, and about how old are they?

At Mehrgarh, an early village in Balochistan, Pakistan. They were preserved inside copper beads buried roughly 7,500 to 8,000 years ago, in the first half of the sixth millennium BCE.

2. What is the difference between Jamdani and ikat?

In Jamdani, the pattern is woven in on the loom, with extra weft threads added motif by motif. In ikat, the threads are tied and dyed in a pattern before weaving, which gives the shapes blurred edges.

3. Name one draped garment and one stitched garment, and say who usually wears each.

Draped: the saree (women), the dhoti or lungi (men). Stitched: the kurta (men and women) or the shalwar kameez (men and women).

4. What are the gho and kira, and when are they required?

They are Bhutan's national dress: the gho is a knee-length belted robe for men, and the kira is an ankle-length wrapped dress for women. Under Bhutan's dress code, men in government offices and schools must wear the gho, and both are worn for formal occasions.

5. Why did Gandhi promote khadi?

He wanted Indians to stop buying British machine-made cloth, which kept India dependent, and to spin and weave their own. Khadi became a symbol of self-reliance and the freedom movement.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the four kinds of silk that India's government recognizes, and name the one that is made almost entirely in Assam.

    Answer

    Mulberry, tasar, eri and muga. Muga, a natural golden silk, is made almost entirely in Assam.

  2. In what year did UNESCO recognize Jamdani weaving, and in which country is it centered?

    Answer
    1. It is centered around Dhaka, Bangladesh.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why ikat patterns have blurry, feathered edges.

    Answer

    The pattern is tied and dyed into the threads before weaving. When the threads are stretched on the loom and woven, they never line up perfectly, so the edges of each shape come out slightly soft.

  2. Explain in your own words why the "paisley" pattern is named after a Scottish town.

    Answer

    The teardrop buta motif came from Kashmir shawls. When factories in Paisley, Scotland, made cheaper copies in the 1800s, English speakers started calling any shawl with that motif a Paisley shawl, and the name stuck to the shape.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Textile Map. Find every dot whose main fiber is silk. What do the places have in common, and how are they different? Hint: look at where each dot sits and what garment each makes.

  2. A friend shows you a white conch-shell bangle and a red bangle her mother wears every day. Using the chapter, explain what they might mean and which region the custom comes from. Hint: look at Section 12.9.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare draped garments (saree, dhoti, lungi) with stitched garments (kurta, shalwar kameez). Give two practical reasons a family might choose one over the other. Hint: think about weather, weaving, fit and occasion.

  2. Ben scored two out of five at culture day. Analyze why guessing someone's country from their clothes is so hard in South Asia, using at least three garments from the chapter as evidence. Hint: compare when the countries were formed with how old the clothes are.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Bhutan requires the gho and kira in certain settings to protect its national identity. Some Bhutanese in the south resented the rule. Evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of a required national dress. Hint: the Whose Story? box gives two viewpoints.

  2. A clothing company sells a cheap machine-printed scarf labeled "pashmina." Evaluate whether that label is fair, using what you learned about pashmina and Geographical Indication tags. Hint: what makes pashmina pashmina?

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a label card for one garment or textile from your own family or from this chapter, as if it were in a museum. Include its name in English and its original script (if you can verify it), the fiber, the technique, where it comes from and one sentence of family or community meaning. Hint: museum labels are short, so choose your details carefully.

  2. Plan a culture day for your own club where people bring clothes from home. Write a one-paragraph guide that helps guests ask good questions instead of guessing countries. Hint: use the "Clothes Speak a Language" list in Section 12.2.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• South Asia has spun and woven cotton for more than 7,000 years. The oldest known cotton fibers come from Mehrgarh in Pakistan, and Bengal's muslin was once famous worldwide.
  • Silk (mulberry, tasar, eri and muga) and pashmina wool from Himalayan goats are the region's other great fibers, behind Banarasi, Kanjivaram and Rajshahi silks and Kashmir and Nepali shawls.
  • Patterns can be woven in (Jamdani, recognized by UNESCO in 2013), dyed into the thread first (ikat) or printed on (ajrak from Sindh).
  • Khadi, hand-spun and hand-woven cloth, became a symbol of self-reliance in India's freedom movement.
  • Draped garments (saree, dhoti, lungi) and stitched ones (kurta, shalwar kameez, dupatta) cross national borders. Bhutan's gho and kira are a clear example of official national dress.
  • Turbans, bindis and bangles can carry religious or marriage meanings, like the Sikh dastar and kara or the Bengali shankha, but meanings vary by family, region and faith.

You can read the cloth now!

You can now look at a saree, a kurta or a gho and ask where its thread came from and how its pattern was made. Next, in Chapter 13, we meet the people who wear these clothes at life's biggest moments: families, names and weddings.

docs.title: Quiz: Clothing and Textiles
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 12. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Where were the oldest known cotton fibers in the world found?

  1. In a tomb near Varanasi, India
  2. Inside copper beads at Mehrgarh, Pakistan
  3. In a weaver's workshop near Dhaka, Bangladesh
  4. In a monastery in Bhutan
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Cotton fibers preserved inside copper beads in a burial at Mehrgarh, in Balochistan, Pakistan, date to the first half of the sixth millennium BCE, roughly 7,500 to 8,000 years ago. Dhaka became famous for fine cotton muslin much later, so it is a tempting but wrong choice.

Concept Tested: Cotton in South Asia Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which of these best defines khadi?

  1. Any cloth made of cotton
  2. A silk saree woven in Varanasi
  3. Cloth printed with wooden blocks in Sindh
  4. Cloth that is both hand-spun and hand-woven
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Khadi is hand-spun and hand-woven cloth, and it can be cotton, silk or wool. Option A is a common misconception: khadi is defined by how it is made, not by the fiber.

Concept Tested: Khadi Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
What are the gho and kira?

  1. The national dress of Bhutan for men and women
  2. Two styles of saree draping from Nepal
  3. Turbans worn by Pashtun men in Afghanistan
  4. Silk weaves from Assam
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The gho is the knee-length belted robe worn by men in Bhutan, and the kira is the ankle-length wrapped dress worn by women. Nepal's national dress for men is the daura-suruwal, not the gho.

Concept Tested: Gho and Kira Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why do ikat patterns usually have soft, feathery edges?

  1. The pattern is painted on with a brush after weaving.
  2. The cloth is washed many times to fade the colors.
  3. The threads are tie-dyed before weaving and never line up perfectly on the loom.
  4. Weavers add extra weft threads one motif at a time.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In ikat, bundles of thread are tied and dyed in a pattern before they are woven, and small shifts on the loom blur the edges. Option D describes Jamdani, where the pattern is woven in with extra weft threads.

Concept Tested: Ikat Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why did Gandhi ask Indians to spin and wear khadi?

  1. Because khadi was cheaper than any other cloth
  2. To make India less dependent on British machine-made cloth and show self-reliance
  3. Because British law banned Indians from wearing silk
  4. To start a new fashion trend for weddings
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Under colonial rule, Indian cotton was often shipped to British mills and sold back as cloth. Gandhi's swadeshi movement urged people to boycott foreign cloth and spin their own. Option A is wrong: hand-spun yarn was often more expensive than mill yarn.

Concept Tested: Khadi Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
What makes the saree and the dhoti "draped" garments rather than "stitched" garments?

  1. They are long unstitched lengths of cloth wrapped and tucked around the body.
  2. They are always made of silk.
  3. They are only worn at weddings.
  4. They are sewn into a tube before being worn.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Both are rectangles of cloth that are wrapped, pleated and tucked rather than cut and sewn. Option D describes the Bangladeshi lungi, which is often sewn into a tube, and even that is wrapped rather than tailored.

Concept Tested: Saree Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
At a community event, you see a man wearing a turban. Based on the chapter, what is the best conclusion?

  1. He must be Sikh.
  2. He must be Muslim.
  3. He must be from Rajasthan.
  4. You can't tell his religion or region from the turban alone; it's best to ask respectfully if you want to know.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Turbans are worn by Sikhs, many Pashtun men, elders in Rajasthan, some Hindu monks and some Muslim scholars, among others. Option A is the most common mistake: the Sikh dastar has a specific meaning, but not every turban is a dastar.

Concept Tested: Turban (Dastar) Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Your friend's mother, who is from Bangladesh, wears a white conch-shell bangle and a red bangle every day. What do they most likely signify?

  1. She has completed a pilgrimage.
  2. She is a member of a weavers' guild.
  3. She is a married Bengali Hindu woman wearing shankha and pola.
  4. She is a Sikh wearing a kara.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Many married Bengali Hindu women in Bangladesh and West Bengal wear the white shankha and the red pola, traditionally given at the wedding. Option D is wrong because the Sikh kara is a single plain steel or iron bangle.

Concept Tested: Bangles Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
The shalwar kameez is Pakistan's national dress, yet Simran's family from Ludhiana, India, wears it too. What does this best show?

  1. Many South Asian garments are older than today's borders and are shared across countries.
  2. Simran's family must have moved from Pakistan recently.
  3. The shalwar kameez was invented in India and later copied by Pakistan.
  4. National dress laws in Pakistan also apply in India.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The shalwar kameez spread across the Punjab region over centuries, long before the 1947 border, so it is worn on both sides. Option C wrongly turns a shared tradition into a contest over who invented it.

Concept Tested: Shalwar Kameez Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Jamdani, ajrak and Banarasi brocade are all patterned cloth. Which comparison is correct?

  1. All three are printed with wooden blocks.
  2. Jamdani and Banarasi patterns are woven in on the loom, while ajrak is block-printed.
  3. Jamdani is silk, ajrak is wool and Banarasi is cotton.
  4. All three are tie-dyed before weaving.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Jamdani motifs are woven in with extra weft threads, Banarasi brocade weaves in zari, and ajrak is printed with carved blocks and natural dyes. Option D describes ikat, and none of these three is ikat.

Concept Tested: Jamdani Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Clothing and Textiles
docs.text:
1. Traditional art of Jamdani weaving - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - The official 2013 listing for Jamdani, Bangladesh's hand-woven cotton. It explains the discontinuous weft technique, how weavers around Dhaka pass the skill from parent to child, and why Bengali women treat the Jamdani saree as a symbol of identity.

  2. First Evidence of Cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh, Pakistan - Christophe Moulherat, Margareta Tengberg, Jérôme-F. Haquet and Benoît Mille, Journal of Archaeological Science 29 (2002) - The original study of the mineralized cotton threads in a copper bead from a Neolithic burial at Mehrgarh, dated to the sixth millennium BCE.

  3. Sericulture (Statistical Year Book, Chapter 11) - Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Government of India - A two-page government summary of India's silk industry that defines mulberry, tasar, eri and muga silk and explains which states produce each.

  4. Khadi and Village Industries Commission - Government of India - The official site of the body that has supported khadi since 1957. It describes khadi as hand-spun, hand-woven cloth tied to the swadeshi spirit of the freedom struggle, and explains the Khadi mark.

  5. Sikh Identity - The Sikh Coalition - A Sikh civil rights organization explains the meaning of the dastar (turban) and uncut hair, and notes that both men and women may wear a turban. Useful before asking a friend about their turban.

  6. Royal Textile Academy of Bhutan - Royal Textile Academy of Bhutan - The home page of the academy founded in 2005 in Thimphu to preserve Bhutanese weaving, with its weaving school, textile museum and conservation center.

  7. Wool Creatives Nepal: Making All the Right Connections - Enhanced Integrated Framework (a multilateral trade program) - A 2018 story about Nepal's chyangra goats and how the Chyangra Pashmina brand was built to mark genuine Nepali pashmina.

  8. Driglam namzha - Wikipedia - Background on Bhutan's code of etiquette and dress, its 17th-century roots, the 1989 rule making it mandatory, and the debate it caused among Lhotshampa in the south. Follow its citations for Bhutanese sources.

  9. Ajrak - Wikipedia - An overview of Sindh's block-printed cloth: carved wooden blocks, resist dyeing and natural dyes led by indigo, the names of its patterns, and its role in Sindhi identity.

  10. Dhaka muslin - Wikipedia - The history of Bengal's "woven air," from Mughal courts to its collapse under colonial rule and recent revival efforts in Bangladesh.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events
Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events
Summary
docs.text: Family sits at the center of social life in much of South Asia, and you can hear that in the words people use. Many South Asian languages have separate words for your father's brother and your mother's brother, for your father's mother and your mother's mother. This chapter explains those kinship words, joint families and respect for elders, then looks at how names are chosen and why not everyone has a surname. It explains caste honestly, including the laws against caste discrimination, and walks through the rituals that mark birth, growing up, marriage and death in Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Buddhist and other families, ending with how gender roles are changing.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Joint Family
  2. Kinship Terms
  3. Respect for Elders
  4. Naming Traditions
  5. Surnames
  6. Varna and Jati
  7. Caste System
  8. Caste Discrimination Laws
  9. Life-Cycle Rituals
  10. Coming-of-Age Rites
  11. Weddings
  12. Arranged Marriage
  13. Mehndi Night and Sangeet
  14. Nikah
  15. Anand Karaj
  16. Funeral Customs
  17. Gender Roles and Change

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia, for the basics of Hinduism, Islam, Sikhism, Buddhism and other faiths.
  • Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts, for the languages and scripts you'll see in the kinship words.
  • It helps to have read Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year, since some family rituals happen at festivals.

Who's Who at the Party?

Hi, I'm Mora! If you've ever stood at a family wedding or a dinner and had no idea what to call the aunt who just pinched your cheek, this chapter is for you. Knowing the right word for each relative, and the story behind your own name, is one of the easiest ways to feel at home in your family. And if your friends are South Asian, it will help you understand why their family events are so big.

docs.title: 13.1 Four Uncles, One English Word
docs.text:
It's a Saturday evening in June, and Zara Hossain's cousin is getting married in a rented hall in St. Paul. Ben Lindqvist is the only guest in a hockey-team blazer, and Zara is steering him through the crowd.

"Ben, this is my Chacha," Zara says, and a smiling man shakes Ben's hand. Five minutes later: "This is my Mama." Another man, another handshake. Then a woman in a green saree hugs Zara and calls her by a name Ben has never heard. "That's my Khala," Zara explains. "And over there by the cake, that's my Fufu." Ben leans in. "Okay, wait. Your mama is a man? And those are all your uncles and aunts? In English I'd just say uncle, uncle, aunt, aunt."

Zara laughs, but then she thinks about it. Chacha is her father's brother. Mama is her mother's brother. Khala is her mother's sister. Fufu is her father's sister. Her Nanu, her mother's mother, is sitting at the head table, and Zara would never mix that word up with Dadi, her father's mother. Ben wants to know why one language needs four words where English uses two. And then he asks the bigger question: what else about a South Asian family works differently from his own?

docs.title: 13.2 One Word or Ten? Kinship Terms
docs.text:
Ben's family already gives him a head start. His relatives are from Sweden and Norway, and in Swedish you don't say "uncle" either. Your father's brother is your farbror ("father-brother") and your mother's brother is your morbror ("mother-brother"). Your father's mother is farmor and your mother's mother is mormor. Swedish speakers can tell, from one word, which side of the family someone is on. Many South Asian languages work the same way, and often go further.

Kinship Terms are the words a language uses for relatives: mother, uncle, cousin, grandmother and so on. Every language has them, but languages slice the family tree differently. English has one word, "uncle," for at least four different people: your father's older brother, your father's younger brother, your mother's brother, and the husbands of your aunts. Many South Asian languages give most of those people their own word.

This table compares a few of them, using Hindi-Urdu, the language family many people in northern India and Pakistan speak (Hindi is usually written in Devanagari script and Urdu in Nastaliq script; see Chapter 6).

Relative English Hindi-Urdu (many families) Father's older brother uncle tau (Hindi) or taya (Urdu) Father's younger brother uncle chacha Father's sister aunt bua (Hindi) or phuphi (Urdu) Mother's brother uncle mama (Urdu also mamun) Mother's sister aunt mausi (Hindi) or khala (Urdu) Father's mother grandmother dadi Mother's mother grandmother nani

Two patterns jump out. First, side matters: the father's side and the mother's side get different words. Second, age matters: in many languages your father's older brother and younger brother are not the same kind of uncle.

Zara's family speaks Bangla, and the words she used at the wedding come straight from that table. In Bangla her mother's mother is নানী (NAA-nee), and Zara uses the affectionate form, নানু (NAA-noo), "Nanu." Her mother's sister is খালা (KHAA-laa), "khala," and her father's sister is ফুফু (FOO-foo), "phuphu" or "fufu."

docs.title: Why separate words for each side?
docs.text:
Part of the answer is about who you live with and who you inherit from. Many South Asian families have traditionally been patrilineal: the family name and property passed mainly through the father's line. Your father's brothers might live in your house, while your mother's brothers live in her birth family's home, often far away. They play different roles in your life, so they get different words.

Languages of South India and Sri Lanka show a second pattern. In Tamil and Sinhala, your father's older brother is literally your "big father" (Tamil பெரியப்பா, peh-ree-YAP-paa; Sinhala ලොකු තාත්තා, LO-ku TAAT-taa), and your mother's older sister is your "big mother." Your father's sister and your mother's brother, though, get completely separate words.

Anthropologists call this a Dravidian kinship system: relatives linked through a same-sex pair of siblings (your father's brother, your mother's sister) are treated almost like extra parents, while relatives linked through an opposite-sex pair (your father's sister, your mother's brother) belong to a different category. In this system, the children of your father's sister or your mother's brother were traditionally seen as possible marriage partners in some communities, which is one reason those relatives have their own terms.

Not every language marks every difference. Tamil and Sinhala use the same word for both grandmothers (Tamil பாட்டி, PAAT-tee; Sinhala ආච්චි, AACH-chee), while Hindi-Urdu, Punjabi and Bangla split them by side (dadi and nani in Hindi-Urdu and Punjabi; many Hindu Bangla speakers say thakuma and didima instead).

Same language, different words

Kinship words change with region and community, even inside one language. Many Muslim Bangla speakers in Bangladesh say chacha and khala, while many Hindu Bangla speakers in West Bengal say kaka and mashi for the same relatives. Ask your family which words they use before assuming the dictionary is right.

docs.title: Words for people who aren't related
docs.text: Kinship words also travel outside the family. Kids are often taught to call a parent's friend "Uncle" or "Auntie," or "khala" or "chacha ji," which turns the whole community into a kind of extended family.

docs.title: 13.3 The Joint Family and Respect for Elders
docs.text:
Imagine living with your parents, your father's parents, and your father's brother with his wife and kids. Meals are cooked for twelve, and your cousins are more like siblings. That is a joint family.

A Joint Family is a household where several generations and branches of one family live together and often share a kitchen, money and property. In the traditional form found in many parts of South Asia, the joint family is built around brothers: married sons stay in their parents' home with their wives and children, while daughters move to their husbands' families when they marry. In India, the law even recognizes a "Hindu undivided family" as a unit for income tax.

Living with extended family is common across the region. A 2019 Pew Research Center study of household types found that extended-family households were the most common household type in the world, covering 38% of people. It also found that the average person in Afghanistan lived in a household of about 9.8 people, and in Pakistan about 8.5, far above the Asia-Pacific average of 5.0 (counting from each individual's point of view).

Not every South Asian family is a joint family. Many city families are nuclear families (parents and children only), and many mix the two, like a diaspora family that brings a grandparent to live with them, as Zara's family did with Nanu.

docs.title: Respect for Elders
