docs.text:
Respect for Elders is the value that older relatives and community members deserve special honor, care and obedience, and that families should look after them as they age. You can see it in small daily habits across South Asia:

  • Speech. In Hindi-Urdu, you address an elder with the polite pronoun आप (aap), not the more casual तुम (tum). Many families add "ji" to a name or title as a mark of respect, like "Chacha ji." In many families children never call an older sibling or relative by their first name alone. They use a kinship word or "bhai" (brother) or "apa," "didi" or "baji" (sister), depending on the language.
  • Greetings. In many Hindu and Sikh families, younger people bend to touch an elder's feet as a greeting of respect, and the elder gives a blessing. In many Muslim families, younger people greet elders first with "salaam" and may be expected to stand when an elder enters.
  • Care. In many families, grown children are expected to care for aging parents at home rather than in a care facility.

Respect for elders doesn't mean elders always get their way, and many teens feel a push and pull between honoring grandparents and making their own choices.

docs.title: 13.4 What's in a Name?
docs.text:
Ben's name is simple: a first name, Ben, and a family name, Lindqvist, which his father and his grandfather also had. Many people assume every name in the world works like that. In South Asia, it often doesn't.

Naming Traditions are the customs a family follows to choose a child's name: who chooses, when, and what the name should mean or sound like. Here are some you might meet:

  • Sikh families. In Sikh tradition, a baby's name is often chosen in a Naam Karan ceremony at a gurdwara. The Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, is opened at random, and the first letter of the first hymn on that page becomes the first letter of the child's name. Most Sikh first names can be used for boys or girls. Then comes a shared name: Singh for men and Kaur for women. Sikh tradition links these names to Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, and one aim of giving everyone the same name was to reduce caste prejudice. That's why Simran, the club's treasurer, is Simran Kaur Gill: Kaur is her Sikh name and Gill is her family name.
  • Muslim families. In many Muslim families, a baby is named in the first week, often on the seventh day, sometimes with an aqiqah, a celebration in which an animal is sacrificed and meat is shared with family and the poor. Many names are Arabic or Persian in origin and are chosen for their meaning or to honor a prophet or a relative.
  • Hindu families. The Hindu naming ceremony, the namakarana, is one of the traditional samskaras (Section 13.6). Some families ask a priest or consult astrology for a lucky first sound for the name.
  • Bengali families, both Hindu and Muslim, often give a child two names: a "good name," ভালো নাম (BHAA-lo naam, "bhalo nam"), used at school and on documents, and a "call name," ডাক নাম (DAAK naam, "dak nam"), a nickname used at home. Zara has one too, but she only lets her family use it.
  • Sherpa families in Nepal, like Nima's, traditionally name a child after the day of the week the baby was born. Nima (also spelled Nyima, "sun") is the name for Sunday, Dawa for Monday, Mingma for Tuesday, Lhakpa for Wednesday, Phurba for Thursday, Pasang for Friday and Pemba for Saturday. That's why so many Sherpas share the same few names.
  • Bhutanese families usually do not have family names at all. A Buddhist lama is often asked to choose the baby's name in the first weeks of life, and most people have two given names, such as Sonam or Tshering, Dorji or Karma, that don't show family or gender.

docs.title: Surnames
docs.text:
A Surname is a family name that is passed down from one generation to the next. In much of South Asia surnames exist, but they don't always work the way they do in Minnesota.

  • Many people have none. Traditionally, many Afghans used only a single given name, and so do many Bhutanese today. In Afghanistan, people were told apart by their tribe, birthplace or profession.
  • Some use the father's name. In many Tamil families in India and Sri Lanka, there is no inherited family name. Instead, a person's father's given name, often written as an initial, comes before their own name. So R. Karthik would be Karthik, son of someone whose name starts with R. His children would then use K as their initial. Some Tamils who move abroad turn the father's name into a last name so forms make sense.
  • Some reflect history. In Sri Lanka, Portuguese rule in the 1500s and 1600s left behind surnames such as Perera and Fernando, which became some of the most common names in the country. Dilan Perera's family name carries that history.
  • Some point to caste or community. In many parts of India and Nepal, a family name can show a person's caste or community. This is one reason some people have dropped their family names, used a religious name like Singh or Kaur, or chosen a new surname.
  • Some change at marriage, and some don't. In many families a woman takes her husband's family name when she marries, but many women keep their own.

Getting a name right

If a South Asian classmate's name doesn't fit the "first name, last name" boxes on a form, it isn't a mistake. Ask them how they'd like their name written and said, and use it.

docs.title: 13.5 Caste: Varna, Jati, and the Law
docs.text: "Is caste still a thing?" Ben asks Ms. Okafor at a club meeting. She tells him it's a fair and serious question, and the honest answer is yes, in different ways, in many places.

docs.title: Varna and Jati
docs.text:
People often use "caste" to mean two different things, so it helps to separate them.

Varna and Jati are the two ideas behind what English speakers call caste. Varna (वर्ण, VAR-na) is a fourfold social classification described in old Brahmanical texts written in Sanskrit, such as the Manusmriti. Those texts list four varnas, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, and assign each one duties and occupations. Jati (जाति, JAA-tee, "birth" or "kind") is the group a person is born into. There are thousands of jatis across South Asia. A jati is usually local, often linked in the past to a traditional occupation, and in many communities people were expected to marry within it. In everyday life, jati is what matters most. Varna is the textbook framework that people later tried to fit the jatis into.

Communities that the varna texts left outside the four varnas were treated as "untouchable" and faced the harshest exclusion: they were kept out of temples, wells, schools and many jobs. Today many of these communities call themselves Dalit (दलित, DUH-lit), a word meaning "broken" or "crushed," which reformers began using in the 1800s and which Dalit activists have made a word of pride and protest.

Mahatma Gandhi used the term "Harijan" ("children of God") for these communities in the 1930s. That word is now a historical term: many Dalits reject it as patronizing, and B. R. Ambedkar, the Dalit leader who chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution, disliked it. Many tribal communities in India and Bangladesh call themselves Adivasi, a 20th-century word meaning "ancient inhabitants." They have their own histories and were largely outside the varna system.

docs.title: The caste system
docs.text:
The Caste System is the social system, built over many centuries, in which people are born into ranked groups that shape whom they marry, what work they are expected to do, and how others treat them. It is historical and continuing: its roots go back more than two thousand years, and it still affects people's lives today. Three points help you understand it fairly.

  1. It isn't only Hindu. A 2021 Pew Research Center survey of about 30,000 adults in India found that Indians of every major religion, including Muslims, Christians and Sikhs, identify with a caste category. Sikh teachings reject caste, and Islam and Christianity teach the equality of believers, yet caste distinctions still appear in many of those communities.
  2. It isn't only in India. Caste shapes society in Nepal too, and caste-based communities also exist in other parts of South Asia and in the diaspora.
  3. It still affects marriage most of all. In the same Pew survey, 64% of Indians said it was very important to stop women in their community from marrying outside their caste, and 62% said the same about men. Most said their close friends were mostly from their own caste. Only about one in five said there was a lot of discrimination against Scheduled Castes, the government's legal term for Dalit communities.

docs.title: Caste Discrimination Laws
docs.text:
Caste Discrimination Laws are laws that ban treating people unfairly because of their caste, and that protect communities who faced untouchability. The most important ones in South Asia are in India's Constitution, which came into effect on 26 January 1950:

  • Article 15 says the state shall not discriminate against any citizen only because of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
  • Article 17 abolished "untouchability" and forbids practicing it in any form. Enforcing any disability that comes from untouchability is a crime.

Parliament later passed laws to enforce these rules, including the Protection of Civil Rights Act (first passed in 1955 as the Untouchability (Offences) Act and renamed in 1976) and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act of 1989. India also reserves a share of seats in legislatures, government jobs and public universities for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other disadvantaged groups, a policy usually called reservations.

Nepal passed the Caste-Based Discrimination and Untouchability (Offence and Punishment) Act in 2011, which made caste discrimination a crime in private places such as homes, not just in public ones. Human rights groups still report that these laws are not always enforced in both countries.

The debate has reached the United States. In February 2023, Seattle became the first US city to add caste to its anti-discrimination laws. In September 2023, Fresno, California, did the same. That October, California's governor vetoed a bill that would have added caste to the state's civil rights law, saying existing protections against discrimination by ancestry already covered it. South Asian Americans were divided: some argued the laws protect people who face real discrimination, and others argued the laws single out South Asians and their faiths.

Whose Story?

People tell the story of caste very differently. Many Dalit writers and activists, following B. R. Ambedkar, describe caste as a system of oppression that religious texts helped justify and that must be ended completely. Many Hindus describe varna as a flexible idea about duty and talent that was later hardened into birth-based caste, and say that caste discrimination goes against their faith. Many Indian Muslims, Christians and Sikhs point out that their faiths reject caste, while researchers have documented caste divisions inside those same communities. In the United States, some South Asian groups see caste laws as civil rights protection, while others see them as unfairly targeting Hindus and Indians. Listening to all of these voices, and especially to people who have faced caste discrimination, is part of understanding the topic.

Handle with care

Never ask a classmate "what caste are you?" or guess someone's caste from their surname. It can be hurtful and is often discriminatory. If caste comes up, talk about the system and the laws, not about ranking any person or community.

docs.title: 13.6 Life-Cycle Rituals and Coming of Age
docs.text: Every family marks big moments in a life: a birth, a first step into adulthood, a wedding, a death. Life-Cycle Rituals are the ceremonies that mark these turning points. In South Asia they are shaped by faith, region and family, and they usually bring the whole extended family together.

docs.title: In Hindu tradition: the samskaras
docs.text:
In Hindu tradition, the life-cycle rituals are called samskaras (संस्कार, sun-SKAA-ruh, "making ready" or "refining"). Old texts list different numbers of them; a list of 16 became the best known, and the number and details vary by region and family. Some you'll hear about:

  • Namakarana, the naming ceremony.
  • Annaprashana ("first eating of rice"), when a baby eats solid food, often sweet rice pudding, for the first time, around six months old. In Nepal this is called pasni.
  • Mundan or chudakarana, a child's first haircut, when the head is shaved.
  • Upanayana, the sacred-thread ceremony (see Coming-of-Age Rites below).
  • Vivaha, marriage.
  • Antyeshti, the "last rite," the funeral.

docs.title: Muslim, Sikh, Buddhist and other traditions
docs.text:
Muslim families mark a birth with prayers, by naming the baby and, in many families, with the aqiqah around the seventh day.

Sikh families mark a birth with Naam Karan. Buddhist families in Sri Lanka, Bhutan and Nepal often invite monks to bless a new baby, and many Christian families in South Asia mark a child's place in the church with baptism.

docs.title: Coming-of-Age Rites
docs.text:
Coming-of-Age Rites are ceremonies that mark the move from childhood toward adulthood or full membership in a community. Some examples from the region:

  • Upanayana (उपनयन, oo-puh-NUH-yun, "initiation"). In this Hindu ceremony, traditionally for boys from certain communities, a child receives the sacred thread, worn over the left shoulder, and is accepted as a student by a teacher. In Nepal it is called Bratabandha (ब्रतबन्ध). Boys have their heads shaved, receive the thread, and make a symbolic first round asking relatives for alms.
  • Amrit Sanchar. In Sikh tradition, people who are ready to commit fully to the faith take amrit (water stirred with a double-edged sword called a khanda) in a ceremony led by five initiated Sikhs, recalling the Panj Pyare ("beloved five") whom Guru Gobind Singh first initiated, and join the Khalsa. There is no fixed age.
  • Puberty ceremonies for girls. In many Tamil families in Tamil Nadu and in the Tamil diaspora, a girl's first period has traditionally been marked by a family celebration, sometimes called manjal neerattu vizha, with a turmeric-water bath, new clothes, food and gifts. Rituals differ by community and region. Some families still hold big celebrations, while others, including some critics in Tamil Nadu, argue the custom puts unfair attention on girls and should change.

Your family counts

Your family might do some of these rituals, all of them, none of them, or a mix of old and new. That's normal. A short ceremony in a Minnesota apartment is just as real as a big one in Lahore or Dhaka.

docs.title: 13.7 Weddings
docs.text: Weddings in South Asia are often multi-day events that join two families, not just two people, with separate ceremonies before, during and after the main rite. Guest lists of hundreds are common. Details differ hugely by faith, region and family budget, but a few pieces show up again and again.

docs.title: Arranged Marriage
docs.text:
An Arranged Marriage is a marriage in which parents or other relatives help find and suggest a partner, and the couple then decides whether to go ahead. Arranged marriage has been common in South Asia for centuries and still is, alongside "love marriages," where the couple meets on their own.

What arranged marriage looks like has changed a lot. In many families today, parents or relatives suggest possible matches, sometimes through friends, community networks or matrimonial websites and apps. The two young people meet, talk, sometimes over months, and either can say no. Some couples meet on their own and then ask their families to "arrange" the rest, which some writers call a "self-arranged" marriage.

The most important word here is consent. An arranged marriage, where both people freely agree, is very different from a forced marriage, where one or both people are pressured or made to marry against their will. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 16) says marriage must be entered into only with the "free and full consent" of both people. Islamic law requires both the bride and the groom to consent, and Sikh teaching expects the couple to agree. In India, the Hindu Marriage Act of 1955 lets a court annul a marriage if consent was obtained by force or fraud. Forced marriage is a human rights abuse, and arranged marriage done with real consent is not.

docs.title: Mehndi Night and Sangeet
docs.text:
The days before a wedding are often the most fun. Mehndi Night and Sangeet are two pre-wedding celebrations popular in many North Indian, Pakistani and diaspora families.

  • At a mehndi night, the bride's hands and feet are decorated with mehndi (henna), a paste made from a plant that stains the skin reddish brown. Artists draw flowers, vines, paisleys and peacocks, and female relatives and friends get small designs too. There's usually music, food and dancing.
  • A sangeet (संगीत, sun-GEET, "music") is a night of singing and dancing. In many families it was once a smaller gathering of women singing folk songs. Today many families stage dance performances by both sides of the family, often to film songs.

In Bangladesh and West Bengal, both Muslim and Hindu families hold a gaye holud (গায়ে হলুদ, GAA-ye HO-lood, "turmeric on the body"), where friends and relatives smear turmeric paste on the bride and groom amid songs and yellow and orange clothes.

docs.title: Nikah
docs.text: A Nikah (نکاح, ni-KAAH) is the Islamic marriage contract and ceremony. At its heart, the bride and groom each give their consent in front of witnesses, and the groom agrees to give the bride the mahr, a gift of money or property that belongs to her alone. An imam or other officiant often leads the ceremony, recites prayers and verses from the Quran, and the couple and witnesses sign a marriage contract, called a nikah nama in Pakistan and Bangladesh. Afterward comes the walima, a wedding feast hosted and paid for by the groom's side. Many South Asian Muslim families combine the nikah with older regional customs like mehndi or gaye holud.

docs.title: Anand Karaj
docs.text: The Anand Karaj (ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ, uh-NUND KAA-raj, "blissful ceremony") is the Sikh wedding ceremony. It takes place in front of the Guru Granth Sahib, usually in a gurdwara. Many Sikh weddings take place in the morning. The center of the ceremony is the laavan, four hymns composed by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru. As each hymn is sung, the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib, the groom leading the bride, who holds one end of a scarf that he holds too. Four hymns, four rounds, and they are married. The Anand Marriage Act of 1909 gave Sikh marriages by this rite legal recognition in British India, and India amended the law in 2012 to let these marriages be registered under it.

docs.title: Hindu and Buddhist weddings
docs.text:
In many Hindu weddings, the couple's marriage is witnessed by a sacred fire. The central moment is often the saptapadi ("seven steps"), when the couple takes seven steps or circles the fire together, making a promise at each one. Rituals vary hugely between, say, a Telugu wedding in Hyderabad like the ones Arjun's cousins have had, a Gujarati wedding and a Nepali wedding. In Sri Lanka, many Sinhala couples marry on a poruwa, a decorated wooden platform, in a ceremony with a traditional officiant, betel leaves and blessings from both families. Buddhist monks do not usually lead the wedding itself, and many Sri Lankans trace the poruwa custom to before Buddhism reached the island.

Wedding Tradition Where the key moment happens Key moment Hindu (many regions) Hindu Around a sacred fire, under a canopy Saptapadi, seven steps or rounds Nikah Muslim Home, mosque or hall Consent before witnesses; mahr; contract signed Anand Karaj Sikh Gurdwara, before the Guru Granth Sahib Four laavan, four rounds of the scripture Poruwa ceremony Sinhala (Sri Lanka) Decorated wooden platform (poruwa) Rituals with an officiant; both families bless the couple

docs.title: 13.8 Funeral Customs
docs.text:
Death is hard to talk about in any culture, but knowing what a friend's family is doing helps you show up for them. Funeral Customs are the rites families follow when someone dies: how the body is cared for, the funeral itself, and the period of mourning afterward.

  • Hindu families usually cremate the body, often within a day. In the Antyeshti, a son or close relative traditionally lights the funeral pyre, and the ashes are later placed in a river, for many families the Ganga. A period of mourning follows, and rituals called shraddha honor the dead in later years. Details vary by region, community and the age of the person who died.
  • Muslim families bury the body as soon as possible, often within a day. The body is washed and wrapped in simple white cloth, a funeral prayer called the janazah is said, and the person is buried facing Mecca. Cremation is not allowed in Islam.
  • Sikh families usually cremate the body. In the Antim Sanskar ("final rite") the family recites prayers, and the ashes are scattered in running water. Sikh tradition discourages gravestones or monuments.
  • Buddhist families in Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan may cremate or bury. In Sri Lanka, families often offer food (dana) to monks on the seventh day after a death, again about three months later, and at the end of a year, dedicating the merit to the person who has died.
  • Parsi (Zoroastrian) families in Mumbai have traditionally placed the dead in a dakhma, or "tower of silence," where the body is exposed to the sun and birds instead of being buried or burned. As vultures have become rare, some families now choose cremation or burial.

If a friend's relative dies, a simple "I'm so sorry" is always welcome. Ask your friend before attending a service so you know what to expect.

docs.title: 13.9 Gender Roles and Change
docs.text:
Back at the wedding, Ben notices that the women are mostly in the kitchen and the men are mostly greeting guests. Then he notices Zara's Khala, a surgeon, giving a speech, and Zara's cousin, the bride, signing her own marriage contract. Both things are true, and that's the story of gender in South Asian families today.

Gender Roles and Change is about the expectations families and societies have for women and men, and how those expectations are shifting. In many traditional South Asian families, men were expected to earn money and represent the family in public, and women were expected to run the home, raise children and care for elders, often in their husband's family's house. Daughters often received less schooling than sons and moved away at marriage.

Surveys show that many of these expectations remain strong, but views differ. In a Pew Research Center survey of about 30,000 Indian adults, carried out in 2019 and 2020 and published in 2022:

  • 54% said both men and women should be responsible for earning money for the family, while 43% said it is mainly men's job.
  • 62% said both parents should share responsibility for taking care of children, while 34% said it is mainly women's job.
  • About nine in ten agreed, at least mostly, that a wife must always obey her husband.

At the same time, South Asia has been home to some of the world's firsts for women in politics. In 1960, Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka (then Ceylon) became the world's first woman elected prime minister. In 1988, Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan became the first woman elected to lead a democratic government in a Muslim-majority country. Women have also led governments in India and Bangladesh, and in 2025 Sushila Karki became Nepal's first woman prime minister, leading an interim government until a new government took office after the March 2026 election.

Change is happening at home too, as more couples choose each other and many diaspora families split chores in new ways, while keeping roles they value, like grandparents' place in raising children. Change looks different in a village in Sindh, an apartment in Dhaka and a Minnesota suburb.

Selecting a relative shows the single English word next to the term many families use in Hindi-Urdu, Bangla, Punjabi, Tamil and Sinhala, in the original script with a respelling. Notes mark where usage varies by family, religion or region (for example, Muslim and Hindu Bangla speakers). Every spelling is logged in the chapter fact log.

Start with "Dad's older brother" and "Dad's younger brother." In English both are "uncle," but notice how many of the five languages give them different words, and how Tamil and Sinhala call them "big father" and "little father." Then click "Mom's brother." Which word stays almost the same across all five languages?

Next, compare "Dad's mother" with "Mom's mother." Then untick the color checkbox and see if you can guess from the words alone which side a relative is on. If your family uses a different word, your family isn't wrong.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about family words, names and big family events. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Bring a sheet of paper and draw a simple family tree together as you talk. Ask if it's okay to take notes.

Questions to ask

  1. What did you call each of your aunts, uncles and grandparents when you were a child? Did anyone have a nickname?
  2. How was your name chosen, and who chose it? Does it have a meaning? How were names chosen for me and my siblings?
  3. Did you grow up in a joint family or a smaller household? Who lived in the house?
  4. Tell me about one wedding, naming ceremony or other family celebration you remember well. What happened, and what did you eat?
  5. How have family roles changed since you were young, or since our family moved? Who cooks, who earns, who decides?
  6. Is there a family custom, word or name you hope I'll keep and pass on?

Listen for: the Kinship Terms your elder uses and whether they split the father's side and mother's side; how the family's Naming Traditions and Surnames work; and any signs of Gender Roles and Change between their childhood and yours.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare the kinship words your elder used with the words in the Kinship Explorer. Which matched, and which were different? If a friend interviewed someone from another language or faith, make a two-column list of the words each family uses for the same relatives.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: All South Asian marriages are forced. Reality: Many marriages are arranged, which means families help find a partner, but in an arranged marriage both people freely agree and can say no. Forced marriage, without real consent, is a human rights abuse that South Asian faiths and laws reject. Many South Asians also choose their own partners.

Myth: Caste only exists in India, and only in the past. Reality: Caste is a historical and continuing system. It still shapes marriage and social life in India and Nepal, appears among people of many faiths, and has become a civil rights issue in the diaspora, including in Seattle and California in 2023. Laws in India and Nepal make caste discrimination a crime.

Myth: Everyone has a first name and a family surname. Reality: Many Bhutanese people and, traditionally, many Afghans have no family name. Many Tamils use their father's name as an initial instead of a surname, and Sherpa children are often named for the day they were born.

Myth: Joint families are disappearing everywhere. Reality: Living patterns are changing, especially in cities and abroad, but extended-family households are still common in South Asia. A 2019 Pew study found that the average person in Afghanistan and Pakistan lived in a household of more than eight people, and many diaspora families still bring grandparents to live with them.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. Why do many South Asian languages have different words for a father's brother and a mother's brother?

In many patrilineal families, the father's brothers belonged to the same household and line of inheritance, while the mother's brothers belonged to another family and played a different role, such as a special part at weddings. Different roles led to different words.

2. What is the difference between varna and jati?

Varna is a fourfold classification described in old Sanskrit texts. Jati is the local birth group a person actually belongs to; there are thousands of them, and they shape marriage and community life.

3. What did Article 17 of India's Constitution do?

It abolished "untouchability," forbade practicing it in any form, and made enforcing any disability arising from it a crime.

4. What is the difference between an arranged marriage and a forced marriage?

In an arranged marriage, families help find a partner, but both people freely consent and can refuse. In a forced marriage, at least one person is made to marry without real consent.

5. What happens during the laavan in an Anand Karaj?

Four hymns by Guru Ram Das are sung, and as each one is sung the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib. After the fourth round, they are married.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Name the four varnas listed in the old Brahmanical texts.

    Answer

    Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.

  2. What is the Sikh name given to all women, and what is the name given to all men?

    Answer

    Kaur for women and Singh for men.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain in your own words what a joint family is and why it might lead to different words for relatives on each side.

    Answer

    A joint family is a household of several generations and branches, traditionally married brothers living with their parents, wives and children. Because the father's relatives live together and the mother's relatives live elsewhere, they play different roles, and languages give them different names.

  2. Explain why a Tamil speaker might call their father's older brother "big father."

    Answer

    In the Dravidian kinship system, relatives linked through same-sex siblings (like a father's brother) are treated almost like parents, so the father's older brother is periyappa, "big father."

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. A new student at your school writes her name as "S. Lakshmi" and seems annoyed when a teacher calls her "Ms. S." Using what you learned about Tamil naming, explain what might be going on and how the teacher could fix it.

    Hint: what might the initial stand for?

  2. Draw your own family tree with at least eight relatives. Label each one with the word your family actually uses, and mark which side they're on.

    Hint: ask a parent if you're not sure of a word.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the Nikah, the Anand Karaj and a Hindu wedding with saptapadi. What do all three require or include, and what is different about where and how the key moment happens?

    Hint: look at consent, witnesses and the role of scripture or fire.

  2. The Pew survey found most Indians say there isn't a lot of caste discrimination, but most also say it's very important to stop inter-caste marriage. What might explain both answers being true at once?

    Hint: think about the difference between how people see discrimination and what they practice.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Seattle added caste to its anti-discrimination law, while California's governor vetoed a similar bill. Using the arguments on both sides from this chapter, which approach do you find more convincing, and why?

    Hint: consider both protection for people who face discrimination and the worry about singling out communities.

  2. Some people say "joint families are disappearing." Evaluate this claim using evidence from the chapter and from your own community.

    Hint: is there one answer for a village, a big city and the diaspora?

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a one-page "Who's Who at a South Asian Wedding" guide for a friend like Ben who has never been to one. Include at least six kinship words, two pre-wedding events and three tips for being a good guest.

    Hint: check each word with someone in your family or a classmate's family.

  2. Write a short scene (one page) in which a teen asks a grandparent how their name was chosen. Show what each of them learns.

    Hint: use real details from your own interview if you can.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Many South Asian languages use different kinship terms for the father's side and mother's side, and for older and younger relatives, while English often uses one word like "uncle."
  • Joint families and respect for elders are strong traditions across the region, but households are flexible and changing, especially in cities and abroad.
  • Naming traditions vary widely: Sikh names chosen from the Guru Granth Sahib, Sherpa day names, Bengali "good names" and "call names," and many people without family surnames.
  • The caste system (built on varna and jati) is historical and continuing. India's Constitution and laws in India and Nepal ban caste discrimination, and the issue now reaches the diaspora.
  • Life-cycle rituals and coming-of-age rites differ by faith and region, from samskaras and Bratabandha to aqiqah and Amrit Sanchar.
  • South Asian weddings often last several days. An arranged marriage depends on the couple's consent, unlike a forced marriage, and the Nikah and Anand Karaj each have their own heart: consent and contract, or four hymns around the scripture.
  • Funeral customs differ by faith, and gender roles are changing at different speeds in different places.

You know the family now!

You can now tell your chacha from your mama and explain why it matters. Next, in Chapter 14, we'll open the books and bedtime stories that families have passed down for centuries.

docs.title: Quiz: Family, Names, and Life Events
Quiz: Family, Names, and Life Events
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 13. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
In Hindi-Urdu, Bangla and Punjabi, what relative do many families call "mama"?

  1. Mother
  2. Father's younger brother
  3. Mother's brother
  4. Mother's mother
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In all five languages in the Kinship Explorer, mama is the word many families use for the mother's brother. It does not mean "mother," which is the misunderstanding Ben has in the chapter's opening scene.

Concept Tested: Kinship Terms Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which article of India's Constitution abolished "untouchability" and forbade its practice in any form?

  1. Article 15
  2. Article 17
  3. Article 16
  4. Article 370
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Article 17 abolished untouchability and made enforcing any disability arising from it a crime. Article 15 is related, since it bans the state from discriminating on grounds such as caste, but it is not the article that abolished untouchability.

Concept Tested: Caste Discrimination Laws Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
What is at the center of the Sikh Anand Karaj wedding ceremony?

  1. Seven steps around a sacred fire
  2. Signing a contract with a mahr before witnesses
  3. Standing on a decorated wooden platform called a poruwa
  4. Four hymns (laavan) sung as the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In the Anand Karaj, four laavan composed by Guru Ram Das are sung, and the couple circles the Guru Granth Sahib once for each hymn. Seven steps around a fire (saptapadi) belong to many Hindu weddings, not the Anand Karaj.

Concept Tested: Anand Karaj Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Which statement best describes the difference between varna and jati?

  1. Varna is a fourfold scheme in old Sanskrit texts; jati is the local birth group people actually belong to, and there are thousands of them.
  2. Varna is the modern legal term for caste; jati is the ancient religious term.
  3. Varna applies only to Muslims and jati only to Hindus.
  4. They are two names for exactly the same four groups.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Varna is the four-part classification described in Brahmanical texts, while jatis are the thousands of local birth groups that shape marriage and community life. Treating them as the same four groups is a common mistake.

Concept Tested: Varna and Jati Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why do Tamil and Sinhala call a father's older brother "big father"?

  1. Because he is always the head of the household by law
  2. Because the languages have no word for uncle at all
  3. Because in the Dravidian kinship pattern, relatives linked through same-sex siblings are treated almost like parents
  4. Because he is usually physically taller than the father
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In the Dravidian pattern, a father's brother or a mother's sister is grouped with the parents ("big father," "big mother"), while a father's sister and a mother's brother get separate words. Tamil and Sinhala do have separate uncle words, such as mama, so option B is wrong.

Concept Tested: Kinship Terms Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
What makes an arranged marriage different from a forced marriage?

  1. Arranged marriages happen only in villages.
  2. In an arranged marriage, families suggest a partner but both people freely consent and can refuse.
  3. Forced marriages are legal if the families agree.
  4. Arranged marriages never involve the couple meeting before the wedding.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Consent is the dividing line: in an arranged marriage the couple decides, while a forced marriage happens without real consent and is a human rights abuse. Many arranged matches today involve long conversations and meetings, so option D is wrong.

Concept Tested: Arranged Marriage Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Nima, a Sherpa student whose family is from Solukhumbu, Nepal, tells the club that her cousin was born on a Monday. Based on Sherpa naming traditions, which name might the cousin have?

  1. Pemba
  2. Nima
  3. Phurba
  4. Dawa
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Sherpa children are traditionally named for the day they were born, and Dawa is the Monday name. Nima (Nyima) is the Sunday name, so a child born on Monday would not usually get it.

Concept Tested: Naming Traditions Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
A teacher is setting up a class roster. A student from Bhutan has two given names and no family name. What is the best way for the teacher to respond?

  1. Ask the student how they'd like their name written and said, since many Bhutanese people have no family surname.
  2. Use the second name as the surname, since every name has one.
  3. Ask the student to choose a new surname for school.
  4. Use the student's father's name as the surname.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Many Bhutanese people have no family name, and names are often chosen by a lama. Assuming the second name is a surname (option B) is the most common mistake, so asking the student is the respectful choice.

Concept Tested: Surnames Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
The 2021 Pew survey of India found that only about one in five Indians said there was a lot of discrimination against Scheduled Castes, yet 64% said it was very important to stop women marrying outside their caste. What does this comparison suggest?

  1. Caste no longer matters in India.
  2. Caste matters only to people who say there is a lot of discrimination.
  3. Caste still shapes choices like marriage, even when many people don't see it as discrimination.
  4. The survey only asked about people living in the diaspora.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Many people did not describe caste discrimination as widespread, but most still wanted to keep marriage within caste, which shows caste continues to shape social life. Option A ignores the marriage finding entirely.

Concept Tested: Caste System Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Compare a Hindu cremation, a Muslim burial and a Sri Lankan Buddhist almsgiving. Which statement correctly analyzes them?

  1. All three require burial within 24 hours.
  2. Muslim tradition calls for prompt burial and forbids cremation, while many Hindu families cremate, and Sri Lankan Buddhist families often offer food to monks at set times after a death.
  3. All three forbid any ritual after the funeral day.
  4. Hindu and Muslim families both scatter ashes in a river.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Islam calls for burial as soon as possible and does not allow cremation. Many Hindu families cremate and place ashes in a river, and Sri Lankan Buddhist families often give dana to monks after seven days, about three months and a year. Option D is wrong because Muslims do not cremate.

Concept Tested: Funeral Customs Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asia has been telling stories for thousands of years, first out loud and later in writing, in dozens of languages. This chapter starts with oral tradition and the two great Sanskrit epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, then follows the animal fables of the Jatakas and the Panchatantra as they travel to Persia, the Arab world and Europe. You'll meet Tamil Sangam poetry, the playwright Kalidasa, the poet-saint Kabir, the ghazals of Mirza Ghalib, and three modern poets who became symbols of nations: Rabindranath Tagore, Kazi Nazrul Islam and Allama Iqbal. The chapter ends with the literature of Partition and with South Asian writing in English and in translation. The big idea is that a good story never stays in one language, faith or country.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 2: Ancient Roots, for the early history behind the epics
  • Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition, for the events behind Partition literature
  • Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia, for Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh and Muslim traditions that shaped many stories
  • Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts, for the languages these works were written in

Pull up a chair

Hi, it's Mora! You probably already know some of these stories, from a bedtime tale, a cartoon, a holiday play or a line your grandparent quotes at dinner. This chapter shows you where those stories came from and how they keep changing, so the next time a relative says "that's not how it goes," you'll know why both of you might be right. Every tradition has a story. Let's find it!

docs.title: 14.1 Two Ramayanas at One Lunch Table
docs.text:
It's Thursday lunch at Prairie Ridge High School. "I watched six episodes of an animated Ramayana series last night," Ben Lindqvist says. "Prince Rama gets sent into the forest, the demon king Ravana kidnaps Sita, and a monkey army builds a bridge to an island to rescue her. It's basically a superhero movie."

Dilan Perera, whose family is Sinhala-speaking and Buddhist and comes from Kandy in Sri Lanka, laughs a little. "That island is supposed to be Lanka," he says. "My grandfather tells some of it differently. In his version Ravana isn't really a monster. He's a brilliant king, a scholar who played music. Some people back home are proud of him."

Zara Hossain jumps in. "My Nanu knows the story too, from growing up in Bangladesh, and she tells it with Bengali details I've never seen in any cartoon." Ben puts his fork down. "Okay, wait. If everyone tells it differently, which one is the real Ramayana?" This chapter is the long answer.

docs.title: 14.2 Stories Are Like Songs With Many Covers
docs.text:
Think about a famous song that many artists have covered. Each cover keeps the melody you recognize but changes the speed, the instruments, maybe a few words, and nobody calls it "fake." Many South Asian stories work the same way. For most of history they were not books. They were performances.

Oral Tradition is the passing of stories, poems, songs and knowledge from person to person by speaking, singing and memorizing, often across many generations, instead of by writing them down. In South Asia, oral tradition has carried everything from holy texts to grandmothers' bedtime stories. Many languages have an everyday word for a story told this way. In Hindi it might be a katha (कथा, KUH-thaa), "story," a word borrowed from Sanskrit. Zara's Nanu calls a story a golpo (গল্প, GOL-po), the everyday Bangla word for "story." In Urdu, a long, adventure-filled tale is a dastan (داستان, daas-TAAN), a word that came from Persian.

Performers learned long poems by heart, often with music and rhythm to help, and sang or acted them at festivals, temples, shrines, courts and village gatherings. Each teller could add local details, jokes and lessons for the audience in front of them.

Oral tradition is still alive. Two examples are on UNESCO's list of the world's living cultural heritage. Ramlila, "Rama's play," is a cycle of open-air plays retelling the Ramayana, performed across northern India during the autumn Dussehra festival. UNESCO first proclaimed it in 2005 and inscribed it on its Representative List in 2008. The Baul songs of Bangladesh (also sung in West Bengal, India) are devotional songs by wandering minstrels called Bauls, passed down orally from teacher to student and recognized by UNESCO on the same timeline.

In Sindh, in today's Pakistan, the poems of the Sufi poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai were passed around by memory and song during his lifetime and only gathered into a book, the Shah Jo Risalo, after he died.

Think about your own family

Is there a story your family only tells out loud, never from a book? Notice which details change when a different relative tells it. That change is oral tradition happening right in your living room.

docs.title: 14.3 The Two Great Epics
docs.text: An epic is a very long poem about heroes, gods, wars and journeys that a culture treats as one of its foundation stories. South Asia's two most famous epics were composed in Sanskrit, the classical language you met in Chapter 6, and for many Hindus they are sacred texts. This section describes what they say and how scholars date them, not whether anyone's beliefs are true.

docs.title: The Ramayana
docs.text:
The Ramayana (रामायण, raa-MAA-yuh-nuh), "the story of Rama," is a Sanskrit epic about Prince Rama of the kingdom of Ayodhya. The best-known version is traditionally credited to the poet-sage Valmiki. Here is the story in brief:

  1. Rama's stepmother persuades his father, King Dasharatha, to send Rama into the forest for fourteen years.
  2. Rama goes, joined by his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana.
  3. Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka, kidnaps Sita and carries her to his island kingdom.
  4. Rama allies with an army of vanaras (monkey-like forest people), including the devoted Hanuman.
  5. They cross to Lanka, defeat Ravana and rescue Sita, and Rama returns home to be crowned.

Valmiki's Ramayana has nearly 24,000 verses, arranged in seven books. Scholars think its oral core took shape around 750 to 500 BCE, with later additions. Many Hindus see Rama as a form of the god Vishnu, and the story's themes of duty, loyalty and doing what is right run through South Asian culture. Diwali, which you met in Chapter 7, is linked in many North Indian families to Rama's return home.

docs.title: The Mahabharata
docs.text:
The Mahabharata (महाभारत, muh-haa-BHAA-ruh-tuh), "the great story of the Bharatas," is a Sanskrit epic about a struggle for a throne between two sets of royal cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, that ends in a huge war at Kurukshetra. It is traditionally credited to the sage Vyasa, who is also a character in the story. Its longest version has more than 100,000 verses, making it one of the longest poems ever composed. Most of it was probably put together between about 300 BCE and 300 CE.

The Mahabharata is famous for being morally complicated: heroes make bad choices, villains have reasons, and characters argue about what is right.

docs.title: The Bhagavad Gita
docs.text:
The most famous section inside the Mahabharata is the Bhagavad Gita (भगवद्गीता, BHUG-uh-vud GEE-taa), "God's song," a poem of about 700 verses found in the epic's sixth book. Just before the great battle, the warrior prince Arjuna sees relatives and teachers on the other side and loses the will to fight. His charioteer, Krishna, whom Hindus revere as a form of Vishnu, answers his doubts in a long conversation about duty, action, devotion and the self. Scholars think it was likely composed in the second or first century BCE.

For many Hindus, the Gita is one of the most important sacred texts. Thinkers over the centuries have written commentaries on it that disagree about its deepest meaning.

Work Language Rough date (scholars' estimate) Size What it's about Ramayana (Valmiki) Sanskrit Oral core about 750 to 500 BCE Nearly 24,000 verses, 7 books Rama's exile, Sita's capture by Ravana, her rescue Mahabharata Sanskrit Mostly about 300 BCE to 300 CE More than 100,000 verses A war between royal cousins and the questions it raises Bhagavad Gita Sanskrit About 2nd to 1st century BCE About 700 verses Krishna's answers to Arjuna's doubts before battle

docs.title: 14.4 One Story, Many Tellings
docs.text:
Now back to Ben's question. Valmiki's Ramayana is the oldest well-known version, but it is far from the only one. Over the centuries, poets retold Rama's story in their own languages, for their own audiences.

  • Tamil: In the 12th century the poet Kamban wrote the Ramavataram, often called the Kamba Ramayanam. Many readers count it among the greatest works of Tamil literature.
  • Bangla: Krittibas Ojha's Bengali Ramayana, the Krittivasi Ramayan, dates from around the 15th century. It is full of the food, customs and village life of Bengal, and for centuries it was one of the most popular books in the region.
  • Awadhi (a language of North India): In the 16th century, Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in everyday Awadhi rather than Sanskrit, so that ordinary people could follow the story. It is the basis of the Ramlila plays.
  • Nepali: Bhanubhakta Acharya (1814 to 1868) made the first Nepali translation of the Ramayana, which spread at first by word of mouth.
  • Beyond South Asia: Around 870 CE, poets on the island of Java (in today's Indonesia) wrote the Kakawin Ramayana. Its second half is very different from Valmiki's. Thailand's Ramakien is one of that country's national epics. The Malay Hikayat Seri Rama mixes in elements from Islamic tradition.

There are also Buddhist and Jain tellings, in which parts of the plot and the meaning change.

In 1987 the scholar A. K. Ramanujan presented an essay called "Three Hundred Ramayanas: Five Examples and Three Thoughts on Translation." He chose the word tellings instead of "versions" on purpose, because "version" suggests there is one true original and the rest are copies. His point was that Valmiki's Ramayana is one telling among many. The essay became controversial: Delhi University assigned it to history students for several years, then voted in October 2011 to remove it from the course after objections. The fight showed how much these stories still matter.

Many tellings is not the same as 'made up'

For many Hindus the Ramayana is sacred, and Rama is worshipped as divine. Saying there are many tellings is a fact about how the story has been passed on, not a claim about whether anyone's faith is true, so talk about it with the same respect you'd want for your own traditions.

So what about Dilan's grandfather? In Sri Lanka, Ravana is remembered in more than one way. Many places on the island are popularly linked with scenes from the Ramayana, and the country's tourism industry promotes a "Ramayana trail" for visitors from India. At the same time, some Sinhala Buddhists have recast Ravana as a wise and noble king of the island, and that view became more popular from the 1980s on. Sri Lanka even named its first satellite, launched in 2019, Raavana-1. In Tamil literature in Sri Lanka and in South India, Ravana also appears in a positive light. One Tamil poet wrote a whole epic in which he is the hero. Historians also debate whether the Lanka of the epic was the same place as today's Sri Lanka.

Whose Story?

The same epic means very different things depending on who is telling it. For many Hindus in India, Nepal and the diaspora, the Ramayana is a sacred story of a divine king, and Ravana's defeat is celebrated each year at Dussehra by burning his effigy. In Thailand the Ramakien is a national epic illustrated on the walls of Bangkok's Wat Phra Kaew temple, and Indonesia, a mostly Muslim country, has its own Ramayana tellings from Java and Bali. Some Sinhala Buddhists in Sri Lanka see Ravana as a proud ancient king of their island, while Tamil writers in South India and Sri Lanka have also honored him as a hero. Scholars like A. K. Ramanujan argue that none of these is the single "real" one, while others feel that treating a sacred text as one telling among many misses what makes it holy to them.

Ben gets it now. "So it's like a song with a hundred covers," he says. "The covers aren't wrong. They're for different crowds." Dilan grins. "And my grandfather would say his cover is the best one."

docs.title: 14.5 Animals Who Teach: Jatakas, Panchatantra and Birbal
docs.text: Some of the most widely traveled stories in history star monkeys, jackals, lions and tortoises.

docs.title: The Jataka Tales
docs.text:
The Jataka Tales (जातक, JAA-tuh-kuh), "birth stories," are Buddhist stories about the earlier lives of the Buddha, before he was born as Prince Siddhartha. In these stories the future Buddha appears as a person or an animal (a monkey, a deer, a parrot, an elephant) and shows qualities like generosity, patience and courage. The Theravada Buddhist collection in the Pali language contains 547 Jatakas in a mix of verse and prose. Scholars think the verses are older than the prose stories around them, and the collection in its present form was put together around 500 CE.

Jatakas were also carved and painted: some of the earliest Jataka pictures are on the stone gateways and railings of the Buddhist stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut in India, and later murals fill the caves at Ajanta. Theravada Buddhism is the main tradition in Sri Lanka, so Jataka stories are part of many Sri Lankan childhoods, Dilan's included, as well as in Myanmar, Thailand and Laos.

docs.title: The Panchatantra
docs.text:
The Panchatantra (पञ्चतन्त्र, PUNCH-uh-TUN-truh), "five treatises," is a Sanskrit collection of animal fables arranged inside a frame story. In the frame, a wise teacher uses clever stories to teach three slow-learning princes how to live and rule wisely. Inside, the animals argue, scheme, make friends and pay for bad choices, and each tale has a lesson about trust, friendship or good judgment. Its author is unknown. Some versions name a teacher called Vishnu Sharma, but that may be a pen name. The Panchatantra shares many of its stories with the Jatakas, which shows how fables flowed between Hindu and Buddhist storytellers.

Then the Panchatantra went on one of the longest journeys of any book:

flowchart LR
    A["Panchatantra<br/>Sanskrit, before 550 CE"] --> B["Middle Persian translation<br/>by Burzoe, about 550 CE"]
    B --> C["Syriac translation"]
    B --> D["Kalila wa Dimna<br/>Arabic, Ibn al-Muqaffa, about 750 CE"]
    D --> E["New Persian, Turkish,<br/>Greek and Latin versions"]
    E --> F["European fables,<br/>credited to Bidpai or Pilpay"]

The Arabic version, Kalila wa Dimna, is named after two jackals who narrate and star in the stories. The Persian scholar Ibn al-Muqaffa's Arabic translation is still admired as a masterpiece of Arabic prose. The Library of Congress holds a digital copy of an illustrated Arabic manuscript of Kalila wa Dimna made in Egypt around 1310, with 73 painted pictures. From Arabic, the stories passed into many other languages, and some European writers openly credited "Bidpai" or "Pilpay, the Indian sage" as their source. One count finds about 200 versions of the Panchatantra in more than 50 languages.

docs.title: Akbar and Birbal Tales
docs.text: Not all South Asian folk stories are ancient. The Akbar and Birbal Tales are funny stories about the Mughal emperor Akbar and his quick-witted minister Birbal, in which Birbal solves impossible puzzles, outsmarts jealous courtiers, and sometimes teases the emperor himself. Birbal was a real person: born Mahesh Das in 1528, he became one of Akbar's closest courtiers and a member of the group of advisers later called the navaratnas, the "nine jewels." He died in 1586, killed in battle in the Swat region of today's Pakistan. Most of the famous tales, though, are folk stories that spread much later, mainly in the 1800s, across what are now India and Pakistan, and they are still retold for children today.

docs.title: 14.6 Classical Poetry: Sangam Poems and Kalidasa
Sangam Literature
docs.text:
Sangam Literature is the earliest known body of Tamil poetry, composed roughly between 300 BCE and 300 CE. The word Sangam (சங்கம், SUNG-gum) means "gathering" or "academy." According to Tamil tradition, the poems were approved by great assemblies of poets in the city of Madurai. Historians treat those legendary assemblies as tradition rather than history, but the poems themselves are very real.

The Sangam collections hold 2,381 poems by 473 poets, 102 of them anonymous. The poems fall into two big kinds:

  • Akam (inner) poems are about love: longing, meeting, separation and jealousy.
  • Puram (outer) poems are about public life: kings, war, generosity, death and fame.

Sangam poets also sorted poems by landscape, such as hills, pastures or seashore, so the setting of a poem helped signal its mood. Many readers find them surprisingly modern: short, vivid and about ordinary emotions. Tamil is spoken today in India's Tamil Nadu, in northern and eastern Sri Lanka, and in a large diaspora, and Sangam poetry is a point of pride for Tamils everywhere.

docs.title: Kalidasa
docs.text:
Kalidasa was a poet and playwright who wrote in Sanskrit, probably in the fourth to fifth century CE, during the time of the Gupta kings. Very little is known about his life, and even his birthplace is debated. His surviving works include three plays and several poems. Two are especially famous:

  • Shakuntala (full title Abhijnanashakuntalam), a play about a king who falls in love with a young woman raised in a forest hermitage, forgets her because of a curse, and finally recognizes her again.
  • Meghaduta, "The Cloud Messenger," a poem in which a yaksha (a nature spirit) exiled for a year asks a passing cloud to carry a message to his wife in the Himalaya, describing the sights the cloud will pass on its way north.

The British scholar William Jones translated Shakuntala into English in the late 1700s, and from English it went into German, where the poet Goethe admired it.

docs.title: 14.7 Poet-Saints and the Ghazal
docs.text: From around the 1400s, some of South Asia's most loved poetry came from poet-saints, devotional poets who wrote in the languages people spoke every day.

docs.title: Kabir
docs.text:
Kabir was a 15th-century poet-saint from Varanasi, in North India. Historians are unsure of his exact dates (some say 1398 to 1448, others 1440 to 1518). Tradition says he was raised by a Muslim weaver family, and he is often described as a weaver himself. Kabir composed songs and short, sharp couplets (called dohe or sakhi) in the everyday Hindi of his time. Many were passed on orally, and later admirers added verses in his name. He questioned empty ritual and hypocrisy in both Hinduism and Islam and taught that the divine is found within each person. During his lifetime he was criticized by both Hindus and Muslims, and after his death both communities claimed him.

Kabir's verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the holy scripture of the Sikhs, and a community called the Kabir Panth ("Path of Kabir") honors him as its founder. Five hundred years later, Rabindranath Tagore was among the writers influenced by him.

docs.title: Mirza Ghalib and the ghazal
docs.text:
To understand the next poet you need one form. A ghazal (غزل, GHUZ-ul) is a poem made of separate two-line couplets that share a rhyme and a repeated ending phrase. Each couplet can stand alone like a tiny poem. The form came to South Asia through Persian and became central to Urdu poetry and music.

Mirza Ghalib (1797 to 1869) is the most famous ghazal poet in the Urdu language. Born in Agra, he lived most of his life in Delhi and wrote in both Urdu and Persian. He wrote far more in Persian than in Urdu, but his fame rests on his Urdu ghazals. He lived through the violence of 1857 in Delhi and spent much of his life short of money.

Before Ghalib, ghazals were mostly about painful love. Ghalib stretched the form to cover philosophy, doubt, faith, loss and the strangeness of life, often with wit. He was also a brilliant letter writer: his chatty, funny Urdu letters helped make Urdu prose more natural and easy to read. Today his couplets are quoted in India, Pakistan and the diaspora, and ghazal singers still perform them.

How to spot a ghazal

Listen for the same word or phrase coming back at the end of every couplet, like a chorus. Many famous film songs and qawwali performances are built on ghazals, so you may have heard one without knowing its name.

docs.title: Poets of the northwest
docs.text:
The northwest of the region, in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan, has its own beloved poets:

  • Rahman Baba (about 1632 to 1706), a Sufi poet from Peshawar, wrote in Pashto about God, kindness and humility. He is among the most popular poets of the Pashto language, loved by Pashto speakers in both Pakistan and Afghanistan.
  • Waris Shah wrote Heer in 1766, the most famous telling of Heer and Ranjha, a tragic Punjabi love story that already existed in oral and earlier written forms.
  • Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, as you saw in 14.2, composed Sindhi Sufi poetry that was sung and memorized before it was ever collected.

docs.title: 14.8 Poets Who Became Symbols of Nations
docs.text: In the late 1800s and early 1900s, three poets became so important that countries now treat them as national symbols. All three were born in British India. Today their memories belong to India, Bangladesh and Pakistan in different ways.

docs.title: Rabindranath Tagore
docs.text:
Rabindranath Tagore (1861 to 1941) was a Bengali poet, songwriter, novelist, playwright, painter and educator from Calcutta (now Kolkata). He wrote some 2,000 songs, many novels and short stories, and founded Visva-Bharati University at Santiniketan. In 1913 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first person from outside Europe to win that prize and the first Asian to win any Nobel Prize. The Nobel committee praised his "profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse," much of it from Gitanjali (Song Offerings), a book of song-poems he translated into English himself.

Tagore wrote the words of two countries' national anthems:

  • India's anthem, "Jana Gana Mana," is the first stanza of a song Tagore wrote in Bengali. It was first sung publicly in Calcutta in 1911 and adopted as India's national anthem in January 1950.
  • Bangladesh's anthem, "Amar Sonar Bangla" (আমার সোনার বাংলা, AA-mar SHO-nar BANG-la), "My Golden Bengal," was written by Tagore and adopted by Bangladesh's provisional government in 1971.

Sri Lanka's anthem has a Tagore connection too, but a debated one. Most historians say the Sri Lankan composer Ananda Samarakoon, who had studied under Tagore at Santiniketan, wrote both the words and music, inspired by his teacher. A minority claim Tagore wrote part or all of it, and some historians in both India and Sri Lanka reject that claim.

docs.title: Kazi Nazrul Islam
docs.text:
Kazi Nazrul Islam (1899 to 1976) was a Bengali poet, songwriter and journalist who is honored as the national poet of Bangladesh. People called him that for decades, and in December 2024 the government made the title official in a gazette notice. Born into a Muslim family in a village in what is now West Bengal, India, he served in the British Indian Army and then became a journalist in Calcutta. In 1922 he published "Bidrohi" ("The Rebel"), a thundering poem against injustice and oppression that earned him the title of Bidrohi Kobi, the "Rebel Poet." His writing against British rule landed him in prison more than once.

Nazrul wrote and composed nearly 4,000 songs, now known as Nazrul Geeti. He brought the ghazal into Bengali and also wrote Islamic devotional songs alongside Hindu devotional songs to the goddess Kali, called Shyama Sangeet, which upset some people on both sides. He looked up to Tagore as a mentor, and in 1923 Tagore dedicated a play, Basanta, to him while Nazrul was in prison. In 1942 an illness began to take away his voice and memory, and he could no longer write. In 1972 Nazrul was brought to the new country of Bangladesh, where he spent his last years.

docs.title: Allama Iqbal
docs.text:
Allama Iqbal (Sir Muhammad Iqbal, 1877 to 1938) was a poet and philosopher born in Sialkot, Punjab, in today's Pakistan. Allama is an honorific meaning "learned scholar." He studied in Lahore, Cambridge and Munich and wrote in Urdu and Persian. In his famous 1930 Allahabad Address he called for a separate political home for Muslims in the northwest of British India, an idea that helped shape the movement for Pakistan, which was founded nine years after his death.

Iqbal is honored as Pakistan's national poet, and his birthday, 9 November, is a public holiday there (the government restored the holiday in 2022 after dropping it in 2015). One of his best-known Persian books, Asrar-e-Khudi (Secrets of the Self), urges readers to build their inner strength, or selfhood. Iqbal's life shows how poetry crosses borders: one of his early Urdu songs, "Saare Jahan Se Achha" (also called "Tarana-e-Hindi"), written for children, is still a popular patriotic song in India, and his Persian poems are so loved in Iran that people there call him Iqbal-e Lahori, "Iqbal of Lahore."

docs.title: And in Nepal
docs.text:
Nepal has its own modern classic. Laxmi Prasad Devkota's long poem Muna Madan (1936) tells of a young husband who leaves Kathmandu for Lhasa, in Tibet, to earn money, and the wife who waits for him. Devkota and Bhanubhakta (14.4) are both major figures in Nepali literature.

Poet Lived Main languages Remembered as Countries that honor him Rabindranath Tagore 1861 to 1941 Bangla, English Nobel laureate (1913); anthem writer India and Bangladesh Kazi Nazrul Islam 1899 to 1976 Bangla The "Rebel Poet"; national poet Bangladesh (and India) Allama Iqbal 1877 to 1938 Urdu, Persian National poet; thinker Pakistan (and admirers in India and Iran)

docs.title: 14.9 Partition Literature
docs.text:
In 1947 British India was divided into India and Pakistan, and in the violence and mass migration that followed, as you read in Chapter 4, huge numbers of people were killed and millions were forced from their homes, with Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs all suffering. Writers on every side tried to make sense of it.

Partition Literature is the poetry, fiction and memoir written about the 1947 Partition and its aftermath, in Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi, Bangla, Sindhi, English and other languages. Rather than heroes and villains, the best of it focuses on ordinary people, loss and the absurdity of drawing a line through a shared home. Three classics:

  • "Ajj Aakhaan Waris Shah Nu" ("Today I Call on Waris Shah," 1947), a Punjabi poem by Amrita Pritam, who left Lahore for India in 1947. In it she calls on the 18th-century poet of Heer to witness the suffering of Punjab. The poem is loved on both sides of the border, and Pritam remained popular in Pakistan all her life.
  • "Toba Tek Singh" (1955), an Urdu short story by Saadat Hasan Manto. It follows patients in a mental hospital in Lahore who are to be divided between India and Pakistan a few years after Partition, and one man who cannot accept that his home village has been assigned to a country. Critics read it as a bitter satire of the whole process.
  • Train to Pakistan (1956), an English novel by Khushwant Singh, set in a fictional village on the new border where Sikhs and Muslims had lived side by side, until trains full of the dead begin to arrive.

Notice the link the Story Web will show you: Amrita Pritam's 1947 poem talks directly to Waris Shah's 1766 Heer. A Partition poem reached back nearly two centuries to a shared Punjabi classic, to say that the land being split had one literature.

docs.title: 14.10 South Asian English Writing
docs.text:
South Asian English Writing is literature written in English by writers from South Asia and its diaspora, as well as works translated into English that reach readers worldwide. Some milestones:

  • 1905: Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, a Muslim writer and reformer born in 1880 in Pairaband, Rangpur (now in Bangladesh), published "Sultana's Dream" in English in a Madras magazine. It imagines "Ladyland," where women run the country and scientists use solar power and flying cars. It is one of the earliest feminist science fiction stories anywhere. Bangladesh marks her birthday, 9 December, as Rokeya Day.
  • 1930s onward: R. K. Narayan (1906 to 2001) created Malgudi, a fictional South Indian town, in his first novel, Swami and Friends, and returned to it again and again. His stories focus on the everyday lives of ordinary people.
  • 1981: Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children, about a boy born at the very moment of India's independence, won the Booker Prize.
  • 2022: Shehan Karunatilaka, from Sri Lanka, won the Booker Prize for The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida, a darkly comic story about a war photographer's ghost in Colombo in 1990, during the civil war.

Translation is also bringing more South Asian books to English readers. The International Booker Prize honors books translated into English. In 2022 Tomb of Sand by Geetanjali Shree, translated from Hindi by Daisy Rockwell, became the first book translated from an Indian language to win it. In 2025 Heart Lamp, Banu Mushtaq's short stories about Muslim women in southern India, translated from Kannada by Deepa Bhasthi, became the first Kannada book and the first story collection to win.

People still debate English's place. Some argue that writing in the colonizers' language cuts writers off from the people they describe. Others answer that English is now a South Asian language too, and that, along with translation, it carries stories to readers who never learned Bangla, Urdu or Kannada.

Your languages count

If you understand your family's language better than you speak it, like Zara does with Bangla, you already have a way into two literatures. Even reading one translated poem or story from your heritage language is a real start.

On the bus home, Zara thinks about her Nanu's golpo, Tagore's songs, Nazrul's rebel poem and Rokeya's Ladyland. They all belong to one Bengali literature, in Bangla and in English, on both sides of a border that didn't exist when most of them were written. She decides the South Asian Student Association needs a story night.
