docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the stories, poems and books they grew up with: bedtime stories, a poet or song they love, and books they read in school. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Ask if you can record or take notes. If they mention a poem or song, write down its title and the poet's name rather than trying to copy the whole thing, and look it up together afterward.

Questions to ask

  1. What stories did someone tell you at bedtime or when you were small? Who told them?
  2. Do you remember a story with talking animals, a clever trickster, or a hero from an epic? How did it go when you heard it?
  3. Is there a poet or a song you love? What is its title, and when do you think of it?
  4. What books or poems did you study in school back home? Which one stuck with you?
  5. Have you heard the same story told differently by someone from another region, faith or country? How has the way you tell it changed since you moved, or since you were young?
  6. Which story would you most like me to remember and someday tell my own kids?

Listen for: signs of Oral Tradition (a story they only know from hearing it), tellings of the Ramayana or Mahabharata, animal fables like the Panchatantra or Jataka Tales, and names like Rabindranath Tagore, Kazi Nazrul Islam, Allama Iqbal or Mirza Ghalib.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare the bedtime story your elder told with a friend's. Did either story come from an epic or a fable collection in this chapter? Find one detail that changed between your two tellings and explain what it might tell you about the place, faith or family it came from.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: There is one true Ramayana, and other versions are copies or mistakes. Reality: Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana is the oldest well-known telling, but the story has been retold for centuries in Tamil, Bangla, Awadhi, Nepali, Thai, Javanese, Malay and more, plus Buddhist and Jain tellings. Scholars such as A. K. Ramanujan call them "tellings" because each is a real performance of the story for its own audience.

Myth: South Asian literature is all religious. Reality: Some of the most famous works are sacred texts, but the region also has Sangam love and war poems, Kalidasa's romantic plays, Ghalib's witty ghazals and letters, Akbar and Birbal comedies, Rokeya's feminist science fiction, Partition stories and modern novels about everyday life.

Myth: Urdu poetry is only about romantic love. Reality: The ghazal began as love poetry, but Mirza Ghalib used it for philosophy, doubt and loss, and Allama Iqbal wrote Urdu and Persian poems about selfhood, faith and politics. Urdu literature also includes Manto's sharp Partition stories.

Myth: Writing in English isn't "real" South Asian literature. Reality: South Asians have written in English for more than a century, from Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain's "Sultana's Dream" (1905) to Booker Prize winners from India and Sri Lanka. Translation into English, such as the International Booker winners of 2022 and 2025, also carries Hindi and Kannada stories to readers worldwide.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What is oral tradition, and why does it lead to many versions of the same story?

Oral tradition is passing stories and poems from person to person by speaking, singing and memorizing. Because each performer adapts the story for a new audience, details change from teller to teller and place to place.

2. How is the Bhagavad Gita related to the Mahabharata?

The Bhagavad Gita is a section of about 700 verses inside the Mahabharata's sixth book. It is the conversation between Krishna and Arjuna just before the great battle.

3. Name two places outside South Asia where the Panchatantra's stories traveled, and what the Arabic version is called.

The stories went to Persia (in a Middle Persian translation around 550 CE) and the Arab world, and from there to Europe. The Arabic version, translated by Ibn al-Muqaffa around 750 CE, is called Kalila wa Dimna.

4. Which poet's words are used in the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh?

Rabindranath Tagore wrote both "Jana Gana Mana" (India) and "Amar Sonar Bangla" (Bangladesh). He also won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.

5. What does Amrita Pritam's Partition poem have to do with an 18th-century poet?

Her 1947 Punjabi poem calls on Waris Shah, who wrote the famous Heer in 1766, to witness the suffering of Punjab during Partition. It links a Partition poem to a classic shared by Punjabis in both India and Pakistan.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List three languages, other than Sanskrit, in which the Ramayana has been retold, and name the poet for each.

    Answer

    Any three of: Tamil (Kamban, 12th century), Bangla (Krittibas Ojha, about 15th century), Awadhi (Tulsidas, 16th century), Nepali (Bhanubhakta Acharya, 19th century).

  2. Match each poet to the country that honors him as its national poet: Kazi Nazrul Islam, Allama Iqbal.

    Answer

    Kazi Nazrul Islam is the national poet of Bangladesh. Allama Iqbal is the national poet of Pakistan.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain the difference between akam and puram poems in Sangam Literature.

    Answer

    Akam ("inner") poems are about love and private feelings such as longing and separation. Puram ("outer") poems are about public life, such as kings, war, generosity and fame.

  2. Explain why A. K. Ramanujan preferred the word "tellings" to "versions."

    Answer

    "Version" suggests there is one original and everything else is a copy. "Telling" treats each Ramayana as a real performance of the story in its own language and setting, with Valmiki's as one telling among many.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Story Web to find every work in the 1700 to 1947 column that is written in Bangla. For each one, write the link the sim shows and the reason for it. Hint: use the language menu, then click each lit dot.

  2. Your little cousin asks why Birbal is in stories with Emperor Akbar if "they're just cartoons." Using facts from 14.5, write a three-sentence answer that separates the real Birbal from the folk tales. Hint: think about dates, and when the stories spread.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the journey of the Ramayana with the journey of the Panchatantra. How are the routes different, and what does each journey tell you about how stories travel (through faith, trade, translation or performance)? Hint: one moved mainly east and the other mainly west.

  2. Tagore, Nazrul and Iqbal were all born in British India, but today they are honored by different countries. Analyze how the borders drawn in 1947 and 1971 changed the way each poet is remembered. Hint: look at the "Countries that honor him" column in the table in 14.8.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Some say students should read South Asian literature only in the original languages, not in translation. Evaluate this claim. What is gained and lost in translation? Hint: think about Heart Lamp, Tomb of Sand and your own family's language.

  2. Delhi University removed A. K. Ramanujan's essay from a course in 2011 after objections. Was that a reasonable decision? Give arguments on at least two sides before stating your own view respectfully. Hint: consider academic study and the feelings of people for whom the Ramayana is sacred.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Plan a 30-minute club "Story Night" with three short pieces from three different countries in this chapter, and write a one-sentence introduction for each. Hint: retell or summarize; don't copy long passages.

  2. Write your own short fable (150 to 250 words) in the style of the Panchatantra or the Jatakas, with animal characters and a lesson for a teen today. Then write two sentences explaining which features of the tradition you used. Hint: a frame story or a clear moral are good places to start.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Oral tradition carried South Asian stories for centuries, which is why a story like the Ramayana exists in many tellings. Ramlila and Baul songs keep oral performance alive today.
  • The Ramayana and the Mahabharata are the two great Sanskrit epics, and the Bhagavad Gita is a 700-verse section of the Mahabharata. For many Hindus these are sacred texts.
  • Animal fables traveled farther than almost any other stories: the Jatakas through Buddhist Asia, and the Panchatantra through Persia and the Arab world (as Kalila wa Dimna) to Europe.
  • Tamil Sangam poems, Kalidasa's Sanskrit plays, Kabir's verses and Ghalib's Urdu ghazals show the range of classical and devotional poetry across languages and faiths.
  • Tagore, Nazrul and Iqbal became national symbols of India, Bangladesh and Pakistan, yet each crossed borders: Tagore wrote two nations' anthems, and Iqbal's song is still sung in India.
  • Partition literature by Pritam, Manto and Khushwant Singh focuses on ordinary people caught in 1947, while South Asian English writing and translation now carry the region's stories worldwide.

You followed the stories!

You can now trace a story from a Sanskrit epic to a Javanese palace, or from a Punjabi love tale to a Partition poem. Next, in Chapter 15, the stories jump onto the big screen and the cricket pitch, from Bollywood and Lollywood to the India-Pakistan rivalry.

docs.title: Quiz: Stories and Literature
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 14. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What is the Bhagavad Gita?

  1. A separate epic that tells the story of Rama's exile
  2. A collection of Buddhist animal fables in Pali
  3. A section of about 700 verses inside the Mahabharata
  4. A book of Urdu ghazals written in Mughal Delhi
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The Bhagavad Gita is a conversation between Krishna and Arjuna found in the sixth book of the Mahabharata. It is not a separate Rama story. That is the Ramayana.

Concept Tested: Bhagavad Gita Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which poet is honored as the national poet of Pakistan?

  1. Allama Iqbal
  2. Kazi Nazrul Islam
  3. Rabindranath Tagore
  4. Kabir
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Allama Iqbal (1877 to 1938), born in Sialkot, is Pakistan's national poet, and his birthday is a public holiday there. Kazi Nazrul Islam is the national poet of Bangladesh, a common mix-up because both wrote in the early 1900s.

Concept Tested: Allama Iqbal Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
What is the Arabic version of the Panchatantra called?

  1. Ramakien
  2. Shah Jo Risalo
  3. Kakawin Ramayana
  4. Kalila wa Dimna
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Ibn al-Muqaffa translated the fables into Arabic around 750 CE as Kalila wa Dimna, named after two jackals. The Ramakien and the Kakawin Ramayana are tellings of the Ramayana in Thailand and Java, not of the Panchatantra.

Concept Tested: Panchatantra Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why do scholars say there are many "tellings" of the Ramayana rather than one original and many copies?

  1. Because Valmiki's Sanskrit text was lost and no one knows what it said
  2. Because the story lived for centuries in performance and was retold in many languages for different audiences
  3. Because every telling was written by the same poet at different times in his life
  4. Because the Ramayana was first written in English and later translated
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Through oral tradition and later retellings in Tamil, Bangla, Awadhi, Nepali, Thai, Javanese and more, each telling became a real performance of the story for its own audience. Valmiki's text survives, so A is wrong. It is one telling among many.

Concept Tested: Ramayana Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
What is the difference between akam and puram poems in Sangam Literature?

  1. Akam poems are in Sanskrit; puram poems are in Tamil
  2. Akam poems are religious hymns; puram poems are comic stories
  3. Akam poems are about love and inner feelings; puram poems are about public life, such as war and kings
  4. Akam poems were written down; puram poems were only spoken
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. "Akam" means inner and covers love, and "puram" means outer and covers public life. Both kinds are Tamil, so A is wrong.

Concept Tested: Sangam Literature Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Which statement best describes the Akbar and Birbal Tales?

  1. They are folk tales about a real courtier of Emperor Akbar, and most of them spread centuries after he lived
  2. They are a Sanskrit epic composed before the Mughal Empire existed
  3. They were written by Birbal himself as a record of his life at court
  4. They are Buddhist stories about the Buddha's earlier lives
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Birbal (1528 to 1586) was a real member of Akbar's court, but most of the funny tales about him spread later, mainly in the 1800s. They are folk tales, not a record Birbal wrote.

Concept Tested: Akbar and Birbal Tales Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
At a club story night, a member reads a poem whose couplets each end with the same repeated phrase, and each couplet makes sense on its own. Which form is she most likely reading?

  1. A Jataka tale
  2. A ghazal
  3. An epic
  4. A frame story
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A ghazal is built from separate two-line couplets that share a rhyme and a repeated ending phrase. Mirza Ghalib is its most famous Urdu master. An epic is a long continuous narrative, not a set of stand-alone couplets.

Concept Tested: Mirza Ghalib Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Zara wants to add a South Asian work written in English to her club's reading list, from a writer born in what is now Bangladesh. Which work fits best?

  1. "Bidrohi" by Kazi Nazrul Islam
  2. "Toba Tek Singh" by Saadat Hasan Manto
  3. Gitanjali in its original Bengali
  4. "Sultana's Dream" by Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, born in Rangpur in today's Bangladesh, published "Sultana's Dream" in English in 1905. "Bidrohi" is a Bangla poem and "Toba Tek Singh" is an Urdu story, so they don't meet the English requirement.

Concept Tested: South Asian English Writing Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Amrita Pritam's 1947 Punjabi poem calls on Waris Shah, who wrote Heer in 1766. What does this link best show about Partition Literature?

  1. That Partition writers mostly ignored older literature
  2. That Punjabi literature only began after 1947
  3. That writers used a classic shared on both sides of the new border to mourn the splitting of one land and culture
  4. That Partition poems were mainly about romantic love, like Heer
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. By calling on the poet of a classic loved across Punjab, Pritam treated the divided land as having one shared literature and asked its old poet to witness the suffering. The poem is about Partition's suffering, not romance, so D is wrong.

Concept Tested: Partition Literature Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Tagore wrote India's and Bangladesh's anthems, and one of Iqbal's early Urdu songs is still sung in India. What does this pattern best suggest?

  1. That only Indian poets are remembered outside their home countries
  2. That poets' work can belong to several countries, because their lives began before the borders of 1947 and 1971 were drawn
  3. That national poets are chosen at random
  4. That poetry has little to do with national identity
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Tagore, Nazrul and Iqbal were all born in British India, so their work crosses today's borders even though each is honored as a national symbol. Iqbal is Pakistan's national poet yet his song is popular in India, which shows A is wrong.

Concept Tested: Rabindranath Tagore Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Stories and Literature
docs.text:
1. Rabindranath Tagore: Facts - NobelPrize.org - The official record of Tagore's 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, with his dates and the prize citation. Its linked pages include his Nobel lecture and a short biography.

  2. Ramlila, the traditional performance of the Ramayana - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - Explains how Ramlila plays based on Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas are staged across northern India at Dussehra, and why UNESCO listed them in 2008. A clear example of oral tradition that is still alive.

  3. Baul songs - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage - Describes the Baul minstrels of Bangladesh and West Bengal, their instruments, and how their songs are passed on orally from teacher to student.

  4. Kalila and Dimna (manuscript, Egypt, about 1310) - Library of Congress - A digitized illustrated Arabic manuscript of Kalila wa Dimna, the Arabic retelling of the Panchatantra, with notes on Ibn al-Muqaffa's translation and its influence on later fables. You can page through its 73 paintings.

  5. Sultana's Dream - A Celebration of Women Writers, University of Pennsylvania Digital Library - The full text of Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain's 1905 English story about "Ladyland." It is short enough to read in one sitting and is a good choice for a club story night.

  6. Why Sri Lanka named its first ever satellite after Ravana - Scroll.in - A news explainer on how Ravana is remembered in Sri Lanka, among Sinhala Buddhists and in Tamil traditions, and why historians debate the link between the epic's Lanka and today's island.

  7. Heart Lamp wins the International Booker Prize 2025 - The Booker Prizes - The prize announcement for Banu Mushtaq's Kannada short stories, translated by Deepa Bhasthi, with the "firsts" the win set for Kannada and for Indian translators.

  8. Three Hundred Ramayanas - Wikipedia - A summary of A. K. Ramanujan's essay, the five tellings it compares, and the 2011 controversy at Delhi University. Follow its citations to the essay itself.

  9. Panchatantra - Wikipedia - An overview of the fable collection's frame story and its journey through Middle Persian, Arabic and European languages, with links to scholarly translations.

  10. Sangam literature - Wikipedia - A starting point on the earliest Tamil poetry: its dates, its anthologies, and the akam and puram kinds of poems.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture
Chapter 15: Cinema, Cricket, and Pop Culture
Summary
docs.text: Movies, songs, TV dramas and sports are how many people around the world first meet South Asian culture, and how many South Asian families spend their evenings. This chapter shows that "Bollywood" is only one of many film industries, introduces the filmmaker Satyajit Ray and the cinemas of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bhutan, and explains playback singing, Pakistani dramas and Coke Studio. It follows South Asian pop as it goes global and asks how South Asians are shown in Western media. Then it teaches the basics of cricket and the India-Pakistan rivalry, plus field hockey, kabaddi and carrom.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Bollywood
  2. Regional Cinemas
  3. Satyajit Ray
  4. Pakistani Cinema
  5. Playback Singing
  6. Pakistani Dramas
  7. Coke Studio
  8. Global South Asian Pop
  9. Streaming Era
  10. Representation in Media
  11. Cricket
  12. India-Pakistan Rivalry
  13. Field Hockey
  14. Kabaddi
  15. Carrom

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts, because each film industry is built around a language.
  • Chapter 9: Music, for film music (filmi) and the classical and folk traditions it borrows from.
  • Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition, for the history behind cricket's arrival and the India-Pakistan rivalry.

Lights, Camera, Cricket!

Hi, I'm Mora! The movies your family watches on weekends, the songs at every wedding, and the cricket match that makes your uncle shout at the TV are culture too, and they're the culture your friends are most likely to ask you about. This chapter gives you the background to explain them, and to enjoy them more.

docs.title: 15.1 "So What's an Over?"
docs.text:
It's a Sunday morning, and the South Asian Student Association is having a watch party in Ms. Okafor's classroom. A cricket match is streaming on the projector, and two club members are already arguing. Ayesha Qureshi, whose family is from Lahore, Pakistan, says the best India-Pakistan match ever was the 2017 Champions Trophy final, when Pakistan beat India by 180 runs in London. Simran Kaur Gill, the club's treasurer, whose grandparents are from Ludhiana, India, insists it was the 2007 T20 World Cup final, which India won. They have clearly had this argument before.

Ben Lindqvist has been watching for twenty minutes. He plays hockey and understands periods, power plays and penalty boxes. But he has no idea what's happening on the screen. "Okay," he finally says. "What's an over? Why did everyone cheer when nothing happened? And why does your whole family, Zara, know the words to every song in that movie you made me watch?"

Zara Hossain laughs. Her Nanu watches Bangladeshi films, her dad follows cricket scores from Dhaka at 3 a.m., and her cousins in London send her Pakistani dramas and Coke Studio songs. She realizes Ben is asking a real question: how do movies, music and sports tie together a region of eight countries, and millions of people far from home?

docs.title: 15.2 Not Just Bollywood
docs.text:
Start with something Ben already knows. "Hollywood" means the big American film studios in Los Angeles. But nobody thinks Hollywood is the same as all film made in English, or all film made in North America. Britain, Canada and Australia have their own film industries, and so do Sweden and Norway, where Ben's family comes from.

South Asia works the same way, only with many more languages.

Bollywood is the popular name for the Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai (formerly Bombay). The word blends "Bombay" and "Hollywood." Bollywood is the best known South Asian film industry outside the region, famous for big stars, long running times, and song-and-dance numbers. But Bollywood means Hindi films only. It is a common mistake to use "Bollywood" for all Indian films, or all South Asian films.

Indian film history starts before sound. Raja Harishchandra (1913), a silent film by Dadasaheb Phalke, is often considered the first full-length Indian feature film. Alam Ara (1931), directed by Ardeshir Irani, was India's first sound film, and it opened the way for songs to become a central part of Indian movies.

docs.title: Regional Cinemas
docs.text:
Regional Cinemas are the film industries that make movies in South Asia's many other languages, each with its own stars, studios, history and fans. Many have their own nicknames, often built on the "-ollywood" pattern.

Industry Language Main center One early landmark Bollywood Hindi Mumbai, India Raja Harishchandra (1913, silent); Alam Ara (1931, first Indian sound film) Telugu cinema ("Tollywood") Telugu Hyderabad, India Bhishma Pratigna (1921), generally called the first Telugu feature Tamil cinema ("Kollywood") Tamil Chennai, India Kalidas (1931), the first sound film with Tamil in it Kannada cinema ("Sandalwood") Kannada Bengaluru, India Sati Sulochana (1934), the first Kannada talkie Malayalam cinema ("Mollywood") Malayalam Kerala, India Vigathakumaran (released 1930), the first Malayalam feature Bengali cinema ("Tollywood") Bengali Tollygunge, Kolkata, India Pather Panchali (1955) by Satyajit Ray Bangladeshi cinema ("Dhallywood") Bangla Dhaka, Bangladesh Mukh O Mukhosh (1956), first Bengali feature made in what is now Bangladesh Pakistani cinema ("Lollywood") Urdu and Punjabi Lahore, and now Karachi, Pakistan See Section 15.4 Nepali cinema Nepali and other languages of Nepal Kathmandu, Nepal Aama (1964), first film produced in Nepal Sri Lankan cinema Sinhala and Tamil Sri Lanka Kadawunu Poronduwa (1947), first Sinhala-language film Bhutanese cinema Dzongkha Thimphu, Bhutan Gasa Lamai Singye (1989), first Bhutanese feature

Notice the two "Tollywoods." The Telugu industry and the Bengali industry in Kolkata (named for the Tollygunge studio neighborhood) both use the nickname, which is a good reminder that these labels are informal. The Tamil nickname "Kollywood" comes from Kodambakkam, a Chennai neighborhood full of film studios.

How big are the regional cinemas? In 2023, India's film certification board (the Central Board of Film Certification, CBFC) listed feature films in more than 25 languages. By our count of its 2023 list (which includes dubbed versions), Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam films together outnumbered Hindi films by more than two to one. Bollywood gets the attention abroad, but it is only one part of Indian film.

Regional films also cross borders. Telugu director S. S. Rajamouli's RRR (2022) became a worldwide hit, and its song "Naatu Naatu," composed by M. M. Keeravaani with lyrics by Chandrabose, won the Academy Award for Best Original Song in 2023. That same year, the Indian documentary The Elephant Whisperers won the Oscar for Best Documentary Short Film.

Name it right

If a friend recommends a movie, ask which language it's in instead of calling it "a Bollywood movie." A Malayalam thriller and a Hindi musical are as different as a Swedish crime drama and a Hollywood blockbuster.

docs.title: 15.3 Satyajit Ray
docs.text:
Not all South Asian cinema is about stars and songs. Satyajit Ray (1921 to 1992) was a Bengali filmmaker from Kolkata who is widely considered one of the greatest directors in the history of cinema. He was also a writer, illustrator, magazine editor and composer.

Ray's first film, Pather Panchali ("Song of the Little Road," 1955), is based on a Bengali novel and follows a poor family in a village through the eyes of a young boy, Apu, and his older sister, Durga. Ray shot much of it outdoors with a small budget and mostly amateur actors, and the sitar player Ravi Shankar wrote the music. Production stopped again and again for lack of money; the West Bengal government finally helped fund it. Pather Panchali became the first part of the Apu Trilogy (1955 to 1959), which follows Apu into adulthood.

Ray's films are quiet, realistic and close to everyday life, and they have influenced filmmakers around the world. In 1992 the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences gave him an honorary Oscar for lifetime achievement. Ray was too ill to travel, so he accepted it by video from a hospital bed in Kolkata. He died a few weeks later, on 23 April 1992.

Ray belongs to a wider tradition of art and "parallel" cinema in South Asia: films that focus on real social problems and often skip the big song numbers. Sri Lanka's Lester James Peries is another example. His film Rekava (1956), about village life and beliefs, is often described as the first Sinhala film shot entirely in Ceylon (as Sri Lanka was then called), and it was selected for the main competition at the 1957 Cannes Film Festival.

docs.title: Pakistani Cinema
docs.text:
Pakistani Cinema is the film industry of Pakistan, making films mainly in Urdu and Punjabi, with Pashto films made in Peshawar. From independence in 1947 until the 2000s, its center was Lahore, and the industry there was nicknamed "Lollywood" (Lahore plus Hollywood). Lahore's studios struggled badly by around 2000, and many filmmakers moved to Karachi, which has since become a major center of new Pakistani film.

In the 2010s and 2020s, a new generation of Pakistani filmmakers drew attention at home and abroad:

  • The Legend of Maula Jatt (2022), directed by Bilal Lashari, is a Punjabi-language action epic based on characters from a famous 1979 film, Maula Jatt.
  • Joyland (2022), directed by Saim Sadiq, became the first Pakistani film in the official selection of the Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Jury Prize in the Un Certain Regard section.

docs.title: Pakistani Dramas
docs.text:
Many South Asians would say Pakistan's biggest screen export is not its films but its TV. Pakistani Dramas are Pakistani television serials, usually in Urdu, known for family stories, romance and social issues, and for running a set number of episodes instead of going on for years.

One famous example is Humsafar (2011 to 2012), a 23-episode drama on Hum TV based on a novel by Farhat Ishtiaq and starring Fawad Khan and Mahira Khan. In 2014 an Indian channel called Zindagi launched and began airing Pakistani dramas, including Humsafar, for Indian audiences, and promoted their short runs compared with India's very long serials. Today many families in the diaspora, like Zara's cousins in London, watch Pakistani dramas online.

Whose Story?

The same films and songs mean different things on different sides of a border. Many films made in Lahore and Bombay before 1947 belong to the shared history of both India and Pakistan, and stars, singers and writers crossed between the two industries in the early years. Before 1971, films made in Dhaka were part of Pakistani cinema; in Bangladesh today, that period is remembered as the start of Bangladeshi film. Politics has often decided who could watch what: after the 1965 war, for example, Pakistan banned Indian films in its cinemas, and political tensions have shaped what audiences on both sides could see ever since. Fans in the diaspora, watching on the same streaming services in Minnesota or London, often feel these borders less sharply than their grandparents did.

docs.title: 15.5 Playback Singing
docs.text:
In most song scenes in South Asian movies, the actor on screen isn't really singing. That surprises a lot of people who are new to these films.

Playback Singing is the practice of recording songs with professional singers, called playback singers, whose voices are then played back while actors lip-sync on camera. Playback singers don't appear in the scene, but in South Asia many of them are as famous as the actors, sometimes more. Many Indian and Pakistani films typically include six or seven songs.

A few of the best known:

  • Lata Mangeshkar (India) recorded songs in more than 36 Indian languages over a career of decades and received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honor, in 2001.
  • Asha Bhosle (India), Lata Mangeshkar's sister, was recognized by Guinness World Records in 2011 as the most recorded artist in music history.
  • Noor Jehan (Pakistan) was a singer and actress whose career began before Partition and continued for decades in Pakistan. She recorded songs in Urdu, Punjabi and Sindhi, and in 1951 became Pakistan's first female film director.
  • Runa Laila (Bangladesh) began her career in Pakistani films in the late 1960s and became popular across Bangladesh, Pakistan and India.
  • Mohammed Rafi (India) and Ahmed Rushdi (Pakistan) are often named as two of the most influential male playback singers.

Film songs, often called filmi (फ़िल्मी, FIL-mee, "of the films") music, have been South Asia's main pop music for most of the last century. They play at weddings, on buses, in shops and in cars, which is why Zara's family knows every word. (You'll find more on filmi music in Chapter 9.)

docs.title: 15.6 Coke Studio, Global Pop, Streaming and Representation
Coke Studio
docs.text: Coke Studio is a TV and online music series in which established and new artists perform live studio recordings, often mixing folk, Sufi, classical, rock and pop. The idea started in Brazil, but Coke Studio Pakistan, launched in 2008 and first produced by Rohail Hyatt, a former member of the band Vital Signs, became the most famous version. It is the longest-running annual TV music show in Pakistan. Its songs, which often pair singers from different regions and generations, have drawn huge audiences online across South Asia and the diaspora.

docs.title: Global South Asian Pop
docs.text:
Global South Asian Pop is South Asian music, film and entertainment that reaches audiences around the world, including people with no South Asian background. Some milestones:

Year Milestone 2009 Slumdog Millionaire, a British film set in Mumbai, wins eight Oscars; A. R. Rahman wins two (Original Score, and Original Song for "Jai Ho" with lyricist Gulzar), and Resul Pookutty shares the award for Sound Mixing 2022 Pakistani American singer Arooj Aftab wins a Grammy for Best Global Music Performance for "Mohabbat," widely reported as the first Pakistani woman to win a Grammy 2022 Bhutan's Lunana: A Yak in the Classroom is nominated for the Oscar for Best International Feature Film 2023 "Naatu Naatu" from RRR wins the Oscar for Best Original Song 2023 Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh performs at the Coachella music festival in California, widely reported as the first Punjabi artist to do so

Bhangra beats, Punjabi pop and Bollywood dance have also become regular parts of college dance competitions and weddings across North America and the UK, performed by teams that include plenty of people like Ben.

docs.title: The Streaming Era
docs.text:
Streaming Era describes the period, mainly since the late 2010s, when films and TV shows began reaching audiences through online services such as Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+ and YouTube instead of only through theaters and TV channels. For South Asian entertainment, streaming changed two things. First, a Malayalam thriller or a Pakistani drama can now be watched with subtitles anywhere in the world on the day it comes out. Second, streaming services began paying for new South Asian shows, so audiences abroad can find stories in many languages, not just Hindi.

For diaspora families, streaming has replaced the stacks of rented DVDs and videotapes that many parents remember. Zara's Nanu watches Bangladeshi films on her tablet, with Zara helping her find them.

docs.title: Representation in Media
docs.text:
Representation in Media is about how a group of people is shown on screen and in the news: how often they appear, what roles they play, who writes their stories, and whether the portrayals are accurate or rely on stereotypes.

For decades, South Asians on American TV were rare and often stereotyped. A well-known example is Apu, the convenience-store owner on The Simpsons, voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria. In 2017, comedian Hari Kondabolu made a documentary, The Problem with Apu, arguing that the character's accent and storylines reinforced stereotypes. In 2020, Azaria announced he would stop voicing Apu.

Since then, South Asian characters created by South Asian writers have become more common:

  • Never Have I Ever (Netflix, 2020 to 2023), co-created by Mindy Kaling, followed Devi, a Tamil Indian American teen in California.
  • Ms. Marvel (Disney+, 2022) made Kamala Khan, a Pakistani American teen in Jersey City, a Marvel superhero on screen.
  • British Pakistani actor Riz Ahmed was nominated for the Oscar for Best Actor in 2021 for Sound of Metal.

Representation is not "solved." Many South Asian Americans point out that most roles still come from a few backgrounds, that some communities (such as Bangladeshi, Nepali or Sri Lankan Americans) rarely appear at all, and that stereotypes still show up.

Count it yourself

Pick the last five shows or movies you watched. How many South Asian characters were there, what languages did they speak, and who wrote them? A simple count like that is how media researchers start.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
Cricket is a bat-and-ball game played between two teams of eleven players on a large oval field. At its center is the pitch, a strip 22 yards (20.12 m) long with a set of three wooden stumps, called a wicket, at each end. One team bats while the other bowls and fields, and then they switch.

If you know baseball, a rough comparison helps. The bowler is like the pitcher, but runs up and bowls the ball with a straight arm, usually bouncing it off the pitch. The batter defends the wicket and tries to hit the ball. Unlike baseball, there's no foul territory: the batter can hit the ball in any direction, all the way around the field.

Scoring works like this:

  • After hitting the ball, the two batters can run between the wickets. Each time they swap ends, they score 1 run.
  • If the ball reaches the boundary rope after bouncing, that's 4 runs. If it crosses the boundary without bouncing, that's 6 runs.
  • A batter is out in several ways. For example, they're bowled if the ball hits the stumps, and caught if a fielder catches the hit before it bounces.

And here's the answer to Ben's question. An over is a set of 6 legal balls bowled by one bowler from one end of the pitch. After each over, the next over is bowled from the other end, and the rules say the same bowler cannot bowl two overs in a row. If a bowler sends down a wide, a ball too far from the batter to hit, the batting side gets 1 extra run and the ball doesn't count toward the six, so it has to be bowled again. That's why everyone cheered when "nothing happened": a dot ball (no runs) under pressure, or a wide that gave away a free run, can be a big moment.

docs.title: Three formats
docs.text:
Cricket comes in different lengths, which is why some matches take an evening and others take days.

Format Overs per side How long it takes Test cricket No limit (up to two innings each) Up to five days One Day International (ODI) 50 overs About a day Twenty20 (T20) 20 overs About three to four hours

docs.title: Cricket across South Asia
docs.text:
The British brought cricket to South Asia during colonial rule, and over the 20th century people across the region made it their own. Today it is a national passion in India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and it has a growing following in Afghanistan and Nepal.

  • Bangladesh became the tenth Test-playing nation on 26 June 2000, and played its first Test against India in Dhaka that November.
  • Afghanistan's team grew up largely among refugees: many of its first players learned the game in camps in Pakistan in the 1980s and 1990s. Afghanistan became a full member of the International Cricket Council (ICC), with Test status, in 2017, and reached the semi-finals of the 2024 T20 World Cup.
  • Nepal played its first One Day International, against the Netherlands, in August 2018.

South Asian teams have won many of cricket's biggest titles (as of October 2026):

Tournament South Asian winners Men's Cricket World Cup (ODI) India (1983, 2011), Pakistan (1992), Sri Lanka (1996) Men's T20 World Cup India (2007, 2024, 2026), Pakistan (2009), Sri Lanka (2014) Women's Cricket World Cup (ODI) India (2025, its first title)

The 2024 Men's T20 World Cup was co-hosted by the United States and the West Indies, and the India-Pakistan match was played at a new stadium in Nassau County, New York. Many of cricket's fans in the US are South Asian Americans, and you might find a cricket league in your own city.

Try it out

You don't need a real pitch to learn cricket. A tennis ball, a flat piece of wood and a trash can for a wicket is how millions of kids in South Asia learned in streets and parking lots.

docs.title: The India-Pakistan Rivalry
docs.text:
The India-Pakistan Rivalry is the competition between the national cricket teams of India and Pakistan, often called the most intense rivalry in the sport. The two teams first played Test matches in 1952, when Pakistan toured India. Politics has shaped the rivalry ever since. No cricket was played between them from 1962 to 1977, a period that included the wars of 1965 and 1971. Cricket has also been used for diplomacy, with leaders and fans crossing the border for matches.

The last full tour with Test matches was Pakistan's tour of India in 2007. After the 2008 Mumbai attacks, bilateral cricket almost stopped: the only series since then was a short one-day and T20 series in India in 2012 to 2013, so the two teams now meet mostly at ICC tournaments and the Asia Cup.

When they do meet, huge audiences watch, and families in the diaspora, including Indian and Pakistani families who are friends and neighbors, often watch together. Ayesha and Simran's argument is part of the fun: each side has its favorite victories, like Pakistan's win in the 2017 Champions Trophy final and India's in the 2007 T20 World Cup final.

Cricket's history in South Asia also includes hard stories about caste and community. Palwankar Baloo (1876 to 1955), born into a Dalit family, was one of the best Indian bowlers of the early 1900s and toured England in 1911. Yet at some matches he was served tea outside the pavilion in a disposable cup while his teammates drank inside. Historians use his story to show how caste discrimination (see Chapter 13) reached even the cricket field.

docs.title: 15.8 Hockey, Kabaddi and Carrom
docs.text: Cricket isn't the only sport people love in South Asia.

docs.title: Field Hockey
docs.text: Field Hockey is a team sport played on grass or artificial turf with curved sticks and a hard ball, eleven players a side. (Ben's ice hockey is a cousin.) For decades, India and Pakistan dominated Olympic field hockey. India's men's team won Olympic gold eight times (1928, 1932, 1936, 1948, 1952, 1956, 1964 and 1980), and Pakistan's men's team won gold three times (1960, 1968 and 1984). In the 1960 final in Rome, Pakistan beat India. After a long gap, India's men won bronze medals at the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Olympics.

docs.title: Kabaddi
docs.text: Kabaddi (Hindi कबड्डी, Bangla কাবাডি, kuh-BUD-dee) is a contact team sport, seven players a side, that combines tag and wrestling. One player, the raider, runs into the other team's half, tries to tag defenders, and must get back to their own side without being tackled, traditionally while chanting "kabaddi, kabaddi" in one breath. Kabaddi was named the national sport of Bangladesh in 1972. It became part of the Asian Games in 1990, and India's professional Pro Kabaddi League, launched in 2014, turned it into a TV sport with big crowds. A circle-style version, often called Punjabi kabaddi, is played on a round field and is popular in Punjab and the Punjabi diaspora.

docs.title: Carrom
docs.text:
Carrom is a tabletop game of Indian origin in which players flick a heavy disc, the striker, to knock smaller wooden pieces into the four corner pockets of a square board. It's a bit like pool played with fingers. Carrom is played by families, at parties and in clubs and cafés across South Asia. Sri Lanka and India both formed carrom federations by 1958, and the International Carrom Federation was founded in Chennai in 1988. Many South Asian American families keep a carrom board in the basement, and it's an easy game to bring to a club meeting.

Sport Players per side Where it's especially popular One fact Cricket 11 India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Nepal An over is 6 legal balls Field hockey 11 India, Pakistan India: 8 Olympic golds; Pakistan: 3 Kabaddi 7 Bangladesh, India, Punjab region National sport of Bangladesh since 1972 Carrom 2 or 4 players Homes and clubs across South Asia International federation founded in Chennai, 1988

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the movies, music, TV and sports they grew up with. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Ask them to pick one favorite song or film scene, and watch or listen to it together before you start your questions. Ask if it's okay to take notes.

Questions to ask

  1. What was the first film you remember seeing in a theater? Who took you, and what was the theater like?
  2. Who was your favorite actor or singer when you were my age? Why?
  3. Do you have a cricket (or hockey, or kabaddi) memory you'll never forget? Where were you, and who were you with?
  4. What TV shows or dramas did the whole family watch together?
  5. How has the way you watch movies and sports changed, from theaters and TV to videotapes, DVDs and streaming, or after moving to a new country?
  6. Is there a film, song or sport you hope I'll love the way you do?

Listen for: whether their favorite films came from Bollywood or one of the Regional Cinemas; names of Playback Singing stars; stories about Cricket or the India-Pakistan Rivalry; and how the Streaming Era changed their habits.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Compare your elder's favorite films and songs with a friend's elder from a different country or language group. Did they grow up with the same industry, or different ones? Did any song or star cross the border between them?

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Bollywood means all Indian films. Reality: Bollywood is the Hindi-language industry in Mumbai. India also has large Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali, Marathi and other industries; in 2023 India certified films in more than 25 languages. Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bhutan have their own cinemas too.

Myth: Cricket is only an Indian sport. Reality: Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and Nepal all have national teams, and Pakistan and Sri Lanka have each won the men's World Cup. The game also has big followings in England, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand and the Caribbean, and is growing in the United States.

Myth: South Asian pop culture is only for South Asians. Reality: "Naatu Naatu" won an Oscar, Arooj Aftab won a Grammy, and Diljit Dosanjh played Coachella. Plenty of fans with no South Asian background love these films, songs and sports, and many dance teams and cricket clubs welcome everyone.

Myth: Representation of South Asians in Western media is now solved. Reality: There are more South Asian characters and creators than twenty years ago, but many communities still rarely appear on screen, and stereotypes haven't disappeared.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What does the word 'Bollywood' refer to?

The Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai. The name blends "Bombay" and "Hollywood." It does not include India's other language industries.

2. What is an over in cricket?

A set of 6 legal balls bowled by one bowler from one end of the pitch. Wides and no-balls don't count toward the six.

3. What is playback singing?

Songs are recorded by professional singers, then played back while actors lip-sync on screen. Many playback singers are as famous as the stars.

4. Why did Satyajit Ray receive an honorary Oscar in 1992?

For his lifetime achievement in filmmaking. His realistic films, starting with Pather Panchali (1955), influenced directors around the world.

5. Which sport is the national sport of Bangladesh, and how does a raid work?

Kabaddi. A raider enters the other team's half, tries to tag defenders, and must return to their own side without being tackled.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Name four film industries in South Asia other than Bollywood, with the language each uses.

    Answer

    Any four, such as Telugu (Hyderabad), Tamil (Chennai), Kannada (Bengaluru), Malayalam (Kerala), Bengali (Kolkata), Bangla (Dhaka, Bangladesh), Urdu and Punjabi (Lahore and Karachi, Pakistan), Nepali (Kathmandu), Sinhala and Tamil (Sri Lanka), Dzongkha (Bhutan).

  2. Which South Asian countries have won the men's Cricket World Cup (ODI), and in which years?

    Answer

    India (1983 and 2011), Pakistan (1992) and Sri Lanka (1996).

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why there are two "Bengali" film industries.

    Answer

    Bengali (Bangla) is spoken in both the Indian state of West Bengal and in Bangladesh. Since 1947, and Bangladesh's independence in 1971, each side of the border has had its own film industry: one centered in Kolkata and one in Dhaka.

  2. Explain why a wide in cricket gives the batting team a run but makes the over longer.

    Answer

    A wide is a ball the batter can't reach, so the batting side gets 1 extra run as a penalty, and because it isn't a legal ball it doesn't count toward the six balls of the over, so another ball must be bowled.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Bollywood is the Hindi film industry in Mumbai; South Asia's regional cinemas in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali and other languages, plus the cinemas of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bhutan, are just as much a part of the story.
  • Satyajit Ray showed the world a realistic, quiet kind of South Asian film and received an honorary Oscar in 1992.
  • Pakistani cinema moved from Lahore toward Karachi, and Pakistani dramas and Coke Studio became some of Pakistan's most loved cultural exports.
  • Playback singing made singers like Lata Mangeshkar, Noor Jehan and Runa Laila stars across borders.
  • Global South Asian pop, the streaming era and new South Asian creators have changed representation in media, but the work isn't finished.
  • Cricket is built on overs of 6 legal balls, comes in Test, ODI and T20 formats, and is shared across the region; the India-Pakistan rivalry is shaped by history and politics as well as sport.
  • Field hockey, kabaddi and carrom are also part of South Asia's sporting life. Hockey brought India and Pakistan Olympic golds, and carrom is played in homes across the region.

That's a wrap!

You can now explain an over, name a dozen film industries, and settle (or start) a debate at the next watch party. Next, in Chapter 16, we'll trade the cricket field for the classroom and look at the numbers and ideas that came from South Asia.

The rivalry has been shaped by history and politics, including no matches from 1962 to 1977 and no bilateral series since a short one in 2012 to 2013, so rare tournament meetings carry huge weight.   3. 13 runs, 6 legal balls

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The digits you write every day, 0 through 9, have a long history that runs through South Asia. This chapter follows that history from Brahmi numerals carved on stone, to the place value system and the zero, to the scholars who carried "Indian reckoning" to Baghdad and on to Europe. It also meets mathematicians such as Aryabhata, Brahmagupta and the Kerala School, the grammarian Panini, healing traditions like Ayurveda and Unani, the board game chaturanga, wootz steel, and modern scientists from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Along the way, it shows how historians test big claims and sometimes change their minds.
