docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia? for the eight countries and the land
  • Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition for India's independence in 1947
  • Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts for language families and the Eighth Schedule
  • Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia is helpful for the faiths mentioned here

One country, many homes

Hi, I'm Mora! India is where my own feathers come from: the peacock is India's national bird. If your family is from India, you've probably noticed that "Indian" can mean very different things to a cousin in Chennai and an uncle in Lucknow. If it isn't, India still touches your world in more ways than you might expect, even the phone in your pocket. This chapter helps you read the whole map, not just one corner of it.

docs.title: 17.1 "Like 28 Countries in One"
docs.text:
It's the first Saturday of the school year, and Arjun Reddy's cousin Kavya is visiting Minnesota from Hyderabad, in India. Arjun brings her to the South Asian Student Association's welcome picnic, where Zara Hossain is handing out samosas and Ben Lindqvist is handing out napkins (and eating most of the samosas).

Ben asks Kavya what India is like. She laughs. "Which part? India is like 28 countries in one. At home we speak Telugu. If I take the train to Bengaluru, the signs are in Kannada. My friend from Kolkata speaks Bengali, and my roommate from Delhi speaks Hindi. We all have to use English or Hindi to talk to each other sometimes." Zara jumps in: "Bengali? That's what my family speaks, and we're from Bangladesh." Kavya nods. "Exactly. Some of India's languages are also other countries' languages."

Ben is confused. He always thought India was one country with one language and one kind of food. Now he's hearing that it has dozens of languages, dozens of governments and a cousin who needs English to talk to her own roommate. So what holds India together, and what does Kavya mean by "28 countries in one"?

docs.title: 17.2 A Country the Size of a Continent
docs.text:
One way to picture it is the European Union, which has 27 member countries, more than 20 official languages, and about 450 million people. Each country has its own government, but they share some laws and many share a currency. Now imagine something with about three times as many people, more than 20 major languages, and 36 states and territories, but with one national government, one constitution, one army, one currency and one passport. That's India.

Or think about the United States, where Minnesota and Texas have their own governors and capitals inside one country. Now imagine if Minnesota's official language were Swedish and Texas's were Spanish. That's closer to India, where many states were drawn around languages.

docs.title: The Republic of India
docs.text:
The Republic of India is the official name of the country: a sovereign, democratic republic and a union of states, with an elected parliament and a constitution that has been in force since 1950. The constitution begins its very first article by naming the country twice: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." Bharat (भारत, BHAH-rut) is the Hindi name for India, borrowed from Sanskrit, and many Indians use it in everyday speech.

India became independent from British rule on 15 August 1947, as you saw in Chapter 4. It became a republic, with an elected president instead of the British king as head of state, on 26 January 1950.

docs.title: How many people?
docs.text:
India had 1,463,865,525 people in 2025 (about 1.46 billion, World Bank). It became the world's most populous country in 2023, passing China. About one in every six people on Earth lives in India.

Most Indians live in villages and small towns. In 2025, about 36% of Indians lived in cities, according to the World Bank. That still means hundreds of millions of city dwellers, in huge cities like Delhi, Mumbai (formerly Bombay), Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

India's last full census was taken in 2011. The next one is under way, with houses counted in 2026 and people counted in early 2027. Until it is finished, many of India's detailed numbers about religion and language come from 2011.

docs.title: A rulebook for a billion people
docs.text:
The Constitution of India is the supreme law of the country: the document that sets up India's government, divides power between the center and the states, and lists the rights of every citizen. It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950, a day Indians celebrate every year as Republic Day. It is famous for being one of the longest written national constitutions in the world.

The constitution was drafted by a committee chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, a lawyer and scholar who was born into a Dalit family and fought against caste discrimination all his life. Among many other things, the constitution:

  • makes all citizens equal before the law;
  • abolishes "untouchability" (Article 17), so discrimination by caste is illegal;
  • protects freedom of religion, speech and assembly;
  • names Hindi in the Devanagari script as the official language of the Union, with English continuing for official use (Article 343);
  • lists the Eighth Schedule of languages, which today has 22 languages (Chapter 6).

India is officially secular, which in India means the state has no official religion and treats all faiths equally. In the 2011 census, about 79.8% of Indians were Hindu, 14.2% Muslim, 2.3% Christian, 1.7% Sikh, 0.7% Buddhist and 0.4% Jain, with smaller Parsi, Jewish, Bahá'í and tribal-faith communities. India has one of the largest Muslim populations of any country in the world.

docs.title: Federal, but with a strong center
docs.text:
India is a federal country: power is shared between the national government (often called "the center" or "the Union") and the state governments. The constitution lists which subjects belong to whom. Defense, foreign affairs and money belong to the center. Police, public health and farming mostly belong to the states. Education is shared. Under Article 345, each state can choose its own official language or languages. That rule is the key to the states you'll meet in Section 17.6.

The Indian system gives the center more power than the American one does. For example, Parliament can create new states, change state borders or rename states by an ordinary law.

Think about it

The constitution let each state pick its own official language. Why might that help a big, many-language country stay united, instead of pulling it apart? Keep your answer in mind for Section 17.7.

docs.title: The Parliament of India
docs.text:
The Parliament of India is the national legislature, the body that makes India's laws. It has two houses, plus the president:

House Hindi name Members How they are chosen House of the People (lower house) Lok Sabha (लोकसभा, LOKE-sub-ha) 543 elected seats Directly elected by voters, one member per constituency, at least every five years Council of States (upper house) Rajya Sabha 245 today, up to 250 allowed (12 appointed by the president) Mostly elected by the members of state assemblies

India uses a parliamentary system, like the United Kingdom and unlike the United States. The prime minister, who runs the government day to day, is the leader of the party or coalition that controls a majority in the Lok Sabha. The president is head of state and has mostly ceremonial powers, acting on the advice of the prime minister and the cabinet.

As of October 2026, India's prime minister is Narendra Modi, in office since 2014 and in his third term, and its president is Droupadi Murmu, in office since 2022. President Murmu, from the Santal community, is the first person from a tribal community to hold the office. Parliament meets in New Delhi, in a new Parliament building opened in May 2023.

docs.title: Elections in India
docs.text:
Elections in India are the regular votes, run by the independent Election Commission of India, in which adult citizens choose members of Parliament and of state assemblies. Every citizen aged 18 or older can vote.

The 2024 general election shows the size of it. Voting took place in seven phases between 19 April and 1 June 2024, and results were announced on 4 June. About 968 million people were registered to vote, and about 642 million voted, the largest number of voters in any election in history. Turnout at polling stations was 65.79%, according to the Election Commission. The highest turnout was in Lakshadweep, at 84.16%, and the lowest in Bihar, at 56.19%.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won 240 seats, short of a majority on its own, and formed a coalition government, the National Democratic Alliance, with 293 seats. The opposition alliance, called INDIA and led by the Indian National Congress, won 234 seats. Like any democracy's, India's politics is lively and argued over; this book describes how the system works and leaves the arguments to the news.

Each state also elects its own legislative assembly, which chooses a chief minister, the state's head of government.

docs.title: 17.5 New Delhi
docs.text:
New Delhi is the capital of India and the seat of its national government, home to Parliament, the President's House (Rashtrapati Bhavan) and the Supreme Court. It sits inside the larger city and union territory of Delhi, on the Yamuna River.

New Delhi is younger than it looks. Under British rule, Kolkata (then Calcutta) was the capital until 1911. That year, King George V announced that the capital would move to Delhi, an old imperial city that had been a Mughal capital (Chapter 3). British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed a new government district south of the old city, and New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931. After independence, the new republic kept it as the capital.

Delhi is a city of layers: Mughal monuments in Old Delhi, the colonial avenues of New Delhi, and huge modern suburbs where people from every state now live.

Delhi or New Delhi?

"Delhi" is the whole city and union territory; "New Delhi" is the district inside it where the national government sits. If someone says India's capital is Mumbai, gently point out that Mumbai is the biggest business city, but the capital is New Delhi.

docs.title: Two kinds of pieces
docs.text:
India is divided into States and Union Territories: 28 states, which have their own elected governments and share power with the center, and 8 union territories, which are governed more directly by the national government. This is the count as of October 2026, according to the National Portal of India.

  • A state has its own elected legislative assembly, a chief minister and a governor appointed by the president. It makes its own laws on state subjects.
  • A union territory (UT) is run by an administrator appointed by the president. Some UTs, like Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir, also have elected assemblies with limited powers.

Why have union territories at all? Some are small islands far from the mainland (the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep). Some were once ruled by France or Portugal and stayed separate after they joined India (Puducherry; Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu). Chandigarh is the shared capital of two states. Delhi holds the national capital. And Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh became union territories in 2019, as you'll see below.

docs.title: All 36 at a glance
docs.text:
Here is the full list, with the capitals given by the National Portal of India. The languages are the main official ones; many states also have additional official languages for some districts or purposes.

State or UT Type Capital Main official language(s) Andhra Pradesh State Amaravati Telugu Arunachal Pradesh State Itanagar English Assam State Dispur Assamese, Bodo (Bengali in the Barak Valley) Bihar State Patna Hindi (Urdu additional) Chhattisgarh State Raipur Hindi Goa State Panaji Konkani, English Gujarat State Gandhinagar Gujarati Haryana State Chandigarh Hindi Himachal Pradesh State Shimla Hindi (Sanskrit second) Jharkhand State Ranchi Hindi (many additional) Karnataka State Bengaluru Kannada Kerala State Thiruvananthapuram Malayalam Madhya Pradesh State Bhopal Hindi Maharashtra State Mumbai Marathi Manipur State Imphal Manipuri (Meitei) Meghalaya State Shillong English (Khasi and Garo associate) Mizoram State Aizawl Mizo, English Nagaland State Kohima English Odisha State Bhubaneswar Odia Punjab State Chandigarh Punjabi Rajasthan State Jaipur Hindi Sikkim State Gangtok Nepali, English and others Tamil Nadu State Chennai Tamil Telangana State Hyderabad Telugu (Urdu additional) Tripura State Agartala Bengali, Kokborok, English Uttar Pradesh State Lucknow Hindi (Urdu additional) Uttarakhand State Dehradun Hindi (Sanskrit second) West Bengal State Kolkata Bengali, English Andaman and Nicobar Islands UT Sri Vijaya Puram (formerly Port Blair) Hindi, English Chandigarh UT Chandigarh English Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu UT Daman Gujarati, Hindi (English used in administration; sources differ) Delhi UT (National Capital Territory) Delhi Hindi, English Jammu and Kashmir UT Srinagar (summer), Jammu (winter) Kashmiri, Dogri, Urdu, Hindi, English Ladakh UT Leh Bhoti, Purgi, Urdu, Hindi, English Lakshadweep UT Kavaratti English (Malayalam widely used) Puducherry UT Puducherry Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam (by area), plus English and French

The map has changed many times since 1947, and it changes still. Dadra and Nagar Haveli merged with Daman and Diu on 26 January 2020. In 2024 the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Port Blair, was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram. In June 2025, a new regulation made Bhoti and Purgi official languages in Ladakh alongside Urdu, Hindi and English.

docs.title: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh
docs.text:
Until 2019, Jammu and Kashmir was a state with special autonomy under Article 370 of the constitution. In August 2019, India's government revoked that special status, and Parliament passed a law splitting the state into two union territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, from 31 October 2019. In December 2023, India's Supreme Court upheld the change and directed that statehood be restored to Jammu and Kashmir "as soon as possible." As of October 2026, both remain union territories.

These two territories are part of a much larger region whose status is disputed, as the box below explains.

Whose Story?

Ask someone in Delhi, Islamabad and Beijing to draw "Kashmir," and you'll get three different maps. In 1947 the Hindu ruler of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, with a Muslim-majority population, joined India during fighting with forces from Pakistan, and war followed. Today India administers about 55% of the region's land, Pakistan about 30% (Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan) and China about 15% (including Aksai Chin). India's position is that the whole former princely state is part of India. China's position is that Aksai Chin is part of China. Pakistan's position is that the region's future should be decided by its people through the vote the United Nations called for in 1948. Many Kashmiris themselves hold their own views, which do not always match either government's, and people of every community there have suffered through decades of conflict.

docs.title: How languages drew the map
docs.text:
Linguistic States are states whose borders were drawn so that most people inside share one main language, which usually becomes the state's official language. Most of India's states today are linguistic states.

At independence, India inherited a patchwork: big British provinces like Madras and Bombay that held speakers of several languages, plus more than 500 princely states. Many people wanted states that matched their languages, so that they could go to school, go to court and deal with officials in their own tongue. India's first leaders worried that language-based states might divide the country, and moved slowly.

In 1952, Potti Sriramulu, an activist demanding a separate state for Telugu speakers, died on the 58th day of a hunger strike. Protests followed, and in 1953 the government created Andhra State from the Telugu-speaking north of Madras State, the first state formed for one language. A States Reorganisation Commission followed, and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew much of the map on linguistic lines from 1 November 1956. Kerala, for example, was created that day for Malayalam speakers.

The process continued:

Year Change 1953 Andhra State formed for Telugu speakers 1956 States Reorganisation Act redraws the map; Kerala, Mysore (later Karnataka) and others formed around languages 1960 Bombay State split into Maharashtra (Marathi) and Gujarat (Gujarati) on 1 May 2000 Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand formed, more for regional and tribal identity than for language 2014 Telangana formed from Andhra Pradesh on 2 June, after a long regional movement; both states speak Telugu 2019 Jammu and Kashmir state split into two union territories

Notice the later changes. Telangana and Andhra Pradesh share the Telugu language, yet they split, because people in Telangana felt their region's history and needs were different. Language matters a great deal, but it isn't the only thing that makes people feel like a "state."

So was Kavya right that India is "28 countries in one"? In one sense, yes: many states have their own language, literature, film industry, food and festivals. But they are not countries. They share one constitution, one parliament and one army, and people move freely between them. Kavya can fly from Hyderabad to Kolkata without a passport.

docs.title: Hindi, English and the language question
docs.text:
India's constitution named Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union and planned for English to be phased out by 1965. In South India, especially in Tamil Nadu, many people strongly opposed having Hindi imposed on them. The Official Languages Act of 1963 settled the issue for the time being: English continues alongside Hindi for official purposes indefinitely.

How many Indians speak Hindi? In the 2011 census, about 43.6% of Indians named Hindi as their mother tongue. That number includes many related regional tongues, such as Bhojpuri and Braj, that the census groups under Hindi. So Hindi is the biggest single language, but more than half of India grows up speaking something else. Bengali came second, at about 8%.

docs.title: 17.8 South India
docs.text:
South India is the southern part of the peninsula, usually meaning the five states of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana, plus Puducherry and Lakshadweep, where the main languages belong to the Dravidian family.

The four big Dravidian languages are Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam, each with its own script, literature and film industry (Chapter 6, Chapter 15). Dravidian languages are a completely different family from Hindi, which is Indo-Aryan, in the same way that Finnish is unrelated to Swedish even though Finland and Sweden are neighbors. That is why a Hindi-speaking student who moves to Chennai has to learn a whole new language.

South India has long faced the sea. Its ports traded with Rome, Arabia and Southeast Asia for centuries (Chapter 3). Kerala has old Christian, Jewish and Muslim communities whose faiths first reached its coast by sea, through trade. The south is also home to big technology cities, Bengaluru and Hyderabad, where many software companies have offices. Arjun's family is from Hyderabad, the capital of Telangana, and he dances Kuchipudi, a classical dance style named after a village in Andhra Pradesh (Chapter 10).

"South Indian" is a useful label, but it has limits: a family from Kochi and a family from Hyderabad may speak, eat, pray and celebrate quite differently.

docs.title: 17.9 Northeast India
docs.text:
Northeast India is the easternmost region of the country, made up of eight states: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura (often called the "Seven Sisters") and Sikkim. It is connected to the rest of India by a narrow strip of land in West Bengal, the Siliguri Corridor, and it borders five countries: China, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal.

The Northeast covers almost 8% of India's area but held only about 4% of its people in 2011. It is one of the most linguistically varied places on Earth. Many of its languages belong to the Tibeto-Burman family, related to Tibetan and Burmese rather than to Hindi or Tamil. Assamese and Bengali are Indo-Aryan, and Khasi in Meghalaya is Austroasiatic. Because no single local language is shared across Nagaland or Arunachal Pradesh, those states chose English as their official language.

Faiths vary widely too. Assam and Tripura have Hindu majorities and Assam has a large Muslim population. Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya have Christian majorities. Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh have important Buddhist communities. Many communities keep Indigenous faiths alongside or instead of these.

Many people from the Northeast who move to big Indian cities have reported facing prejudice and being treated as "foreigners" in their own country. This chapter treats the Northeast as a full part of India's story, not a footnote.

Not all Indians look alike

If a classmate says they're from India and they don't match the picture you had in your head, that picture is too small. India includes people from Ladakh, Nagaland, Kerala and Gujarat, and none of them is "less Indian" than the others.

docs.title: 17.10 Adivasi Communities
docs.text:
Adivasi Communities are India's Indigenous or tribal peoples, many of whom have their own languages, faiths, governance and ways of life tied to forests, hills and land. Adivasi (आदिवासी, AH-dee-VAH-see) means "original inhabitants" in Hindi. The government's official term is Scheduled Tribes, groups listed in a schedule under the constitution for special protection and support. Some officials avoid the word Adivasi, but many communities and activists use it with pride, and this book uses both respectfully.

In the 2011 census, about 104 million Indians, 8.6% of the population, belonged to Scheduled Tribes, and hundreds of different groups are listed. That is more than the entire population of most countries. Madhya Pradesh has the largest tribal population of any state (about 15 million in 2011), and in several northeastern states tribal peoples are the majority. Most live in rural areas.

Adivasi communities include the Santal, Gond, Bhil, Munda, Oraon and many more, with very different histories. Santali, an Austroasiatic language, was added to the Eighth Schedule in 2003. The state of Jharkhand was created in 2000 partly in response to a long movement for tribal self-rule; its first chief minister took office on 15 November 2000, the birth anniversary of the Munda leader Birsa Munda, who led a movement against British rule and the loss of tribal land in the 1890s.

Adivasi communities have faced serious problems, especially losing land and forests to dams, mines and other projects. They have also shaped Indian art, music and politics, and today an Adivasi woman, Droupadi Murmu, is president of India.

docs.title: 17.11 Unity in Diversity
docs.text:
Unity in Diversity is the idea that a country can hold many languages, faiths, peoples and cultures and still be one nation, with the differences seen as a strength rather than a threat. Indian leaders, schools and textbooks have used the phrase since independence to describe what India hopes to be.

You've already seen the diversity: 22 scheduled languages and hundreds more spoken; Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and others; deserts, rainforests, Himalayan valleys and coral islands. What provides the unity?

  • Shared institutions: one constitution, one parliament, one Supreme Court and one election system.
  • Shared history: the independence movement, which brought people from every region together against colonial rule.
  • Shared culture across lines: cricket (Chapter 15), Hindi and regional films, festivals that neighbors of different faiths often celebrate together, and food that travels between states.

Unity in diversity is a goal, not an automatic fact. India has seen violence between religious communities, conflicts in Kashmir and parts of the Northeast, and arguments over language. Indians debate, loudly, how a big democracy should balance majority and minority, center and state. Those debates are part of how a diverse country works out living together.

docs.title: 17.12 National Symbols of India
docs.text:
National Symbols of India are the official emblems, chosen by the government, that stand for the country as a whole: a flag, an emblem, an anthem, a song, an animal, a bird, a flower and more.

Symbol What it is Adopted or notes National flag The tricolor, or tiranga (तिरंगा, ti-RUNG-ah): saffron, white and green bands with a navy blue wheel (the Ashoka Chakra) in the center Adopted 22 July 1947 State emblem Three lions from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, with the motto Satyameva Jayate, "Truth alone triumphs" Adopted 26 January 1950 National anthem "Jana Gana Mana," written in Bengali by Rabindranath Tagore Adopted 24 January 1950 National song "Vande Mataram," by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee Honored equally with the anthem National animal Tiger National bird Indian peafowl (peacock) Since 1963 National flower Lotus National calendar The Saka calendar, used alongside the Gregorian calendar Adopted 22 March 1957

Many of these symbols reach back into older history. The wheel on the flag and the lions on the emblem come from the reign of the emperor Ashoka in the 200s BCE (Chapter 2). The anthem connects India to its neighbors: Tagore also wrote "Amar Shonar Bangla," the national anthem of Bangladesh, which you'll meet in Chapter 19.

docs.title: 17.13 The Indian Economy and the Rupee
The Indian Economy
docs.text:
The Indian Economy is the system of farms, factories, services and trade through which India's 1.46 billion people make and buy goods. It is huge in total but still modest per person. In 2025, India's gross domestic product (GDP), the value of everything produced in a year, was about 3.96 trillion US dollars, the sixth-largest in the world by the World Bank's figures in US dollars, close behind the United Kingdom. But because that output is shared among so many people, India's income per person (gross national income per person) was about 2,760 US dollars in 2025, according to the World Bank, far below that of the United States.

India's economy has many layers at once:

  • Farming still employs a very large share of Indians, growing rice, wheat, cotton, sugarcane, tea and spices.
  • Services are the biggest part of the economy, including software and IT companies in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune, banking in Mumbai, and call centers that serve customers worldwide.
  • Manufacturing includes cars, medicines and, increasingly, phones.
  • The informal economy: millions of street vendors, small shops and family workshops that are not registered businesses.

Since economic reforms in 1991 opened India more to trade and investment, its economy has grown fast, and hundreds of millions of people have risen out of extreme poverty. At the same time, India still has many people living in poverty, and the gaps between rich and poor, and between booming and struggling states, are large.

docs.title: The Indian Rupee
docs.text:
The Indian Rupee is India's currency, written ₹ and divided into 100 paise. The word "rupee" comes from the Hindi rupaya (रुपया, ROOP-yah), from a Sanskrit word for wrought silver. The rupee goes back to a silver coin called the rupiya, first issued by the ruler Sher Shah Suri between 1540 and 1545 and later by the Mughals, and several neighbors also call their money rupees: Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka all do.

The ₹ symbol is new. In 2010, India's government held an open competition for a rupee sign, and on 15 July 2010 it chose a design by D. Udaya Kumar, a young designer from IIT Bombay. The symbol blends the Devanagari letter र (ra) with the Latin letter R, and its two horizontal lines echo the flag. In October 2026, about 95 rupees bought one US dollar, according to Britannica.

docs.title: 17.14 ISRO and India in Space
docs.text:
ISRO, the Indian Space Research Organisation, is India's national space agency, which builds and launches rockets and satellites and sends missions to the Moon and beyond. It grew out of a space research committee set up in 1962, at the urging of the physicist Vikram Sarabhai, and took the name ISRO in 1969. Its headquarters are in Bengaluru, and it launches rockets from Sriharikota, an island on the coast of Andhra Pradesh.

ISRO is known for doing ambitious things on small budgets. Its satellites forecast weather, map crops, guide fishing boats and broadcast TV across the country.

Its most famous recent mission is Chandrayaan-3 ("Moon craft"). Launched on 14 July 2023, it landed its Vikram lander near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, and a small rover called Pragyan drove across the surface. India became the fourth country to land softly on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China, and the first to land near the lunar south pole, a region scientists study because it may hold water ice. The rover's instruments confirmed sulfur in the soil near the pole.

Connect the dots

Chandrayaan-3 was built by engineers from many states and launched from Andhra Pradesh by an agency based in Karnataka. Why might a national science project like this be a good example of "unity in diversity"?

Controls: "Color the tiles by" menu (Language family, Region); "Highlight the 8 union territories" checkbox; click or tap any tile.

Behavior: A tile cartogram shows 36 equal tiles (squares for the 28 states, rounded tiles for the 8 union territories), placed roughly where each sits in India, with no borders drawn. Tiles are colored by the language family of each place's main official language(s) (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman, mixed families) or by informal region. Tapping a tile shows its capital, official languages, family, region and a short note. A card summarizes India's capital, 2025 population (World Bank), 28 + 8 units and languages. The caption "Schematic map, not to scale. Not an official depiction of borders." and a neutral note that the wider Kashmir region is disputed appear inside the drawing area.

Start with the Language family coloring. Look at the teal block in the south (Dravidian) and the purple tiles in the northeast (Tibeto-Burman). Then tap Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Notice that each southern state has its own language, but they all belong to the same family. Now tap the gray tiles: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Sikkim and Ladakh. Each one has official languages from two different families.

Then switch to Region and check Highlight the 8 union territories. Tap each union territory and ask why it isn't a state. Is it an island group, a former French or Portuguese territory, a capital city, or a place that changed in 2019? Finally, find Hyderabad in the Telangana tile and imagine Kavya's train ride to Bengaluru in Karnataka: how many tiles, and how many languages, would she pass?

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about the place in India their family comes from: which state, which language, and what makes it different from the rest of India. If your family isn't from India, ask an elder about a place in India they have visited or would like to visit. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Pull up the India Explorer MicroSim on a phone or tablet so your elder can tap their home state. It gives you an easy way to start talking.

Questions to ask

  1. Which state, city or village is our family (or your family) from? What is one thing you remember most about it?
  2. Which language did you speak at home there? Which languages did you learn at school?
  3. What food, festival or custom from your state do you think people from other states don't really know about?
  4. When you met people from other parts of India, what surprised you about them, or about yourself?
  5. How has your home state changed since you were young, or since you moved away?
  6. What is one thing from your state that you hope I keep, even if I never live there?

Listen for: whether their state is one of the Linguistic States and which language it was drawn around; whether they are from South India, Northeast India or another region; and moments where they describe Unity in Diversity, like friends from different states or faiths celebrating together.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Find your elder's state in the table in Section 17.6. Does the official language there match the language your family speaks at home? If a friend interviewed someone from a different state, compare the two: what is different, and what do they share as Indians?

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: India has one culture. Reality: India has 28 states and 8 union territories, 22 scheduled languages and hundreds more, and many faiths, cuisines and festivals. A family in Kerala and a family in Punjab can differ in language, food and customs as much as Swedes and Spaniards do, while sharing one country, one constitution and a lot of history.

Myth: Everyone in India speaks Hindi. Reality: Hindi is the largest language, but in the 2011 census only about 44% of Indians named it as their mother tongue. Most people in South India, Northeast India, West Bengal, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Punjab and Odisha grow up speaking another language, and English is widely used to bridge the gaps.

Myth: India's capital is Mumbai. Reality: The capital is New Delhi, inside the National Capital Territory of Delhi. Mumbai, the capital of Maharashtra, is India's biggest business and film city.

Myth: India is mostly big cities. Reality: India has some of the world's largest cities, but in 2025 only about 36% of Indians lived in urban areas, according to the World Bank. Most Indians still live in villages and small towns.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. How many states and union territories does India have, and what is the difference between them?

As of 2026, India has 28 states and 8 union territories. States have their own elected governments that share power with the center; union territories are governed more directly by the national government through an administrator, though some also have elected assemblies.

2. What is a linguistic state, and which was the first?

A linguistic state is one whose borders were drawn around a shared language, which usually becomes its official language. Andhra State, formed in 1953 for Telugu speakers, was the first.

3. What are the two houses of the Parliament of India?

The Lok Sabha (House of the People), with 543 directly elected seats, and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States), mostly elected by state assemblies.

4. What happened on 23 August 2023, and why did it matter?

ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole. India became the fourth country to make a soft landing on the Moon and the first to land near the lunar south pole.

5. What are Adivasi communities, and what share of India's population did they make up in 2011?

Adivasi communities are India's Indigenous or tribal peoples, officially called Scheduled Tribes. In the 2011 census they made up about 8.6% of the population, about 104 million people.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Name India's capital, its 2025 population (World Bank) and the date its constitution came into effect.

    Answer

    New Delhi; 1,463,865,525 (about 1.46 billion); 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.

  2. List the eight states of Northeast India.

    Answer

    Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh use English as their official language.

    Answer

    Each is home to many peoples speaking many different languages, mostly Tibeto-Burman, with no single local language shared by everyone, so English works as a neutral common language for government.

  2. Explain the difference between Delhi and New Delhi.

    Answer

    Delhi is the whole city and the National Capital Territory, a union territory. New Delhi is the district inside it, built by the British and inaugurated in 1931, that holds Parliament and the national government.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the India Explorer MicroSim. Switch the coloring to Language family and list every gray ("mixed families") tile. For each, name the two families its official languages come from.

    Hint: tap each gray tile and read the note.

  2. A new student says her family is from Thiruvananthapuram and speaks Malayalam at home. Using the table in Section 17.6, write two sentences that show you know which state she is from and how that state got its borders.

    Hint: think about 1 November 1956.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the creation of Telangana in 2014 with the creation of Andhra State in 1953. Why was language the main reason for one but not the other?

    Hint: both states speak Telugu.

  2. Kavya said India is "like 28 countries in one." Analyze what is accurate and what is misleading about that statement, using at least two facts from the chapter.

    Hint: think about languages and governments, then about the constitution, Parliament and passports.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Some Indians argue that Hindi should be used more widely as a common national language; others, especially in South India, argue that this would be unfair to non-Hindi speakers. Evaluate both positions and say which you find more convincing, and why.

    Hint: use the 2011 census number and the history of the Official Languages Act of 1963.

  2. India's national symbols include a flag, an emblem from Ashoka's era, an anthem in Bengali and a calendar. Evaluate how well this set of symbols represents a country of many languages and faiths. What would you add or change, and why?

    Hint: look at where each symbol comes from.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a "welcome to my state" poster for one of India's 36 states or union territories. Include its capital, its official language, one festival or food, and one fact that would surprise someone from another state.

    Hint: start from the MicroSim card, then add from your own research or interview.

  2. Write a short news report (150 to 200 words) of the Chandrayaan-3 landing as it might have been told in two different Indian languages' newspapers. What would be the same in both, and what local detail might each add?

    Hint: use the dates and facts in Section 17.14.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The Republic of India, with 1,463,865,525 people in 2025 (World Bank), is the world's most populous country; its constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950.
  • India is a federal parliamentary democracy: the Lok Sabha's 543 seats are directly elected, and in 2024 about 642 million people voted in the largest election in history.
  • India has 28 states and 8 union territories (2026), and its capital is New Delhi, inside the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
  • Many states are linguistic states, drawn around a shared language, beginning with Andhra State in 1953 and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956.
  • South India's main languages are Dravidian, Northeast India's are largely Tibeto-Burman, and Hindi was the mother tongue of about 44% of Indians in 2011.
  • Adivasi communities (Scheduled Tribes) made up 8.6% of Indians in 2011, and India's national symbols, economy, rupee and space program all reflect the goal of unity in diversity.
  • Kashmir is disputed: India, Pakistan and China each administer part of the region, and their positions differ.

You toured India!

You can now explain how 36 states and territories, 22 scheduled languages and 1.46 billion people fit into one republic, and why Kavya's "28 countries in one" is half right. Next, in Chapter 18, we cross India's western border to tour Pakistan and Afghanistan.

docs.title: Quiz: India
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 17. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
As of 2026, how is India divided?

  1. 29 states and 7 union territories
  2. 28 states and 8 union territories
  3. 36 states and no union territories
  4. 22 states, one for each scheduled language
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. India has 28 states and 8 union territories, according to the National Portal of India. The count of 29 states and 7 union territories was correct before 2019, when Jammu and Kashmir became a union territory and Ladakh was separated from it.

Concept Tested: States and Union Territories Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
When did the Constitution of India come into effect?

  1. 15 August 1947
  2. 26 November 1949
  3. 1 November 1956
  4. 26 January 1950
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, now celebrated as Republic Day. It was adopted on 26 November 1949, which is why option B is tempting, and 15 August 1947 is Independence Day.

Concept Tested: Constitution of India Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
What did ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 mission achieve on 23 August 2023?

  1. It made India the first country to land near the Moon's south pole.
  2. It made India the first country ever to land on the Moon.
  3. It put the first Indian astronaut on the Moon.
  4. It sent India's first spacecraft into orbit around Mars.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touched down near the lunar south pole, making India the fourth country to land softly on the Moon and the first near the south pole. It was not the first Moon landing overall: the Soviet Union, the United States and China landed first, and the mission carried no astronauts.

Concept Tested: ISRO Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Which statement best explains what a linguistic state is?

  1. A state where English is banned from government use
  2. A state where everyone must learn Hindi first
  3. A state whose borders were drawn so that most people share one main language
  4. A state created for people who speak more than three languages
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Linguistic states were drawn around a shared language, which usually became the state's official language, starting with Andhra State in 1953. They do not require Hindi; in fact, many linguistic states have non-Hindi official languages such as Telugu, Tamil or Marathi.

Concept Tested: Linguistic States Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why do Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh use English as their official language?

  1. Because English is the only language taught in their schools
  2. Because each is home to many peoples with different languages and no single shared local language
  3. Because they were British colonies until 2000
  4. Because the constitution requires all northeastern states to use English
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. These states are home to many communities speaking many languages, mostly Tibeto-Burman, so English works as a neutral common language. The constitution does not require it; each state chooses its own official language under Article 345.

Concept Tested: Northeast India Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Which statement about Hindi in India is accurate?

  1. In the 2011 census, about 44% of Indians named Hindi as their mother tongue, so most Indians grow up speaking another language.
  2. Hindi is the mother tongue of almost every Indian.
  3. Hindi is the only official language of India's national government.
  4. Hindi belongs to the Dravidian language family.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Hindi is the largest single language, but about 43.6% of Indians named it as their mother tongue in 2011. English continues alongside Hindi for national official use under the Official Languages Act of 1963, and Hindi is Indo-Aryan, not Dravidian.

Concept Tested: Unity in Diversity Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A new classmate tells you her family is from Chennai and speaks Tamil at home. Using the chapter, which description fits her family's home region?

  1. Northeast India, where most languages are Tibeto-Burman
  2. A union territory governed directly from New Delhi
  3. The capital region, where Hindi and English are the official languages
  4. South India, where the main languages belong to the Dravidian family
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Chennai is the capital of Tamil Nadu, a state in South India, and Tamil is a Dravidian language. Tamil Nadu is a state, not a union territory, so option B does not fit.

Concept Tested: South India Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Your club is making a poster about India's government. Which pair correctly describes India's leaders as of October 2026?

  1. President Narendra Modi and Prime Minister Droupadi Murmu
  2. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and President Asif Ali Zardari
  3. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Droupadi Murmu
  4. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Rabindranath Tagore
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Narendra Modi is prime minister (in his third term) and Droupadi Murmu has been president since 2022. Option A swaps their offices, and option B names Pakistan's leaders.

Concept Tested: Parliament of India Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Telangana was split from Andhra Pradesh in 2014, even though both states mainly speak Telugu. What does this case show?

  1. Language matters, but regional history and identity can also shape how states are drawn.
  2. The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 required every state to split in two.
  3. Telugu speakers do not live in Telangana.
  4. Linguistic states were abolished in 2014.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Telangana's movement was about regional history and needs, not a different language, so it shows that language is only one reason states form. Linguistic states were not abolished, and Telugu is Telangana's official language.

Concept Tested: Linguistic States Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
The India Explorer MicroSim draws Goa and Rajasthan as tiles of the same size. What is the best reason a tile cartogram is used instead of a traced map?

  1. Goa and Rajasthan really are the same size.
  2. Equal tiles make every state and territory easy to see and compare, and avoid drawing disputed borders.
  3. Tile cartograms show each state's exact population.
  4. Traced maps of India are not allowed to show capitals.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Equal tiles let tiny places like Goa or Chandigarh be seen and tapped as easily as big ones, and a schematic layout avoids drawing official borders, including the disputed Kashmir region. Goa is actually India's smallest state by area, and Rajasthan its largest.

Concept Tested: States and Union Territories Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Pakistan and Afghanistan are neighbors on the western side of South Asia, with a long mountain frontier between them and a famous road that crosses it. This chapter tours Pakistan first: how the country is governed, its capital, its four provinces, and the many languages that sit beside Urdu, its national language. Then it turns to Afghanistan: its mountains and capital, its two official languages, the Pashtun code of Pashtunwali, its heritage sites and its carpets, along with a brief, dated look at who governs it today. Along the way you'll see how cultural regions like the Punjab and the Pashtun belt cross the lines on a modern map.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What Is South Asia? for the eight countries, the Hindu Kush and the Indus River
  • Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters for the Mughal Empire
  • Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition for how Pakistan was created in 1947
  • Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts is helpful for the Perso-Arabic script

Two neighbors, one old road

Hi, I'm Mora! Pakistan and Afghanistan show up in the news a lot, usually in short, scary headlines that leave out the people, the poetry, the food and the festivals. If your family is from either country, this chapter gives you words for the places you hear about at home. If it isn't, it helps you see your classmates' homelands as more than a headline.

docs.title: 18.1 Dinner at the Qureshis'
docs.text:
On a Saturday in October, Ayesha Qureshi's family invites Zara Hossain and Ben Lindqvist over for dinner. Ayesha's family is from Lahore, in Pakistan, and they speak Urdu at home. The table is crowded: a big pot of biryani, a bowl of chickpeas, flatbread still warm from the pan, and a plate of kebabs. Ayesha spends most of dinner arguing with her cousin about cricket.

Ben sits next to Ayesha's uncle, who asks him what he knows about Pakistan. Ben admits that he knows almost nothing, except that it is next to India and next to Afghanistan, "which I always thought was in the Middle East." The uncle laughs. "Afghanistan is our neighbor, beta. Lahore and Kabul were tied together by the same roads and the same empires for centuries. The first Mughal emperor ruled from Kabul before he ever saw Lahore, and he chose to be buried in Kabul. My grandfather bought carpets that came down through the Khyber Pass."

Ben looks at Zara. Zara shrugs; her family is from Bangladesh, at the other end of South Asia. "I know Pakistan and Bangladesh used to be one country," she says. "But I don't really know what's in Pakistan, or in Afghanistan." Ben pulls out his phone and opens a map. There's a line between the two countries. So how can two places on either side of a border, with different governments and different flags, be "tied together"?

docs.title: 18.2 Borders and Cultural Regions
docs.text:
Start with an example from closer to home. The Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) people have lived around the Great Lakes for centuries, on land that today is split between Minnesota, other US states and Canada. The US-Canada border runs right through their homeland. A family in northern Minnesota and a family in Ontario can share a language, ceremonies and relatives, even though they carry different passports.

South Asia is full of situations like this. A country is a political unit with a government and borders, as you learned in Chapter 1. A cultural region is an area where people share a language, customs or history, whether or not a border runs through it. In this chapter you'll meet two big cultural regions that cross borders:

  • The Punjab, split in 1947 between Pakistan and India.
  • The Pashtun homeland, split in 1893 between British India (today Pakistan) and Afghanistan.

So when you compare Pakistan and Afghanistan, ask two kinds of questions. How are the two countries governed, and what are their official languages and capitals? And which cultures, roads and families reach across the line?

docs.title: 18.3 Pakistan: A Country Born in 1947
docs.text: Pakistan became independent on 14 August 1947, the day Pakistan celebrates as Independence Day, when British India was divided (Chapter 4). At first Pakistan had two wings, West Pakistan and East Pakistan, on opposite sides of India. In 1971, after a war, East Pakistan became the independent country of Bangladesh, which you'll meet in Chapter 19. Today's Pakistan is the old western wing.

docs.title: The Islamic Republic of Pakistan
docs.text:
The country's full name is the Islamic Republic of Pakistan: a federal, parliamentary republic in which Islam is the state religion. The name was adopted in Pakistan's first constitution, which took effect on 23 March 1956. The constitution in force today dates from 1973. Federal means power is shared between a national government and provincial governments. Parliamentary means the prime minister, who runs the government day to day, is chosen by the elected National Assembly, while the president is head of state.

As of October 2026, Pakistan's prime minister is Shehbaz Sharif, in office since March 2024, and its president is Asif Ali Zardari, who took the oath of office on 10 March 2024. Like any country's politics, Pakistan's is lively and contested, and this book leaves the arguments to the news.

docs.title: How many people?
docs.text:
Pakistan had 255,219,554 people in 2025 (about 255 million, World Bank), making it one of the ten most populous countries on Earth. Pakistan's own 2023 census, the country's seventh, counted 241.49 million people, with a growth rate of 2.55% a year. (The two numbers differ because they are from different years and use different methods.)

About 96% of Pakistanis are Muslim, most of them Sunni, with a large Shia minority. The 2023 census counted Hindus at 1.61% of the population, the largest religious minority, and Christians at 1.37%. Some Christian leaders believe their community was undercounted. There are also smaller communities of Sikhs, Parsis and Ahmadis.

docs.title: Islamabad
docs.text:
Islamabad (is-LAHM-ah-bahd) is the capital of Pakistan. Its name means "City of Islam" or "City of Peace." It is a planned city, which means it was designed from scratch rather than growing over centuries. When Pakistan was founded, the capital was Karachi, a busy port on the Arabian Sea. In 1959 a commission chose a new site in the north, on the Potwar Plateau below the Margala Hills, next to the older city of Rawalpindi, which served as the temporary capital. Construction began in 1961. The city is laid out in zones, including government, diplomatic, residential and commercial areas, a greenbelt and a national park.

Just outside Islamabad lie the ruins of Taxila, an ancient city on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1980. From the 400s BCE to the 100s CE it was an important Buddhist center of learning, shaped in turn by Persia, Greece and Central Asia. Keep that in mind; we'll come back to those roads in Section 18.9.

docs.title: 18.4 The Provinces of Pakistan
docs.text:
The Provinces of Pakistan are the four large regions, each with its own elected assembly and government, into which the country is divided: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. The capital city has its own federal territory, the Islamabad Capital Territory. In the far north, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir are areas administered by Pakistan that are part of the larger Kashmir region, whose status is disputed among Pakistan, India and China. Pakistan regards them as its territory with special arrangements, India claims them, and the dispute is unresolved.

Province Capital Population (2023 census) Main first languages Punjab Lahore 127.68 million Punjabi, Saraiki Sindh Karachi 55.69 million Sindhi, Urdu Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Peshawar 40.85 million Pashto Balochistan Quetta 14.89 million Balochi, Pashto Islamabad Capital Territory (Islamabad) 2.36 million Punjabi, Urdu and others

More than half of all Pakistanis live in Punjab, and each province has its own main language: Pakistan is a country of several large peoples.

docs.title: Punjab and the Punjab Region
docs.text:
The Punjab Region is the cultural and geographic region of the five rivers that feed the Indus, today divided between Pakistan's Punjab province and India's Punjab state. The name comes from Persian words for "five" and "water." The five rivers are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Their water and rich soil made the Punjab one of the great farming regions of the subcontinent.

In 1947 the British province of Punjab was split in two. West Punjab, slightly more than half, went to Pakistan, and East Punjab went to India. Millions of people crossed the new line in both directions, a painful story told in Chapter 4. Today most people in Pakistani Punjab are Muslim, and Sikhs are the majority in Indian Punjab. Yet people on both sides still share the Punjabi language, much of the same music and food, and in many cases family memories of the other side. Even the script tells this story: Punjabi in Pakistan is written in Shahmukhi, a Perso-Arabic script, while in India it is mostly written in Gurmukhi.

docs.title: Lahore
docs.text:
Lahore (لاہور, lah-HOR) is Pakistan's second-largest city and the capital of Punjab province. It sits on the Ravi River in the upper Indus plain. Lahore has been a royal city many times: a Ghaznavid capital in the 1100s, a favorite Mughal residence in the 1500s and 1600s, and the seat of the Sikh ruler Ranjit Singh from 1799 to 1839.

Lahore's Mughal buildings are its pride. The Lahore Fort was built in part by the emperor Akbar and expanded by the emperors who followed him. The Shalamar Gardens, laid out in 1642 for the emperor Shah Jahan, are terraced, walled gardens with hundreds of fountains. Together the fort and the gardens became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1981. Nearby stands the Badshahi Mosque, built by the emperor Aurangzeb in 1671 to 1673, still one of the largest mosques in the world. A popular Punjabi saying claims that whoever hasn't seen Lahore hasn't really been born, and Ayesha's uncle repeats it at every family dinner.

docs.title: Sindh
docs.text:
Sindh is Pakistan's southeastern province, the land of the lower Indus River and its delta, with Karachi as its capital. The province even takes its name from the river, which is known as the Sindhu in Pakistan. Sindh was one of the heartlands of the Indus Valley Civilization more than 4,000 years ago, and its most famous city, Mohenjo-daro, is a UNESCO World Heritage site (1980) (Chapter 2).

Sindh also has a special place in the history of Islam in South Asia: the Arab conquest of Sindh in 711 CE was one of the first ways Islam came into the subcontinent. Today Karachi, on the Arabian Sea, is Pakistan's largest city and main port, drawing people from every part of the country. In the 2023 census, about 60% of people in Sindh spoke Sindhi as their first language and about 22% spoke Urdu.

docs.title: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
docs.text:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KY-ber pukh-TOON-khwah) is Pakistan's northwestern province, bordering Afghanistan, with Peshawar as its capital. Until 2010 it was called the North-West Frontier Province. Its new name joins two ideas: "Khyber," after the famous pass, and "Pakhtunkhwa," roughly "land of the Pashtuns."

The province rises from the fertile Vale of Peshawar into the Hindu Kush. Most people are Pashtuns, Pashto is the main language (spoken by 81% as a first language in the 2023 census), and nearly everyone is Muslim. Peshawar is one of the oldest cities in the region and a center of Pashtun culture.

In October 2026 the province was in the news: on 11 October the federal government declared an emergency there and suspended the provincial government, which had been led by the PTI party, citing security concerns. PTI leaders called the move undemocratic. Events were still unfolding as this book was written.

docs.title: Balochistan
docs.text:
Balochistan is Pakistan's westernmost province, bordering Iran and Afghanistan, with Quetta as its capital. It is the largest province by area and the most thinly populated. Much of it is dry plateau, desert and mountains outside the reach of the monsoon, and sheep raising is a major way of life.

Balochistan has two main peoples: the Baloch and the Pashtuns. In the 2023 census, about 40% of the province spoke Balochi as their first language and about 34% spoke Pashto. Brahui and Sindhi are also spoken.

Try this

Look back at the province table. If you only met people from Lahore, what would you assume "Pakistani food" or "the Pakistani language" is? Now imagine a friend from Quetta or Karachi reading your answer. What would they add?

docs.title: 18.5 Urdu and Pakistan's Many Mother Tongues
Urdu as National Language
docs.text:
Urdu as National Language means that Urdu (اردو, OOR-doo) is the language Pakistan's constitution names as the language of the whole nation, even though only a small share of Pakistanis speak it as their first language. Article 251 of the 1973 constitution says that Urdu is the national language of Pakistan, that English may be used for official purposes, and that provinces may promote their own provincial languages alongside Urdu.

Urdu is written right to left in a flowing Perso-Arabic style called Nastaliq, and everyday spoken Urdu is very close to everyday Hindi, as you saw in Chapter 6.

docs.title: What people speak at home
docs.text:
In practice, most Pakistanis grow up speaking another language at home and learn Urdu at school, on TV and in the city. Here are the most common first languages in the 2023 census:

First language (mother tongue) Share of Pakistan's population, 2023 census Punjabi about 37% Pashto about 18% Sindhi about 14% Saraiki about 12% Urdu about 9% Balochi about 3% Other languages about 6%

So Urdu is everybody's second language more than it is anybody's first. That's exactly why it works as a national language: it belongs to no single province. Urdu's share has been growing, though, from about 7% in the 2017 census to about 9% in 2023, as more families in big cities raise their children in Urdu. Ayesha's family is one of them: her grandparents spoke Punjabi at home in Lahore, but her parents mostly spoke Urdu to her. English is widely used in government, law and higher education, and many Pakistanis switch between two or three languages in one conversation.

One country, many languages

If a Pakistani friend says "my language is Punjabi" or "Pashto" instead of "Urdu," they aren't being unusual. Ask "What do you speak at home?" instead of assuming.

docs.title: 18.6 Afghanistan: Mountains, Valleys and Many Peoples
docs.text:
Afghanistan is a landlocked, mountainous country where South Asia meets Central Asia and Iran, and the eighth member of SAARC, which it joined in 2007. Landlocked means it has no coastline; the nearest sea, the Arabian Sea, is about 480 km to the south. Afghanistan had 43,844,111 people in 2025 (about 44 million, World Bank).

The Hindu Kush runs through the middle of the country (Chapter 1), and most of the land gets its rain and snow in winter and spring rather than from the monsoon. For thousands of years, Afghanistan's passes linked South Asia, Central Asia, Iran and China.

Afghanistan has many peoples. Pashtuns are the largest group. Tajiks, Hazaras, Uzbeks and Turkmen are other large communities, along with many smaller ones. Nearly all Afghans are Muslim: most are Sunni, and a Shia minority (estimates range from about 10% to 15%) includes most Hazaras. Afghanistan once had Sikh and Hindu communities estimated in the hundreds of thousands in the 1970s, but nearly all have left; only small numbers remain, mostly in Kabul, Jalalabad and Ghazni.

Afghanistan was never formally colonized. Britain fought wars there in the 1800s and controlled Afghanistan's foreign relations until the Treaty of Rawalpindi in 1919.

docs.title: Kabul
docs.text:
Kabul (کابل, KAH-bool) is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan. It sits about 1,800 m (5,900 ft) above sea level in a valley ringed by mountains, along the Kabul River, which flows east to join the Indus in Pakistan. People have lived at or near Kabul for about 3,500 years.

Kabul has long depended on trade, and its bazaars are famous across the region. It is also a city of many peoples: Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras, Uzbeks, Turkmen and others live side by side. Babur, who founded the Mughal Empire in 1526, ruled from Kabul before he marched into India, and he chose a garden in Kabul as his final resting place. That garden, Bagh-e Babur, was restored between 2003 and 2007 and now draws more than 400,000 visitors a year.

docs.title: Dari and Pashto
docs.text:
Dari and Pashto are Afghanistan's two official national languages, a status first set out in the 1964 constitution.

  • Dari (دری, dah-REE) is the form of Persian spoken in Afghanistan. It is close enough to the Persian of Iran (Farsi) that speakers understand each other easily. Dari has long been the language that Afghans of different groups use to talk to each other, and it is understood by most people in the country.
  • Pashto (پښتو, PUSH-toh) is the language of the Pashtuns, spoken on both sides of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. As you saw above, it is also Pakistan's second-most-common first language.

Both are written in versions of the Perso-Arabic script, right to left, and both belong to the Iranian branch of the Indo-European language family. Many Afghans speak both, and many also speak Uzbek, Turkmen or another language. The 2004 constitution of the former republic gave several of these, including Uzbek, Turkmen and Balochi, official status in areas where most people speak them.

docs.title: 18.7 Afghanistan Today
docs.text:
Afghanistan's last half century has been marked by war: a Soviet invasion and occupation (1979 to 1989), civil war, the first Taliban government (1996 to 2001), a US-led war that removed it in 2001, and two decades of an internationally backed republic.

In August 2021, as US and NATO forces withdrew, the Taliban, an Islamist movement, took control of Kabul and the country. The Taliban call their government the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. It is led by a supreme leader and rules by its own interpretation of Islamic law.

Most countries have not formally recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan's government. In July 2025 Russia became the first country to do so, and as of October 2026 it was still the only one, though several countries, including China and the United Arab Emirates, keep diplomatic ties and talk with Taliban officials. Much of the world's hesitation centers on restrictions on women and girls. Girls have been barred from secondary school since March 2022, and women from universities since December 2022. In August 2026, UNESCO estimated that about 2.4 million girls were shut out of secondary education, and said Afghanistan was the only country in the world with such a ban. The government has rejected calls to lift the ban, calling it an internal matter.

Culture has changed too. For example, Nowruz, the spring new year on 21 March that many Afghans have celebrated for centuries, is no longer an official public holiday. In 2025 the government said people could still mark it privately.

Ordinary Afghans carry on, keeping traditions alive at home and in a large worldwide diaspora. Millions of Afghans have lived as refugees in Pakistan and Iran over the decades. Since 2023, Pakistan has sent more than a million Afghans back across the border under a campaign against people living in Pakistan without legal status.

Check the date on the news

This section describes Afghanistan as of October 2026, and news here changes fast. When you read about the Taliban, remember that a government and a people are not the same thing: many Afghan families, at home and abroad, hold very different views about how their country should be run.

docs.title: 18.8 Pashtunwali: The Pashtun Way
docs.text:
The Pashtuns (also called Pakhtuns, and in older English "Pathans") are an ethnic group of tens of millions of people who live mainly in the region between the Hindu Kush in Afghanistan and the Indus River in Pakistan. They are the largest group in Afghanistan, and in fact the word "Afghan" once meant a Pashtun before it came to mean anyone from Afghanistan. What unites Pashtuns is their language, Pashto, along with Islam (most Pashtuns are Sunni) and a shared code of conduct.

Pashtunwali (push-toon-WAH-lee) is that code: the traditional, unwritten rules of honor, hospitality and justice that guide Pashtun social life. It is older than Islam in the region and is a matter of custom, not religious law, though for most Pashtuns it sits comfortably alongside their faith. Its main ideas include:

Idea Pashto word What it means Hospitality melmastia (mel-mus-TEE-ah) Welcome every guest generously, whoever they are, and expect nothing back. Sanctuary nanawatai (nah-nah-wah-TAI) Protect someone who comes to you asking for shelter, even from their enemies. Honor nang (nung) Defend your family's honor and protect the weak. Justice badal (BAH-dul) A wrong must be answered; this can mean revenge, but often it is settled by compensation instead. Council jirga (JEER-gah) Settle disputes in an assembly of elders who talk until they reach agreement.

Kinship is the base of Pashtun society. Tribes trace descent from a common ancestor and are divided into clans and families.

Like any code, Pashtunwali is lived differently by different families, in the city and the village, at home and abroad. Outsiders often focus on badal and blood feuds, but hospitality is just as central. Ben's welcome at the Qureshis' table (a Punjabi family, not a Pashtun one) shows how seriously hospitality is taken across this whole region.

Whose Story?

The border between Pakistan and Afghanistan is called the Durand Line, after the British official who negotiated it with Afghanistan's ruler in 1893. It runs about 2,600 km and split the Pashtun homeland in two. Pakistan inherited the line in 1947 and treats it as a settled international border; it began building a fence along it in 2017. Every Afghan government since 1947, whoever was in power, has said the line is void because it was imposed by the British, and some Pashtuns on both sides see it as cutting through one people. In 2025 and again in early 2026, fighting along the border led Pakistan to close crossings such as Torkham for weeks. Ask a Pakistani and an Afghan to draw "the border," and you may get two different answers, and two different histories.

docs.title: 18.9 The Khyber Pass
docs.text:
The Khyber Pass (KY-ber) is the mountain pass that connects Peshawar in Pakistan with Kabul in Afghanistan, crossing the hills at the end of the Spin Ghar ("White Mountains") range. The pass winds about 53 km (33 miles) from near the town of Jamrud, Pakistan, to the border post of Torkham. In places it is a narrow gorge between cliffs of shale and limestone 180 to 300 m high. Its highest point, at Landi Kotal, is about 1,072 m above sea level.

Few mountain passes in the world have seen so much history:

  • In the 500s BCE, the Persian king Darius I conquered the area around Kabul and marched through the pass to the Indus.
  • In the 200s BCE, under the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, Buddhism flourished in and around the Khyber, and Buddhist stupas still stand near the pass.
  • The pass was part of the Silk Road, linking Taxila (near today's Islamabad) with Kabul.
  • In 1526 Babur, then ruler of Kabul, came through the Khyber before defeating the Delhi sultan at the First Battle of Panipat and founding the Mughal Empire.
  • The British fought for control of the pass during the Anglo-Afghan wars of the 1800s. A railway with 34 tunnels opened in 1925 from Peshawar to near the border, though services stopped in 2007.

The pass carried traders and goods as well as armies, and it carried ideas and faiths too: Buddhism spread through these valleys in Ashoka's time, and later Muslim rulers, scholars and artists came the other way. That's what Ayesha's uncle meant when he said Lahore and Kabul were tied together. The road ran from Kabul down the Kabul River valley to Jalalabad, through the Khyber to Peshawar, past Taxila and on across the Punjab plain to Lahore and beyond to Delhi.

Since 1947 the pass has been in Pakistani territory. It is still an important road, but traffic is often interrupted by violence and by disputes between the two governments.

docs.title: 18.10 Heritage in Stone: Bamiyan, Jam and Pakistan's Ancient Sites
The Buddhas of Bamiyan
docs.text:
The Buddhas of Bamiyan were two giant standing statues of the Buddha carved into a sandstone cliff in the Bamiyan Valley of central Afghanistan, destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001. The larger statue was 55 m (180 ft) tall and the smaller one 38 m (125 ft). Radiocarbon dating suggests they were made in the late 500s and early 600s CE.

Why were giant Buddhas in the middle of the Hindu Kush? Bamiyan was a stopping place on a branch of the Silk Road linking China and India. Buddhist monks carved many caves into the cliffs as monasteries and chapels, some with wall paintings mixing Indian, Greek, Roman and Persian influences in the style called Gandharan art. Later, Muslim dynasties built fortresses in the valley.

In March 2001, during its first period in power, the Taliban ordered the destruction of all statues in Afghanistan and blew up both Buddhas. The destruction was condemned around the world. In 2003 UNESCO added the Cultural Landscape and Archaeological Remains of the Bamiyan Valley to the World Heritage List and to its List of World Heritage in Danger. Today the two empty niches remain. People still debate whether the statues should be rebuilt from fragments, or whether the empty niches should stay as a memorial.

docs.title: The Minaret of Jam
docs.text: In a remote river valley in central Afghanistan, about 1,900 m above sea level, stands the Minaret of Jam, a brick tower 65 m tall built in 1194 by the Ghurid sultan Ghiyas-od-din. It is covered in geometric patterns and a band of Arabic calligraphy in turquoise tile. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage site in 2002, Afghanistan's first.

docs.title: Pakistan's World Heritage sites
docs.text:
Pakistan's heritage stretches across every era of South Asian history. Here are four of its UNESCO World Heritage sites:

Site Where Inscribed What it shows Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro Sindh 1980 A planned city of the Indus Valley Civilization Taxila Punjab, near Islamabad 1980 An ancient city and Buddhist center on the old trade routes Buddhist Ruins of Takht-i-Bahi Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 1980 A Buddhist monastery founded in the 1st century CE on a high hilltop Fort and Shalamar Gardens in Lahore Punjab 1981 Mughal palaces and gardens

Put these next to Bamiyan and Jam and a pattern appears. The Buddhist sites of Takht-i-Bahi and Taxila in Pakistan and Bamiyan in Afghanistan belong to the same Gandharan world, joined by the same roads. Modern borders cut across a shared past.

docs.title: 18.11 Afghan Carpets
docs.text:
Afghan Carpets are hand-knotted wool rugs woven in Afghanistan, especially in the north and west, in traditions passed down within families for generations. They are one of the country's best-known crafts and an important source of income for many households.

How is a knotted carpet made? A weaver stretches strong threads on a loom. Then, row by row, she ties small knots of colored wool around those threads and cuts them short, so the cut ends stand up to form a soft, tufted surface called the pile. Weavers also make flatweave rugs, whose threads aren't knotted, along with bags and animal trappings for daily use.

Most Afghan carpet weaving was traditionally done by women of nomadic and semi-nomadic herding groups, such as the Turkmen and the Baluch, in the north and west of the country. Each tradition has its own look:

  • Turkmen carpets are mostly red, with rows of repeated abstract motifs called guls (goolz). Each gul pattern was linked to a particular clan.
  • Baluch carpets are more colorful and, while mostly abstract, often include floral designs and figures.

Hazara, Uzbek and Kyrgyz communities have their own weaving traditions too. Weaving was a family skill, passed down at home; red dyes were long made from the root of the madder plant. In refugee families of the 1980s, boys and young men also wove alongside women.

During the wars of the 1980s, millions of Afghans fled to Pakistan, and refugee weavers kept the craft alive in camps there. After Soviet troops invaded in December 1979, some weavers began making "war rugs," which worked tanks, helicopters and other military images into traditional patterns, a record of what weavers lived through. The British Museum has exhibited them as a form of history told in wool. Peshawar became the biggest market for Afghan carpets, and the carpets traveled down the same Khyber road that Ayesha's great-grandfather knew.

Carpets aren't Afghanistan's only famous craft. In 2025 UNESCO added Afghanistan's tradition of miniature painting in the style of Kamal ud-Din Behzad, a famous painter whose style many Afghan artists still use as their model, to its list of intangible cultural heritage. In 2024 it listed the art of crafting and playing the rubab, a string instrument carved from mulberry wood and one of the oldest instruments in the region, as heritage shared by Afghanistan, Iran, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

docs.title: 18.12 Putting It Together
docs.text:
Back at the Qureshis', Ben has stopped eating to listen to Ayesha's uncle, which, for Ben, is a big deal. He finally understands the line on the map. It's real: it marks two countries with different governments, laws and official languages. But it doesn't mark where Punjabi or Pashto stops, where the old road ends, or where hospitality begins.

This table compares the two countries:

Pakistan Afghanistan Capital Islamabad Kabul Population (2025, World Bank) 255,219,554 (about 255 million) 43,844,111 (about 44 million) Official or national languages Urdu (national), English (official) Dari and Pashto Most common first language Punjabi Dari is the most widely understood Main faith Islam (about 96%) Islam (nearly all) Coastline? Yes, on the Arabian Sea No, landlocked Government (October 2026) Federal parliamentary republic Taliban government, recognized only by Russia A UNESCO site Fort and Shalamar Gardens in Lahore Minaret of Jam; Bamiyan Valley
