docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter draws on the whole book, but these chapters help most:

  • Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition, for why some family memories are painful
  • Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts, for heritage languages and what happens when they fade
  • Chapter 13: Family, Names, and Life Events, for kinship words and family roles
  • Chapter 21: The South Asian Diaspora, for how families came to live outside South Asia

Last chapter, biggest project

Hi again, it's Mora! You've spent 21 chapters learning about the region, and maybe 21 conversations learning from the people around you. Right now, the grandparents and great-aunts who remember 1947, 1971, a village festival or a first winter in Minnesota are still here to ask. This chapter shows you how to keep their stories safe and how to use what you've learned to make your school a little better for everyone.

docs.title: 22.1 Twenty-One Pages of Nanu
docs.text:
It's the last week of May. The Prairie Ridge South Asian Student Association has one meeting left this year, and Zara Hossain is sitting on her bedroom floor with a stack of notebook pages. There are 21 of them, one for every Ask Your Elders interview she did with her Nanu. One page has the smell of the first monsoon rain in Chattogram. One has the Bangla word for the river ferry. One has a story about 1971 that Nanu told only once, very quietly, and then asked Zara to keep "just for the family."

Zara wants to do something with all of it. A booklet? A club night? A post? But she's not sure what she's allowed to share, or how.

Ben Lindqvist has a different worry. He's been the club's first non-South Asian member all year. He ran the quiz games, learned to count Teentaal and ate more biryani than anyone. Now some new freshmen are asking to join, and one of them asked him, "Is it weird that you're in it?" Ben texts Zara: "How do I help the club without being the guy who takes over? Like, what's my actual job?"

Two questions, one evening. How do you turn what you've learned into something that lasts, and how does everyone, whatever their background, take part in a way that's fair? This chapter answers both.

docs.title: 22.2 Who Am I? Cultural Identity
docs.text:
Start with something familiar: your favorite playlist. Some songs came from your parents' car, some from friends, some from a movie or a trip. You didn't write any of them, but you chose which ones to keep, and the list keeps changing. Nobody else's playlist is exactly like yours.

Identity works a lot like that.

Cultural Identity is a person's sense of belonging to one or more cultural groups, built from family, language, faith, food, place, history and the people around them. It is partly given (you didn't choose your grandparents) and partly chosen (you decide what to carry forward), and it changes over a lifetime.

For a teen with roots in South Asia, it might include a home region like Punjab, Kerala, Kandy or Chattogram, a language a grandparent speaks, a faith or a family's values, festival foods, and a Minnesota suburb with long winters and hockey. None of these makes someone "more" or "less" South Asian. Zara understands Bangla but answers in English, and that bothers her a little. She is not alone: in a Pew Research Center analysis of 2021-23 Census Bureau survey data, 28% of Indian Americans ages 5 and older spoke only English at home. Many heritage speakers understand far more than they say. That still counts.

docs.title: Labels and the hyphen
docs.text:
People name this kind of identity in many ways.

Label What it usually means Notes Bangladeshi American, Pakistani American, Sri Lankan American, Indian American Someone in the US with roots in one country The most specific. Many people prefer naming their own country. South Asian American Roots anywhere in the eight countries Common in clubs and archives. It doesn't center one country. Desi An informal word many in the diaspora use for themselves Not everyone uses it (see below). Bengali, Punjabi, Tamil, Pashtun A language or regional community Often older and more personal than any country name.

The word desi (देसी, DAY-see) comes from Hindi-Urdu and means "of the homeland" or "local." Many young people use it warmly, but not everyone from South Asia uses it or likes it for themselves. So ask people what they call themselves before you choose a label for them.

Hyphenated Identity means belonging to two or more cultures at once, sometimes written with a hyphen, as in "Indian-American." The hyphen has a history. In the United States from about 1890 to 1920, "hyphenated American" was a put-down suggesting immigrants were not fully loyal. In March 2019 the Associated Press, whose stylebook many newspapers follow, dropped the hyphen from dual-heritage terms like "Asian American." Some people see the hyphen as a bridge between two homes; others say it makes them sound like half of each. Zara writes "Bangladeshi American." Her cousin in London says "British Bangladeshi." Both are right for them.

docs.title: Third culture kids
docs.text:
Third Culture Kids are people who spent a large part of their childhood living in a culture different from their parents', usually because a parent's job moved the family between countries. The term comes from Ruth Useem, a sociologist at Michigan State University, who first used it in the 1960s for the children of Americans working abroad. She had developed the idea of a "third culture" with her husband, John Useem, after a year-long research stay in India. The "first culture" is the parents' home culture, the "second" is where the family lives, and the "third" is the blend the child builds from both.

Strictly speaking, children of immigrants who settle in one country, like Zara, aren't usually called third culture kids. But many second-generation teens say the idea fits how they feel: at home in two places, and fully at home in neither. Arjun Reddy, a friend from school, says he's "Hyderabad at dinner and Minnesota at practice." That in-between space isn't a problem to fix. A lot of creativity comes from it.

Culture moves

If culture never changed, nobody in South Asia would cook with chilies, which arrived from the Americas, probably with Portuguese traders, in the 1500s. When you mix traditions, you aren't breaking your culture. You're doing what every generation before you did.

docs.title: 22.3 Stereotypes and Colorism
docs.text:
Identity is how you see yourself. Other people also have ideas about you, and some of those ideas are unfair.

Stereotypes are fixed, oversimplified beliefs about a whole group of people, applied to every member of it. "South Asian kids are all good at math." "Every South Asian family wants a doctor." "They all speak Indian." (There is no language called "Indian." India alone lists 22 languages in its Constitution's Eighth Schedule, as Chapter 6 showed.)

Some stereotypes sound like compliments, but they still hurt. A student who struggles in chemistry may be ashamed to ask for help because everyone "expects" them to be good at it. And every stereotype erases the differences you've read about in this book, between eight countries, dozens of languages and many faiths. Stereotypes also live inside communities: a Punjabi family might joke about Bengalis, or a Pakistani family about Indians, and the other way around.

To push back without starting a fight, try asking a question ("What makes you say that?"), adding a real example ("My cousin is a pastry chef, actually") or naming the range ("South Asia is eight countries. Which one do you mean?"). And never ask the only South Asian student in a room to speak for everyone.

docs.title: Colorism
docs.text:
One stereotype deserves its own section, because it often lives inside families.

Colorism is prejudice or unfair treatment based on skin tone, usually favoring lighter skin over darker skin, including among people of the same background. The American writer Alice Walker is widely credited with bringing the word into use in the early 1980s, writing about the African American community. The same pattern shows up in many places, including South Asia.

In many South Asian families and media, lighter skin has long been praised and darker skin treated as something to fix. You may have heard an aunty warn a cousin not to play in the sun, or seen matrimonial ads asking for a "fair" bride. Writers and researchers trace this preference to several roots, including older social hierarchies and the legacy of colonial rule.

One well-documented example is Fair & Lovely, a skin-lightening cream made by Hindustan Unilever. It went on sale in India in 1975 and is sold in India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and beyond. After years of criticism that its name and ads linked "fair" skin to success, the company renamed it Glow & Lovely in 2020 and said its ads would show women of many skin tones. The cream itself is still sold. The renaming shows that public pressure can change how a company talks about beauty, even when the product stays.

Be careful with this one

Colorism can be very personal. If you talk about it in a club, talk about patterns and media, not about any member's skin, and never make a joke of it.

docs.title: 22.4 Appreciation or Appropriation?
docs.text:
Picture a jacket. In one version, a friend asks to borrow your grandfather's old jacket, learns the story behind it and tells people, "This was Zara's grandfather's." In another, someone takes it without asking, wears it as a joke costume and later sells copies under their own name. Same jacket, very different relationship.

Cultural Appropriation is when someone, usually from a more powerful or dominant group, takes an element of another group's culture (clothing, symbols, music, sacred practices) in a way that ignores its meaning, gives no credit, or turns it into a costume or product without the community's involvement. It stings most when the people who created a tradition were mocked for the very same thing.

Cultural Appreciation is learning about, honoring and taking part in another culture with respect: understanding what something means, being invited or welcome, giving credit, and supporting the people the tradition comes from.

Situation Leans toward appreciation Leans toward appropriation Saree, salwar kameez or kurta A friend's family invites you to a wedding and helps you wear it Wearing it as a "costume" for a theme party Bindi Wearing one when invited to a festival by people who explain it Using it as a sparkly sticker for a music festival look, unaware it has religious meaning for many Hindus Mehndi (henna) Getting mehndi at a friend's Eid or wedding celebration Calling it a "tribal tattoo" and selling designs without credit Yoga Practicing it and learning its roots in South Asian traditions Marketing it as a brand-new Western fitness invention Food Learning a friend's family recipe and naming where it comes from Claiming you "invented" a dish after stripping out what makes it South Asian

About yoga: it grew out of South Asian religious and philosophical traditions, and in 2014 the United Nations declared 21 June the International Day of Yoga. Yoga is a tradition, not a proven treatment for any disease, and nothing here is medical advice.

When you're not sure, ask yourself: Do I know what this means to the people it comes from? Was I invited? Is it sacred to anyone? Who gets the credit and the money? Would I do this the same way in front of a grandparent from that community?

Whose Story?

People inside South Asian communities don't all agree on where the line is. Many families are thrilled when a non-South Asian friend wears a lehenga to a wedding, and see it as a welcome. Others feel hurt seeing a bindi or a turban used as a costume, especially if they were teased for wearing the same thing at school. Some scholars argue that "appropriation" is used too loosely, since cultures have always borrowed through trade and migration, like chilies, tea and cricket. Others argue that borrowing is different when one side holds much more power and money. The questions above won't settle every case, but they help you think it through with the people most affected.

docs.title: 22.5 Being a Good Ally
docs.text:
Back to Ben's question: "What's my actual job?"

Allyship is the ongoing practice of supporting a group you are not part of, by listening, learning, showing up and using whatever voice or access you have to back that group, while letting its members lead and speak for themselves. It's something you do again and again, not a title you give yourself.

For Ben, that looks like:

  • Listening first. When a member describes being stereotyped, he doesn't jump in with "I'm sure they didn't mean it."
  • Doing his homework, so members don't have to teach him everything.
  • Taking real jobs, not the microphone. He runs the quiz and sets up chairs. He doesn't present "what Diwali is" to the school while South Asian members sit in the audience.
  • Speaking up where they aren't. If a hockey teammate mocks an accent, Ben can say "Not funny" in a room no club member is in.
  • Taking correction well. If he mispronounces a name, he says "Thanks, I'll get it right," and moves on.

Allyship works inside the club too. A Bangladeshi member can be an ally to a Sri Lankan Tamil member, and a Hindu member to a Muslim member. Nima Sherpa, whose family is from Nepal, may notice when "South Asian night" is really just "Indian night" and say so. Being South Asian doesn't make anyone an expert on all of South Asia.

A simple rule for allies

Back people up instead of replacing them. If you're about to speak for a group, first ask whether someone from that group would rather speak.

So what should Ben tell the freshman? "No, it's not weird. The club is for anyone who wants to learn. My job is to show up, listen and help."

docs.title: 22.6 Culture Lives in People: Oral History
docs.text:
Now for Zara's 21 pages.

A book can explain the monsoon, Partition or a wedding custom. It can't tell you what your Nanu smelled on the first rainy morning in Chattogram. That kind of knowledge lives in people, which is why every chapter ended with Ask Your Elders.

Intergenerational Dialogue is conversation between people of different generations, such as grandparents, parents and teens, in which each side learns from the other. Teens ask, elders tell, and sometimes elders ask back: "Why does your club do Diwali in October? We did it differently." A structured interview often opens up stories that never come out at the dinner table.

Oral History is the practice of recording people's memories of their own lives, in their own words, and keeping those recordings or notes so others can learn from them later. Memory isn't a database: two people can remember the same day differently. Oral history doesn't replace documents. It adds what documents leave out, like feelings, daily life and the voices of people who rarely appear in official records.

The Bangla word for "story" is গল্প (GOL-po), and the Urdu word is کہانی (ka-HAA-nee). Families across South Asia have passed down golpo and kahani for generations without writing them down. Oral history makes sure they aren't lost when the storytellers are gone.

docs.title: Oral history projects in South Asia and the diaspora
docs.text:
You won't be the first to do this.

Project Where What it collects South Asian American Digital Archive (SAADA) United States, founded 2008 Documents and stories of South Asian Americans. Its First Days Project, launched in 2013, collects short stories of people's first days in the US and has gathered hundreds of them. The 1947 Partition Archive Based in Berkeley, California Life stories of people who lived through Partition. It reports preserving over 12,000 oral histories, many recorded by volunteer "citizen historians." Liberation War Museum Dhaka, Bangladesh, established 1996 Eyewitness accounts of 1971. Since 2007 a mobile exhibit on a bus has visited schools, and students then interview elders and send in what they hear. One of its founding trustees reported more than 60,000 student-collected narratives in 2021. Citizens Archive of Pakistan Karachi, Pakistan, founded 2007 Its Oral History Project records memories from across Pakistan; the archive reports more than 5,000 oral histories.

Notice the Liberation War Museum's method. It's almost exactly what you've been doing: a student learns some history, goes home, asks an elder and writes it down. Tens of thousands of Bangladeshi teens have done what Zara did.

docs.title: 22.7 The Method: Consent, Listening, Preservation
docs.text:
The Oral History Project page has the short version and a consent script. Here is the full method, with the reasons behind it.

flowchart LR
    A[Prepare<br/>theme and questions] --> B[Ask for consent<br/>explain, get a yes]
    B --> C[Interview<br/>listen, follow up]
    C --> D[Save it<br/>date, first name, their words]
    D --> E[Check back<br/>show them what you wrote]
    E --> F{Did they agree<br/>to share?}
    F -- Yes --> G[Share with first names only]
    F -- No --> H[Keep it in the family]

docs.title: Step 1: Informed consent
docs.text:
Informed Consent means the person you interview understands what you are doing, why, how their words will be used and who might see them, and freely agrees, with the right to skip questions, stop at any time or change their mind later.

The Oral History Association, the main professional group for oral historians in the US, sets out these expectations in its Principles and Best Practices (revised in 2018) and its ethics statement: explain the purpose first, get consent (ideally in writing), tell narrators they can decline any question, and let them review the interview and limit or remove parts before anything is made public.

For a student project, that means:

  • Explain it simply and say what you'll do with it: notes or audio, and who, if anyone, will see it.
  • Make "no" easy. "You can skip anything, and we can stop whenever you want."
  • Get a parent or guardian's OK if you're under 18 and plan to share anything outside the family. The Story Archive requires it.
  • Protect privacy. First names or initials only. Never share a full name, address, phone number or photo without clear permission.
  • Let consent change. If Nanu later says, "Don't share that part," you don't.

Nanu asked Zara to keep the 1971 story "just for the family." Informed consent means it stays there. Zara can still use the other 20 pages.

docs.title: Step 2: Active listening
docs.text:
Active Listening is giving a speaker your full attention and showing that you understand, by focusing on their words, asking follow-up questions, reflecting back what you heard and leaving room for silence, instead of planning what you'll say next.

In an interview, that means:

  • Ask open questions. "What was a school day like?" gets a story. "Did you like school?" gets "yes."
  • Follow the energy. If they light up about a ferry ride, ask about the ferry. "What happened next?" and "What did that look like?" bring out the best details.
  • Let silence sit. Count to five before your next question. Elders often add the best part after a pause.
  • Don't correct. Memory isn't a test. If their story differs from this book, write the difference down. That's interesting, not wrong.
  • Read the room. Partition, 1971, the Sri Lankan civil war or leaving home can bring up grief. If someone goes quiet, say "We can stop or move on," and mean it.

If your elder is more comfortable in Bangla, Urdu, Sinhala, Nepali or Pashto, let them answer in that language, and ask a parent to help translate later. You don't need to be fluent to listen well.

You're more ready than you think

If you've done even one Ask Your Elders interview in this book, you've already practiced consent and listening. This chapter just adds the "why."

docs.title: Step 3: Preservation
docs.text:
Cultural Preservation is the work of keeping a community's traditions, knowledge, languages and memories alive for future generations, by recording them, practicing them and passing them on.

In a family, preservation can be a recipe card in Nanu's handwriting or a voice memo of a grandfather singing. For your interviews, label each one with the date, theme and the person's relationship and first name. Keep it in a private folder with a backup, and give the person a copy. Some families make a small printed booklet as a gift.

At a larger scale, UNESCO keeps lists of intangible cultural heritage, meaning living practices rather than buildings, to help protect them:

Tradition Country Added to UNESCO's lists Durga Puja in Kolkata India 2021 Mangal Shobhajatra, the Pohela Boishakh new year procession (renamed in Dhaka in April 2025 to an earlier name, Barshabaran Ananda Shobhajatra) Bangladesh 2016 Suri Jagek, the Kalasha people's way of reading the sun, moon and stars to plan the farming year Pakistan 2018 Rūkada Nātya, string puppet drama Sri Lanka 2018, the country's first element Drametse Ngacham, the mask dance of the drums from Drametse Bhutan proclaimed 2005, inscribed 2008

When the Drametse mask dance was first proclaimed, the listing noted that fewer people were practicing it, partly because young people were losing interest. Lists help, but a tradition survives only when people, often young people, keep doing it.

Preservation is not the same as freezing. Durga Puja in Kolkata today, with its giant themed pandals, looks different from a century ago, and it's still Durga Puja. A family that serves biryani next to the turkey at Thanksgiving is a living culture adapting, not one being lost.

docs.title: 22.8 Bring It Home: Clubs, Organizing and Impact
docs.text:
The last step is the one in the chapter's title: doing something with what you've learned.

Student Clubs are student-run groups at a school, usually with a faculty advisor, that meet regularly around a shared interest or identity. A South Asian Student Association is one kind. Clubs give students a place to belong and a chance to practice leading. Under a 2023 Minnesota law, every Minnesota high school must offer an ethnic studies course starting in the 2026-27 school year, and a club can be a natural partner for that class. The Club Kit has a two-year plan of 45-minute meetings mapped to the chapters, officer roles, food and allergy notes, and a guide to Ask Your Elders nights.

Community Organizing is people working together, in a planned way, toward a shared goal for their community, by finding out what people need, building relationships, dividing up the work and acting together. For a club, it might go like this:

  1. Listen first. Maybe new students from Nepal feel invisible, or the library has no books by Pakistani or Sri Lankan authors.
  2. Pick one goal. "A South Asian author display during Mother Language Day week."
  3. Build relationships. Meet the librarian, and invite another club, such as the Black Student Union, to co-host.
  4. Divide the work and act. One person makes the book list, one checks dates, one makes posters.
  5. Reflect. Ask what worked and what didn't.

Community Impact is the real difference a project makes in people's lives, the changes you can see or measure, not just how busy you were. Ten meetings is activity. Five new members who say they finally feel they belong is impact.

Activity (what you did) Impact (what changed) Held an Ask Your Elders night Elders said nobody had asked about their childhood before; three families started their own story booklets Ran Two Truths and a Myth for a middle school class Students could name all eight countries afterward Collected 12 stories for a family booklet Grandparents and grandchildren now share a printed copy of stories that lived only in memory

A simple habit: before each project, write down one question you'll ask and one number you'll count, then check them afterward.

At the last meeting, Zara brings a stapled booklet, "Nanu's Stories, Year One." It has 20 stories, not 21; the 1971 page stayed home, as promised. Nanu comes too, and when Zara reads the ferry story aloud, she adds a detail nobody had heard before. Ben runs the "best of the year" Jeopardy game and makes sure the Nepal category is worth as many points as the India one. When a freshman asks how to join, he points at Zara and Simran Kaur Gill, the treasurer: "Talk to them. They run it. I just help."

docs.title: Diagram: Interview Builder
docs.text:
Open the Interview Builder fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Interview Builder

sim-id: ch22-interview-builder Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Create Bloom Verb: design Learning Objective: The learner will design an ethical oral history interview plan, with a consent script, theme questions, follow-up prompts and a note-taking grid, for a chosen theme, narrator and length.

Canvas: responsive width; 640 px drawing area plus 120 px control area.

Controls: Theme menu (the 21 chapter themes plus a "life story" capstone), Narrator menu (grandparent, parent, aunt or uncle, community member), Length menu (10, 20 or 30 minutes), New questions button, Print plan button; click or tap the Consent, Questions and Notes tabs on the canvas.

Behavior: A plain-text question bank in the sim, written from each chapter's Ask Your Elders topics, feeds a plan of 6, 8 or 10 questions (a warm-up, theme questions, a "how has it changed" question and a closing question), plus a consent script adjusted for the narrator, follow-up prompts and a note grid. Print calls window.print() on a clean, print-only layout. Nothing is saved or sent anywhere.

Choose the chapter you enjoyed most and the person you want to interview. Read the Consent tab first, and notice how the script changes when you switch from a grandparent to a community member. Then open the Questions tab and change the length: a 10-minute plan keeps only a few theme questions, while a 30-minute plan adds room to warm up and reflect.

Press New questions to see other questions from the same theme, then Print plan and take the page to your interview. Notice what never changes, whatever you pick: a consent script, the right to skip questions and the rule of first names only.

docs.title: Ask Your Elders
docs.text:
Your interview for this chapter

Talk with a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, family friend or community elder about their life story: where they grew up, the moments that changed their life, what they carried with them and what they hope the next generation keeps. This is the capstone, a full oral history interview using everything in this chapter. If you don't have a South Asian elder to ask, interview a club advisor, a local temple, mosque, gurdwara or cultural center volunteer, or a classmate's family (with permission). Ten minutes is enough.

Before you start: Use the Interview Builder to print a plan with the "Life story" theme, read the consent script aloud first, and ask whether you may take notes or record audio. Bring a photo or object from their past if they have one.

Questions to ask

  1. What is your earliest memory? Where were you, and who was with you?
  2. Who were the most important people in your life when you were my age, and what did they teach you?
  3. What was the biggest change you lived through, and how did it change your everyday life?
  4. Is there a tradition, recipe, song or saying from your childhood that you still keep? Why that one?
  5. How have you changed since you were young, or since you moved to a new place? What surprised you most?
  6. What do you hope I, and people my age, keep from your life and from our family's traditions?

Listen for: moments where they describe their Cultural Identity changing over time, signs of Intergenerational Dialogue (stories passed down from their own elders), and anything they say they want kept, which is Cultural Preservation in their own words.

Save it: Write down one quote or story in their words, with their permission. If they agree, you can share it with the Roots & Rivers Story Archive.

Your turn: compare two answers

Look back at an earlier Ask Your Elders interview you did, from any chapter. Compare it with this life-story interview: did the same person tell a story differently, or add something new, when asked about their whole life instead of one topic? If a friend interviewed someone from a different country or generation, compare what each elder said they most want kept.

"Every family does it a little differently, and there is no wrong answer here."

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Culture is fixed. If you change a tradition, you lose it. Reality: Cultures have always changed through trade, migration and new ideas. Chilies came from the Americas, and Durga Puja and Eid celebrations look different in each generation. Adapting a tradition to a new home is a normal part of keeping it alive.

Myth: Appreciation and appropriation are the same thing, so it's either all fine or all wrong. Reality: The difference lies in meaning, invitation, credit and power. Wearing a saree to a friend's wedding when invited is very different from wearing a bindi as a party costume or selling a tradition without credit.

Myth: You need to speak your heritage language fluently to really belong. Reality: Many heritage speakers understand more than they speak, and in 2021-23, 28% of Indian Americans ages 5 and older spoke only English at home (Pew Research Center). Belonging comes from connection, curiosity and relationships, not a language test.

Myth: One person's story speaks for the whole community. Reality: Every oral history is one person's experience and memory. A Partition story from one family in Lahore and another from a family in Amritsar can both be true and still be very different. That's why oral historians collect many voices.

Myth: Being an ally means speaking for the group you support. Reality: Allyship means listening, showing up and backing a group's members while they speak for themselves. Allies use their voice most in rooms where those members aren't present.

docs.title: Check Yourself
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between cultural identity and a stereotype?

Cultural identity is a person's own sense of belonging to cultural groups, partly given and partly chosen. A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified belief that outsiders (or insiders) apply to every member of a group.

2. Why did the Associated Press drop the hyphen from terms like \"Asian American\" in 2019?

AP made the change after talking with journalists and community groups. Many argued that the hyphen splits a person's identity in half, and it echoes the old "hyphenated American" put-down that questioned immigrants' loyalty. Without the hyphen, the heritage word simply describes the American.

3. Name two things that separate cultural appreciation from cultural appropriation.

Any two of: understanding the meaning, being invited or welcome, giving credit, making sure the community benefits, and treating sacred items with care instead of as costumes.

4. What does informed consent require in an oral history interview?

The person must understand what the project is, how their words will be used and who may see them, and must freely agree. They can skip questions, stop at any time and change their mind later, and they should be able to review what is shared.

5. Give one example of activity and one example of impact for a student club.

Activity: holding an Ask Your Elders night. Impact: elders said they had never been asked about their childhood, and families started their own story booklets. (Other pairs that show a real, visible change also work.)

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the three steps of the oral history method described in Section 22.7.

    Answer

    Informed consent, active listening and preservation (keeping the record safe and giving it back to the narrator).

  2. Name two oral history projects from this chapter and the country where each is based.

    Answer

    Any two of: SAADA and its First Days Project (United States), The 1947 Partition Archive (United States, Berkeley), the Liberation War Museum (Bangladesh, Dhaka), the Citizens Archive of Pakistan (Pakistan, Karachi).

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain in your own words why children of immigrants who settle in one country are usually not called third culture kids, and why many still relate to the idea.

    Answer

    Strictly, third culture kids grow up moving between countries because of a parent's job, and the term isn't usually used for permanent immigrants. Many second-generation teens still relate because they also build a blended "third" culture between their parents' home culture and the one they live in.

  2. Explain why "preservation" doesn't mean keeping a tradition exactly the same forever.

    Answer

    Living traditions change as people practice them in new times and places. Preservation means keeping the knowledge, meaning and practice alive and passed on, which often requires adapting, like celebrating Eid or Durga Puja in a new setting.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Use the Interview Builder to create a 20-minute plan for the theme you enjoyed most in this book. Print it (or save it as a PDF), then mark one question you would cut and one you would add for your specific narrator. Hint: think about what your narrator knows best and what might be painful for them.

  2. A classmate says, "You're Pakistani, so you must love spicy food and be good at cricket." Write a short, calm reply that uses one of the moves from Section 22.3. Hint: asking a question or adding a real example often works better than arguing.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare the Liberation War Museum's student oral history program with the Ask Your Elders method in this book. Identify two ways they are alike and one risk that comes with student-collected history. Hint: think about who asks, who answers and how stories are checked.

  2. Look at the Fair & Lovely to Glow & Lovely renaming in 2020. Analyze what changed and what stayed the same, and what that suggests about how colorism can (and can't) be changed by a company. Hint: separate the name and ads from the product and the beliefs behind it.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Choose two rows from the appreciation and appropriation table in Section 22.4. For each, judge whether the "appreciation" column is enough, or whether you'd add a condition. Defend your choices. Hint: the Whose Story? box shows that people in the community disagree.

  2. A club officer wants to post a member's grandmother's Partition story on the club's Instagram because "it's so powerful." Evaluate this plan using the rules of informed consent and privacy. Hint: who agreed to what, and who might see it?

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a one-semester community organizing plan for your club with one clear goal, a list of partners, a division of work and one way to measure community impact. Hint: use the five organizing steps and the activity versus impact table.

  2. Conduct the capstone life-story interview from Ask Your Elders, then create a one-page "story card" from it: a title, the narrator's first name or relationship, one story in their words (with permission), and one sentence on what you learned about your own cultural identity. Hint: show the card to your narrator before sharing it with anyone.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Cultural identity is partly given and partly chosen, and it changes over a lifetime. Labels like "South Asian American," "Bangladeshi American" or "desi" are personal, so ask people what they call themselves.
  • Stereotypes, even ones that sound like compliments, erase the huge variety within South Asia. Colorism, a preference for lighter skin, is a stereotype that often lives inside families and media.
  • Appreciation and appropriation differ in meaning, invitation, credit and power. Allyship means listening, showing up and backing others while they speak for themselves.
  • Oral history records people's memories in their own words. Projects in the United States, Pakistan and Bangladesh have collected thousands of these stories, many gathered by students or volunteers.
  • Good oral history rests on informed consent, active listening and careful preservation: explain, get a real yes, follow the story, use first names only and give the story back.
  • Cultural preservation keeps traditions alive by practicing and adapting them, not by freezing them.
  • Student clubs can turn learning into community organizing and real community impact. The Club Kit and Oral History Project pages show you how to start.

You brought it home!

You've finished all 22 chapters, and every tradition you met had a story behind it. Now go find the ones in your own family, ask with care, and keep them safe. That's the next chapter, and you get to write it.

docs.title: Quiz: Bring It Home
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 22. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What is oral history?

  1. A collection of official government documents about a community
  2. The practice of recording people's memories of their own lives, in their own words, and keeping them for others to learn from
  3. Stories that are made up and passed around without anyone writing them down
  4. A news interview with a famous person about current events
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Oral history records people's own memories in their own words and preserves them, with permission, for the future. It is not made-up storytelling (C). It adds personal experience to what official documents (A) leave out.

Concept Tested: Oral History Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which description matches the term "third culture kids" as Ruth Useem first used it?

  1. Any child of immigrants who settles permanently in a new country
  2. Children who speak three languages at home
  3. Children of parents from three different countries
  4. Children who spent much of their childhood in a culture different from their parents', usually because a parent's job moved the family abroad
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Ruth Useem used the term in the 1960s for children of Americans working abroad. Strictly, children of immigrants who settle in one country (A) aren't usually called third culture kids, although many second-generation teens relate to the idea.

Concept Tested: Third Culture Kids Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
In 2020, Hindustan Unilever renamed its skin-lightening cream Fair & Lovely as Glow & Lovely. Which concept from the chapter does this example mainly illustrate?

  1. Colorism
  2. Cultural preservation
  3. Hyphenated identity
  4. Community impact
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The cream was criticized for linking lighter, "fair" skin to beauty and success, which is colorism: favoring lighter skin over darker skin. The renaming was a response to that criticism; it is not an example of preserving a tradition (B).

Concept Tested: Colorism Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why did many people object to the hyphen in terms like "Indian-American"?

  1. Hyphens are grammatically wrong in all English writing
  2. The hyphen was required only for South Asian Americans
  3. "Hyphenated American" had been used as a put-down suggesting immigrants weren't fully loyal, and some felt the hyphen split them in half
  4. The Constitution of India bans hyphens in names
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. From about 1890 to 1920, "hyphenated American" was used as an insult, and many people felt the hyphen made them sound only partly American. In March 2019 the Associated Press dropped the hyphen from dual-heritage terms. Hyphens aren't wrong in general (A); this is about history and identity.

Concept Tested: Hyphenated Identity Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Which statement best explains the difference between cultural appreciation and cultural appropriation?

  1. Appreciation means never taking part in another culture; appropriation means taking part at all
  2. Appreciation involves understanding meaning, being invited, giving credit and supporting the community; appropriation takes elements while ignoring meaning, credit or the community
  3. Appreciation applies only to food, and appropriation applies only to clothing
  4. There is no real difference; both words mean borrowing from another culture
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter separates the two by meaning, invitation, credit and power. Appreciation does not mean staying away entirely (A); wearing a saree to a friend's wedding when invited is an example of appreciation.

Concept Tested: Cultural Appreciation Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why does the chapter say that preservation is "not the same as freezing"?

  1. Living traditions survive by being practiced and adapted, so a tradition can change and still be itself
  2. UNESCO forbids any change to traditions on its lists
  3. Traditions only count if they are exactly as they were a thousand years ago
  4. Preservation means storing objects in a museum and no longer using them
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Durga Puja in Kolkata looks different from a century ago and is still Durga Puja, and families adapt festivals to new homes. Option C is the "culture is fixed" myth the chapter corrects.

Concept Tested: Cultural Preservation Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Dilan is about to interview his grandfather about growing up in Kandy. Which step should come first?

  1. Start recording audio so nothing is missed
  2. Ask the hardest question first while his grandfather has the most energy
  3. Post a photo of his grandfather to the club's page to build excitement
  4. Explain the project, how the notes will be used and who might see them, and ask whether it's OK, making clear he can skip questions or stop
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Informed consent comes before anything else. Recording without asking (A) skips consent, and posting a photo (C) breaks the privacy rule of sharing nothing without clear permission.

Concept Tested: Informed Consent Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
During an interview, Ayesha's grandmother mentions a train ride to Lahore and her voice changes. Ayesha's next planned question is about cricket. What is the best active listening move?

  1. Move straight to the cricket question to stay on schedule
  2. Correct her if the date she gives doesn't match the textbook
  3. Pause, then gently ask something like "Can you tell me more about that?" while being ready to stop or move on if the memory is painful
  4. Tell her own story about a train ride to keep the conversation going
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Active listening means following the speaker's lead, leaving room for silence and reading the room, especially with possibly painful memories. Sticking rigidly to the list (A) misses the story, and correcting memory (B) treats the interview like a test.

Concept Tested: Active Listening Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
The Liberation War Museum in Dhaka asks school students to interview elders about 1971 and send in their accounts. How is this most similar to the book's Ask Your Elders method?

  1. Both rely on official government records instead of personal memories
  2. Both have teens ask older relatives or community members about their own experiences and write the stories down
  3. Both are run only by professional historians
  4. Both collect stories only from people who left South Asia
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In both, young people learn some history, then gather memories from elders in their own words. Option A describes the opposite of oral history. Option D is wrong because the museum's accounts come from people in Bangladesh, not only from people who left.

Concept Tested: Intergenerational Dialogue Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
A club reports two results at the end of the year: "We held 10 meetings" and "Five new members said they finally feel they belong at school." Which analysis is correct?

  1. Both are community impact, because both are numbers
  2. Neither matters, because clubs can't measure anything
  3. The first is activity; the second is community impact, because it describes a real change in people's lives
  4. The first is community impact, because more meetings always means more change
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter defines community impact as the real difference a project makes, not just how busy a group was. Counting meetings (D) measures activity; impact shows up in what changed for people.

Concept Tested: Community Impact Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Bring It Home
docs.text:
1. OHA Statement on Ethics - Oral History Association - The professional standard for oral history in the US: informed consent, the narrator's right to decline questions and review an interview, privacy, and archiving. Read this before your capstone interview.
  2. Principles and Best Practices (revised 2018) - Oral History Association - The overview page that links the association's full guidance, including a document written for people being interviewed. Good for club officers who run Ask Your Elders nights.
  3. AFC Plans to Enhance Resources for Higher Education - Library of Congress, American Folklife Center (Folklife Today blog) - Points students and teachers to Folklife and Fieldwork, the Library of Congress's free step-by-step fieldwork guide in English and Spanish, and to other interview resources.
  4. South Asian American Digital Archive - Wikipedia - A short overview of SAADA, founded in 2008, and its First Days Project (2013), which collects immigrants' stories of their first days in the US. Use it as a starting point, then visit saada.org.
  5. About The 1947 Partition Archive - The 1947 Partition Archive - Explains how volunteer "citizen historians" recorded more than 12,000 life stories of people who lived through Partition, and how anyone can train to record one.
  6. Liberation War Museum - Mofidul Hoque, HURIGHTS OSAKA FOCUS Vol. 105 (September 2021) - A founder-trustee of Dhaka's Liberation War Museum describes its mobile museum for schools and the 60,000-plus 1971 accounts that students collected from elders.
  7. The Citizens Archive of Pakistan - Citizens Archive of Pakistan - A Karachi-based nonprofit, founded in 2007, that runs an Oral History Project and reports more than 5,000 oral histories collected. Shows how a country-wide archive works.
  8. Indians in the U.S. Fact Sheet - Pew Research Center - Population, language use and other data on Indian Americans, including the share who speak only English at home (2021-23 data). Pew has matching fact sheets for Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan and Nepalese Americans.
  9. Why Hyphenation of Dual Heritage Terms Has Been a Point of Contention in Newsrooms - Daily Bruin (UCLA student newspaper), April 2019 - A clear, student-written explainer on the history of the "hyphenated American" insult and the Associated Press's 2019 decision to drop the hyphen.
  10. Third culture kid - Wikipedia - Explains Ruth Useem's term, its link to her research in India, and why second-generation immigrants are usually not counted as third culture kids. Follow its footnotes to the original research.

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
A learning graph is a map of every idea in this book and which ideas you need first. Each of the 368 concepts is a node. An arrow from one concept to another means "learn this one first". For example, Diwali points to Lunisolar Calendar, because you need the calendar to understand why Diwali moves each year.

The graph keeps the book honest: no chapter uses an idea before the book has taught it.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
Every chapter has one interactive simulation. They work on phones and computers, need no login, and save nothing about you. Click a picture to open the sim.

  • Region Explorer

    A schematic tile map of the eight countries of South Asia, with mountains, rivers, seas and an animated southwest monsoon.

    Chapter 1: What Is South Asia?

  • Ancient Timeline

    A scrubbable timeline of South Asia from about 7000 BCE to 550 CE, linked to a schematic map of eleven ancient places.

    Chapter 2: Ancient Roots

  • Empire Swim Lanes

    A swim-lane timeline of ten South Asian powers from 600 to 1800 CE, with a moving year line that shows which powers existed at the same time.

    Chapter 3: Empires and Encounters

  • Borders Then and Now

    A schematic block diagram showing how British India, the princely states and Ceylon became India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka between 1857 and 1972.

    Chapter 4: Colonialism, Independence, and Partition

  • Faith Explorer

    Compare eight South Asian faith traditions through the same five lenses (origins, sacred texts, place of worship, a major festival, a core idea) without ranking them.

    Chapter 5: Faiths of South Asia

  • Script Family Tree

    A simplified family tree of South Asian scripts, from Brahmi and Aramaic to the scripts used today, showing how each one writes ka, ki, ku and k.

    Chapter 6: Languages and Scripts

  • Festival Wheel

    A 12-month calendar wheel of South Asian festivals that shows why solar, lunisolar and lunar festival dates move in different ways.

    Chapter 7: Festivals Through the Year

  • Thali Builder

docs.title: Region Explorer
docs.text: Run the Region Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Region Explorer is a schematic tile map of South Asia. Each of the eight countries (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka) is a colored tile placed roughly where it sits in the region. The map also shows the Hindu Kush, the Himalaya, the Western and Eastern Ghats, the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers, the Thar Desert, the Deccan Plateau, and the three big bodies of water around the region: the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean.

Click or tap a tile (or pick a country from the menu) to see its capital, its population in 2025 (World Bank) and its main languages. Press Start monsoon to watch the southwest monsoon spread over the region on its normal schedule, from the sea near Sri Lanka and Kerala in late May, to all of India by about 8 July. The dates follow the India Meteorological Department's normal onset dates, but the shape of the spreading rain is simplified.

The map is schematic, not to scale, and does not draw any national borders.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the map before touching anything. Find the eight country tiles and the two big mountain chains across the north.
  2. Click or tap any country tile. Read its capital, 2025 population and main languages in the panel.
  3. Use the menu under the map to jump to a country you can't find.
  4. Press Start monsoon and watch the shaded rain zone grow from the southwest sea. Use Pause to stop at any date.
  5. Notice which places the monsoon reaches first, which it reaches last, and which it barely reaches at all.
  6. Press Reset to start the monsoon again. Untick the checkbox to hide the mountain, river and sea labels and test yourself.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to locate the eight countries of South Asia on a schematic map and explain how the region's mountains and the southwest monsoon shape where water arrives and where people live.

Bloom level: Understand (locate, explain).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch01-region-explorer/main.html" height="702px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world geography, world history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Students open the sim and, without clicking, write down the names of any countries they already know. Most will list India and maybe Pakistan.
  2. (5 min) Students click all eight tiles and fill in a quick table: country, capital, population (2025), one main language.
  3. (5 min) Students run the monsoon and pause it three times: once when it reaches Kerala, once when it reaches Bangladesh, and once at the end. At each pause they write which countries are getting rain.
  4. (5 min) Pairs discuss: Why does Afghanistan stay mostly dry? Why are the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta so crowded with people?

Assessment questions:

  1. Name the eight countries of South Asia. Which two are island countries?
  2. Which mountain range runs across the north of Nepal and Bhutan? Which one crosses Afghanistan?
  3. Where does the southwest monsoon arrive first in India, and about when?
  4. Which South Asian country does the summer monsoon barely reach, and why might that matter for farming there?
  5. Using the map, explain why so many people live along the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra.

docs.title: Ancient Timeline
docs.text: Run the Ancient Timeline MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Ancient Timeline links time to place. Across the top is a timeline from about 7000 BCE, when farmers settled at Mehrgarh, to about 550 CE, when the Gupta Empire faded. Eight colored bands mark the major periods: Mehrgarh farming, the Indus Valley Civilization, the Vedic Period, the Mahajanapadas, the Maurya Empire, the Sangam Age, the Kushan Empire and the Gupta Empire. Overlapping periods sit in two rows so you can see when they ran at the same time.

Below the timeline is a schematic map with eleven places: Mehrgarh, Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Taxila (Pakistan), Kandahar (Afghanistan), Lumbini (Nepal), Pataliputra and Nalanda (India), Mahasthangarh (Bangladesh), Madurai (India) and Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka). As you move the year, places light up while they mattered, and an event card explains what was happening.

All dates are approximate and follow the sources in Chapter 2. To fit the crowded later centuries, the timeline gives them more space than the long early period. The map is schematic, not to scale, and draws no borders.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with the slider at the far left (about 7000 BCE). Read the event card.
  2. Drag the slider slowly to the right, or press Play to move through time automatically. Press Pause to stop.
  3. Watch which dots light up on the map and which period bands are highlighted.
  4. Click or tap any dot to read about that place and see which present-day country it is in.
  5. Use the Jump to an era menu to go straight to a period.
  6. Stop at 100 CE and notice which two periods overlap.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to put the major ancient periods of South Asia in order, from Mehrgarh (about 7000 BCE) to the end of the Gupta Empire (about 550 CE), and connect each period to the places, and present-day countries, where it happened.

Bloom level: Remember and Understand (sequence, locate, explain).

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Before touching the sim, students write down what they think is the oldest event in South Asian history.
  2. (6 min) Students drag the slider from left to right and fill in a table with three columns: period, approximate dates, places lit.
  3. (5 min) Students stop at 2200 BCE, 250 BCE, 100 CE and 500 CE, and for each write one sentence from the event card in their own words.
  4. (5 min) Pairs click every dot and sort the eleven places by present-day country. Discuss: why is it misleading to call all of this "ancient India"?

Assessment questions:

  1. Put these in order: Gupta Empire, Indus cities, Mehrgarh, Maurya Empire, Vedic Period.
  2. Name one ancient place in Pakistan, one in Nepal, one in Bangladesh and one in Sri Lanka.
  3. Which two periods overlap around 100 CE, and where was each one?
  4. About when was Nalanda founded, and by which empire?
  5. Why does the timeline say "about" in front of almost every date?

docs.title: Empire Swim Lanes
docs.text: Run the Empire Swim Lanes MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Empire Swim Lanes is a timeline of South Asia from 600 to 1800 CE drawn as ten horizontal lanes, one for each major power or group of powers: the Cholas, the Sri Lankan kingdoms, the Delhi Sultanate, the Bengal Sultanate, the Vijayanagara Empire, the Deccan sultanates, the Mughal Empire, the Maratha Empire, the Durrani Empire, and the European trading companies. Each colored bar shows roughly when a power existed. Bars with an arrow at the right end continued after 1800.

An orange year line moves with the slider. Bars that are active in the chosen year light up, and the panel below lists every power active in that year. Click or tap a bar to read its dates, its capital and one key fact.

The lanes are a selection. Many other kingdoms, such as the Rajput kingdoms, the Ahom kingdom in Assam, the kingdoms of Nepal and the Sikh kingdom of Punjab, are not shown. Dates are approximate, and the sources are listed in the chapter's fact log.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the panel at the starting year, 1600. Count how many powers were active.
  2. Drag the year slider to 1000, then to 1450, then to 1750. Count the active powers each time.
  3. Press Play to sweep the year line from 600 to 1800. Press Pause to stop at any year.
  4. Click or tap any bar to read its dates, capital and one key fact. Click an empty spot in a lane to go back to the year summary.
  5. Look for years when new powers appeared while older ones were still active.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to compare the dates of major South Asian powers between 600 and 1800 CE and explain, with examples, that many powers coexisted and overlapped rather than replacing each other one at a time.

Bloom level: Analyze (compare, explain).

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Before opening the sim, students write down how many empires they think ruled South Asia between 600 and 1800, and whether they think those empires came one after another.
  2. (7 min) Students set the slider to 1000, 1450, 1600 and 1750 and record the powers active in each year in a table.
  3. (5 min) Students click three bars from different lanes and write one fact about each, including its capital.
  4. (5 min) Pairs discuss: Was any year ruled by only one power? What does the picture suggest about the idea of one empire "replacing" another?

Assessment questions:

  1. Name two powers that existed in South Asia at the same time as the early Mughal Empire.
  2. Which lane shows two kingdoms existing at the same time on one island? Name them.
  3. In which year on the timeline did the Delhi Sultanate end, and which power began that same year?
  4. Which power in the sim continued after 1800, and how can you tell?
  5. Explain, using two examples from the sim, why "one empire replaced another" is a misleading way to describe this period.

docs.title: Borders Then and Now
docs.text: Run the Borders Then and Now MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Borders Then and Now is a schematic block diagram, not a map. It shows how the political units of South Asia split, joined and changed names in six steps: 1857, 1858, 1947, 1948, 1971 and 1972.

In 1857 and 1858, one large block stands for East India Company territory and then British India under the Crown. Small purple tiles inside it stand for the princely states, which kept their own rulers. Ceylon sits below as a separate British colony, and Afghanistan, Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives appear as gray outside blocks because they were never part of British India. In 1947 the big block splits into West Pakistan, India and East Pakistan, and the princely-state tiles change color as they join a side. Hyderabad stays purple until 1948, and Jammu and Kashmir becomes a striped "disputed" tile. In 1971, East Pakistan becomes Bangladesh, and in 1972, Ceylon becomes Sri Lanka.

A panel explains each step with dates and, for 1947 and 1971, the sourced ranges historians give for deaths and displacement. The diagram draws no borders and is not to scale.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the 1857 panel and find the large block, the princely-state tiles, Ceylon and the gray neighbors.
  2. Press Next (or tap the diagram) to move forward one step. Press Back to go back.
  3. At each step, decide whether a block split, joined or only changed its name.
  4. Leave Show 1947 migration arrows ticked to see that people crossed the new borders in both directions.
  5. Press Play to watch all six steps in order. Press Pause to stop.
  6. Drag the slider to jump straight to any year.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain how one colonial territory, British India, became several nations in separate steps, especially the two events of 1947 and 1971, and how Ceylon and the princely states fit into that story.

Bloom level: Understand (explain, summarize).

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Before opening the sim, students write down when they think Bangladesh became a country. Many will guess 1947.
  2. (8 min) In pairs, students step through all six years and fill in a three-column table: year, what split or joined, what only changed name.
  3. (5 min) Students stop at 1947 and 1971 and read the ranges in the panel aloud. Discuss why historians give ranges instead of single numbers.
  4. (4 min) Exit ticket: in two sentences, explain how a person could live in three countries without moving.

Assessment questions:

  1. In which year did the East India Company's rule end, and what replaced it?
  2. Which two new countries were created in 1947, and how was Pakistan divided?
  3. What happened to Hyderabad and to Jammu and Kashmir after 1947?
  4. Did Partition create Bangladesh? Explain using the diagram.
  5. How was Ceylon's path to independence different from East Pakistan's?

docs.title: Faith Explorer
docs.text: Run the Faith Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Faith Explorer shows eight faith traditions of South Asia as equal-sized tiles in alphabetical order: Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Jainism and Sikhism, plus a row of smaller communities, Jewish communities and Zoroastrians (Parsis). The order and the equal sizes are deliberate: the sim compares, it does not rank.

Pick a faith and a lens (Origins, Sacred texts, Place of worship, A major festival, or A core idea) to read a short card. Every card is written the way followers usually describe their own faith ("Muslims believe...", "In Sikh tradition..."), not as the book's own claim. Tick Compare to see two faiths side by side through the same lens. Each card is a starting point, not a full description: practice varies a great deal within every faith.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. The sim opens in Compare mode with Sikhism (faith 1, orange) and Islam (faith 2, teal) through the Place of worship lens. Read both cards.
  2. Change the lens menu to Sacred texts, A major festival and A core idea, and read both cards each time.
  3. Tap a tile to change faith 2, or use the two faith menus. In Compare mode, tapping a tile sets faith 2; untick Compare to tap a tile and set faith 1.
  4. Untick Compare to read one faith's card in a larger size.
  5. For each pair you compare, write one sentence that names a similarity and one that names a difference, without using words like "better" or "truer."

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to compare South Asian faith traditions on the same five dimensions (origins, sacred texts, place of worship, a major festival and a core idea), describing each in its followers' own terms and without ranking them.

Bloom level: Analyze (compare, distinguish).

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world history, world religions, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Set ground rules as a group: describe, don't judge; no ranking; practice varies; anyone may pass on sharing personal beliefs.
  2. (8 min) In pairs, students choose two faiths and fill in a five-row table (one row per lens) using Compare mode.
  3. (7 min) Each pair writes two comparison sentences, one similarity and one difference, using neutral language ("Both...", "In contrast...").
  4. (5 min) Pairs share one sentence with the class. The teacher or club leader notes any wording that slips into ranking and asks the group how to rephrase it.

Assessment questions:

  1. Name the place of worship for Sikhism, Islam, Hinduism and Zoroastrianism.
  2. According to their Origins cards, which two faiths in the sim have old communities in Kerala?
  3. Compare the core ideas of Jainism and Buddhism in two sentences.
  4. Why does the sim show the faiths in alphabetical order with equal-sized tiles?
  5. Choose one lens and explain what it leaves out about how people actually live their faith.

docs.title: Script Family Tree
docs.text: Run the Script Family Tree MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Bangla, Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil and Sinhala letters look nothing alike at first glance. This MicroSim shows that most of them are cousins. The tree has two roots.

  • Brahmi, in use by the 3rd century BCE, splits into a northern branch (through the Gupta script) and southern branches (through the Kadamba and Pallava scripts). Its living descendants on the tree are Gurmukhi, Devanagari, Gujarati, Bengali-Assamese, Odia, Tibetan, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam and Sinhala.
  • Aramaic, the script of the Persian Empire's government, leads to Kharoshthi (no longer used) and, through Arabic, to the Perso-Arabic script used for Urdu, Pashto, Sindhi and more. Thaana, the script of the Maldives, took the shapes of its first letters from Arabic numerals, so it hangs from the Arabic branch with a dashed line.

Every modern script on the tree shows a real Unicode character for the syllable "ka." Click any script to see how it writes ka, ki, ku and a bare k, and which languages use it. Most scholars think Brahmi itself was inspired by an Aramaic-family script, but this is debated, so that link is hidden until you tick the checkbox.

The tree is simplified. Scholars draw some of the middle branches differently, and many scripts are left out.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with Bengali-Assamese selected. Read the panel: the same letter ক gets different vowel marks for ka, ki and ku.
  2. Use the Show ka menu to switch every script on the tree to ki. Notice that each script adds a vowel mark to the same base letter.
  3. Switch to k (no vowel). Most Brahmi-family scripts add a small "vowel-killer" mark. Which script shows "none," and why?
  4. Click Devanagari, then Gujarati. They share a parent. What is the most obvious difference?
  5. Click Tamil, Telugu and Sinhala. Follow the lines back to Brahmi. Telugu and Tamil are Dravidian languages, and Sinhala is Indo-Aryan, yet all three scripts are Brahmi's grandchildren.
  6. Click Perso-Arabic and Thaana. Which direction are they written? How are vowels handled?
  7. Tick Show debated link to see where many scholars think Brahmi's idea of writing came from.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain that many South Asian scripts share Brahmi as a common ancestor, and explain how an abugida writes a consonant with an inherent vowel that vowel marks can change or remove.

Bloom level: Understand (explain, compare).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch06-script-family-tree/main.html" height="782px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world history, world languages, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Ask students who can read or write any South Asian script to write their name or the name of their language on the board. Ask the class: are these scripts related?
  2. (6 min) Students explore the tree and fill in a three-column table: script, its parent on the tree, one language that uses it.
  3. (6 min) Students switch the menu from ka to ki to ku to k. In pairs, they write one sentence explaining what stays the same and what changes. Introduce the word abugida.
  4. (5 min) Discussion: Hindi and Urdu sound very close in everyday speech but sit on different roots of the tree. Tamil and Telugu are not Indo-Aryan languages but use Brahmi-family scripts. What does that tell us about the difference between a language and a script?

Assessment questions:

  1. Name three modern scripts that descend from Brahmi and one that does not.
  2. In Devanagari, क is read "ka" and कि is read "ki." Explain what the extra mark does.
  3. Why does the tree show Telugu (a Dravidian language) on the same root as Devanagari (used for Indo-Aryan languages)?
  4. Thaana writes every vowel with a mark. Why do some linguists say it is not a true abugida?
  5. Why is the link from Aramaic to Brahmi shown as "debated"?

docs.title: Festival Wheel
docs.text: Run the Festival Wheel MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Festival Wheel is a 12-month calendar drawn as a circle, with 1 January at the top and the months running clockwise. Fourteen festivals and festival groups from across South Asia sit on the wheel: Pongal, Losar, Holi, Nowruz, Vaisakhi and Pohela Boishakh, Vesak, Onam, Navaratri and Dashain, Diwali and Tihar, Christmas, Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha and Ashura.

Drag the Year slider from 1990 to 2060 and watch what happens. Festivals set by the sun (gold) stay in the same place. Festivals set by a lunisolar calendar (teal) jump back and forth by a few weeks but stay in the same season. Islamic festivals (orange), which follow a purely lunar calendar, slide about 11 days earlier every year and travel all the way around the wheel in about 33 years.

None of the moving dates are typed in. The sim calculates new and full moons from a standard astronomy formula (Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, chapter 49), then applies simple calendar rules: for example, Diwali falls on the new moon that ends the lunar month in which the sun enters Libra, and an Islamic month starts the day after the new crescent could first be seen in South Asia. For 2026 these rules give the same dates as the Government of India's holiday list for Eid al-Fitr (21 March), Buddha Purnima (1 May), Eid al-Adha (28 May, after the moon-sighting change), Muharram (26 June), Dussehra (20 October) and Diwali (8 November). Holi comes out one day early in 2026. Real dates can differ by a day because local calendars and moon sighting decide them.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with the year 2026. Click or tap any dot (or pick a festival from the menu) to read its date, where it is celebrated and why it moves.
  2. Drag the Year slider one year at a time. Watch the gold dots, then the teal dots, then the orange dots.
  3. Select Eid al-Fitr and read the orange line in the panel: it tells you next year's date and how many days earlier it is.
  4. Press Play years to step through the years automatically. Press Pause to stop.
  5. Keep Show Islamic dates from the past 4 years ticked to see faint dots trailing behind the Islamic festivals.
  6. Switch the menu to Color by faith to see which traditions each festival belongs to. Several are shared by many faiths.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain why solar festivals keep the same Gregorian date, lunisolar festivals move within a season, and Islamic lunar festivals move about 11 days earlier each year.

Bloom level: Understand (explain, compare).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch07-festival-wheel/main.html" height="734px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world history, world religions, ethnic studies, math connections, or a South Asian student club planning its calendar)

Duration: 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Before opening the sim, students guess: "Will Diwali and Eid be on the same dates next year?"
  2. (5 min) Students set the year to 2026 and record the dates of Vaisakhi, Holi and Eid al-Fitr. Then they move to 2027 and 2028 and record the same three festivals.
  3. (5 min) Students sort the 14 markers into three groups: never moves, moves a little, moves a lot. They compare their groups with the color key.
  4. (4 min) Students find the year when Eid al-Fitr falls in December, and the year when Ramadan comes back to roughly the same month as in 2026.
  5. (3 min) Exit ticket: "In one or two sentences, explain to a club member why Eid is 'early' this year."

Assessment questions:

  1. Which festivals on the wheel never move from their Gregorian date? What do they have in common?
  2. Why does Holi always stay in spring even though it follows the moon?
  3. Eid al-Fitr is on about 21 March 2026. About when will it fall in 2027, and why?
  4. About how many years does it take Ramadan to move all the way around the calendar?
  5. The sim says "about" for most dates. Give two reasons the real date can differ from the computed one.

docs.title: Thali Builder
docs.text: Run the Thali Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A thali is a round plate that holds a whole meal: a staple grain in the middle and small bowls, called katori, around the edge. This MicroSim fills a thali for seven regions: Punjab (Pakistan and India), Bengal (Bangladesh and India), Kerala (India), Gujarat (India), Sindh (Pakistan), Sri Lanka and the hills of Nepal.

Each plate has the same seven slots: staple, dal, vegetable, main dish, side, sweet and main spices. Because the slots stay the same, you can switch regions and see what changes. A "Why here?" note explains how each region's grain, rain, coast or mountains, and trade history shape its food. A checkbox swaps the main dish between a common vegetarian dish and a common non-vegetarian dish from the same region, marked with a green or brown symbol.

Every plate is one common example. Real families in each region cook many more dishes, and no plate here is the "correct" one. No map or borders are drawn.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with the plate that loads (Bengal). Read the "Why here?" note.
  2. Click or tap the center of the plate, then each bowl, and read what is in it.
  3. Choose another region from the menu, or use Previous and Next to step through all seven.
  4. Compare two regions slot by slot. Start with the staple in the center: is it rice or bread?
  5. Tick Non-vegetarian version to see a common meat or fish dish in the main bowl. Notice which regions use fish and which use meat.
  6. Look for ingredients that came from the Americas, like maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chili.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to compare the everyday meals of different South Asian regions and explain how staple grains, climate, geography, faith and trade shape what each region eats.

Bloom level: Analyze (compare, connect causes to differences). Supports Understand (explain).

Activity:

  2. (7 min) In pairs, students fill a table with one row per region and columns for staple, dal, main dish and one spice.

  1. Which regions in the sim have rice as their staple, and which have bread? What do the rice regions have in common?
  2. Name two ingredients on these plates that came from the Americas.
  3. Why does the Bengal plate feature fish, while the Gujarat plate is usually vegetarian?
  4. Which two regions in the sim lie in Pakistan, at least in part?
