docs.title: Tala Clapper
docs.text: Run the Tala Clapper MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A tala is a repeating cycle of beats in South Asian music. This MicroSim draws one cycle as a circle of beat dots, like a clock face, so you can see how the beats come back around to the start. The first beat of the cycle, called sam, is the large star-marked dot at the top. Claps (tali) are filled orange dots, waves (khali) are hollow teal dots, and the other beats are small dots. Colored bands show the sections of the cycle, with their traditional markings (X, 2, 0, 3 for Hindustani talas; laghu and drutam for Adi tala).

You can choose four talas:

Tala System Beats Sections Teentaal Hindustani 16 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 (wave on beat 9) Rupak Hindustani 7 3 + 2 + 2 (starts on a wave) Dadra Hindustani 6 3 + 3 (wave on beat 4) Adi tala Carnatic 8 4 + 2 + 2 (palm, three finger counts, palm-flip, palm-flip)

The MicroSim starts paused and silent. When you press Start, each beat lights up in turn and the center shows what your hand does. Short clicks are synthesized in your browser with WebAudio (no recordings are used): a low, longer tone marks sam, a bright click marks a clap, a soft tick marks a wave, and a quiet tick marks the other beats. Untick Sound on to mute it.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose a tala from the menu. Teentaal is selected first.
  2. Read the panel to learn how the tala is divided. Click any beat dot to see what your hand does on that beat.
  3. Press Start. Count the beats out loud and clap, wave or tap your fingers when the center tells you to.
  4. Use the Tempo slider to slow down (40 beats per minute) or speed up (160).
  5. Watch the cycle counter. Try to land on sam with a big clap (or, in Rupak, a wave) every time the cycle comes around.
  6. Press Pause to stop, switch talas, and compare.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to count through a full cycle of four common talas, perform the clap, wave and finger-count gestures in the right places, and identify sam, the first beat, when the cycle returns.

Bloom level: Apply (count, perform, keep time).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch09-tala-clapper/main.html" height="632px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (music, world cultures, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Warm-up: the class claps a steady 4/4 beat together. Ask: where is "one"?
  2. (5 min) Project the sim with Teentaal at 60 bpm. The class claps and waves along for two cycles, counting aloud. Point out the wave on beat 9 and the "arrival" on sam.
  3. (5 min) In pairs, students try Dadra and Rupak. Before pressing Start on Rupak, each pair predicts what happens on beat 1.
  4. (5 min) Students learn Adi tala with palm, finger counts and hand flips, then try to keep the tala going with the sound muted while a partner watches the screen to check.

Assessment questions:

  1. How many beats are in Teentaal, and which beat is the wave (khali)?
  2. Why is Rupak described as starting on khali?
  3. In Adi tala, what does the hand do on beats 2, 3 and 4?
  4. If a tala is played at 60 beats per minute, how many seconds does one cycle of Teentaal take? Of Dadra?
  5. Why might musicians smile or nod when they land on sam together?

docs.title: Classical Dance Map
docs.text: Run the Classical Dance Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Classical Dance Map has two views. The Dance map places the eight classical dances recognized by India's Sangeet Natak Akademi (Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Kathakali, Sattriya, Manipuri and Mohiniyattam) as tiles in roughly their home regions. A checkbox adds Chhau, which India's Ministry of Culture also lists, so you can see that the "official" number depends on who is counting. A "Beyond India" row adds Kandyan dance from Sri Lanka, Attan from Afghanistan (also danced by Pashtuns in Pakistan), Bhangra and Luddi from Punjab (in both India and Pakistan), and Manipuri dance as it is performed in Sylhet, Bangladesh. Click or tap any tile to read where the dance comes from, how to spot it, and what dancers wear.

The Hand gestures view draws six single-hand mudras with simple shapes: Pataka, Tripataka, Ardhapataka, Kartarimukha, Mayura and Alapadma. Their meanings come from the Abhinaya Darpana, a classic handbook of gesture, in the 1917 English translation by Ananda Coomaraswamy and Gopala Kristnayya Duggirala.

The map is schematic, not to scale, and draws no borders.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start in the Dance map view. Click or tap each of the eight tiles and read the panel.
  2. Find one feature for each dance that helps you tell it apart from its neighbors. Compare Kathakali with Mohiniyattam (both from Kerala) and Bharatanatyam with Kuchipudi.
  3. Tick Show Chhau and notice the dashed tile. Read why it is on one list but not the other.
  4. Click the four Beyond India tiles to meet dances from Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Punjab and Bangladesh.
  5. Press Hand gestures. Click each hand, read its meanings, and make the shape with your own hand.
  6. Notice how Pataka, Tripataka and Ardhapataka differ by just one bent finger at a time.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to distinguish the eight classical dances recognized by the Sangeet Natak Akademi by home region, key movement features and costume, and identify six basic single-hand mudras and some of their meanings.

Bloom level: Remember and Understand (identify, distinguish).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch10-classical-dance-map/main.html" height="802px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world cultures, world history, fine arts, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Ask students to name any South Asian dance they know. Most will say "Bollywood" or "Bhangra." Write the answers on the board.
  2. (8 min) In pairs, students click all eight classical tiles and fill in a table: dance, home region, one movement clue, one costume clue.
  3. (4 min) Students tick the Chhau checkbox and discuss: why might two government bodies count differently?
  4. (6 min) Students switch to Hand gestures, practice all six mudras with their own hands, and then tell a three-gesture story to a partner (for example: Pataka for waves, Alapadma for the moon, Kartarimukha for lightning).
  5. (3 min) Exit ticket: name two dances from outside India and the country each belongs to.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which classical dance comes from Andhra Pradesh, and what is its famous brass-plate feat called?
  2. Kathakali and Mohiniyattam both come from Kerala. Give one way to tell them apart.
  3. Why does the number of Indian classical dances depend on who is counting?
  4. Which mudra means "flag," and how is Tripataka different from it?
  5. Name the dance that is widely called Afghanistan's national dance, and one place outside Afghanistan where it is danced.

docs.title: Kolam Maker
docs.text: Run the Kolam Maker MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A kolam is a line drawing made with rice flour on the ground outside a home, drawn fresh each morning by many women in Tamil Nadu and across South India, and by Tamil families in Sri Lanka and around the world. Many kolams start with a grid of dots called pulli. The artist then draws lines that loop around the dots without touching them.

This MicroSim gives you a square of dark, swept "ground" and a grid of white dots. It starts with a demo pulli kolam already drawn. On a 5 x 5 grid, the demo is one single unbroken line that loops around all 25 dots. Press Trace demo to watch it being drawn.

Then draw your own. With 4-fold symmetry switched on, every line you draw is copied three more times, turned a quarter, a half and three quarters of the way around the center (the small gold circle). That's rotational symmetry, the same kind you see in many kolams and rangolis.

The demo is computed, not stored as a picture. It uses a "mirror curve": diagonal lines pass through the gaps between dots and bounce off the edge of the grid. On odd-sized grids (3 x 3, 5 x 5, 7 x 7), the sim also adds a few inner "walls," always in sets of four placed symmetrically, which join all the loops into one line. On even-sized grids, the same rules give several separate closed loops.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the demo on the 5 x 5 grid. Follow the line with your finger. Does it ever touch a dot? Does it ever end?
  2. Press Trace demo to watch the line drawn from start to finish. Press Pause to stop partway.
  3. Press Clear, then draw your own lines with your mouse or finger. Keep your lines in the spaces between dots.
  4. Watch how each stroke appears four times around the gold center point. Untick 4-fold symmetry and draw again to compare.
  5. Change the grid from 3 x 3 to 7 x 7 dots. On which grid sizes does the demo use one line, and on which does it use several loops?
  6. Pick a different ink color, finish a design you like, and press Save to download it as a picture.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to create a symmetric dot-grid design and explain how the grid of dots and rotational symmetry guide the drawing of a kolam.

Bloom level: Create (design, construct), supported by Understand (explain).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch11-kolam-maker/main.html" height="682px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (art, geometry, world cultures, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Show the demo. Ask: "How do you think the artist planned this?" Point out the dots.
  2. (5 min) Students press Trace demo on the 3 x 3 and 5 x 5 grids and describe in their own words the two rules the line follows (it goes around the dots without ever touching them, and it bounces back at the edge).
  3. (8 min) With 4-fold symmetry on, students design their own kolam on a 5 x 5 grid. Then they turn symmetry off and try to copy their design by hand.
  4. (4 min) Pairs compare designs and identify the center of rotation and the four repeated parts.
  5. (3 min) Optional: draw a real kolam with chalk on the sidewalk using a dot grid, then share a saved image with the club.

Assessment questions:

  1. What are the dots (pulli) for in a pulli kolam?
  2. What does "4-fold rotational symmetry" mean? How many times does each line appear?
  3. Why might a kolam artist prefer one continuous line that never ends?
  4. The demo uses one line on 5 x 5 dots but four separate loops on 4 x 4 dots. Describe what you notice.
  5. How is a kolam different from a rangoli made with colored powder?

docs.title: Textile Map
docs.text: Run the Textile Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Textile Map places ten South Asian textiles and garments on a schematic tile map of the eight countries. The dots are Jamdani (Bangladesh), ajrak (Sindh, Pakistan), the perahan tunban (Afghanistan), pashmina shawls from the Kashmir and Ladakh region, Chyangra Pashmina (Nepal), kira weaving (Bhutan), Banarasi silk, ikat and Kanjivaram silk (India), and the osariya or Kandyan saree (Sri Lanka).

Click or tap a dot, or choose a textile from the menu, to see where it is made, what fiber it uses, how its pattern is made, and what garment it usually becomes. The panel draws a simple garment in the textile's colors and a pattern swatch drawn by code: scattered woven flowers for Jamdani, feathery diamonds for ikat, teardrop buta shapes for pashmina, indigo and crimson stars for ajrak, and so on. The swatches are simplified illustrations, not copies of real pieces.

Quiz me hides the textile's name and place. Read the swatch, the fiber and the technique, then click the dot you think matches.

The map is schematic, not to scale, and does not draw any national borders.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the map. Find the eight country tiles and the ten orange dots.
  2. Click or tap each dot (or use Previous and Next). Read the place, fiber, technique and "worn as" lines.
  3. Compare the pattern swatches. Which patterns are woven in, which are dyed into the thread first, and which are printed on?
  4. Untick Show place names and see if you can still name every dot.
  5. Press Quiz me. Study the mystery swatch and garment, then click the matching dot. Your score shows under the buttons.
  6. Press Stop quiz to go back to exploring.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to connect ten South Asian textiles and garments to the regions where they are made and to their fiber (cotton, silk or wool) and technique (woven, tie-dyed before weaving, or block-printed).

Bloom level: Remember and Understand (identify, explain).

docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch12-textile-map/main.html" height="842px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (world geography, world history, art, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Ask students to name any South Asian clothing they know. Write the list on the board.
  2. (6 min) Students click all ten dots and fill in a table with four columns: textile, country, fiber, technique.
  3. (3 min) Students sort the ten into three groups: patterns woven in, patterns dyed into the thread before weaving, and patterns printed on.
  4. (5 min) Students play Quiz me in pairs, taking turns, and aim for 8 out of 10.
  5. (3 min) Discussion: Why are the pashmina dots in the mountains and the fine cotton dots in hot, low places?

Assessment questions:

  1. Which textile is woven around Dhaka, and what did UNESCO do in 2013?
  2. What is the difference between how ikat and Jamdani patterns are made?
  3. Which two dots use wool from mountain goats? Why do those goats grow such fine undercoats?
  4. Which textile is block-printed in Sindh, and what colors is it known for?
  5. Name the national dress of Bhutan and the Kandyan saree's Sinhala name.

docs.title: Kinship Explorer
docs.text: Run the Kinship Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Kinship Explorer is a small family tree centered on "You." Dad's side sits on the left in teal and Mom's side on the right in marigold. There are nine relatives to explore: both grandfathers and both grandmothers, Dad's older brother, Dad's younger brother, Dad's sister, Mom's brother and Mom's sister.

Click or tap a relative (or choose one from the menu) to see the single English word for them, such as "uncle," next to the word many families use in five South Asian languages: Hindi-Urdu, Bangla, Punjabi, Tamil and Sinhala. Each word appears in its own script with a simple respelling. Notes point out where usage differs, for example between many Muslim and many Hindu Bangla speakers, or between older and younger aunts in Tamil and Sinhala. Every spelling was checked against a dictionary and is listed in the chapter's fact log.

Kinship words vary by family, region and community. If your family uses a different word, your family isn't wrong.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the tree. Find "You," your parents, and the relatives on each side.
  2. Click or tap "Dad's older brother." Compare the English word with the five South Asian words.
  3. Press Next relative to step through all nine relatives, or choose one from the menu.
  4. Compare "Dad's older brother" with "Dad's younger brother," and "Dad's mother" with "Mom's mother." Which languages use different words? Which use the same one?
  5. Untick Color Dad's side and Mom's side. Pick a relative and see if you can tell which side they're on from the words alone.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain why many South Asian languages have separate words for relatives on the father's side and the mother's side, and for older and younger relatives, by comparing kinship terms in five languages.

Bloom level: Understand (compare, explain).

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (world languages, ethnic studies, sociology, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Students list every English word they know for relatives. Most lists will have about ten words, with "uncle," "aunt" and "cousin" doing a lot of work.
  2. (6 min) In pairs, students click all nine relatives and fill in a chart: relative, English word, and the word in one South Asian language of their choice.
  3. (4 min) Students find two relatives who share one English word but get different words in at least three of the five languages.
  4. (5 min) Discussion: Why might a family where married brothers live together need different words for each side? Why do Tamil and Sinhala call a father's brother "big father" or "little father"? Students who speak a South Asian language at home share the words their own family uses.

Assessment questions:

  1. In Hindi-Urdu, what is the difference between dadi and nani?
  2. Which relative is called "mama" in all five languages?
  3. Name one language that uses the same word for both grandmothers.
  4. Explain one reason a language might have separate words for the father's side and the mother's side.
  5. Bangla speakers sometimes use different words for the same relative. Give one example from the sim and explain why.

docs.title: Story Web
docs.text: Run the Story Web MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Story Web places thirty works and writers of South Asian literature on a timeline, in five era columns from before 1 CE to today. Each dot is colored by language group: Sanskrit and Pali; Tamil and Kannada; Bangla; Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi and related languages; Nepali and Pashto; English; and Persian, Arabic and Javanese (for tellings that traveled beyond South Asia).

Lines link works that retell, translate, answer or share stories with each other: the Valmiki Ramayana to its Tamil, Bangla, Awadhi, Nepali and Javanese tellings; the Jatakas to the Panchatantra and the Panchatantra to Kalila wa Dimna; Kabir to Tagore and Tagore to Nazrul; Waris Shah to Amrita Pritam's Partition poem; and more. Click or tap any dot to read its card: language, date, place, a one-line summary, and the reason for each of its links. Dates for early works are scholars' estimates.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with the Valmiki Ramayana, which is already selected. Read its card and follow the orange lines to the five later tellings.
  2. Click each linked dot. Note its language, its century and where it was composed.
  3. Click the Panchatantra and follow its link out of South Asia to Kalila wa Dimna.
  4. Use the language menu to show only one language (for example Persian, Bangla or English). Works in other languages fade.
  5. Untick Show all links to see only the links of the selected dot.
  6. Find the two dots with no links (Kalidasa, Akbar and Birbal) and propose a link of your own.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to trace how a story or literary form traveled across languages, faiths and borders by following links between works on a timeline.

Bloom level: Analyze (trace, compare).

Activity:

  2. (7 min) Pairs follow the Ramayana's links and fill in a table: telling, language, century, place.
  3. (5 min) Pairs follow the Panchatantra to Kalila wa Dimna and discuss how a Sanskrit fable book reached Europe.
  4. (5 min) Each pair uses the language filter to pick one language and writes two sentences about which eras it appears in and why.
  5. (5 min) Share: each pair proposes one new link for Kalidasa or Akbar and Birbal, with a reason.

Assessment questions:

  1. Name three languages, besides Sanskrit, in which the Ramayana was retold, and the century of each.
  2. Trace the route of the Panchatantra from India to the Arab world. Which two steps does the web show?
  3. Which link in the web crosses the border created in 1947? What does it tell you?
  4. Why do the English dots appear only in the last two eras?
  5. Pick one link and explain whether it shows retelling, translation or a writer answering an earlier writer.

docs.title: Film Industries Map and Cricket Basics
Film Industries Map and Cricket Basics
docs.text: Run the Film Industries MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim has two tabs.

Film industries. Eleven colored tiles sit roughly where South Asia's language-based film industries are centered: Urdu and Punjabi (Lahore and Karachi, Pakistan), Nepali (Kathmandu), Dzongkha (Thimphu, Bhutan), Hindi (Bollywood, Mumbai), Bengali (Kolkata), Bangla (Dhaka, Bangladesh), Telugu (Hyderabad), Kannada (Bengaluru), Tamil (Chennai), Malayalam (Kerala) and Sinhala and Tamil (Sri Lanka). Click or tap a tile to see the language, the center, a landmark film or figure with its year, and a short note. The Hindi tile, Bollywood, is just one of eleven. The map is schematic, not to scale, and draws no borders.

Cricket: one over. A simple cricket field shows the bowler, the batter and the 22-yard (20.12 m) pitch. Press Start to watch one over: a single, a dot ball, a four, a wide (1 extra run that does not count as a ball), two runs, a wicket and a six. The scoreboard adds up the runs and counts legal balls, ending at 14 runs for 1 wicket from 6 legal balls. The over starts paused.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. On the film tab, click or tap every tile and read the panel. Count the languages and countries.
  2. Find the two tiles for Bengali-language film, one in Kolkata and one in Dhaka. Why might one language have two industries?
  3. Click Cricket: one over, then press Start.
  4. Watch the "Legal balls" counter. Pause after each delivery and predict the score before the next one.
  5. When the over ends, explain why there were seven deliveries but only six legal balls. Press Reset or Replay to watch again.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain that Bollywood is one of many language-based film industries in South Asia, and describe the basic structure of a cricket over (6 legal balls, with runs adding up and wides not counted).

Bloom level: Understand (explain, describe).

docs.title: Zero and Place Value
docs.text: Run the Zero and Place Value MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows one number three ways at once. The top of the screen is a place value table with four columns: thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Each column holds one digit and the same number of colored counters. Below the table, the number appears in our everyday digits (Hindu-Arabic numerals), in a South Asian digit set you choose (Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil or the Eastern Arabic style used for Urdu), and in Roman numerals.

When a column inside the number is empty, it glows and its 0 turns orange: the zero is holding that place. Tick Hide the zeros to remove every zero symbol. The digits slide together and the number turns into a different number, which is exactly the problem a zero solves. Roman numerals never need a zero, because their letters keep the same value wherever they sit, but they get long and are hard to calculate with. (Standard Roman numerals stop at 3,999; for bigger numbers the sim simply repeats M, which is a modern shortcut rather than how Romans wrote them.)

The digit sets use real Unicode characters (U+0966 to U+096F for Devanagari, U+09E6 to U+09EF for Bengali, U+0BE6 to U+0BEF for Tamil and U+06F0 to U+06F9 for the Eastern Arabic style). Your device's fonts decide exactly how they look.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Tap or click the up arrow at the top of a column to add one to that place, or the down arrow to take one away.
  2. Build 507. Read all three rows: the table, the digits, and the Roman numeral DVII.
  3. Tick Hide the zeros. Read the warning and notice what number you seem to see now.
  4. Untick it. Use the menu to switch between Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil and Urdu digits.
  5. Press Random to get new numbers (many will have an empty place). Press Clear to start from 0.
  6. Try 3,888 and 1,000 and compare how long each Roman numeral is.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain why a symbol for zero makes a place value system work, by comparing the same number written in a place value table, in a South Asian digit set and in Roman numerals.

Bloom level: Understand (explain, compare).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch16-zero-place-value/main.html" height="642px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world history, math history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Without the sim, students write 507 in Roman numerals and try to multiply DVII by XII on paper. Discuss how hard it is.
  2. (5 min) Students build 507, 2,026 and 9,009 in the sim and record each in Devanagari, Bengali and Roman numerals.
  3. (5 min) Students tick "Hide the zeros" for each number and write down what the number seems to become.
  4. (5 min) Pairs discuss: Why didn't Roman numerals need a zero? Why does our system need one? Which system would you choose for doing taxes, and why?

Assessment questions:

  1. In the number 2,006, what places are the two zeros holding?
  2. Why does 507 turn into 57 when the zero is removed, but DVII stays DVII?
  3. Write 1,947 in Devanagari or Bengali digits.
  4. Brahmi numerals had separate signs for 10, 20 and 30. Why don't they need a zero?
  5. Explain in two sentences why historians say the zero was one of the most useful ideas in the history of mathematics.

docs.title: India Explorer
docs.text: Run the India Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
India Explorer shows India's 28 states and 8 union territories as a tile cartogram: every state or territory gets one tile of the same size, placed roughly where it sits in the country. It is not a traced map. Tiny Goa gets the same tile as huge Rajasthan, and no borders are drawn. Squares are states; round tiles are union territories.

The menu colors the tiles in two ways:

  • Language family: the family of each place's main official language or languages (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman, or a mix of families).
  • Region: an informal grouping into North, Northeast, East, West, Central and South. Different sources group states a little differently.

Tap any tile to see its capital, its official language or languages, its language family and a short note. The checkbox highlights the 8 union territories. The list and capitals follow the National Portal of India (checked October 2026).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the "India at a glance" card on the right (or below, on a phone).
  2. Look at the Language family colors. Find the block of teal tiles in the south and the purple tiles in the northeast.
  3. Tap Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Telangana. Compare their official languages.
  4. Switch the menu to Region and see which regions the colors now show.
  5. Check Highlight the 8 union territories and tap each one. Notice which ones are islands, cities or former colonies.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain how India's federal structure of states and union territories connects to its languages, using the idea of linguistic states.

Bloom level: Understand (explain, classify).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch17-india-explorer/main.html" height="842px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world geography, civics, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (4 min) In pairs, students tap five tiles in different colors and record each capital and official language.
  2. (5 min) Students sort the five southern states and the five largest northern states by language family and write one sentence about the pattern.
  3. (4 min) Students highlight the union territories and list two reasons a place might be a union territory instead of a state.
  4. (5 min) Class discussion: why would a country draw its internal borders around languages?

Assessment questions:

  1. How many states and union territories does India have in 2026?
  2. What is the capital of Telangana, and what is its official language?
  3. Which language family do the official languages of Kerala and Tamil Nadu belong to?
  4. Name two union territories that are groups of islands.
  5. Why does a tile cartogram show Goa and Rajasthan the same size?

docs.title: Country Compare
docs.text: Run the Country Compare MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Country Compare puts Pakistan and Afghanistan side by side. The map is schematic: labeled dots for cities and heritage sites (Kabul, Bamiyan, the Minaret of Jam, Kandahar, the Khyber Pass, Peshawar, Islamabad, Lahore, Quetta, Mohenjo-daro and Karachi), the Hindu Kush, and the Indus and Kabul rivers. Two soft colored areas stand for the two countries. No borders are drawn.

A comparison card shows each country's capital, its population in 2025 (World Bank), its languages, main faith, a UNESCO World Heritage site, some well-known foods and its main festivals. The menu can also switch the card to two cultural regions that cross today's border: the Punjab region and the Pashtun belt. When you pick one, it lights up on the map.

Press Start the Khyber road to send a traveler along the old route from Kabul, past Jalalabad, through the Khyber Pass to Peshawar, Islamabad and Lahore. A line under the map describes each stop.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the Pakistan card. Then use the menu to switch to Afghanistan and compare the two cards row by row.
  2. Switch the menu to Punjab region, then Pashtun belt. Notice where each shaded area sits compared with the two countries.
  3. Click or tap any dot to read about that city or site.
  4. Press Start the Khyber road. Pause at the Khyber Pass and at Peshawar and read the line under the map.
  5. Press Reset to start the journey again.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to compare Pakistan and Afghanistan using the same set of features (capital, population, languages, faith, heritage, food, festivals) and analyze how cultural regions such as the Punjab and the Pashtun belt connect places that today's border separates.

Bloom level: Analyze (compare, connect).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch18-pakistan-afghanistan-compare/main.html" height="802px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9-12 (world geography, world history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (5 min) In pairs, students fill a two-column table (Pakistan, Afghanistan) with the seven rows from the card.
  2. (4 min) Students circle one row where the two countries are most alike and one where they differ most.
  3. (4 min) Students switch to the two cultural regions and list which cities on the map belong to each.
  4. (5 min) Students run the Khyber road and write two sentences on why a mountain pass could matter for trade, faith and empire.

Assessment questions:

  1. What are the official languages of Afghanistan? What is Pakistan's national language?
  2. Which city is the capital of Pakistan's Punjab province, and which UNESCO site is there?
  3. Name two cities that sit in the Pashtun belt, one in each country.
  4. Why does a comparison by country alone miss part of the story in this region?
  5. Which cities does the old road connect, and which pass does it cross?

docs.title: Delta and Island
docs.text: Run the Delta and Island MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Delta and Island puts two very different kinds of land side by side.

  • Bangladesh: the Bengal Delta. Three great rivers, the Padma (Ganges), the Jamuna (Brahmaputra) and the Meghna, meet and flow into the Bay of Bengal. A monsoon river level slider raises the water, and the lowest land, near the rivers and the coast, floods first. The share of land under water is illustrative, not real data, because the land heights are made up to show the idea. The two preset buttons match two documented figures: about 21% of Bangladesh floods in an average year, and more than two-thirds of the country flooded in 1998.
  • Sri Lanka: an island. A stylized island (not a traced outline) with schematic central highlands and dots for Jaffna, Anuradhapura, Kandy, Sri Pada (Adam's Peak), Colombo and Galle.

Tap any dot to read a short card about that place. No borders are drawn, and the caption "Schematic map, not to scale. Not an official depiction of borders." appears inside the drawing area.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the "Compare the two" card at the bottom.
  2. Press Average year. Notice which land floods: the land along the rivers, around Dhaka and toward the coast.
  3. Press Extreme year (1998). Which parts stay dry?
  4. Tap Dhaka, Chattogram and the Sundarbans.
  5. On the island, tap Anuradhapura, Kandy, Sri Pada, Colombo, Galle and Jaffna. Notice how the highlands sit in the south-center and the old capitals moved over time.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to explain how geography shapes life in Bangladesh (a low, flat river delta where floods are both a danger and a source of fertile soil) and in Sri Lanka (an island with central highlands, coasts and an ancient dry-zone heartland).

Bloom level: Understand (explain, compare).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch19-bangladesh-srilanka-compare/main.html" height="932px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (world geography, environmental science, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (5 min) Students press Average year and Extreme year and sketch which parts of the delta flood first and which stay dry.
  2. (4 min) In pairs, students list two ways a flood can hurt a farm and one way it can help.
  3. (5 min) Students tap every Sri Lanka dot and sort the places into "ancient capital," "port," "hill country" and "north."
  4. (4 min) Exit ticket: one sentence comparing how water shapes life in each country.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which three rivers meet in the Bengal Delta?
  2. About how much of Bangladesh floods in an average year, and how much flooded in 1998?
  3. Why does the eastern part of the schematic delta stay dry longest?
  4. Which Sri Lankan place is sacred to Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians?
  5. Why is the flooded share in the simulation called "illustrative"?

docs.title: Mountains to Atolls
docs.text: Run the Mountains to Atolls MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives sit at opposite ends of South Asia's "staircase." This MicroSim draws a schematic elevation profile that starts at a low coral atoll in the Maldives (average ground about 1.5 m, highest natural point about 2.4 m), crosses the Indian Ocean, and climbs through Nepal's Terai plains (about 67 to 300 m), Kathmandu (about 1,400 m) and Bhutan's capital Thimphu (about 2,250 to 2,650 m) to the summit of Mount Everest (8,848.86 m, 2020 China-Nepal survey). The places are lined up as steps on one staircase, and horizontal distances are not to scale.

The sea-level slider raises the ocean by up to 2 m. On the mountain-scale panel, the sea line barely moves (the sim reports how many pixels). In the close-up below, a sample atoll island, shaped from the Maldives' average and highest elevations, floods as the sea rises, and the sim reports how much of the island's width lies below the new sea level. Optional bands show the IPCC's likely global sea-level rise by 2100: 0.28 to 0.55 m with very low emissions and 0.63 to 1.01 m with very high emissions (IPCC AR6, 2021).

The island is schematic, so its percentages are not a forecast for any real island. No borders are drawn.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click or tap each marker on the top panel, or pick a place from the menu, and read its elevation and a short description.
  2. Notice the axis: the top panel runs from 0 to about 9,000 m.
  3. Drag the Sea-level rise slider to 1.00 m. Watch the top panel and read how many pixels the sea line moved.
  4. Now look at the close-up. Read how much of the sample island is below the new sea level.
  5. Keep Show IPCC 2100 ranges ticked and compare the green (very low emissions) and orange (very high emissions) bands with the island's shape.
  6. Try 2.00 m, a rise scientists cannot rule out under very high emissions but consider unlikely by 2100.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to compare how altitude and sea level shape life in Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives by reading a schematic elevation profile and testing how a given sea-level rise affects a low atoll island.

Bloom level: Analyze (compare, explain).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch20-mountains-to-atolls/main.html" height="792px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (world geography, environmental science, world history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Before opening the sim, students guess how many times taller Everest is than the Maldives' highest natural ground.
  2. (5 min) Students tap all six places and record each elevation in a table. They check their guess (about 3,700 times).
  3. (5 min) Students set the slider to 0.55 m, 1.01 m and 2.00 m and record the pixel shift on the top panel and the share of the sample island below sea level.
  4. (5 min) Pairs discuss: Why does a rise that is invisible from Kathmandu matter so much in Malé? What climate worry do Nepal and Bhutan face instead?

Assessment questions:

  1. Which place on the profile is highest, and what is its elevation? Which is lowest?
  2. About how high is the Maldives' highest natural ground, and how does that compare with the IPCC's likely range for sea-level rise by 2100?
  3. Why does the sea line on the top panel barely move, even at 2 m?
  4. Name one way that rising seas threaten an atoll island besides covering it with water.
  5. Compare one climate risk for Nepal or Bhutan with one for the Maldives.

docs.title: Migration Waves
docs.text: Run the Migration Waves MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Migration Waves shows the big movements of South Asian people around the world as arcs between labeled region tiles. South Asia sits in the middle, with tiles for the United States, the Caribbean, Britain, the Gulf, East Africa, Mauritius and Fiji around it. The tiles are not a map. Their positions are only rough, and no borders are drawn.

Drag the year slider from 1830 to 2020, or press Play, and arcs light up for each wave while it is active: indenture to Mauritius (from 1834), the Caribbean (1838 to 1917) and Fiji (1879 to 1916); railway workers and traders in East Africa (from 1896); Punjabi workers on the US West Coast (about 1900 to 1917); postwar migration to Britain; the 1972 expulsion from Uganda to Britain; the Gulf oil boom (from the 1970s); and the United States after the Immigration Act of 1965. Finished waves stay faintly visible, so you can see how the diaspora built up layer by layer.

Click or tap a region, or pick a wave from the menu, to read a card with its dates, its main cause and one fact. Every date and number comes from the sources listed in Chapter 21's references.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the tiles first. Find South Asia in the middle and the seven destination regions around it.
  2. Press Play and watch the arcs appear as the years pass. Press Pause to stop at any year.
  3. Pause at 1850, 1910, 1960, 1980 and 2010. Read the "Active in" line at the bottom of the card each time.
  4. Click or tap each region tile to read why people went there.
  5. Use the wave menu to find the arc that does not start in South Asia (East Africa to Britain, 1972).
  6. Press Reset to go back to 1830, or drag the slider to any year you want to check.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to identify the major waves of South Asian migration (indenture, East Africa, early North America, Britain, the Gulf and the post-1965 United States) and explain the main cause of each.

Bloom level: Understand (identify, explain).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch21-migration-waves/main.html" height="762px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (US history, world history, ethnic studies, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Students write down when they think South Asians first came to the United States, then check their guess against the "Early United States" wave.
  2. (7 min) Students play the timeline and pause at 1850, 1910, 1960, 1980 and 2010, filling in a table of active waves for each year.
  3. (5 min) Students click every region and sort the waves by cause: empire and plantations, railways and trade, postwar labor, oil, a new law, or expulsion.
  4. (5 min) Pairs discuss: Which waves were tied to the British Empire? Which wave might match their own family's story, or a friend's?

Assessment questions:

  1. Which three destinations received indentured workers in this sim, and why did indenture begin?
  2. Why does one arc start in East Africa instead of South Asia?
  3. Which wave began in the 1970s, and what caused it?
  4. What changed in US law in 1965, and how does the sim show its effect?
  5. In 1975, which waves were active? For each one, name its main cause.

docs.title: Interview Builder
docs.text: Run the Interview Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Interview Builder turns the book's Ask Your Elders sections into a complete oral history interview plan. Choose a theme (any of the 21 chapters, or a "life story" capstone), a narrator (a grandparent, a parent, an aunt or uncle, or a family friend or community member) and a length (10, 20 or 30 minutes). The sim assembles:

  • a consent script to read aloud, adjusted for the narrator,
  • 6, 8 or 10 questions, color coded as warm-up, theme, change and closing questions, drawn from a plain-text question bank written from each chapter's Ask Your Elders topics,
  • follow-up prompts for active listening, and
  • a note-taking grid with one row per question.

Some themes add a care note, for example on painful memories of 1947 and 1971, on asking about values in families that aren't religious, or on recording home remedies as traditions rather than medical advice.

Print plan prints a clean, one- to three-page version of the whole plan, with blanks for the date, first names and the narrator's permissions. Nothing you choose is saved or sent anywhere.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Pick a Theme from the menu. Start with the chapter you enjoyed most.
  2. Pick a Narrator. Open the Consent tab and read the script. Switch to "Family friend or community member" and notice what the script adds.
  3. Open the Questions tab. Change the Length and watch how many questions the plan keeps.
  4. Press New questions to see a different mix and order, and keep the set that fits your narrator.
  5. Open the Notes tab to see the follow-up prompts and the grid you'll fill in during the interview.
  6. Press Print plan (or print to PDF) and take the page to your interview.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to design an ethical oral history interview plan, including informed consent, open questions, follow-up prompts and a plan for notes, for a chosen theme, narrator and length.

Bloom level: Create (design, plan).

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/south-asian-culture-textbook/sims/ch22-interview-builder/main.html" height="762px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (ethnic studies, social studies, English, or a South Asian student club meeting)

Duration: 25 to 30 minutes in class, plus an interview at home

Activity:

  1. (5 min) In pairs, students read the consent script aloud. Then they list what the narrator is told and what rights they keep.
  2. (10 min) Each student builds a plan for one theme and narrator, then changes the length. They write one sentence on which questions they would drop for a 10-minute interview and why.
  3. (5 min) Pairs swap plans and suggest one follow-up question for each other.
  4. (5 min) Students print or save the plan and set a date for their interview.
  5. (Follow-up meeting) Students share one story from their interview, only with the narrator's permission and using first names only.

Assessment questions:

  1. Name three things the narrator is told before the interview begins, and explain why each matters.
  2. Why does the plan start with warm-up questions instead of the hardest question?
  3. Which questions in your plan are open questions? Rewrite one closed question to make it open.
  4. What would you do if your narrator became upset during a question about the past?
  5. Your narrator agrees to notes but not to sharing. What can you do with the interview, and what can't you do?
